concepts.name: Abbreviation
concepts.definition: A Planguage parameter meaning 'abbreviation'.
concepts.overview: An **Abbreviation** is a short form (e.g., `SQC`) of a longer Planguage term (e.g., `Specification Quality Control`).

concepts.name: Absolute Specification
concepts.definition: An absolute specification of a term can be understood fully without reference to other definitions.
concepts.overview:
An **Absolute Specification** is a value that needs no further lookup.
Its opposite is a [[Relative-Specification.402|Relative Specification]] which depends on other definitions.

concepts.name: Abstract Strategy
concepts.definition: An abstract strategy is an idea or state, without itself containing or being a [[Concrete-Strategy.661|Concrete Strategy]] (*661).
concepts.overview:
An **Abstract Strategy** names a desired *direction or level*, not a *means*.
"Achieve higher reliability" is abstract; "deploy redundant servers in two zones" is concrete.

concepts.name: Acceptable Level
concepts.definition: Any numeric level in the [[Acceptable-Range.545|acceptable range]].
concepts.overview:
An **Acceptable Level** is "tolerable" — neither a win nor a loss.
It lives in the band between Fail (lower bound) and Goal (success threshold).

concepts.name: Tolerable Range

relatedConcepts.name: Tolerable
relatedConcepts.note: Tolerable is the lower bound of the Tolerable Range — the project-viability threshold

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Goal is the upper bound of the Tolerable Range — reaching it declares success

relatedConcepts.name: Status
relatedConcepts.note: Status in the Tolerable Range means the project is alive but below the committed target

relatedConcepts.name: Failure Range
relatedConcepts.note: in STG, Failure Range is the lower portion of the Tolerable Range (between Tolerable/Survival and Tom's Fail)

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe Range
relatedConcepts.note: in STG, Catastrophe Range = Intolerable Range; it is below the Tolerable Range

relatedConcepts.name: Success Range
relatedConcepts.note: Success Range begins at Goal — it is above the Tolerable Range

relatedConcepts.name: Acceptable Level
relatedConcepts.note: any numeric level in the Tolerable/Acceptable Range

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: Fail sits inside the Tolerable Range in STG — it is a fine-grained marker within the alive-but-below-Goal zone

concepts.definition: The **Tolerable Range** is the band on a scalar attribute axis where the project is alive — at or above the [[Tolerable.539|Tolerable]] threshold — but below the committed success level ([[Goal.109|Goal]]). The project is not failing, but it has not yet reached its target.
concepts.overview:
The **Tolerable Range** is the "alive but not yet successful" band: at or above [[Tolerable.539|Tolerable]], below [[Goal.109|Goal]].
Land here and the project is still viable — but improvement work must continue toward Goal.

concepts.name: Acquisition
concepts.definition: Acquisition is the activity of obtaining a [[Component.022|component]]. Acquisition is part of the [[Development-Cycle.413|Development Cycle]].
concepts.overview: **Acquisition** is *how a component arrives in your system* — by purchase, build, license, contract, or any other lawful means.

concepts.name: Act

relatedConcepts.name: Act
relatedConcepts.note: noun form (general use); not the same as PDSA Act

concepts.definition: Act [PDSA] is part of the [[Plan-Do-Study-Act-Cycle.168|Plan-Do-Study-Act Cycle]]. The 'Act' phase decides on what course of action should be taken based on the information supplied by the 'Study' phase. It is to standardize the process at a new level, to draw new conclusions about the original theory, or to determine and select new theories (to design or modify processes).
concepts.overview:
**Act** is the fourth (and decisive) phase of the PDSA cycle.
Take what `Study` taught and *decide what to do next*: standardise, revise theory, or design new theories.

concepts.name: Act

relatedConcepts.name: Act
relatedConcepts.note: PDSA-cycle phase; not the same concept

concepts.definition: An 'act' is a process of doing something, by means of humans or other Agents.
concepts.overview:
**Act (noun)** is a generic "doing of something" by an Agent.
Not to be confused with [[Act-PDSA.172\|Act [PDSA]]] *172, the cycle phase.

concepts.name: Action

relatedConcepts.name: Act
relatedConcepts.note: noun form

relatedConcepts.name: Act
relatedConcepts.note: PDSA phase

concepts.definition: Action is a specification parameter which describes an action to be taken under defined circumstances.
concepts.overview:
An **Action** parameter says *"when X, do Y"*.
The keyed icon is `^[Y]`.

concepts.name: Actual Step Content
concepts.definition: The design ideas, modified by [actual qualifiers] and functionality modified by [actual qualifiers], which are actually delivered in a specific [[Evo-Step.141|Evo step]].
concepts.overview:
**Actual Step Content** is *what was delivered*, in contrast to *what was specified*.
Tom's stated rationale: "we needed a concept to distinguish between plans and reality."

concepts.name: Adaptive

relatedConcepts.name: Agile
relatedConcepts.note: sister adjective; movement-oriented

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: Evo systems are inherently adaptive

concepts.definition: 'Adaptive' refers to the set of concepts which are interesting in relation to changing a system from one defined state to another. This can be while a system is in operation (user changes operational parameters). It can refer to system modification such as porting, extending, improving, correcting.
concepts.overview:
**Adaptive** is the umbrella adjective for everything to do with *changing the system from state A to state B*.
Whether at runtime (user changes a parameter) or design-time (extending, porting, fixing).

concepts.name: Add
concepts.definition: Add is a Planguage verb indicating the addition of some specification to a defined set of specifications.
concepts.overview:
**Add** is the verb that puts something *into* a defined specification set.
Keyed icon: `+`.

concepts.name: After
concepts.definition: 'After' is a parameter used to indicate a planned sequencing of events, including [[Evo-Step.141|Evo steps]] and [[Task.149|tasks]].
concepts.overview:
**After** is the precedence relation: `B After A` ≡ `A => B`.
Reads as "do A, then do B."

concepts.name: Agent System

relatedConcepts.name: Target System
relatedConcepts.note: the Target System is the entity being changed; Agent System and Target System are a paired mandatory distinction

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architect
relatedConcepts.note: the Systems Architect role is typically part of the Agent System directing architectural change

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: the Agent System produces and applies the Systems Architecture that governs the Target System

concepts.definition: An **Agent System** is the entity — organisation, team, process, or programme — that is responsible for directing deliberate change at a [[Target-System.610|Target System]] (*610). The Agent System drives the change; the Target System is what changes.
concepts.overview: **Agent System** (*611) is one half of the fundamental Planguage distinction between *who changes* and *what is changed*. The Agent System is the entity with authority and responsibility for the change effort: it sets the objectives, applies the resources, and manages the change process. The [[Target-System.610|Target System]] (*610) is what the Agent System acts upon. Explicitly naming both in any project charter or specification eliminates the common confusion about accountability that plagues unclear change efforts.

concepts.name: Agent
concepts.definition: Any combination of person, group, and/or machine, which carries out a defined (written) procedure, thus doing a task, which is a part of a process (other parts being entry and exit sub-processes).
concepts.overview:
An **Agent** is whoever (or whatever) actually does the task.
Person, team, machine, AI, or any combination — Planguage doesn't care, as long as the procedure is followed.

concepts.name: Agile

relatedConcepts.name: Adaptive
relatedConcepts.note: sister adjective; system change-ability vs process change-readiness

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: Tom's specific Agile process

concepts.definition: Any set of tactics that enable a prioritized stream of useful results, in spite of a changing environment.
concepts.overview:
**Agile** is *what your process does* when it keeps producing prioritised useful results in a changing environment.
No specific framework required. The proof is in the result-stream.

concepts.name: Aim
concepts.definition: An 'aim' is a stated desire to achieve something by certain stakeholders. An aim is usually specified informally and non-numerically.
concepts.overview:
An **Aim** is the qualitative ambition: "what life looks like when we win."
It is informal by design. The numbers come later, in [[Objective-noun.100\|Objectives]] and [[Goal.109\|Goals]].

concepts.name: Alternative Designs

relatedConcepts.name: Supplementary Designs
relatedConcepts.note: complementary, not alternative

concepts.definition: Alternative designs will have satisfactory, but *different*, performance and cost attributes. The alternative design idea attributes will be so significant that they do not need any *other* alternative design ideas in addition, or cannot afford it.
concepts.overview:
**Alternative Designs** are *competing* solutions — each enough on its own.
Their counterpart, [[Supplementary-Designs.589\|Supplementary Designs]], are *complementary* — used together.

concepts.name: Ambition
concepts.definition:
'Ambition' is a parameter, which can be used to summarize the ambition *level* of a performance or budget target requirement.
Ambition must state the requirement concerned (like 'Usability') and it must contain a notion of the kind of level being sought (like 'high').
concepts.overview:
An **Ambition** is the *one-sentence summary* of a requirement's level.
Read the Ambition first; the detailed numbers come right after.

concepts.name: And
concepts.definition: 'And' is used as a logical operator to join any two expressions within a statement.
concepts.overview:
**And** joins two expressions; both must hold.
Keyed icon: `&`. Case-insensitive: `And`, `AND`, `and` are all the same operator.

concepts.name: Architectural Description

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture Specification
relatedConcepts.note: abstract specs only; no models/systems

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: the parent collective concept

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: the real artifacts that the description describes

concepts.definition: Architectural description is "a collection of products to *document* an architecture."
concepts.overview:
An **Architectural Description** is *whatever you assemble to document an architecture*.
Models, blueprints, spec text, prototypes, even working systems — if it documents the architecture, it counts.

concepts.name: Architecture Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: the product that Architecture Engineering creates and maintains

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: upstream process; provides requirements the architecture must satisfy

relatedConcepts.name: Design Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: downstream process; operates within the framework Architecture Engineering establishes

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture Specification
relatedConcepts.note: the written artefact produced by Architecture Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: the broader discipline; Architecture Engineering is a focused sub-process

concepts.definition: The architecture engineering process puts in place the systems architecture, which is a controlling mechanism for the design engineering of any project.
concepts.overview:
**Architecture Engineering** establishes the strategic design framework — the Systems Architecture — that all lower-level design work must conform to.
It operates at the highest design level: technologically neutral, tradeoff-governing, cross-system synchronising.

concepts.name: Architecture Review
concepts.definition: An architecture review is a review process which looks at the *entire* set of engineering artifacts for a given system at a given level of process or development.
concepts.overview:
An **Architecture Review** is the review that looks at *everything together*.
Where Clarity Review checks one spec, and Content Review checks one artefact, Architecture Review checks the *whole engineering picture*.

concepts.name: Architecture Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: the collective noun — the real artefacts

relatedConcepts.name: Architectural Description
relatedConcepts.note: broader; includes models and real systems

relatedConcepts.name: Design Specification
relatedConcepts.note: Architecture Specification is a specialised form

concepts.definition: An architecture specification is the written definition of an architectural component.
concepts.overview:
An **Architecture Specification** is the *written* definition of an architectural component.
Strictly text/spec; models and real systems live under [[Architectural-Description.618\|Architectural Description]].

concepts.name: Architecture

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: the process

concepts.definition:
The 'architecture' is the set of entities that:
- in fact exist and impact a set of system attributes directly,
- or indirectly, by
- constraining, or influencing, related engineering decisions.
concepts.overview:
An **Architecture** is *the set of design components that, together, determine what the system can do and at what cost*.
Includes whatever was deliberately specified, accidentally inherited, or just visibly present.

concepts.name: Artifact

relatedConcepts.name: Artifact
relatedConcepts.note: Planguage Artifact — distinct concept

concepts.definition: Development artifacts are engineering information and tools such as specifications, test cases, user documentation which are not regarded as product components, but can potentially be reused to develop products and product components.
concepts.overview:
A **Development Artifact** is engineering output that supports building products but isn't itself a product part.
Specs, test cases, docs, scripts — all reusable, none shipped.

concepts.name: Artifact

relatedConcepts.name: Artifact
relatedConcepts.note: [Development] — different concept

concepts.definition: A collective term for all Planguage "Planguage" {books, slides, translations, variants, dialects, and other related things}.
concepts.overview:
A **Planguage Artifact** is anything that is *part of the Planguage corpus*: books, slides, translations, dialects.
Different from [[Artifact-Development.583\|Artifact (Development)]] *583 — which is project engineering material.

concepts.name: Aspect, in [ASPECT] book 2026
concepts.definition: Any distinguishable property, perspective, or dimension used to describe, analyze, or evaluate an entity.
concepts.overview:
An **Aspect** is *any way you can describe, analyse, or evaluate something*.
Includes parameters (measurable), qualitative, structural, relational, contextual.

concepts.name: Assertion

relatedConcepts.name: Assumption
relatedConcepts.note: stronger neighbour — Assumption is taken as given for planning

relatedConcepts.name: Evidence
relatedConcepts.note: what an Assertion lacks until proof is supplied

relatedConcepts.name: Claim
relatedConcepts.note: more formal kin

concepts.definition: An assertion is a statement that something is true, without necessarily backing it up with evidence or proof.
concepts.overview:
An **Assertion** is "I say it's so" — recorded but not yet proved.
Common variant: an *Impact Assertion* — claiming a design's expected impact without proof.

concepts.name: Asset

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: what an Asset can become when used

concepts.definition: An asset is a potential resource.
concepts.overview:
An **Asset** is *potential* — what could become a Resource if you decide to use it.
Owned or not, in use or not — the defining property is *availability*.

concepts.name: Assumption
concepts.definition: Assumptions are unproven conditions, which if not true at some defined point in time, would threaten something, such as the validity of a specification or the achievement of our requirements.
concepts.overview:
An **Assumption** is *what we treat as true so we can move forward*.
If the Assumption later turns out false, the specification it sits under may be invalid.

concepts.name: Attached Specification
concepts.definition: Attached specifications are directly and visibly present specification elements to one given specification.
concepts.overview:
An **Attached Specification** is *directly written-in* — not inherited, not global, not implied.
Its visibility is its defining property.

concepts.name: Attack
concepts.definition: Attacks are [[Threat.671|Threats]] activated. They attempt to cause negative consequences in a system.
concepts.overview:
An **Attack** is what happens when a [[Threat.671\|Threat]] activates and engages the system.
The system responds with [[Mitigation.670\|Mitigation]]; success or failure determines [[Damage.673\|Damage]].

concepts.name: Attribute Level Icon Point
concepts.definition: The exact point in space, in a diagram, which represents a given attribute level.
concepts.overview:
An **Attribute Level Icon Point** is the *exact location* on a scalar diagram where a named level (Goal, Fail, Past, Stretch...) lives.
Drawn as the arrow tip; optionally emphasised with `--|--`.

concepts.name: Attribute
concepts.definition: An attribute is an observable characteristic of a system.
concepts.overview:
An **Attribute** is something *observable* about a system: how good, what it does, what it costs, how built.
Four canonical categories — Performance, Function, Resource, Design.

concepts.name: Authority

relatedConcepts.name: Source
relatedConcepts.note: different concept — Source can carry no authority

concepts.definition: Authority is a specific level of power to 'decide' or 'influence' or 'enforce' a specific matter requiring some degree of judgment or evaluation. For example, the status of a specification is usually the responsibility of some 'authority' (some set of individuals holding the specific authority).
concepts.overview:
**Authority** is the *power to decide, influence, or enforce* — distinct from being merely the source of information.
Held by individuals, groups, roles, or authorised documents.

concepts.name: Background

relatedConcepts.name: Implementable Specification
relatedConcepts.note: synonym for Core specification

concepts.definition: Background information is the part of a specification which is *useful* related information, but is not *central* (*core*) to the implementation, nor is it commentary.
concepts.overview:
**Background** is the third tier of specification: not implementation-driving (Core), not commentary, but useful framing.
Examples: Past, Trend, Record, Owner, Version, Ambition, Gist.

concepts.name: Backroom
concepts.definition: Backroom is an adjective or noun, referring to a conceptual place, used to describe any processes or activities in Evo that are not necessarily visible to the Evo step recipients.
concepts.overview:
The **Backroom** is what stakeholders *don't* see — engineering work running in parallel with the visible Evo delivery cycle.
Counterpart: [[Frontroom.343\|Frontroom]] *343, what stakeholders *do* see.

concepts.name: Baseline To Target Pair
concepts.definition: In [[Impact-Estimation.283|Impact Estimation]], this is a set of two numeric values associated with a specific requirement under stated conditions: the Scale value for the benchmark reference point (0%) and the Scale value for the target (100%).
concepts.overview:
A **Baseline-to-Target Pair** is a *0% → 100%* anchor pair on a Scale.
Pegs the start and end of an improvement and lets every other measurement read as a percentage.

concepts.name: Baseline
concepts.definition: A Baseline is a stable well-defined benchmark *set* (one or more system attributes) that serve as a comparison for system change.
concepts.overview:
A **Baseline** is the *reference state* against which all subsequent change is compared.
Can be a single attribute's benchmark, or a whole set of attributes describing a system state.

concepts.name: Basic Planguage
concepts.definition: Basic Planguage is the original specification of Planguage — the generic, un-tailored form of the language, as opposed to project-specific tailored variants.
concepts.overview:
**Basic Planguage** is the *un-tailored kernel* of the language: the shared parameters, icons, and grammar.
Projects extend it with [[Tailored-Planguage.226\|Tailored Planguage]] *226.

concepts.name: Basis
concepts.definition: A basis is an underlying idea that is a foundation for a specification.
concepts.overview:
A **Basis** is the *foundation belief* under a specification — *deeper* than an Assumption, *stabler* than a Rationale.
Make it explicit so it can be challenged.

concepts.name: Before
concepts.definition: 'Before' is a parameter used to indicate planned sequencing of events, including Evo steps and tasks.
concepts.overview:
**Before** is the predecessor relation: `A Before B` ≡ `A => B`.
Same `=>` icon as [[After.313\|After]]; only the position of the tags differs.

concepts.name: Benchmark Cost
concepts.definition: A benchmark cost is an expenditure of resource that has been determined by some means for purposes of comparison and analysis.
concepts.overview:
A **Benchmark Cost** is a *reference cost figure* used for comparison and analysis.
Drawn from observation, measurement, estimation, or any cost-effective means.

concepts.name: Benchmark
concepts.definition: A benchmark is a specified reference point, or baseline. There are two main types: scalar and binary benchmarks.
concepts.overview:
A **Benchmark** is a *reference point on a system attribute*.
Scalar (Past/Record/Trend) or binary (was the function there before, yes/no?).

concepts.name: Benefit
concepts.definition: Benefit is value delivered to stakeholders.
concepts.overview:
A **Benefit** is *value delivered* to a stakeholder.
Without a stakeholder who values it, no Benefit. Without a Cost beside it, no economic decision.

concepts.name: Binary Constraint
concepts.definition: A Binary Constraint is a constraint that only has two possible status conditions: complied with or not.
concepts.overview:
A **Binary Constraint** is *all-or-nothing*: complied with, or not.
Two kinds: Veto (forbid) and Demand (require).

concepts.name: Binary
concepts.definition: Binary is an adjective used to describe objects, which are specified as observable in two states.
concepts.overview:
**Binary** = two possible observable states. Yes/no. Present/absent. True/untrue.
The opposite of [[Scalar.198\|Scalar]] *198 (numeric).

concepts.name: Binding
concepts.definition: A formal engineering decision type which constrains variability of product line artifacts or components in order to improve the potential for reuse and commonality.
concepts.overview:
A **Binding** is a deliberate decision to *fix variation* across product-line artefacts.
Trade flexibility for reuse and commonality.

concepts.name: Black Box

relatedConcepts.name: Component
relatedConcepts.note: a Component can be treated as a Black Box when its internals are unknown or irrelevant

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: Black Box testing is fundamental to systems-level verification

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: a Specification describes a Black Box interface — what it must do, not how

relatedConcepts.name: Scale
relatedConcepts.note: measuring Black Box behaviour requires a Scale against which outputs are observed

concepts.definition: A Black Box is a conceptual interface to any system of perhaps unknown, or unknowable, internal complexity and/or construction.
concepts.overview:
A **Black Box** is any system viewed purely through its external interface — inputs, outputs, and observable behaviour — without regard to internal implementation.
It enables requirements-based evaluation independent of design.

concepts.name: Budget Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Budget
relatedConcepts.note: the resource target that Budget Constraint limits from below

relatedConcepts.name: Budget Target
relatedConcepts.note: the parent concept grouping Budget Targets and Budget Constraints together

relatedConcepts.name: Budget Cycle Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: a specific form of constraint on when and how budgets are allocated

relatedConcepts.name: Cost Level Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: sibling constraint operating on cost levels

concepts.definition: *\<this was found missing, and is messy in other terms, check all \*421\> tg*
concepts.overview:
A **Budget Constraint** is a hard limit on resource expenditure — the resource-axis equivalent of a Fail or Survival constraint on a performance scale.
It defines the boundary beyond which budget overspend constitutes a defect.

concepts.name: Budget Cycle Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Budget Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: the scalar spending limit; Budget Cycle Constraint adds timing and governance dimensions

relatedConcepts.name: Budget
relatedConcepts.note: the committed resource allocation that Budget Cycle Constraint governs

relatedConcepts.name: Binary Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: sibling class of constraint; Budget Cycle Constraint is constraint-by-form

concepts.definition: A restriction regarding budget, which is related to the budget cycle process, such as when, who, how much.
concepts.overview:
A **Budget Cycle Constraint** restricts the *process* of budgeting — specifically: *when* funds may be committed, *who* has authority to commit them, and *how much* may be committed per cycle.
It governs the governance and timing of budget allocation, not merely the spending level.

concepts.name: Budget Target

relatedConcepts.name: Target
relatedConcepts.note: the generic scalar target class; Budget Target is a resource-expenditure specialisation

relatedConcepts.name: Budget
relatedConcepts.note: the committed resource-allocation level within the Budget Target family

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Target
relatedConcepts.note: sibling target class on the performance axis rather than the resource axis

relatedConcepts.name: Stretch
relatedConcepts.note: also *480 — the motivating-but-not-committed level in a Budget Target spec

relatedConcepts.name: Wish
relatedConcepts.note: also *480 — the aspirational level in a Budget Target spec; no commitment

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: also *480 — the committed level; Planned Budget is the resource-axis Goal

relatedConcepts.name: Budget Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: the Fail/Crash/Survival limits that form the constraint half of a Budget Target spec

concepts.definition: A Budget Target is a numeric resource-expenditure allocation plan. They are expressed with target levels {Budget, Wish, Stretch}.
concepts.overview:
A **Budget Target** is the complete resource-axis specification: all levels (Wish, Stretch, Budget) plus the constraint boundaries (Fail/Crash/Survival).
It is to resource management what a performance specification is to quality.

concepts.name: Budget

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: performance-axis counterpart; Budget is to resource allocation what Goal is to performance targets

relatedConcepts.name: Budget Target
relatedConcepts.note: the collective class grouping Wish, Stretch, Budget, and resource constraint levels

relatedConcepts.name: Stretch
relatedConcepts.note: motivating-but-not-committed resource level; more ambitious than Budget

relatedConcepts.name: Wish
relatedConcepts.note: aspirational resource level; no commitment; the most ambitious

relatedConcepts.name: Budget Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: the resource Fail/Crash/Survival limit; defines when resource expenditure becomes a defect

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: performance-axis structural counterpart to Budget Constraint on the resource axis

relatedConcepts.name: Scale
relatedConcepts.note: a Budget is always specified on a Scale (the resource measure)

concepts.definition: A 'budget' is an allocation of a limited resource.
concepts.overview:
**Budget** is the *committed* resource allocation level — the Goal on the resource axis.
Wish and Stretch are more ambitious (less resource used); Budget Constraint is the outer Fail boundary.

concepts.name: Bug

relatedConcepts.name: Error
relatedConcepts.note: origin — a human Error is the root cause that may become a Bug in the implemented system

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Issue
relatedConcepts.note: intermediate — an Error may be detected as a Specification Issue before becoming a Bug

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Defect
relatedConcepts.note: intermediate — a Specification Defect may propagate into a Bug in the implemented system

relatedConcepts.name: Malfunction
relatedConcepts.note: consequence — a provoked Bug may result in a Malfunction

relatedConcepts.name: Fix Probability
relatedConcepts.note: metric — Fix Probability measures the likelihood that an attempt to correct a Bug will succeed

relatedConcepts.name: Issue
relatedConcepts.note: detection point — an Issue is the observable symptom upstream of a Bug in the defect chain

relatedConcepts.name: Risk
relatedConcepts.note: a Bug is a latent Risk; when provoked, it becomes a realised Malfunction

concepts.definition:
A **Bug** is a defect in a real system which, if *provoked* by an agent or specific data, can result in a system [[Malfunction.275|Malfunction]].
*Fault* is a synonym for Bug; in Planguage both terms name the same concept at *339.
concepts.overview: **Bug** (*339) — also called **Fault** — is a latent defect in a *live, implemented system*. It does not cause harm until it is *provoked* by an agent or a specific data condition, at which point it may produce a [[Malfunction.275|Malfunction]]. This provocation model is the key insight: a system may contain many Bugs that never manifest, and every Malfunction can be traced back through the chain to an originating human [[Error.274|Error]]. The distinction between Bug and Malfunction matters for defect management and reporting: a Bug is invisible until triggered; a Malfunction is the event that stakeholders observe. [[Fix-Probability.067|Fix Probability]] (*067) measures the likelihood that an attempt to correct a Bug will succeed without introducing a new one.

concepts.name: Business Level
concepts.definition: Business Level is the topmost layer of the Value Delivery Tree. It expresses what the Business stakeholder values: profit, market position, growth, sustainability, regulatory compliance. Business outcomes are the effects produced by everything below; they are the ultimate justification for the work.
concepts.overview: **Business Level** (*801) is part of HumanAgent Gilb's Value Delivery framework, an extension to Tom Gilb's original Planguage. It is not in the source PlanguageGlossary.pdf — it has been authored to capture concepts the framework needs but the PDF did not name.

concepts.name: Business Rules

relatedConcepts.name: System Rules
relatedConcepts.note: the generic containing concept; Business Rules is a sub-class

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rules
relatedConcepts.note: sibling sub-class; rules about specification best practice rather than business operations

relatedConcepts.name: Condition
relatedConcepts.note: the left side of a Business Rule: [Conditions] ->

relatedConcepts.name: Process
relatedConcepts.note: business rules constrain or define how processes operate

concepts.definition: Business Rules are specifications or practices that define or constrain some aspect or principle of how a business operates or should operate — its 'rules of behavior'.
concepts.overview:
A **Business Rule** defines how a business *must* behave under given conditions — expressed as `[Conditions] -> {Actions}`.
Business Rules are the bridge between governance policy and executable system behaviour.

concepts.name: Case

relatedConcepts.name: Artifact (Planguage)
relatedConcepts.note: broader category of Planguage corpus artefacts; a Case is one kind

relatedConcepts.name: Case Study
relatedConcepts.note: a more structured, extensive form of Case

concepts.definition: Cases are real or doctored-for-discretion (originally real) examples of practice of Planguage (this method).
concepts.overview:
A **Case** is a real (or lightly anonymised) Planguage usage example, used to ground theory in practice.
Any size — from a single snippet to a full project archive.

concepts.name: Catastrophe Range Start

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe Range
relatedConcepts.note: the range that begins at this point

relatedConcepts.name: Failure Range
relatedConcepts.note: the range immediately above the Catastrophe Range

relatedConcepts.name: Success Range
relatedConcepts.note: the range that lies above the Failure Range

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: generic scalar range; Catastrophe Range Start marks one boundary of a Range

concepts.definition: The exact numeric point where a Catastrophe Range begins.
concepts.overview:
**Catastrophe Range Start** is the boundary level below (or beyond) which the system enters a [[Catastrophe-Range.603|Catastrophe Range]].
It is the numeric threshold that separates the Failure Range from organisational non-survival territory.

concepts.name: Catastrophe Range
concepts.definition: The catastrophe range is the full numeric extent of all catastrophe levels — the zone beyond the [[Survival.440|Survival]] limit where the system is no longer salvageable.
concepts.overview: A **Catastrophe Range** (*603, STG primary name: **Intolerable Range**) is the open-ended band of values past the [[Survival.440|Survival]] limit. In the [[Tolerable.539|STG simplified model]], this is the zone below the [[Tolerable.539|Tolerable]] threshold — where the *whole project* fails, not just a single attribute value. The Intolerable Range is the most severe zone: Status here means the project is in terminal danger. Anchored by a single Start point; extends in the direction of "worse" without bound.

concepts.name: Catastrophe

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: the level immediately better than Catastrophe; the two are 'two sides of the same level

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: Catastrophe Range — the open band of values past Catastrophe

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe Range
relatedConcepts.note: the full extent of Catastrophe levels; Catastrophe is a single level inside it

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe Range Start
relatedConcepts.note: the exact numeric anchor where the Catastrophe Range begins

concepts.definition: A catastrophe level of an attribute is where disaster threatens all, or part, of a system.
concepts.overview:
A **Catastrophe** is a single numeric level on a scale at which the system is effectively dead — illegal, unpaid, useless, or worse than [[Survival.440|Survival]].
If a design risks reaching it, abandon the design or the requirement; do not negotiate.

concepts.name: Cause-Effect Level
concepts.definition: A Cause-Effect Level is a layer in HumanAgent Gilb's Value Delivery hierarchy where causes at one level produce effects at the next level. Five levels stack: Business -> Stakeholder -> Product -> Solution -> Evo. Effects at lower levels become causes for the level above; this chain enables traceable value delivery from operational deliveries up to business outcomes.
concepts.overview: **Cause-Effect Level** (*800) is part of HumanAgent Gilb's Value Delivery framework, an extension to Tom Gilb's original Planguage. It is not in the source PlanguageGlossary.pdf — it has been authored to capture concepts the framework needs but the PDF did not name.

concepts.name: Cell

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation
relatedConcepts.note: the table technique that contains Cells at every requirement × design intersection

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation Table
relatedConcepts.note: the structural container; a Cell is one intersection inside this table

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimate
relatedConcepts.note: the numeric estimate that lives inside a Cell

relatedConcepts.name: Design Ideas
relatedConcepts.note: one axis of the table; the column whose impact a Cell records

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: the other axis; the row a Cell measures impact against

concepts.definition: In an Impact Estimation table, a cell is an intersection between a requirement attribute (usually a performance or a resource/cost attribute) and a design idea.
concepts.overview:
A **Cell** is one row × column intersection in an Impact Estimation Table — the unit where a single design's impact on a single requirement is estimated, evidenced, and made auditable.
It carries the estimate *plus its supporting metadata*: uncertainty, evidence, source, credibility.

concepts.name: Chance Cause

relatedConcepts.name: Special Cause
relatedConcepts.note: primary canonical name; this is a synonym pointer entry sharing the same number

concepts.definition: Synonym of Special Cause "Special Cause" (*019).
concepts.overview: A pure synonym pointer: **Chance Cause** is another name for [[Special-Causes.019b|Special Cause]] — a non-systemic, identifiable, removable disturbance distinct from common-cause variation.

concepts.name: Change Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Problem
relatedConcepts.note: the trigger — Change Requirements are usually the answer to a stated Problem

relatedConcepts.name: Need
relatedConcepts.note: the underlying motivation; a Need typically generates one or more Change Requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Baseline To Target Pair
relatedConcepts.note: the structure that anchors a Change Requirement: from where to where

relatedConcepts.name: Gap
relatedConcepts.note: the scalar distance between baseline and target; relevant only for scalar Change Requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Design Target
relatedConcepts.note: the destination side of the change; what the Change Requirement aims to reach

concepts.definition: A 'change requirement' represents a 'differential' change with reference to a defined 'baseline' system.
concepts.overview:
A **Change Requirement** is a *differential* — it specifies *what should be different* from a known [[Baseline-To-Target-Pair.220|baseline]], not an absolute end-state.
Always read against a baseline: "from X to Y", not just "Y".

concepts.name: Changing

relatedConcepts.name: State
relatedConcepts.note: the parent concept; Changing is one predefined value of State

relatedConcepts.name: Unstable
relatedConcepts.note: sibling state — flux that is *not* predictable; Changing is predictable, Unstable is not

relatedConcepts.name: Dynamic
relatedConcepts.note: sibling state — also describes change, but emphasises responsiveness rather than transience

concepts.definition: Predefined State. The state is in continuous but predictable flux, not stable.
concepts.overview:
A **Changing** state means *flux you can plan around* — the system is not stationary, but its motion is predictable.
Distinguished from [[Unstable.630|Unstable]] (flux that is *not* predictable).

concepts.name: Check, To

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: the parent process; Check is the core verb of Specification Quality Control

relatedConcepts.name: Checker
relatedConcepts.note: the role that performs the check

relatedConcepts.name: Checking
relatedConcepts.note: [SQC] — the named sub-process inside SQC where checking predominantly occurs

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rules
relatedConcepts.note: the standards a specification is checked against

relatedConcepts.name: Checklist
relatedConcepts.note: interpretive aid that supports correct application of rules during checking

concepts.definition: To 'check' a specification means to determine if it is consistent with any applicable specification rules (standards), which it *should* be consistent with.
concepts.overview:
The **verb form**: "to check" is the act of comparing a specification against the rules it is *supposed* to obey.
Rules are primary; checklists support correct rule interpretation; other documents (sources, kin) supply the evidence.

concepts.name: Checker

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: parent process; Checker is a defined role within SQC

relatedConcepts.name: Check
relatedConcepts.note: the verb the Checker performs

relatedConcepts.name: Checking
relatedConcepts.note: [SQC] — the named sub-process where Checkers most visibly act

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rule
relatedConcepts.note: the standards a Checker tests a specification against

relatedConcepts.name: Checking Rate
relatedConcepts.note: the work-rate constraint that governs how a Checker performs the role

concepts.definition:
A checker is a person, who performs checking within Specification Quality Control (SQC). It is a defined role in the process, and the checking activity can occur in most of the SQC sub-processes, not just the predominant 'checkers' process itself.
Checkers check specifications against rules, according to defined checking processes, looking mainly for major defects. They will also note and later report, process improvement suggestions; and report 'questions of intent' to the author/writer.
concepts.overview: A **Checker** is the named role inside SQC. They check a specification against rules, looking mainly for *major* defects, and additionally report process improvements and questions of intent.

concepts.name: Checking Rate

relatedConcepts.name: Rate
relatedConcepts.note: the parent concept; Checking Rate is one specialised kind of Rate

relatedConcepts.name: Optimum Checking Rate
relatedConcepts.note: the per-checker speed that empirically maximises defect-finding for that individual

relatedConcepts.name: Checking
relatedConcepts.note: [SQC] — the activity whose throughput Checking Rate governs

relatedConcepts.name: Checker
relatedConcepts.note: the role whose work this rate measures

concepts.definition: The checking rate is the *average* speed at which a specification is checked by a checker, using all the relevant related specifications and standards {the main specification, rules, checklists, source documents and kin documents}.
concepts.overview:
An **average** speed (not peak) measured in significant words of main specification per hour.
Default working figure: **~300 sig-words/hour**, with a tolerance of 0.1–1.9 hours per 300 words depending on document load.

concepts.name: Checking

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: the parent process; Checking is one of its named sub-processes and a pervasive activity throughout

relatedConcepts.name: Check
relatedConcepts.note: the verb that names what happens during Checking

relatedConcepts.name: Checker
relatedConcepts.note: the role that performs Checking

relatedConcepts.name: Checking Rate
relatedConcepts.note: the work-rate that governs how Checking is performed effectively

relatedConcepts.name: Optimum Checking Rate
relatedConcepts.note: the per-individual rate at which an individual Checker performs Checking best

concepts.definition:
Checking is the name of a sub-process within Specification Quality Control (SQC).
'Checking' is also the name of a widespread SQC activity, ('checking' with a small 'c'), which although *predominantly* carried out within the Checking [SQC] sub-process, is also used to some degree within all the other SQC sub-processes. Carrying out 'checking' is a core activity in SQC.
concepts.overview:
**Two senses, one word.** Capital-C **Checking** is a named sub-process inside SQC. Lower-case "checking" is the activity itself, which appears in *every* SQC sub-process to some degree.
The activity uses formal written rules, supported by checklists, against source and kin documents — all governed by an [[Optimum-Checking-Rate.126|Optimum Checking Rate]].

concepts.name: Checklist

relatedConcepts.name: Check
relatedConcepts.note: the verb a Checklist supports — Checklists guide how to check rules

relatedConcepts.name: Checking
relatedConcepts.note: [SQC] — the activity inside which Checklists are predominantly used

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rule
relatedConcepts.note: rules are primary; a Checklist supports correct interpretation of specific rules

relatedConcepts.name: Role-SQC
relatedConcepts.note: SQC roles use Checklists as a process aid

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: the parent process where Checklists are most heavily used

concepts.definition: A checklist is a list of items to be checked or verified, used as a standard to guide quality control processes and reviews.
concepts.overview:
A **Checklist** is a *rule-interpretation aid*, not a rule. It enumerates items to verify so that ad-hoc review cannot silently skip them.
Checklists are an SQC artefact — generic or project-specific — supporting the verb [[Check-To.013|Check]].

concepts.name: Chunk

relatedConcepts.name: Checking
relatedConcepts.note: [SQC] — the activity that operates on Chunks of a specification

relatedConcepts.name: Checking Rate
relatedConcepts.note: the ~300 sig-words/hour rate that motivates chunking — a session can only cover so much

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: parent process; chunking is a sampling tactic within SQC

concepts.definition: A 'chunk' is a portion of a document being evaluated by SQC, where the intent is to continue checking other chunks after the first chunk is checked, unless the defect data from a chunk is extreme ('too many' or 'zero' defects).
concepts.overview:
A **Chunk** is a manageable portion of a larger spec, checked one at a time so that SQC can adapt mid-stream — escalating, stopping early, or changing strategy based on defect density in the first chunks.
Chunking exists because the [[Checking-Rate.015|Optimum Checking Rate]] caps how much one human can check per sitting.

concepts.name: Claim

relatedConcepts.name: Assumption
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — like Claim, marks information as risk-bearing rather than verified

relatedConcepts.name: Evidence
relatedConcepts.note: the upgrade path: Claims become Evidence-backed when verified

relatedConcepts.name: Source
relatedConcepts.note: every Claim names a source; the source's credibility is part of the Claim's risk

relatedConcepts.name: Credibility
relatedConcepts.note: the score that quantifies how much a Claim should be trusted

relatedConcepts.name: Assertion
relatedConcepts.note: synonym in everyday usage; Claim emphasises low credibility, Assertion is a more neutral term

concepts.definition:
'Claim' is an assertion by a defined source, about a system attribute or an event. The Claim parameter is used to emphasize that the credibility of the claim is not high, and the reader should exercise their judgement and caution, because there is a risk that the claim might not be correct.
A scalar claim might be so vague that it is non-numeric, and is put in fuzzy brackets.
concepts.overview:
A **Claim** is *flagged-as-risky* information. The `?` icon explicitly says "trust this with caution."
Use Claim as a prefix to any other parameter to mark it as risk-bearing — and as a starting point to upgrade later to Past, Record, Trend, or Evidence.

concepts.name: Clarity Review

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: the parent process; Clarity Review can be carried out as an SQC instance with rules tuned to clarity

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Content Review
relatedConcepts.note: the next stage in the review chain; checks engineering goodness once clarity is established

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture Review
relatedConcepts.note: the third stage; checks architectural fitness after content has been validated

relatedConcepts.name: Clarity
relatedConcepts.note: the property the review is testing for

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: the artefact under review

concepts.definition:
A Clarity Review is a specification review which is primarily used to make sure the specification is clear enough to be interpreted correctly by the intended spec readership, as intended by the spec writers.
In particular, a clarity review is not initially concerned with the engineering goodness of the spec. This is left to later Specification Content Reviews. Clarity Reviews are trying to establish that a specification can be trusted because it is clear, unambiguous, correct, and complete. If so, the basis is laid for deciding if it is good engineering, good architecture and 'good for business' – with other analytical processes, which include Specification Content Reviews, experiments, prototypes, Evolutionary Step Delivery, competitive bidding and any other processes which determine how powerful an idea is.
A Clarity Review can be carried out using the generic Specification Quality Control process (SQC). The Rules we check against will tune into these issues. But a clarity review can be less formal – something like a friend checking quickly and declaring it to be fine for them.
concepts.overview:
A **Clarity Review** asks one question: *can readers interpret this specification as the writer intended?* It does **not** ask whether the spec is good engineering — that comes next.
Clarity is the **first gate** in the review chain: Clarity → Content → Architecture.

concepts.name: Clarity

relatedConcepts.name: Clarity Review
relatedConcepts.note: the review type that tests a specification for Clarity

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: the artefact whose Clarity is measured

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rule
relatedConcepts.note: rules encode what 'clear' means; rules drive the Clarity test

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: Clarity is a defect metric used in SQC processes

concepts.definition: The specification quality of 'being understood by a defined readership as intended by the writer'.
concepts.overview:
**Clarity** is a property of the *specification* relative to a *defined readership*: it asks whether the reader receives the writer's intended meaning.
Tom's working extension: a clear spec also makes it *obvious how to test for the existence of what it specifies*.

concepts.name: Class

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: the parent concept; a Class is a category of qualifier terms

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: Tags often act as qualifier-class members; e.g., Date, Place, Time

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier Condition
relatedConcepts.note: Conditions inside qualifier brackets resolve against Class memberships

concepts.definition: A class is a defined qualifier term category.
concepts.overview:
A **Class** is a *category of qualifier terms* — `Date`, `Place`, `Time`, `Task`, etc. — that lets a writer tag scope-defining values inside `[...]` qualifier brackets.
Classes can be predefined, project-defined, or informal — but the **Planguage Classification Principle** is: things are what they are, regardless of how we class them.

concepts.name: Client Stakeholder

relatedConcepts.name: Server Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: the dual role; the Server produces what the Client requests

relatedConcepts.name: Client
relatedConcepts.note: narrower business sense — a paying client; Client Stakeholder is the broader Stakeholder role

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: the parent concept; Client Stakeholder is one defined Stakeholder role

concepts.definition: A Client Stakeholder states needs, approves requirements and receives benefits or results produced by a Server Stakeholder.
concepts.overview:
A **Client Stakeholder** is the role that *requests, approves, and receives*. Its dual is the [[Server-Stakeholder.651|Server Stakeholder]], which delivers.
Multiple levels possible: a Server can be the Client of a deeper Server (chains and tiers).

concepts.name: Client

relatedConcepts.name: Consumer
relatedConcepts.note: also has 'Customer' as a synonym; the term Customer was diluted by use for non-paying internal recipients

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: the parent role; Client is one specific Stakeholder type

relatedConcepts.name: Client Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: the broader role concept; a Client is one paying instance of Client Stakeholder

relatedConcepts.name: Server Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: the dual; the Server delivers what the Client commissions

concepts.definition: A client is a person or group who has requested some defined work, system, or product, and will pay for it, directly or indirectly.
concepts.overview:
A **Client** is the *commissioning, paying* stakeholder — distinct from the broader [[Client-Stakeholder.650|Client Stakeholder]] role, which can be unpaid.
Tom prefers "Client" to "Customer" because the term *Customer* has been diluted by internal-process usage (see [[Consumer.038]]).

concepts.name: Combine

relatedConcepts.name: Generate
relatedConcepts.note: antonym; Generate uses `{`, Combine uses `}` — same axis, opposite direction

concepts.definition: Combine means: to put together, in some sense and manner.
concepts.overview:
A **Combine** operator (icon `}`) maps multiple inputs to a single output: `A } B` means *A combines / compresses / condenses / summarises / implodes to B*.
Antonym: [[Generate.392|Generate]] (`{`) — one source, many products.

concepts.name: Comment

relatedConcepts.name: Note
relatedConcepts.note: the canonical entry; Comment is a synonym pointer to Note *018 — same concept, same number

relatedConcepts.name: Commentary
relatedConcepts.note: the broader category Comments fall under — non-binding remarks on other specifications

concepts.definition: See Note *018.
concepts.overview: A pure synonym pointer: **Comment** is another name for [[Note.018b|Note]] — same number, same concept. Counts as [[Commentary.632|Commentary]] (non-binding remarks).

concepts.name: Commentary

relatedConcepts.name: Non-Commentary
relatedConcepts.note: the dual category — content that *does* carry binding consequences

relatedConcepts.name: Core Specification
relatedConcepts.note: the binding part of a spec; Commentary surrounds and supports it

relatedConcepts.name: Background
relatedConcepts.note: Background is one kind of Commentary — context that frames the spec

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: the artefact whose Commentary supplies non-binding annotation

relatedConcepts.name: Note
relatedConcepts.note: individual instance of Commentary — a single non-binding remark

concepts.definition: Commentary specifications are remarks about other specifications. Commentary specifications will probably not have any economic, quality or effort consequences if they are incorrect: defects in commentary are almost always of minor severity.
concepts.overview:
**Commentary** is the part of a spec that *talks about* the spec — Notes, Comments, quoted text, Sources. Defects here are almost always minor.
Sits opposite the binding [[Non-Commentary.294|Non-Commentary]] / [[Core-Specification.633|Core Specification]].

concepts.name: Commitment Parameters

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: Commitment parameter — the minimum acceptable level

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Commitment parameter — the planned target level

relatedConcepts.name: Limit
relatedConcepts.note: Commitment parameter — a binding constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Wish
relatedConcepts.note: non-Commitment counterpart of Fail — valued but not promised

relatedConcepts.name: Ideal
relatedConcepts.note: non-Commitment counterpart of Goal — perfection target, noted but not promised

relatedConcepts.name: Stretch
relatedConcepts.note: non-Commitment counterpart of Limit — aspirational, not promised

concepts.definition: Future requirements specification levels which are 'promised' at some level.
concepts.overview:
**Commitment Parameters** are the *promised* targets: [[Fail.098b|Fail]], [[Goal.109|Goal]], [[Limit.606|Limit]]. Their dual is the non-Commitment family ([[Wish.244|Wish]], [[Ideal.328|Ideal]], [[Stretch.404|Stretch]]) — valued but unpromised.
The distinction prevents engineers from misreading every spec value as a binding obligation.

concepts.name: Common Causes

relatedConcepts.name: Special Causes
relatedConcepts.note: the dual category — non-systemic, identifiable, removable disturbances. Special / Common cover all variation.

relatedConcepts.name: Statistical Process Control
relatedConcepts.note: the framework that distinguishes Common from Special causes via control-chart limits

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Survival Limit
relatedConcepts.note: scalar boundary often crossed when Common-Cause variation exceeds tolerance

concepts.definition:
These are repetitive systemic causes of consistent measurable process output levels of performance or cost.
"Common causes: of variation, produce points on a control chart that over a long period all fall inside the control limits. Common causes of variation stay the same day to day, lot to lot." (Deming, 1993, p.178).
Dr. Shewhart (Deming's teacher, who invented the concept) called them "assignable causes".
concepts.overview:
**Common Causes** are *systemic* — built into the process, not the worker. They produce control-chart points that stay *inside* the limits.
Deming's contention: only management can remove them. Workers cannot.

concepts.name: Commonality

relatedConcepts.name: Variability
relatedConcepts.note: the dual concept; together Commonality + Variability define a product-line architecture

concepts.definition: If any two products share any common assets they have commonality.
concepts.overview:
**Commonality** is the *shared-assets* dimension of a product line. The dual is [[Variability.582|Variability]] — the dimension along which products differ.
Maximising commonality (without losing necessary variability) is the central economic question of product-line architecture.

concepts.name: Competitive Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: the parent discipline; Competitive Engineering is the win-focused specialisation

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: the comparison anchor — competitive levels are defined relative to Benchmarks

relatedConcepts.name: Risk
relatedConcepts.note: Competitive Engineering explicitly analyses and avoids undesired risks

concepts.definition: A Systems Engineering discipline that is focused on 'winning', relative to some competitor, some enemy, some challenges, some events, or some Benchmarks.
concepts.overview:
**Competitive Engineering** is [[Systems-Engineering.223|Systems Engineering]] with an explicit *win condition*. The win is defined relative to a [[Benchmark.007|Benchmark]] — competitor, enemy, event, or challenge.
Tom names eight constituent activities, all oriented around outperforming the chosen reference.

concepts.name: Complex

relatedConcepts.name: Compound
relatedConcepts.note: near-synonym for structural complexity; both denote 'consisting of parts

relatedConcepts.name: Elementary
relatedConcepts.note: antonym pair via Compound; an Elementary thing has no parts to interconnect

relatedConcepts.name: Simple
relatedConcepts.note: direct antonym (defined 2022-07-29)

relatedConcepts.name: Complicated
relatedConcepts.note: distinct concept — Complicated = hard to understand; Complex = structurally interconnected. Tom keeps these strictly separate.

concepts.definition: Compound in structure; consisting of interconnected parts.
concepts.overview:
**Complex** is a *structural* property: many interconnected parts. It says nothing about understandability — that's [[Complicated.676|Complicated]].
Antonym: [[Simple.689|Simple]] (defined 2022-07-29).

concepts.name: Complicated

relatedConcepts.name: Risk
relatedConcepts.note: Complicated systems are intrinsically risk-bearing — unpredictable behaviour quantifies as Risk

relatedConcepts.name: Uncertainty
relatedConcepts.note: Complicated implies Uncertainty about current and future system behaviour

relatedConcepts.name: Complex
relatedConcepts.note: orthogonal — Complex is structural (parts), Complicated is epistemic (understanding). Tom keeps these strictly separate.

relatedConcepts.name: Intelligible
relatedConcepts.note: antonym pair — Intelligible specs are not Complicated; Complicated systems lack Intelligibility

relatedConcepts.name: Compound
relatedConcepts.note: structural sibling; orthogonal to Complicated

relatedConcepts.name: Elementary
relatedConcepts.note: structural sibling; an Elementary thing can still be Complicated if poorly understood

relatedConcepts.name: Simple
relatedConcepts.note: structural sibling; Simple things can be Complicated

concepts.definition: Anything, that is difficult to understand, estimate or predict the actions, reactions, and attributes of.
concepts.overview:
**Complicated** is *epistemic* — about our ability to understand, estimate, predict.
Independent of structure: a [[Complex.021|Complex]] system can be intelligible; an [[Elementary.055|Elementary]] one can be Complicated.

concepts.name: Component

relatedConcepts.name: Elementary
relatedConcepts.note: structural class — a Component can be Elementary (no further parts)

relatedConcepts.name: Complex
relatedConcepts.note: structural class — a Component can be Complex (interconnected parts of its own)

relatedConcepts.name: Consists Of
relatedConcepts.note: the inverse relation — 'X consists of y' iff 'y is a Component of X

relatedConcepts.name: Includes
relatedConcepts.note: weaker relation — Includes can be a *partial* list; Component is a single member of the whole

concepts.definition: A component is a potential, or actual, part of some larger system, or specification.
concepts.overview:
A **Component** is *any identifiable individual part* of a larger whole. It can be Elementary or Complex; potential or actual.
Notation: `X: {y}` means *y is a Component of X*.

concepts.name: Compound

relatedConcepts.name: Elementary
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — an Elementary entity has no parts; Compound has two or more

relatedConcepts.name: Complex
relatedConcepts.note: near-synonym — Complex adds 'interconnected'; Compound is the broader structural class

relatedConcepts.name: Simple
relatedConcepts.note: structural sibling — Simple is the antonym of Complex; all four sit in the Partitioning family

relatedConcepts.name: Complicated
relatedConcepts.note: orthogonal epistemic concept — Compound describes structure, Complicated describes difficulty of understanding

concepts.definition: Compound entities contain two or more elements.
concepts.overview: **Compound** is a *structural* property: any entity that has two or more parts. It is the antonym of [[Elementary.055|Elementary]] and a near-synonym of [[Complex.021|Complex]] (which adds interconnection). Entirely orthogonal to [[Complicated.676|Complicated]] (epistemic difficulty).

concepts.name: Concept

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage Concept
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — a Concept defined in Planguage notation

relatedConcepts.name: Engineering Concept
relatedConcepts.note: sub-category — a Concept of an engineering artifact (design idea, requirement idea); self-referential in source

concepts.definition: A concept is an idea.
concepts.overview: **Concept** is the general class: *any defined idea*. Defined concepts can be reused, redefined, and referenced across languages — from any term back to the same numbered definition. [[Planguage-Concept.188|Planguage Concept]] is the specialisation for concepts defined in Planguage notation.

concepts.name: Concrete Strategy

relatedConcepts.name: Abstract Strategy
relatedConcepts.note: counterpart — Abstract Strategy is non-material (goals, aims, objectives); Concrete Strategy is material

relatedConcepts.name: Strategy
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Concrete Strategy is the material specialisation of Strategy

relatedConcepts.name: Aim
relatedConcepts.note: what a Concrete Strategy exists to support — it is a means toward stated Aims

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Objective
relatedConcepts.note: the higher-level objectives a Concrete Strategy's real-world attributes impact

relatedConcepts.name: Means Objective
relatedConcepts.note: Concrete Strategy is the how — the material means by which Means Objectives are achieved

concepts.definition: A concrete strategy [is] any device or means for supporting specified aims, which is existing in a real or material form, and is not abstract.
concepts.overview: **Concrete Strategy** is the *material half* of the strategy pair. It includes organisations, technology, and resources — anything that exists in the physical or operational world. It is distinguished from [[Abstract-Strategy.660|Abstract Strategy]] (goals, aims, objectives) by materiality, not by level of detail.

concepts.name: Condition Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Condition
relatedConcepts.note: related but distinct — a Condition is a pre-requisite for validity; a Condition Constraint imposes a binding restriction with failure consequences

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Condition Constraint is a binary specialisation of Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Status
relatedConcepts.note: the result of evaluating any Condition; Condition Constraint evaluation yields a binary pass/fail status

concepts.definition:
A condition constraint is a requirement that *imposes a conscious restriction* for a specified system scope.
A condition constraint, also called a 'restriction,' is a binary type of requirement.
concepts.overview:
**Condition Constraint** (synonym: **Restriction**) is a *binary requirement* — either the constraint is met or it isn't. Failing a Condition Constraint signals a problem, risk, invalidity, or dependency. Distinguished from a plain [[Condition.024|Condition]] by consequence: violating a Condition Constraint causes failure; a Condition is simply a pre-requisite for validity.
Notation: `[<Condition Tag Name>]` — square brackets, same icon as Condition.

concepts.name: Condition

relatedConcepts.name: Condition Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: distinct — a Condition is a pre-requisite for validity; a Condition Constraint is a binding restriction with failure consequences

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: application — one or more Conditions form a statement Qualifier

relatedConcepts.name: Status
relatedConcepts.note: the result of evaluating a Condition — the current true/false answer

concepts.definition: A condition is a specified pre-requisite for making a specification or a system component valid.
concepts.overview:
**Condition** is a *pre-requisite for validity* — a true/false test. Evaluating a Condition yields a [[Status.174b|Status]]. Three distinct kinds exist: Reusable Conditions (define conditional terms), Qualifier Conditions (validate a statement qualifier), and Pre-requisite Conditions (entry/exit gates for a process).
Notation: `[?]` alone; also `[   ]` (square brackets) containing conditions in qualified statements.

concepts.name: Confidentiality

relatedConcepts.name: Complete
relatedConcepts.note: sibling status parameter — Complete asks 'is anything missing?'; Confidentiality asks 'who may read this?

relatedConcepts.name: Clarity
relatedConcepts.note: sibling spec quality — a spec can be Confidential and still be Clear (or not)

concepts.definition: The level of readership to which a specification is restricted.
concepts.overview: **Confidentiality** is a *status parameter* that scopes who may read a specification. It is not a quality of the specification's content — it is an access control label. A specification can be any confidentiality level regardless of how complete, clear, or accurate it is.

concepts.name: Consists of

relatedConcepts.name: Component
relatedConcepts.note: inverse relation — 'X consists of y' iff 'y is a Component of X'; Consists Of states the full set, Component names one member

relatedConcepts.name: Includes
relatedConcepts.note: weaker relation — Includes may list some but not necessarily all components; Consists Of commits to the complete set

concepts.definition: Parameter: Describes the *complete* set of elements that a concept consists of.
concepts.overview:
**Consists Of** is the *exhaustive enumeration* relation: `X = {a, b, c}` means the complete set of X's elements is exactly {a, b, c} — no more, no less. It is the inverse of [[Component.022|Component]] and stronger than [[Includes.391|Includes]] (which admits partial lists).
Notation: `= { . . . }` — "is equal to the set."

concepts.name: Constraint Attribute Impact

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint Attribute
relatedConcepts.note: parent — a Constraint Attribute Impact is the acknowledged effect of a specific Constraint Attribute *687

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: grandparent — Constraint Attributes belong to Constraints; Impact extends that chain

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimate
relatedConcepts.note: quantification link — Impact Estimate *433 provides the formal estimation methodology for quantifying Impact

concepts.definition: An acknowledgement, probably by conscious analysis and explicit specification — and perhaps by quantitative estimation of the degree — that a specific [[Constraint-Attribute.687|Constraint Attribute]] has an impact on one or more system objects or sets of objects of interest.
concepts.overview: **Constraint Attribute Impact** maps a [[Constraint-Attribute.687|Constraint Attribute]] to the system objects it affects. The acknowledgement is explicit — not assumed. The impact may be named, categorised, or quantified (via [[Impact-Estimate.433|Impact Estimate]]). Notation: `->` as in `Constraint X, Attribute Y -> {system objects affected}`.

concepts.name: Constraint Attribute

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint Attribute Impact
relatedConcepts.note: extension — each Constraint Attribute can carry a Constraint Attribute Impact *688 on identified system objects

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: parent — a Constraint possesses Constraint Attributes; analysis of Attributes reveals downstream consequences

concepts.definition: A constraint can possess a number of potentially interesting attributes. Analysis of these Constraint Attributes can help us understand the full consequences of a particular constraint specification earlier, perhaps avoiding unnecessary negative consequences.
concepts.overview: **Constraint Attribute** characterises *how* a [[Constraint.218|Constraint]] constrains — not just *what* it restricts. Constraint Attributes are variables (degrees, not binary); each attribute tends to impact specific system objects, tracked via [[Constraint-Attribute-Impact.688|Constraint Attribute Impact]]. Identified attribute types include: Governing, Enabling, Fixed, Interdependent, Mappable, Manageable, Robustness, Resilience.

concepts.name: Constraint Design

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: the requirement being satisfied — Constraint Design is design aimed at meeting Constraint *218

relatedConcepts.name: Design Specification
relatedConcepts.note: parent form — Constraint Design is a specialised Design Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Function Design
relatedConcepts.note: sibling design type — satisfies Function requirements; same multiple-impact principle applies

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Design
relatedConcepts.note: sibling design type — satisfies Performance requirements; same multiple-impact principle applies

relatedConcepts.name: Cost Design
relatedConcepts.note: sibling design type — satisfies Cost requirements; all design types share the multiple-impact reality

relatedConcepts.name: Design Process
relatedConcepts.note: the process in which Constraint Design is produced

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: one of many quality dimensions a Constraint Design simultaneously impacts

relatedConcepts.name: Function Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: function requirements are impacted by Constraint Design as a side effect

concepts.definition: Constraint Design is design specification aimed at, or as a side effect, satisfying Constraint requirements.
concepts.overview: **Constraint Design** is [[Design-Specification.586|Design Specification]] whose primary or incidental purpose is satisfying [[Constraint.218|Constraint]] requirements. The defining principle: *any design specification, regardless of its intent, impacts many requirements simultaneously* — not just the one it targets. Constraint Design is not isolated from Function, Performance, or Cost design.

concepts.name: Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Constraint is a specialised Requirement whose primary intent is to restrict

relatedConcepts.name: Function Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: binary sub-type — restriction on what the system must or must not do

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: scalar sub-type — Fail/Survival levels on a quality-attribute scale

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: scalar sub-type — restriction on resource consumption (time, money, people)

relatedConcepts.name: Design Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: binary sub-type — restriction on which designs are permissible

relatedConcepts.name: Condition Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: binary sub-type — named-scope restriction; synonym Restriction

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: scalar mechanism — the lower bound a system must not breach

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: scalar mechanism — the level at which breach constitutes unacceptable failure

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint Attribute
relatedConcepts.note: analysis extension — attributes (Governing, Fixed, etc.) characterise how a Constraint constrains

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint Attribute Impact
relatedConcepts.note: analysis extension — maps Constraint Attributes to affected system objects

concepts.definition:
A constraint is a requirement that explicitly and intentionally tries to directly restrict any system or process.
A key property of a constraint is that a **penalty or loss** of some kind applies if the constraint is not respected.
Constraints include limitations on the engineering process, a system's operation, or its lifecycle.
concepts.overview: **Constraint** is *restriction with penalty*. Two forms: **Binary** (must/must not — Function, Design, Condition) and **Scalar** (Fail/Survival levels — Performance, Resource). Unlike a Goal or Target, a Constraint does not motivate — it *limits*. Violating it has a named consequence.

concepts.name: Consumer

relatedConcepts.name: Client
relatedConcepts.note: sibling stakeholder — Client also uses 'Customer' as a synonym; distinct from Consumer in that Client implies a commissioning/paying relationship

relatedConcepts.name: User
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — the Consumer at the end of a chain who makes practical use of the final real system is termed a User

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Consumer is a stakeholder role in the downstream chain

concepts.definition: A consumer is a person or group who makes use of ('consumes') a process output (product).
concepts.overview: **Consumer** is *any stakeholder downstream in a process chain* who consumes an output. The term applies throughout systems engineering processes — not just to end-users. The synonym **Customer** is used to remind colleagues that their internal downstream counterparts deserve the same treatment as paying customers. The [[User.234|User]] is the Consumer at the *end* of the chain.

concepts.name: Content

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: container — Content is what a Specification contains; the Specification is the formal housing for Content

relatedConcepts.name: Concept
relatedConcepts.note: source — a Concept is the idea; Content is its specification; the Content may intentionally simplify or partially represent the Concept

relatedConcepts.name: Context
relatedConcepts.note: companion — a Context is a particular view; Content may reflect just one contextual view of a Concept

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Review Rule
relatedConcepts.note: quality standard — Content Rules specify engineering standards for deriving, specifying, and analysing Content (as distinct from Clarity Rules *129 which govern expression)

concepts.definition:
Content is the meaning or message contained in a specification as distinct from its appearance, form, or style.
Actual specification content may or may not totally reflect a concept we have in mind. It might intentionally simplify the concept, or specify a particular view of it.
concepts.overview: **Content** is *what a specification means*, separated from how it looks or is formatted. A specification's Content is its meaning and message — which may intentionally simplify or partially represent the underlying [[Concept.595|Concept]]. Content quality is measured by Content Rules; expression quality is measured by Clarity Rules.

concepts.name: Context

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: sub-class — stakeholders are a particular class of Context; a Stakeholder is an active, responsible Context

relatedConcepts.name: View
relatedConcepts.note: synonym / companion — a Context is a system view; View *484 extends this concept

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: specification mechanism — Planguage Qualifiers are the primary way of specifying a Context in formal statements

concepts.definition: A context is a system view from any useful perspective.
concepts.overview: **Context** is a *deliberate perspective* from which requirements or designs are considered. Contexts are established to force completeness — to surface requirements we might otherwise forget. Context analysis is therefore a risk management technique. [[Stakeholder.233|Stakeholders]] are a special class of Context; [[Qualifier.124|Qualifiers]] are the Planguage notation for specifying a Context formally.

concepts.name: Continuous Process Improvement

relatedConcepts.name: Defect Prevention Process
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — Defect Prevention is a core activity of CPI; systematically preventing recurring defects

relatedConcepts.name: Statistical Process Control
relatedConcepts.note: mechanism — SPC provides the measurement and control infrastructure that makes CPI evidence-based

concepts.definition: Continuous Process Improvement (CPI) includes any and all continuous long-term effort to systematically improve an organisation's work processes.
concepts.overview: **CPI** is the sustained, systematic commitment to making work processes better — indefinitely. It is not a project with an end date; it is an ongoing discipline. [[Defect-Prevention-Process.042|Defect Prevention]] is a core activity within CPI; [[Statistical-Process-Control.466|Statistical Process Control]] provides the measurement infrastructure that makes improvement evidence-based rather than opinion-based.

concepts.name: Control Axis

relatedConcepts.name: Input/Output Axis
