relatedConcepts.note: companion axis — the vertical axis in a Planguage process diagram; Control Axis is horizontal, I/O Axis is vertical

concepts.definition: The Process Control Axis is the horizontal, left-to-right direction of 'process flow' in a Planguage process diagram.
concepts.overview: **Control Axis** is the *horizontal dimension* of a Planguage process diagram. Processes flow left-to-right along this axis: precedent processes enter from the left (Control Entry, CE); subsequent processes exit to the right (Control Exit, CX). The companion vertical axis handles data in/out. The Control Axis coincides with the Plan and Study components of the PDSA quadrangle.

concepts.name: Control Chart

relatedConcepts.name: Control Limits
relatedConcepts.note: component — Control Limits are the upper and lower bounds drawn on a Control Chart

relatedConcepts.name: Statistical Process Control
relatedConcepts.note: parent framework — a Control Chart is the primary visual tool of SPC

relatedConcepts.name: Common Causes
relatedConcepts.note: inside the limits — observations within Control Limits are attributed to Common Causes

relatedConcepts.name: Chance Cause
relatedConcepts.note: related — Chance Cause is the underlying mechanism of Common Cause variation within limits

concepts.definition: "A control chart is a graphic comparison of process performance data to computed 'control limits' drawn as limit lines on the chart." [JURAN74]
concepts.overview: **Control Chart** is the *primary visual tool of SPC*: a time-series graph of process measurements with computed [[Control-Limits.028|Control Limits]] overlaid. Observations within the limits are attributed to [[Common-Causes.020|Common Causes]] (normal process variation); observations outside the limits signal probable Special Causes requiring investigation. Invented by Walter Shewhart in 1924.

concepts.name: Control Limits

relatedConcepts.name: Control Chart
relatedConcepts.note: host — Control Limits are drawn as lines on a Control Chart

relatedConcepts.name: Common Causes
relatedConcepts.note: inside relation — observations within Control Limits are attributed to Common Causes (normal variation)

relatedConcepts.name: Chance Cause
relatedConcepts.note: inside relation — Chance Cause is the mechanism of Common Cause variation; observations within limits are Chance-Cause-driven

relatedConcepts.name: Statistical Process Control
relatedConcepts.note: parent framework — Control Limits are the boundary mechanism in SPC

concepts.definition: Control limits are the upper and lower bounds on a control chart. Control limits should contain, within those boundaries, all observations of 'variation due to common causes'. Observations *outside* the control limits are *probably* due to special causes.
concepts.overview: **Control Limits** are the computed upper (UCL) and lower (LCL) bounds on a [[Control-Chart.029|Control Chart]], set at ±3 standard deviations (3-sigma) by Shewhart convention. Observations within the limits are attributed to [[Common-Causes.020|Common Causes]] (normal process variation); observations *outside* are flagged as *probably* due to Special Causes — triggering investigation, not automatic action.

concepts.name: Control Point

relatedConcepts.name: Design Problem
relatedConcepts.note: application domain — Control Points are the dimensions of a Design Problem that must all be addressed in the solution

relatedConcepts.name: Problem Definition
relatedConcepts.note: companion — Problem Definition establishes the Control Points that the solution must address

concepts.definition:
Control points are the specified elements that must be considered in solving a problem. They include requirements, constraints, qualifiers, and inherited specification elements.
The number of problem control points that must be considered is a measure of the complexity of the problem to be solved.
concepts.overview: **Control Point** (synonyms: Problem Control Points, Problem Dimensions) is *any specified element that the solution to a problem must address* — requirements, constraints, qualifiers, or inherited specifications. The count of Control Points is a proxy measure of problem complexity. More Control Points = a more constrained solution space.

concepts.name: Controllability

relatedConcepts.name: Controllable
relatedConcepts.note: application — Controllable *232 is the binary property derived from Controllability: a component is Controllable or it is not

relatedConcepts.name: Observable
relatedConcepts.note: paired concept — Observability is defined alongside Controllability in feedback control theory; a state component is Observable if it can be estimated from output

concepts.definition:
A component of the system state vector is **Controllable** if there exists a control signal which can bring the system from the current state to a desired state.
It is **Observable** if it is possible to compute or estimate the state from a finitely long observation of the system output.
concepts.overview: **Controllability** is a *systems engineering property* from feedback control theory: a system component is Controllable if it can be driven to any desired state via a control input. Its companion property, **Observability**, is whether the state can be determined from outputs alone. Both are binary: either possible in finite time or not.

concepts.name: Controllable

relatedConcepts.name: Controllability
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — Controllability *175 defines the formal property; Controllable *232 is its binary application to an objective type

concepts.definition: *Controllable* is the type of objective where the Design Ideas chosen are capable of influencing Fundamental Objectives at all.
concepts.overview: **Controllable** (after Keeney) classifies an objective by whether Design Ideas can *influence it at all*. If no design choice affects an objective, specifying a requirement against it is pointless — it cannot be satisfied by engineering. Pairs with [[Controllability.175|Controllability]] *175 (the formal control-theory formulation of the same property).

concepts.name: Core Ideology

relatedConcepts.name: Core Purpose
relatedConcepts.note: first component — Core Ideology = Core Purpose + Core Values

relatedConcepts.name: Core Values
relatedConcepts.note: second component — Core Ideology = Core Purpose + Core Values

relatedConcepts.name: Vision
relatedConcepts.note: companion — Vision *422 is typically built on Core Ideology; source lists *442 (Ultimate) but *422 (Vision) is the intended link

concepts.definition: Core Ideology consists of Core Purpose and Core Values.
concepts.overview: **Core Ideology** is the *durable identity* of an organisation: the fixed conjunction of [[Core-Purpose.662|Core Purpose]] (why we exist) and [[Core-Values.663|Core Values]] (how we operate). Introduced by Collins & Porras in *Built To Last*, it is the stable foundation on which Vision and strategy are built.

concepts.name: Core Purpose

relatedConcepts.name: Core Ideology
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Core Purpose is the 'why' component of Core Ideology

relatedConcepts.name: Core Values
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Core Values are the 'how' constraints; Core Purpose is the 'why' direction

relatedConcepts.name: Objective and Performance Requirements
relatedConcepts.note: engineering link — Core Purpose is the most fundamental Objective; it implies a performance dimension

relatedConcepts.name: Mission
relatedConcepts.note: companion — Mission is 'what we do'; Core Purpose is 'why we do it

concepts.definition:
A Core Purpose is the most fundamental 'why?' the organisation exists. It can be viewed as the most fundamental *objective*; the most fundamental *measure* of progress or improvement; the measure that all supporting strategies intend to improve. We must always aim to improve in that dimension, while keeping loyal to our Core Value constraints.
Part of the Core Ideology.
concepts.overview: **Core Purpose** is *why the organisation exists* — framed not as a goal to be achieved and retired, but as a direction of improvement that is permanently valid. It serves two roles: defining the core **mission** (what we do) and implying a **performance dimension** (improvement is always better). Contrasted with [[Mission.097|Mission]] (*097) — Mission is *what* we do; Core Purpose is *why*.

concepts.name: Core Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Commentary
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Commentary is non-binding and low-severity; Core Specification is binding and high-severity

relatedConcepts.name: Non-Commentary
relatedConcepts.note: parent category — Core Specification is a type of Non-Commentary (it produces real system changes)

relatedConcepts.name: Background
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Background is supporting context; Core Specification is the binding 'meat

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: parent form — Core Specification is the binding, high-consequence subset of all Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: measurement framework — SQC defects in Core Specification are almost always major severity

concepts.definition: Anything classed as 'core specification' will result in real system changes being made: incorrect core specification would materially and negatively affect the system in terms of costs, effort, or quality. Specification defects in core specification are almost always of major severity.
concepts.overview: **Core Specification** (synonyms: **Implementable Specification**, **Critical**) is the *binding, high-consequence subset* of a specification. It is what gets built. A defect here — wrong value, wrong scale, wrong constraint — propagates directly into the system. Distinguished from [[Commentary.632|Commentary]] (non-binding remarks) and [[Background.507|Background]] (supporting context) by consequence: Core Specification errors cost money, time, or quality.

concepts.name: Core Values

relatedConcepts.name: Core Ideology
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Core Values are the constraint component of Core Ideology

relatedConcepts.name: Core Purpose
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Core Purpose is the 'why'; Core Values are the 'how' constraints on pursuing it

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: Planguage equivalent — Core Values function as the highest-priority Constraints on all planning and activity

concepts.definition:
Core Values are a handful of basic ingrained beliefs about how to run a given organisation. They are almost unchangeable for the lifetime of the organisation. They are the strongest guidelines that all other activity in the organisation must try to align with. They are the highest priority. Core Values can be viewed as **constraints** on planning and activity. Anything that violates these constraints is not acceptable — it is out of alignment with the Core Values. Essentially they are constraints on reaching the Core Purpose.
Part of the Core Ideology.
concepts.overview: **Core Values** are *the highest-priority Constraints on organisational activity* — not aspirational but operative. They are ingrained beliefs about how to act, and they do not change with strategy, market, or leadership. In Planguage terms, they are the supreme [[Constraint.218|Constraints]] that bound the pursuit of [[Core-Purpose.662|Core Purpose]].

concepts.name: Cost Budget

relatedConcepts.name: Budget Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: sub-type — Budget Constraints (Cost-Level Constraints *186 and binary cost constraints *467) are the restriction half of Cost Budget

relatedConcepts.name: Budget Target
relatedConcepts.note: sub-type — Budget Targets {Goal, Wish, Stretch} are the motivational half of Cost Budget

relatedConcepts.name: Cost-Level Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: implementation — Fail and Limit specifications express Cost-Level Constraints within the Cost Budget framework

concepts.definition: A cost budget is a requirement level set for a resource. Cost budgets are either Budget Constraints or Budget Targets.
concepts.overview: **Cost Budget** (synonym: **Cost Requirement**) is the complete framework of resource-level requirements: it encompasses both the **binding** side ([[Budget-Constraint.421|Budget Constraints]] — Fail/Limit levels) and the **motivational** side ([[Budget-Target.481|Budget Targets]] — Goal/Wish/Stretch). The two halves are distinct: constraints must be respected; targets motivate but allow variation.

concepts.name: Cost Design

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: target type — Cost Design satisfies cost constraints; every design also impacts other constraints as a side effect

relatedConcepts.name: Design Specification
relatedConcepts.note: parent form — Cost Design is a specialised Design Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Design
relatedConcepts.note: sibling design type — same multiple-impact principle; Performance Design also affects cost

relatedConcepts.name: Function Design
relatedConcepts.note: sibling design type — Function Design also carries cost side effects

relatedConcepts.name: Design Process
relatedConcepts.note: the process context in which Cost Design is produced

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Target
relatedConcepts.note: Cost Design may incidentally satisfy or impact Performance Targets as a side effect

concepts.definition: Cost design is conscious design specification aimed at, or at least incidentally resulting in, the achievement of specified cost targets and cost constraints.
concepts.overview: **Cost Design** is [[Design-Specification.586|Design Specification]] whose primary purpose or incidental effect is satisfying cost targets and cost constraints. Like all design types, it carries the **multiple-impact principle**: any design decision — however narrowly cost-focused — simultaneously affects Performance, Function, and other Constraints. Cost Design cannot be isolated from other requirement dimensions.

concepts.name: Cost-Level Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Budget Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Cost-Level Constraint is the scalar form of Budget Constraint; Budget Targets (*481) are set within its framework

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Type Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Resource Type Constraint restricts the *type* of resource used (binary); Cost-Level Constraint restricts the *level* (scalar)

relatedConcepts.name: Cost Budget
relatedConcepts.note: parent framework — the Cost-Level Constraint is the binding half of the Cost Budget

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: specification mechanism — Fail and Limit express Cost-Level Constraints on the resource scale

concepts.definition: A cost-level constraint specifies a cost-level limitation on a defined resource scale. It is a numeric cost requirement constraint on the costs of design ideas, for a specified function or system.
concepts.overview:
**Cost-Level Constraint** (synonym: **Cost Constraint**) is a *scalar binding restriction* on resource consumption — expressed using `Fail` and `Limit` parameter levels on a cost scale. It is a fundamental requirement handed down from an authority level above the project; it cannot be traded off without that authority's approval. [[Budget-Target.481|Budget Targets]] (Goal, Wish, Stretch) are set *within* this constraint framework.
Notation: `-----[-->>----]-->O` — `[` lower limit, `]` upper limit, `>>` Fail-type constraint.

concepts.name: Cost

relatedConcepts.name: Cost Level
relatedConcepts.note: application — Cost Level *033 is a specific numeric level of the cost attribute

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: adjective synonym — 'resource constraint' and 'resource requirement' use Resource as the adjective form of this concept

concepts.definition: 'Cost' as an adjective is used to signify that *Resources*, rather than *Qualities*, *Functions*, or *Designs*, are the category of the noun being used.
concepts.overview: **Cost** (adjective, *185) is a *category marker*: it signals that the following noun belongs to the resource-consumption dimension — not the quality, function, or design dimension. Its synonym is **Resource** (also adjective). The essential distinction: a *Resource* is a latent capability or fuel; a *Cost* is the expense incurred (resource consumed).

concepts.name: Cost, to

relatedConcepts.name: Estimate
relatedConcepts.note: general synonym — 'to estimate' applies to any attribute or parameter; 'to cost' carries an implied financial or resource scope

relatedConcepts.name: Cost
relatedConcepts.note: noun counterpart — the output of 'costing' is a Cost (noun) specification for a set of requirements

concepts.definition: To 'cost' something is specifically to estimate the *resources* needed to achieve a planned set of requirements. To estimate costs.
concepts.overview: **Cost, to** (*184) is the *estimation activity* for resource consumption — especially financial resources. Its synonym is **to estimate** (*059), but *to estimate* is broader: it applies to any attribute. *To cost* implies resource (and typically financial) estimation unless otherwise specified.

concepts.name: Cost

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Resource is potential available; Cost is quantity consumed (Cost ≠ Resource)

relatedConcepts.name: Cost Level
relatedConcepts.note: specific application — Cost Level *033 is a numeric point on a defined cost scale

relatedConcepts.name: Cost, to
relatedConcepts.note: verbal form — 'to cost' is the process of estimating resource requirements

concepts.definition: Cost is an *expense* incurred in building or maintaining a system. It is consumption of a resource.
concepts.overview: **Cost** (*033) is *resource consumed* — the expense of development or maintenance. Its synonyms are Price and Expense. The critical distinction: **Cost ≠ Resource**. A Resource is a *potential source* of inputs (hours available, capital allocated). A Cost is the *quantity of that resource consumed*. The keyed icon `-|->O` places a level `|` on a resource flow arrow, showing consumption.

concepts.name: Creativity

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: application — Architecture is one major output of purposeful creativity applied to structural design

relatedConcepts.name: Design Idea
relatedConcepts.note: product — Creativity generates Design Ideas (*047) as its evaluable output

relatedConcepts.name: Design Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: process context — Design Engineering is the discipline in which purposeful creativity operates

relatedConcepts.name: Design Process
relatedConcepts.note: possible synonym — Design Process overlaps significantly with the Creativity process

relatedConcepts.name: Innovation
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Innovation is the applied outcome of creativity; creativity is the generative process

concepts.definition:
The process of identifying, defining, and evaluating ideas, with respect to defined criteria.
The *degree* of creativity is the degree of effects on defined performance requirements, and on defined constraints.
concepts.overview: **Creativity** (*680) is not idea generation for its own sake — it is a *purposeful, criteria-driven process* for identifying, defining, and evaluating ideas against defined requirements and constraints. Its measure — the **degree of creativity** — is the degree of effect on those requirements. An idea that meets no requirement has zero degree of creativity; an idea that satisfies an extreme requirement has a high degree. Newness and originality are irrelevant unless specifically required.

concepts.name: Credibility Rating

relatedConcepts.name: Credibility
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Credibility Rating is the numeric assignment on the Credibility scale (0.0–1.0)

concepts.definition: A credibility rating is the assignment of a number on a defined credibility scale that ranges from 0.0 (no credibility for an impact estimate) to 1.0 (perfect credibility of an impact estimate).
concepts.overview: **Credibility Rating** (*272) is *the numeric act of assigning a credibility value* to an impact estimate. It operationalises **Credibility** (*035): where Credibility is the concept, Credibility Rating is the number placed on the 0.0–1.0 scale. Each level in the scale has a defined evidential meaning — from "wild guess" (0.0) to "reliable in-house measurements corroborated by independent external measurements" (0.8+). The rating then directly adjusts impact estimates: `Credibility-Adjusted Estimate = Impact Estimate × Credibility Rating`.

concepts.name: Credibility

relatedConcepts.name: Credibility Rating
relatedConcepts.note: child — Credibility Rating is the numeric assignment of a credibility value on the Credibility scale

relatedConcepts.name: Evidence
relatedConcepts.note: basis — Credibility is assessed for the Evidence and Sources supporting an impact estimate

relatedConcepts.name: Source
relatedConcepts.note: subject — Sources receive credibility ratings that cascade to and adjust impact estimates

concepts.definition:
Credibility expresses the strength of 'belief in' and hence 'validity of', information.
Within Impact Estimation, credibility is usually assessed for the *evidence* and *sources* supporting each specific impact estimate. Credibility is expressed as a numeric value, on a range from 1.0 (perfect credibility) to 0.0 (no credibility at all). These credibility values can be used to credibility-correct the impact estimates: each impact estimate is multiplied by its relevant credibility.
concepts.overview: **Credibility** (*035) is the *adjustment mechanism* for impact estimates — it converts a raw estimate into a credibility-corrected estimate by multiplying by a 0.0–1.0 value. The Credibility value is assigned via **Credibility Rating** (*272), which has a calibrated scale from "wild guess" (0.0) to "perfectly verified" (1.0). The keyed icon `±?.#` represents an uncertainty estimate. Credibility is assessed for the *evidence* and *sources*, not for the estimate itself.

concepts.name: Critical Factor

relatedConcepts.name: Critical Success Factor
relatedConcepts.note: child — Critical Success Factor is the success-direction specialisation; specified as Goal/Budget or binary Target

relatedConcepts.name: Critical Failure Factor
relatedConcepts.note: child — Critical Failure Factor is the failure-direction specialisation; specified as Fail/Survival or binary Constraint

concepts.definition:
A Critical Factor is an attribute level or condition in a system which can, on its own, determine the success or failure of the system under specified conditions.
A critical *failure* factor is usually specified as a constraint level (for example a 'Fail' or 'Survival' level), or as a binary constraint.
A critical *success* factor is usually specified as a target level (a 'Goal' or 'Budget' level), or as a binary target.
concepts.overview: **Critical Factor** (*036) is the *parent concept* for [[Critical-Success-Factor.418|Critical Success Factor]] (*418) and [[Critical-Failure-Factor.025|Critical Failure Factor]] (*025). A Critical Factor is any attribute level or condition that, *on its own*, determines whether a system succeeds or fails under specified conditions. Direction distinguishes the two types: Critical Success Factors are specified as goals and targets; Critical Failure Factors are specified as constraints (Fail/Survival levels). The word "critical" means the factor is *determinative* — not just influential.

concepts.name: Critical Failure Factor

relatedConcepts.name: Critical Success Factor
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Critical Success Factor is the success-direction counterpart; together they span the Critical Factor space

relatedConcepts.name: Critical Factor
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Critical Failure Factor is the failure-direction specialisation of Critical Factor *036

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: specification parameter — Fail level is the primary scalar specification for a Critical Failure Factor

concepts.definition:
A Critical Failure Factor is any factor that determines any degree of failure of a system. This includes, and can be specified and articulated using, both scalar levels and binary conditions.
A critical failure factor may be specified as a constraint level (for example a 'Fail' or 'Survival' level), or as a binary constraint ('Constraint').
concepts.overview: **Critical Failure Factor** (*025) is the failure-direction child of **Critical Factor** (*036). It is *any* factor — scalar or binary — that *determines any degree* of system failure. This includes both numeric threshold breaches (Fail or Survival levels on a scale) and binary violations (Constraint). The phrase "any degree" is intentional: a Critical Failure Factor need not cause total collapse — a partial or conditional failure also qualifies.

concepts.name: Critical Success Factor

relatedConcepts.name: Critical Factor
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Critical Success Factor is the success-direction child of Critical Factor *036

relatedConcepts.name: Critical Failure Factor
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — CFF is the failure-direction counterpart of CSF

concepts.definition: Any attribute level or condition of a system that can itself, *alone or in combination with other factors*, determine practical or total system success, is a Critical Success Factor.
concepts.overview: **Critical Success Factor** (*418) is the success-direction child of **Critical Factor** (*036). A CSF is any attribute level or condition — scalar or binary — that *alone or in combination* determines system success. The key extension over the parent concept: *Critical Factor* says "on its own"; CSF adds "or in combination with other factors" — recognising that success often requires a threshold of combined conditions, not a single decisive factor. Credit: Chris Dale (February 2007).

concepts.name: Culture

relatedConcepts.name: Environment System
relatedConcepts.note: container — Culture is a property of the Environment System that a target system must operate within and respect

relatedConcepts.name: System
relatedConcepts.note: host — Culture is a System Property; it characterises the human/organisational system in which technical systems are embedded

concepts.definition:
"Culture is an umbrella term which encompasses the social behavior, institutions, and norms found in human societies, as well as the knowledge, beliefs, arts, laws, customs, capabilities, and habits of the individuals in these groups. Culture is often originated from or attributed to a specific region or location."
**Planguage Viewpoint:** Culture can be described by an interesting set of Visions, Objectives, Constraints, Strategies, Processes, Procedures, Rules, Stakeholders.
concepts.overview: **Culture** (*692) is, in Planguage, a **System Property** of the human and organisational system surrounding a technical system — described through the same vocabulary as any other system: Visions, Objectives, Constraints, Strategies, Processes, Rules, Stakeholders. It is not mere background context; it is a specifiable, structured property that technical systems must operate within and align with. Culture is *learned, shared, symbolic, integrated, and dynamic* — not innate, not fixed, and not reducible to a simple classification.

concepts.name: Cumulative Defect Removal Effectiveness

relatedConcepts.name: Defect-Detection-Process
relatedConcepts.note: the series of DDP stages whose combined effectiveness this metric measures

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Quality-Control
relatedConcepts.note: SQC process series — cumulative effectiveness of SQC passes is a primary use case

relatedConcepts.name: Critical-Factor
relatedConcepts.note: context — defect removal effectiveness is a critical factor in system quality delivery

relatedConcepts.name: Defect-Specification
relatedConcepts.note: related — defects are what is being removed; specification of defect types governs what is measured

concepts.definition: The cumulative defect-removal percentage of a defined series of defect-removal processes. For example, a series of specification defect-removal stages, plus various testing stages.
concepts.overview: **Cumulative Defect Removal Effectiveness** (*037) measures what a *series* of defect-removal processes achieves together — not what any single pass achieves in isolation. A single Specification Quality Control (SQC) pass may remove 60–88% of defects of a given type; but a planned series of SQC passes can reach 95% cumulative removal before testing begins. This metric motivates the design of multi-pass QC strategies rather than over-relying on a single stage, and provides the empirical basis for planning how many passes are needed to meet quality targets. The concept can also apply to any cumulative effectiveness metric outside defect removal.

concepts.name: Cycle-Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Cycle-Constraint is a planning Constraint specialised to evolutionary cycles

relatedConcepts.name: Cycle-Priority
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — determines which cycles run; Cycle-Constraint restricts how they run

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary-Project-Management
relatedConcepts.note: context — cycles are the delivery vehicle of evolutionary projects

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary
relatedConcepts.note: foundational — the evolutionary paradigm within which cycles operate

concepts.definition: A planning constraint on an evolutionary project cycle of any kind. Typically expressed in a planning policy, and requiring a cycle to be planned within certain time or financial limits.
concepts.overview: **Cycle-Constraint** (*039) is a specialisation of Constraint (*218) applied to the planning of evolutionary delivery cycles. It restricts how large, long, or expensive any single cycle may be. Without cycle constraints, teams expand scope and duration until iterations cease to be iterative. The classic form is a budget or time cap expressed as a policy applicable to all result cycles.

concepts.name: Cycle Priority

relatedConcepts.name: Cycle-Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — constrains cycle size; Cycle-Priority ranks which cycle to run

relatedConcepts.name: Quality-to-Cost-Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: calculation basis — Cycle-Priority is typically the benefit/cost ratio for the next cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Benefit
relatedConcepts.note: numerator — benefit delivered is the basis of the ratio

relatedConcepts.name: Impact-Estimation-Table
relatedConcepts.note: tool — used to estimate expected benefit/cost to compute Cycle-Priority

relatedConcepts.name: Impact-Estimation
relatedConcepts.note: method — estimates the numerator (quality/benefit impact) for Cycle-Priority calculation

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary-Project-Management
relatedConcepts.note: context — cycles are the delivery units whose priority this concept ranks

concepts.definition: The calculated relative (to other potential cycles) importance of a specific planned evolutionary delivery cycle.
concepts.overview: **Cycle Priority** (*040) is a quantified ranking of an evolutionary delivery cycle relative to other candidate cycles. It is computed — not guessed — using the expected benefit/cost ratio (also called the quality-to-cost ratio) for the upcoming cycle. The higher the ratio, the higher the priority. Cycle Priority can be scoped to a specific stakeholder or market qualifier, allowing prioritisation that serves narrower interests when needed.

concepts.name: Damage

relatedConcepts.name: Threat
relatedConcepts.note: origin — threats are the source of attacks that cause damage

relatedConcepts.name: Attack
relatedConcepts.note: proximate cause — a successful attack results in damage

relatedConcepts.name: Mitigation
relatedConcepts.note: countermeasure — built-in mitigation reduces gross damage; post-damage mitigation reduces net damage

relatedConcepts.name: Gross-Damage
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — damage remaining after built-in mitigation fails to stop an attack

relatedConcepts.name: Net-Damage
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — damage remaining after post-damage mitigation (insurance, recovery)

relatedConcepts.name: Risk
relatedConcepts.note: quantification — risk is the degree to which an attack succeeds in causing damage despite mitigation

concepts.definition:
Damage is the negative consequences of successful Attacks to a system. If built-in mitigation fails to deal with attacks, some damage of some sort, by definition, results.
**Gross Damage**: damage remaining after built-in Mitigation (i.e., attacks that succeeded despite it).
**Net Damage**: damage remaining after Post-Attack Mitigation strategies (such as Insurance, Recovery).
concepts.overview: **Damage** (*673) is the negative outcome when a [[Threat.671]] escalates into an [[Attack.672]] that defeats the system's built-in [[Mitigation.670]]. Damage is not a binary event — it has two measured levels: **Gross Damage** (*673a) is what survives built-in mitigation, and **Net Damage** (*673b) is what remains after post-attack recovery strategies (insurance, backups, business continuity). **Risk** (*309) is precisely defined as the degree to which an attack succeeds in causing damage despite mitigation — i.e., risk is the *probability and magnitude of Damage*. Specifying Damage quantitatively is what transforms risk management from a narrative into an engineering discipline.

concepts.name: Data

relatedConcepts.name: Dataware
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — data that can be or is processed by a computer

relatedConcepts.name: Logicware
relatedConcepts.note: sibling tech-material — active computer logic; all logicware is also dataware

relatedConcepts.name: Infoware
relatedConcepts.note: sibling tech-material — information of any kind, a superset of computer-processable data

relatedConcepts.name: Planware
relatedConcepts.note: sibling tech-material — plans/information for humans, not computers

relatedConcepts.name: Documentation
relatedConcepts.note: sibling tech-material — primarily for human not computer consumption

concepts.definition: Data is any form of signal which humans or machines can *usefully* distinguish from other signals. Data is interpreted by some sensing agent, a reader, or a computer, which tries to convert it into useful information. Data can be viewed as a necessary system resource, and also as a process input and a process output. Data can be characterised in terms of its function ('to warn', 'to give costs'), volume (bits), cost (to acquire, store, keep updated), and performance characteristics (accuracy, updatedness, credibility, precision, correctness).
concepts.overview: **Data** (*319) is the Planguage system element that covers any distinguishable signal — for humans or machines — that carries potential meaning. The key qualifier is "usefully": random noise is not data. Data is multi-dimensional: it has a function, a volume, a cost, and a set of quality characteristics (accuracy, currency, credibility). In the Tech Material family, **Data** is the broadest category — **Dataware** (*576) is the computer-processable subset, while **Infoware** (*578) is the human-interpretable superset.

concepts.name: Dataware

relatedConcepts.name: Data
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — Dataware is the computer-processable subset of Data

relatedConcepts.name: Logicware
relatedConcepts.note: sub-type — all logicware is also dataware (code is readable by a computer)

relatedConcepts.name: Infoware
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — information of any kind; only a small subset of infoware is used by computers

relatedConcepts.name: Planware
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — plans and information for humans, not computers

relatedConcepts.name: Documentation
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — primarily for human not computer consumption

concepts.definition: Dataware includes any data which can be or is in fact processed by a computer.
concepts.overview: **Dataware** (*576) is the computer-processable subset of [[Data.319]]. Where Data is the broadest category covering any distinguishable signal for humans or machines, Dataware narrows to what a computer can process. Crucially, all [[Logicware.575]] (program code) is also Dataware — code is readable by computers — but not all Dataware is Logicware. This distinguishes Dataware from sibling concepts: [[Planware.577]] (plans for humans), [[Infoware.578]] (information primarily for humans), and [[Documentation.579]] (human-facing documents).

concepts.name: Debugging

relatedConcepts.name: Defect-Detection-Process
relatedConcepts.note: upstream — DDP identifies faults that Debugging then removes

relatedConcepts.name: Fault
relatedConcepts.note: subject — Debugging removes faults (not defects) from a built system

relatedConcepts.name: Bug
relatedConcepts.note: common synonym for Fault — the origin of the term 'debugging

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Quality-Control
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — SQC removes defects from specs, not faults from systems

relatedConcepts.name: Edit-Audit-SQC
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — upstream SQC process that fixes spec defects; Debugging is the downstream system analogue

relatedConcepts.name: Edit-SQC
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — upstream SQC editing process; Debugging operates on built systems not specifications

concepts.definition: A process of removing identified faults (bugs) from a system. The process should include fault-consequent revalidation (regression testing) confirming that the fault removal succeeded and has not inadvertently injected additional faults.
concepts.overview: **Debugging** (*293) is the downstream Quality Control process that removes faults from a *built system* — not from its specifications. It is activated when QC processes (testing, field trials, user complaints, service analysis) have already identified a fault. The critical discipline is revalidation: after removing a fault, the system must be retested to confirm the fix worked and no new faults were introduced. Debugging is well downstream of the specification-level processes ([[Edit-SQC.288]], [[Edit-Audit-SQC.289]]), which remove defects from documents before they become system faults.

concepts.name: Decision-maker

relatedConcepts.name: Sponsor
relatedConcepts.note: often the decision-maker for funding and strategic commitments

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — all decision-makers are stakeholders with decision authority

concepts.definition: A decision-maker is a person or group who will make a specific defined decision. Also referred to as a decision-taker.
concepts.overview: **Decision-maker** (*237) is the Planguage stakeholder role assigned to whoever holds authority over a named decision. The definition is deliberately narrow: a decision-maker is defined *relative to a specific decision*, not as a general title or organisational rank. The same person can be a decision-maker for one decision and a stakeholder without decision authority for another. The [[Sponsor.396]] is often (but not always) the decision-maker for funding and strategic commitments.

concepts.name: Default

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: Default is a fallback qualifier — it specifies the value to use when no explicit Qualifier is stated

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: Defaults are declared on a Scale, bounding the measurement context

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: A Default is attached to a Tag in a specification statement

concepts.definition: A **Default** specification is a term to be used as a value when none is explicitly specified.
concepts.overview: **Default** (*447) is a specification mechanism that provides a fallback value for a qualifier or parameter when the author does not supply an explicit one. Its rationale is economy: it reduces repetition, keeps specs concise, and allows a single canonical assumption to be stated once and inherited everywhere. When an author wants a different value for a specific context, they simply state an explicit qualifier that overrides the Default. The Default is thus both a shorthand and a formal contract — anyone reading the spec knows exactly what was assumed in the absence of explicit qualification.

concepts.name: Defect Detection Process

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: parent process — DDP is one of the two components of SQC

relatedConcepts.name: Defect Prevention Process
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — DPP uses the defect data stream produced by DDP to drive process improvement

relatedConcepts.name: Major Defect
relatedConcepts.note: primary concern of DDP — major defects are the priority removal targets

relatedConcepts.name: Estimated Remaining Defects
relatedConcepts.note: metric produced by DDP activity — tracks the defect backlog

concepts.definition: The **Defect Detection Process (DDP)** is part of Specification Quality Control (SQC), which also includes the Defect Prevention Process (DPP). It is the systematic, project-focussed process of identifying and fixing specification defects.
concepts.overview: **Defect Detection Process** (*041, DDP) is the project-level component of Specification Quality Control that finds and removes defects from specifications *before* they propagate to code, test, or the field. DDP is economically motivated: late defect removal is many times more costly than early removal — "a stitch in time saves nine." While DDP is focused on the current project's economics, it feeds real defect data into the [[Defect-Prevention-Process.042|Defect Prevention Process]] (DPP), enabling systemic process improvement across future projects. DDP does not improve the process itself; DPP does. DDP removes the defects.

concepts.name: Defect Prevention Process

relatedConcepts.name: PDSA Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: methodological basis — DPP operates as a PDSA cycle of continuous improvement

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: parent — DPP is one of the two components of SQC

relatedConcepts.name: Defect Detection Process
relatedConcepts.note: sibling and data source — DPP is fed defect data from DDP to identify process improvements

relatedConcepts.name: Continuous Process Improvement
relatedConcepts.note: purpose — DPP is the primary mechanism for Continuous Process Improvement in SQC

relatedConcepts.name: Process Improvement Suggestion
relatedConcepts.note: output of DPP meetings — suggestions are logged and actioned from DPP sessions

relatedConcepts.name: Process Improvement
relatedConcepts.note: what DPP delivers — measurable reductions in defect rates across future projects

relatedConcepts.name: Process Meeting
relatedConcepts.note: forum where DPP operates — the regular meeting at which defect data is reviewed and process changes decided

relatedConcepts.name: Process Change Management Team
relatedConcepts.note: governance — the team that owns and implements DPP process changes

concepts.definition: The **Defect Prevention Process (DPP)** is a specific IBM-originated process of continuous process improvement. It is part of Specification Quality Control (SQC).
concepts.overview: **Defect Prevention Process** (*042, DPP) is the organisation-level component of Specification Quality Control that works towards continuous process improvement for on-going and future projects. Where the [[Defect-Detection-Process.041|Defect Detection Process]] (DDP) removes defects from the current project, DPP asks why defects recur and changes the process to prevent them from appearing in the first place. DPP was developed at IBM Research Triangle Park by Carole Jones and Robert Mays from 1983 onwards, and directly inspired the CMM Level 5 / CMMI Level 5 process capability model. IBM's data shows 50% reduction in historical defect rates in year one of DPP use, and 70% within two to three years.

concepts.name: Specification Defect

relatedConcepts.name: Defect Detection Process
relatedConcepts.note: DDP — the formal inspection/review process that identifies and removes Specification Defects

relatedConcepts.name: Defect Prevention Process
relatedConcepts.note: DPP — the process improvement activity that eliminates root causes of Specification Defects

relatedConcepts.name: Defect (Specification)
relatedConcepts.note: index-form alias entry at the same concept number; same concept, different naming order

relatedConcepts.name: Major Defect
relatedConcepts.note: a Specification Defect significant enough to prevent release or cause serious rework

relatedConcepts.name: Minor Defect
relatedConcepts.note: a Specification Defect of low severity; correctable without blocking delivery

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Issue
relatedConcepts.note: a candidate defect raised for review; becomes a Specification Defect once confirmed

relatedConcepts.name: Report-SQC
relatedConcepts.note: SQC reports record Specification Defects found per page/unit — the primary metric for defect density

concepts.definition: A **Specification Defect** is any error, omission, ambiguity, inconsistency, or rule violation found in a specification document. It is a defect in the *specification itself* — not in the code, system, or product — and is the primary target of the [[Defect-Detection-Process.041|Defect Detection Process]] (DDP).
concepts.overview: **Specification Defect** (*043) is any flaw in a specification document — an error, omission, ambiguity, inconsistency, or violated specification rule. Specification Defects are the primary target of the [[Defect-Detection-Process.041|Defect Detection Process]] (DDP, *041), which finds and removes them through formal inspection before they propagate downstream into design, code, or test artefacts. Early removal is orders of magnitude cheaper than late removal: a defect found in a requirements document costs far less to fix than the same defect discovered as a system failure in production. The [[Defect-Prevention-Process.042|Defect Prevention Process]] (DPP, *042) acts on the root causes of Specification Defects to prevent their recurrence.

concepts.name: Define

relatedConcepts.name: Definition
relatedConcepts.note: the parameter that formalises the act of defining — 'Defined As' is the Planguage keyword

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: a Tag is the named target of a definition; defining always produces a tagged term

relatedConcepts.name: Defined Term
relatedConcepts.note: what results from the act of defining — a Term that has been defined

concepts.definition: To **define** is to officially explain a specified concept in writing.
concepts.overview: **Define** (*240) is the fundamental Planguage act of giving a concept an official written explanation, anchored to a unique Tag. In Planguage, every defined concept receives a capitalised Tag and, in the glossary, an asterisk-number identifier. The capitalisation of the Tag at point of use signals to any reader that a formal definition exists elsewhere — in a Glossary or project specification — and should be consulted rather than assumed. Defining is not explaining; it is creating a reusable, unambiguous anchor for a term within a specified scope.

concepts.name: Definition

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: a Definition anchors to a Tag — the Tag is the reusable named reference

relatedConcepts.name: Term
relatedConcepts.note: a Definition creates a Defined Term (Term *151) — a reusable, precisely scoped concept

relatedConcepts.name: Define (verb)
relatedConcepts.note: the verb of which Definition is the noun — defining produces a Definition

relatedConcepts.name: Default
relatedConcepts.note: Defaults are often embedded within a Definition on a Scale, providing the fallback qualifier

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: Definitions frequently scoped to a Scale — see Reliability example in source

concepts.definition: **Definition** (or **Defined As**) is a parameter that is used to define a tagged term. The tagged term can then be re-used anywhere else within scope, and will always carry this precise definition. The keyed icons are `:` (primary) or `=` (less common).
concepts.overview: **Definition** (*044) is the Planguage parameter that formalises the act of defining — it gives a [[Tag.146|Tag]] an official, reusable written meaning within a specified scope. Once defined, the tag can appear anywhere in the specification and inherits the definition exactly — not approximately. The three synonymous forms (`Defined As:`, `Definition:`, `Def:`) and the icon shortcuts (`:` and `=`) are interchangeable; the choice is stylistic. The `Definition` parameter is what separates a Planguage specification from ordinary prose: it turns named terms into precision instruments.

concepts.name: Degree of Target Fulfillment

relatedConcepts.name: Target
relatedConcepts.note: the Target level is the 100% reference point — full fulfillment equals the Target

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: the Benchmark level is the 0% reference point — the baseline from which progress is measured

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation
relatedConcepts.note: primary use — Degree of Target Fulfillment quantifies partial-credit impact in Impact Estimation

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Goals are the targets whose fulfillment degree is measured

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: fulfillment is measured on the Scale on which the Target is specified

concepts.definition: This is the degree, expressed as % of a [qualified] **Target** level (100%), which it has been met, in relation to a defined **Benchmark** level (0%).
concepts.overview: **Degree of Target Fulfillment** (*191) is a percentage measure of how far a delivered level has progressed between a defined Benchmark (0%) and a Target (100%). It allows partial credit: 50% means half the distance to the Target has been achieved; −50% means the delivered level has moved in the opposite direction by the same magnitude. This concept is essential in [[Impact-Estimation.283|Impact Estimation]], where design alternatives rarely deliver 100% of any target and their partial contributions must be compared. The fulfillment can be real (measured), estimated (forecast), or hypothetical (scenario analysis).

concepts.name: Delivered Level

relatedConcepts.name: Past
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Delivered Level is a specialised Past benchmark, specific to Evo delivery steps

relatedConcepts.name: Goal Step
relatedConcepts.note: the planned future counterpart — Goal Step is where you are going; Delivered Level is where you arrived

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: the delivery unit — each Evo Step produces a Delivered Level on each tracked Scale

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: the target the Delivered Level is measured against — progress toward Goal is tracked via Delivered Levels

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: Delivered Levels are numeric values on a Scale — the Scale defines what is measured

concepts.definition:
For a scalar attribute, the **Delivered Level** is the numeric value on a scale of measure 'delivered' by an Evo step (that is, the resulting level after system enhancement). A Delivered Level is a **Past** benchmark. It is a result of project measurement of progress towards a required Goal/Budget level.
*Rationale:* The reason for this term, instead of a simple 'Past', is to emphasise the series of Evo deliveries on a particular project, and distinguish them from other Past levels benchmarked in the project.
concepts.overview: **Delivered Level** (*533, keyed `•`) is a specialised [[Past.106|Past]] benchmark that records the measured scalar value produced by a completed [[Evo-Step.141|Evo Step]]. It answers the question: "After this delivery, what level did the system actually achieve on this attribute?" A series of Delivered Levels across Evo Steps provides a quantified progress trace toward the [[Goal.109|Goal]], making project advancement visible and measurable at each step. Delivered Level is a Past — but a Past associated with a specific delivery, not arbitrary historical measurement.

concepts.name: Delivered Value

relatedConcepts.name: Value
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — Delivered Value is the realised form of Value; what was actually delivered to stakeholders

relatedConcepts.name: Delivery
relatedConcepts.note: the mechanism — Delivered Value is the value consequence of a Delivery event

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: the recipient — Delivered Value is received by a specific stakeholder group

relatedConcepts.name: Delivered Level
relatedConcepts.note: the scalar form — Delivered Level measures system attribute improvement; Delivered Value measures stakeholder value consequence

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: the delivery unit — each Evo Step potentially delivers value to stakeholder groups

concepts.definition: **Delivered value** is the value delivered by a set of delivery steps to a stakeholder group, as a *consequence* of changing the system attributes.
concepts.overview: **Delivered Value** (*371) is the value realised by a [[Stakeholder.233|stakeholder group]] as a result of system attribute changes made through [[Delivery-Cycle.049|Delivery]] steps. It is the measurement that closes the loop between engineering decisions (what system attributes were improved) and stakeholder outcomes (what benefit was actually received). Delivered Value is a Scalar Benchmark — it can be measured, tracked, and compared across Evo Steps. Critically, it is a *consequence* of system changes, not the system changes themselves: improving system attributes is the mechanism; Delivered Value is the result experienced by stakeholders. This distinction is central to Tom's value-first design philosophy.

concepts.name: Delivery Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Result-Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: parent — the Delivery Cycle is a subset of a Result Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Deployment
relatedConcepts.note: final stage — Deployment is the last stage of the Delivery Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Evo-Step
relatedConcepts.note: subject — a Delivery Cycle implements and hands over one Evo Step

concepts.definition: A delivery cycle contains the initial operational implementation of an Evo Step, and its handover to stakeholders. A delivery cycle is a subset of a Result Cycle. A delivery cycle involves implementation activities such as training, installation and field-testing.
concepts.overview: **Delivery Cycle** (*049) is the structured process by which a single Evo Step transitions from development to live use in the hands of real stakeholders. It is a subset of the broader [[Result-Cycle.122]], adding the operational handover layer — training, installation, field-testing, and ultimately [[Deployment.358]] — that a pure build iteration would omit. The cycle is deliberately kept small: Tom's guidance is that each delivery cycle should consume between 2% and 5% of the project's total cost and time budgets. This constraint enforces incrementalism and limits the blast radius of any individual delivery failure.

concepts.name: Demand Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Design-Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Design Constraint restricts design choices; Demand Constraint mandates a behaviour or action

relatedConcepts.name: Veto-Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Veto Constraint is 'You must NOT do X'; Demand Constraint is 'You must DO X

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Demand Constraint is a constraint classified by its source/nature

concepts.definition: A demand is a constraint of type 'You must do X'. It is a non-scalar, affirmative constraint — it mandates a specific behaviour, action, or condition, rather than setting a numeric limit.
concepts.overview: **Demand Constraint** (*461) is a mandatory affirmative directive: it says *do this*, as opposed to *do not exceed this level* (a scalar constraint) or *do not do this* (a Veto Constraint). It is the "must" in requirements language — law, regulation, policy, or stakeholder insistence that forces a specific action or condition. Demand Constraints are non-scalar: they are not expressed on a numeric scale; they are either satisfied or they are not. The parameter `Do` (or plain `Constraint:`) is used in Planguage to flag them explicitly, though they also arise implicitly in natural language requirements phrased as "shall," "must," or "is required to."

concepts.name: Dependency

relatedConcepts.name: Depends-On
relatedConcepts.note: parameter form — Depends On is the explicit Planguage parameter for expressing a dependency

relatedConcepts.name: Before
relatedConcepts.note: related — Before implies a temporal dependency between specifications

relatedConcepts.name: After
relatedConcepts.note: related — After implies a temporal dependency between specifications

relatedConcepts.name: Impacts
relatedConcepts.note: related — Impacts describes causal influence; often co-occurs with Dependency

relatedConcepts.name: Impacted-By
relatedConcepts.note: inverse of Impacts — Impacted By is the receiving end of a dependency chain

concepts.definition: A 'dependency' is a reliance of some kind, of one set of components on another set of components. Any given component can be part of numerous dependencies (either having one or more dependencies, and/or having one or more dependencies placed on it). The parameter 'Dependency,' or its synonym 'Depends On,' is used to *explicitly* specify a dependency.
concepts.overview: **Dependency** (*189) is the Planguage concept for capturing reliance relationships between specification components — requirements, functions, design ideas, conditions, or values. A dependency says: "component A only holds, applies, or succeeds if component B is also true or in force." Dependencies can be implicit (expressed through Qualifiers) or explicit (expressed through the `Dependency` or `Depends On` parameter). Tom's rationale is explicit: making dependencies visible promotes planning realism, enables risk identification, and allows teams to model the conditions under which requirements actually apply. Unmarked dependencies are a common source of requirements failures when conditions change.

concepts.name: Deployment

relatedConcepts.name: Delivery-Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Deployment is the final stage of the Delivery Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Evo-Step
relatedConcepts.note: subject — each Deployment delivers one Evo Step to stakeholders

concepts.definition: 'Deployment' means *actually delivering* an Evo step to a set of stakeholders. Deployment is the last stage of a Delivery Cycle.
concepts.overview: **Deployment** (*358) is the final, irreversible act of a [[Delivery-Cycle.049]] — the moment at which an Evo Step transitions from field trials and preparation into full operational use by its intended stakeholders. Everything that precedes deployment (planning, training, installation, field trials, evaluation) is preparation; deployment is the commitment. It is the point at which users, customers, or operators begin using the upgraded system at full scale, and the point at which operational data collection can genuinely begin. Deployment is distinct from installation or field testing: it means *going live* with the real system for the real audience.

concepts.name: Derivative Source

relatedConcepts.name: Derived-adjective
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — Derived (adj) is the meta-qualifier that Derivative Source supports

relatedConcepts.name: Derivative
relatedConcepts.note: output — Derivative Source is the input; Derivative is the output of the same derivation process

relatedConcepts.name: Derived-Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: application — the Derivative Source for a Derived Constraint is its Generic or Global Constraint

concepts.definition: The source of the Derived (*449) specification or plan. The 'source' implies the resource and the rule for conversion into the derivative.
concepts.overview: **Derivative Source** (*450) identifies *where* a derived specification element comes from and *how* it is produced — it names both the originating information and the conversion rule that transforms that information into the [[Derivative.452]]. Without a traceable Derivative Source, a derived requirement is an assertion without a basis; with it, the derivation is auditable and the derived element is automatically invalidated if the source changes. The synonym "Derivation" should be avoided because it is ambiguous: it can refer to the source (*450), the output (*452), or the act of deriving — Tom Gilb's own warning.

concepts.name: Derivative

relatedConcepts.name: Derivative-Source
relatedConcepts.note: input side — Derivative Source is where the Derivative originates

relatedConcepts.name: Derived-adjective
relatedConcepts.note: meta-qualifier — 'Derived' (adj) is the label applied to the Derivative

relatedConcepts.name: Derived-Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: application — Derived Constraint is a Derivative in the constraint domain

concepts.definition: The thing derived from its Derivative Source (*450). The source is the initial information or resource, and some rules or process for derivation.
concepts.overview: **Derivative** (*452) is the output side of a derivation process: the specification element, requirement, constraint, or value that results from applying a conversion rule to a [[Derivative-Source.450]]. The Derivative is the *result*; the Derivative Source is the *origin + rule*. Together they form a traceable derivation chain: `Source × Rule → Derivative`. The Derivative inherits a validity dependency from its source — if the source changes, the Derivative must be re-evaluated. In Planguage specifications, Derivatives appear as derived requirements, derived constraints (*451), or derived impacts (requirements generated by design choices).

concepts.name: Derived Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Derived-adjective
relatedConcepts.note: parent qualifier — 'Derived' (adj) is the property that classifies this constraint as derived

relatedConcepts.name: Derivative-Source
relatedConcepts.note: input — the Generic or Global Constraint that the Derived Constraint is produced from

relatedConcepts.name: Derivative
relatedConcepts.note: output type — the Derived Constraint is a Derivative in the constraint domain

relatedConcepts.name: Demand-Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Demand Constraint is a constraint by source/nature; Derived Constraint is classified by origin

concepts.definition: A specific local constraint derived from a Generic 'template' Constraint or Global 'wide scope' Constraint.
concepts.overview: **Derived Constraint** (*451) is a constraint that does not arise from independent stakeholder demand but is produced by applying a broader, more general constraint to a specific local scope. The [[Derivative-Source.450]] is the Generic Constraint (a template) or Global Constraint (wide-scope rule); the Derived Constraint is the [[Derivative.452]] that results from applying that source to a particular product, system, region, or condition. This classification matters for change management: if the Generic or Global Constraint changes, the Derived Constraint changes with it — automatically, if the derivation chain is recorded. A Derived Constraint that loses touch with its source becomes a hard-coded local rule with no traceable authority.

concepts.name: Derived

relatedConcepts.name: Derivative-Source
relatedConcepts.note: companion — Derivative Source is where a Derived specification comes from

relatedConcepts.name: Derivative
relatedConcepts.note: companion — Derivative is the thing produced by derivation

relatedConcepts.name: Derived-Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: application — Derived Constraint is a constraint produced by derivation from a Generic or Global Constraint

concepts.definition: Something resulting from processing other information according to defined rules. A derived requirement is a specific requirement obtained by applying a generic requirement to a local range.
concepts.overview: **Derived** (*449, adjective) is the meta-qualifier applied to any specification element that results from applying a rule or transformation to another (more generic or higher-level) source. It is not a parameter itself but a *type label*: a derived requirement, a derived constraint, a derived impact. The derivation chain always involves a [[Derivative-Source.450]] (the source information and conversion rule) and produces a [[Derivative.452]] (the result). Understanding whether a requirement is primary or derived matters for traceability — change the source, and derived requirements may become invalid. It also matters for design analysis: design choices can themselves generate derived requirements (derived impacts) that must be tracked and specified.

concepts.name: Descendant

relatedConcepts.name: Parent
relatedConcepts.note: inverse — a Descendant always has at least one Parent in the hierarchy

relatedConcepts.name: Kid
relatedConcepts.note: subset — a Kid is an immediate Descendant; Descendant is the generalisation

concepts.definition:
An artifact descended from another artifact; immediately, or via several levels of process.
A Kid is always a descendant of a Parent. A design could be the descendant of a set of requirements.
concepts.overview: **Descendant** (*268) names the directional, downward relationship in any Planguage hierarchy — whether that hierarchy is a system decomposition, a requirements tree, or a process lineage. A Kid (*266) is an immediate Descendant; a grandchild or further-removed artifact is a Descendant via multiple levels. The concept captures both immediate and transitive ancestry, making it applicable wherever traceability across levels is required. The upward counterpart — a path to the originating artifact — is traversed by following Parent (*267) links upward through the hierarchy.

concepts.name: Description

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: container — Description is one parameter within a full Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: context — Description partially defines a requirement component alongside other parameters

relatedConcepts.name: Design Idea
relatedConcepts.note: context — Description partially defines a design idea; full definition requires additional parameters

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Description is a Planguage parameter type

relatedConcepts.name: Design Content Rules
relatedConcepts.note: governance — Content Rules constrain what a Description should contain

concepts.definition:
A description is a set of words and/or diagrams that describe, and *partially* define, a component.
The parameter 'Description' (or synonyms Detail, Detailed Description) is used to specify description.
concepts.overview: **Description** (*416) is a Planguage specification parameter that provides a natural-language or diagrammatic partial account of a component — what it is, what it does, what it means. The key word is *partially*: a Description alone is never the full definition of a component. Full definition requires all relevant parameters (Scale, Meter, Goal, Constraint, and inherited or implied definitions from related components) acting together. Models, real systems, and prototypes may also serve as a form of Description. The parameter name may be substituted with the synonyms Detail or Detailed Description.

concepts.name: Design Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Design Constraint is a specific type of Constraint that acts directly on design choices

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: home — Design Constraint belongs in requirement specifications, not design specifications

relatedConcepts.name: Design Idea
relatedConcepts.note: target — Design Constraint directly restricts which Design Ideas are mandatory or prohibited

relatedConcepts.name: Condition Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Condition Constraint restricts conditions, not design choices directly

relatedConcepts.name: Design Specification
relatedConcepts.note: separation — optional design ideas belong in Design Specifications, not in requirement specs

concepts.definition:
A design constraint is an explicit and direct restriction regarding the choice of design ideas. It either declares a design idea to be compulsory (**Mandatory Design**) or to be excluded (**Prohibited Design**).
Design constraints are dictated from an earlier system development stage (a higher level or a more specialised level). They are binary requirements — a specific design is either required or forbidden.
concepts.overview: **Design Constraint** (*181) is the only type of requirement that makes design decisions directly. While all requirements limit design choices to some degree (a performance requirement eliminates designs that cannot meet it, a resource constraint eliminates expensive ones), a Design Constraint bypasses this indirect effect and names a design idea as either mandatory or prohibited — full stop. This binary nature is what distinguishes it from every other requirement type. Design Constraints belong in requirement specifications, not in design specifications; that separation is what tells each level of design responsibility what it is and is not free to choose.

concepts.name: Design Content Rules

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rule
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Specification Rules govern how designs are written up; Content Rules govern what they contain

relatedConcepts.name: Design Specification
relatedConcepts.note: target — Design Content Rules apply to the substance of Design Specifications

relatedConcepts.name: Review Criteria
relatedConcepts.note: instrument — violation of Design Content Rules provides the basis for design review findings

relatedConcepts.name: Design Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: related — Design Constraints are one category of content that Design Content Rules may govern

relatedConcepts.name: Design Idea
relatedConcepts.note: subject — the design ideas that Design Content Rules apply to

concepts.definition:
Design rules state expected design practices.
Design (content) rules give advice on best practices and recommended practices when designing (or architecting, or design engineering, or finding means or strategies). Deviation from Design Content Rules should be the basis for a design review. Unjustified violation of Design Content Rules is classified as a design *defect*.
concepts.overview: **Design Content Rules** (*593) govern the *substance* of design — what makes a good design choice, how design ideas should be structured, and what best practices apply when architecting or engineering solutions. They are distinct from Specification Rules (*129), which govern how clearly a design is *written up*; Content Rules govern whether the design itself is sound. Violations become design defects, and defect density against these rules is the primary quantitative measure of design quality, as well as the criterion for entering and exiting design processes.

concepts.name: Design Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Design Process
relatedConcepts.note: generalisation — Design Engineering is the rigorous, quantified form of the Design Process

relatedConcepts.name: Design Idea
relatedConcepts.note: output — Design Engineering produces a selected set of Design Ideas estimated against requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Design Specification
relatedConcepts.note: output — the main output of Design Engineering is a set of Design Specifications

relatedConcepts.name: Design Problem
relatedConcepts.note: input — Design Engineering works to close the requirement gap (Design Problem)

relatedConcepts.name: Design Target
relatedConcepts.note: evaluation reference — Design Targets define the levels Design Ideas must satisfy

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Architecture Engineering applies the same rigour at structural/system level

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: parent discipline — Systems Engineering encompasses Design Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — Engineering is the broad discipline; Design Engineering is its application to design

relatedConcepts.name: Creativity
relatedConcepts.note: process context — Design Engineering is the discipline in which purposeful creativity operates

concepts.definition:
Design Engineering is an iterative process of determining a set of designs, with rigorous attention to quantified and measurable control of their impact on requirements.
The design engineering process implies the matching of potential and specified design ideas with quantified performance requirements, quantified resource requirements, and defined design and condition constraints.
concepts.overview: **Design Engineering** (*501) is what separates disciplined engineering from intuitive design. Where the Design Process (*046) describes *what* to do — search, specify, evaluate, select — Design Engineering prescribes *how* to do it: with quantified performance requirements, credibility-weighted impact estimates, evolutionary delivery, and post-delivery measurement. It contrasts explicitly with conventional design practice, which relies on intuition, tradition, and trial-and-error, naming objectives without quantifying them and naming designs without estimating their effects. Design Engineering insists that every design choice is justified by measurable, estimated impact on defined requirements.

concepts.name: Design Problem
concepts.keyedIcon: -----<====>----> (the gap between < a past and > a target is an iconic symbol of a design problem)

relatedConcepts.name: Control Point
relatedConcepts.note: measurement context — Control Points measure progress against the requirement targets that define the Design Problem

relatedConcepts.name: Problem
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — Design Problem is the engineering-specific form of a Problem

relatedConcepts.name: Design Idea
relatedConcepts.note: solution — Design Ideas are selected to close the gaps that constitute the Design Problem

relatedConcepts.name: Design Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: process — Design Engineering is the iterative process of solving the Design Problem

relatedConcepts.name: Design Target
relatedConcepts.note: component — Design Targets are the specific requirement levels that define the gap in a Design Problem

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: source — the Design Problem is expressed as a complete set of requirement specifications

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar Target
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Design Problem is a type of Scalar Target

concepts.definition: A design problem is expressed as a requirement specification that includes a 'complete set' of valid targets and constraints, together with updated information about the degree of satisfaction in the design or the implementation. A design problem is the 'set of gaps' (to meet required levels) that remain to be designed for.
concepts.overview: **Design Problem** (*654) is the engineering-precise definition of what remains to be solved: not a narrative of difficulties, but a *quantified set of requirement gaps* — the difference between where each requirement currently stands and where it must reach. Under Evolutionary Project Management, the Design Problem is dynamic: each implemented Design Idea closes some gaps and the remaining gaps become the new Design Problem. A Design Problem is never solved by a single Design Idea; it requires a *set* of Design Ideas whose cumulative impacts close all gaps within all constraints.

concepts.name: Design Process

relatedConcepts.name: Design Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — Design Engineering is the rigorous, quantified form of the Design Process

relatedConcepts.name: Design Idea
relatedConcepts.note: output — Design Ideas are the primary output of the Design Process

relatedConcepts.name: Design Problem
relatedConcepts.note: problem — the Design Process works toward solving the Design Problem (the requirement gap set)

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: input — stakeholder requirements are the input that the Design Process works to satisfy

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: parent discipline — Systems Engineering encompasses the Design Process at system level

relatedConcepts.name: Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: parent discipline — Engineering is the broader discipline of which Design Engineering is a sub-process

relatedConcepts.name: Creativity
relatedConcepts.note: possible synonym — Creativity overlaps significantly with the Design Process

concepts.definition:
The design process is the act of searching for, specifying, evaluating and selecting design ideas, in an attempt to satisfy specified stakeholder requirements.
Design is finding a set of solutions (design ideas) for a set of defined requirements.
concepts.overview: **Design Process** (*046) is the general-purpose description of how requirements are converted into design solutions. It covers the full sequence: acquire requirements, identify candidate designs, evaluate them, select a set, review, implement, and revise. It is deliberately process-agnostic about *how* those steps are executed — by tradition, intuition, heuristics, or engineering logic. Its more rigorous sibling, Design Engineering (*501), specifies *how*: with quantified impact estimation, credibility-weighted selection, and evolutionary delivery. The Design Process is the *what*; Design Engineering is the *how*.

concepts.name: Design Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Design Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: process — Design Engineering produces a set of Design Specifications as its main output

relatedConcepts.name: Design Idea
relatedConcepts.note: content — a Design Specification is the written definition of a specific Design Idea

relatedConcepts.name: Design Process
relatedConcepts.note: process — the Design Process generates Design Specifications as its output

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Systems Architecture Specifications are Design Specifications at structural level

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: related — Architecture is the structural class of Design Idea that Architecture Specifications document

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture Specification
relatedConcepts.note: sibling type — Architecture Specification is the Design Specification at architecture level

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Design Specification is a type of Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Design Content Rules
relatedConcepts.note: governance — Design Content Rules govern what a Design Specification should contain

relatedConcepts.name: Design Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: distinction — Design Constraints live in requirement specs; optional designs live in Design Specifications

concepts.definition:
A design specification is the written specification of a design idea.
A set of design specifications is the main output of a design engineering process.
A specific set of design specifications, when implemented, will, to some degree, meet the stated requirements.
