concepts.overview: **Design Specification** (*586) is the document that makes a Design Idea (*047) engineering-grade: it records not just what the design is, but what the design is *expected to do* — its estimated impact on requirements, its cost attributes, its constraint compatibility. A single design idea with no specification is an unverifiable intent; a Design Specification is the verifiable commitment. The set of Design Specifications produced by a Design Engineering process (*501) constitutes the solution to the Design Problem (*654) — each specification contributing an estimated portion of the requirement gap-closure.

concepts.name: Design Target

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: companion — Benchmark records the starting level; Design Target records the level to reach

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Target
relatedConcepts.note: parent — a Design Target for a performance attribute is a Performance Target

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: component — the qualifier (scope, condition, time-box) is an integral part of the Design Target

relatedConcepts.name: Budget Target
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Budget Target is the resource-dimension form of a Design Target

relatedConcepts.name: Condition Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: complement — Condition Constraints define operating conditions that scope Design Target applicability

relatedConcepts.name: Design Problem
relatedConcepts.note: context — Design Targets define the gap boundaries within a Design Problem

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar Target
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Design Target is a Scalar Target applied in a design context

concepts.definition: A Design Target is the specific target *level*, including *qualifier*, of an attribute requirement that is being worked towards, in the design or implementation process.
concepts.overview: **Design Target** (*338) is the level and qualifier combination that defines what the designer must achieve: not merely a number, but a number *in a context* — qualified by scope, condition, and time-box. Design Targets are the bridge between abstract requirements and concrete engineering decisions: they tell the designer exactly what "good enough" means for this attribute, in this context, at this stage. They may incorporate a safety factor (e.g., designing for 2× the nominal requirement) to provide headroom for estimation uncertainty. A Design Target is specified using one of the Planguage target parameters — Goal, Stretch, or Wish — combined with a qualifier.

concepts.name: Design To Cost

relatedConcepts.name: Design Process
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Design To Cost is a strategy within the Design Process

concepts.definition: 'Design To Cost' is an engineering strategy of consciously selecting design ideas, which will allow you to stay within any and all resource budgets.
concepts.overview: **Design To Cost** (*472) is the engineering discipline of choosing design ideas specifically to remain within all resource budgets — time, money, materials, energy, and any other constrained resource. Rather than designing freely and then cutting costs afterwards, Design To Cost builds the budget constraint into the selection criteria from the start. It is a strategy within the broader Design Process (*046), directing the designer's choices rather than describing the process steps. The key insight is that cost compliance must be a first-class selection criterion during design, not a post-hoc constraint applied after choices have been made.

concepts.name: Designer

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architect
relatedConcepts.note: sibling/specialisation — Systems Architect is a more specific engineering role than Designer

concepts.definition: A designer is a person or group who specifies design ideas, in an effort to satisfy specified requirements.
concepts.overview: **Designer** (*190) is the generic Planguage role for any person or group responsible for producing design ideas aimed at satisfying specified requirements. The role is intentionally broad: a designer may be a solo engineer, a cross-functional team, or an outsourced vendor. More specific role names — systems engineer, planner, systems architect — are specialisations of this generic term. The key characteristic of a Designer in Planguage is that they work from requirements; they do not set requirements, they satisfy them.

concepts.name: Development Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: parent framework — Development Cycle is one of the optional sub-cycles within Evo

concepts.definition: A development cycle is an optional backroom cycle, within the result cycle of Evo. It is concerned with acquiring/purchasing and developing, any products required for the production and/or delivery cycles.
concepts.overview: **Development Cycle** (*413) is one of the optional specialised sub-cycles inside the Evo result cycle. Where the production cycle builds what will be deployed and the delivery cycle deploys it to stakeholders, the development cycle is the "backroom" cycle responsible for acquiring or creating any products — software components, tools, platforms, purchased subsystems — that the production or delivery cycles need. It is optional because not every Evo increment requires new development work; if the required products already exist, the development cycle can be skipped. For example, any new systems development project would be carried out within this cycle.

concepts.name: Deviation
concepts.definition: Deviation is the amount (estimated or actual) by which some attribute differs from some specific benchmark or target. Deviation is usually expressed numerically using either absolute or percentage difference.
concepts.overview: **Deviation** (*475) is a Planguage quantification parameter that expresses how far an attribute value lies from a specified benchmark or target. Its keyed icon is ±, reflecting that deviation can be positive (above benchmark) or negative (below benchmark). Deviation may be estimated in advance — expressing expected variance before measurement — or actual, expressing measured difference after observation. It is expressed numerically, either as an absolute difference (e.g. ±15 ms) or as a percentage (e.g. ±5%). Deviation enables specifications to acknowledge and quantify uncertainty or tolerable variation without abandoning precise definition.

concepts.name: Diagram
concepts.definition: A set of icons, symbols and terms, which pictorially explains how something works, or tries to clarify the relationship between parts of the whole.
concepts.overview: **Diagram** (*228) is any visual artefact that uses icons, symbols, and/or terms to explain how something works or to show the relationships between parts of a system. In Planguage, a Diagram is a type of Software and Technology Material — a technical artefact, not a requirement or a design decision. Diagrams support communication and comprehension; they clarify structure, behaviour, or relationships that would be harder to express in prose. The definition is intentionally broad: any pictorial representation that explains or clarifies qualifies.

concepts.name: Dialect
concepts.definition: A 'Dialect' is a local variation in Planguage symbols or terminology due to local culture, habit, traditions or language variation.
concepts.overview: **Dialect** (*204) is the Planguage concept for any locally sanctioned variation in the symbols or terminology of Planguage, arising from the culture, habits, traditions, or language of a local group. A dialect is not a violation of Planguage — it is a recognised adaptation of it. The "local group" can be a project, a division, a company, a charity, or a national language community — any group that finds it necessary or useful to vary or specialise from the canonical Planguage definitions. Dialect enables Planguage to be adopted across diverse organisations without requiring universal symbol uniformity.

concepts.name: Direct Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Indirect Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Indirect Constraint is any constraint not in direct constraint format; the two together exhaust constraint types by source

concepts.definition: Any constraint which is specified in the *format of a constraint*, and is intended to directly constrain performance, function, costs or design.
concepts.overview: **Direct Constraint** (*510) is the class of constraints that are explicitly stated *as constraints* — using the constraint format — and are intended to directly limit performance, function, cost, or design. The "direct" in the name distinguishes it from its sibling **Indirect Constraint** (*511), which encompasses all other specifications (Goals, Authority parameters, qualifiers) that have the effect of constraining the solution space without being stated in constraint format. The Direct/Indirect distinction classifies constraints by their *source format*, not by their domain or severity.

concepts.name: Do [PDSA]

relatedConcepts.name: PDSA Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Do is one phase of the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Plan [PDSA]
relatedConcepts.note: preceding phase — Plan produces the plan that Do executes

relatedConcepts.name: Study [PDSA]
relatedConcepts.note: following phase — Study analyses the results of Do

relatedConcepts.name: Act [PDSA]
relatedConcepts.note: final phase — Act responds to Study findings before cycling back to Plan

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: application context — in Evo, Do corresponds to step implementation

relatedConcepts.name: Statistical Process Control (SPC)
relatedConcepts.note: related domain — PDSA originates in SPC (Shewhart/Deming cycle)

concepts.definition: Do [PDSA] is part of the 'Plan Do Study Act' Cycle (See Plan Do Study Act Cycle *168). It involves implementing (Do…ing) what you have planned, that is, carrying out the 'experiment' to see how your plan measures up to reality.
concepts.overview: **Do [PDSA]** (*170) is the second phase of the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle (*168), the improvement loop derived from Shewhart's process-cycle model and popularised by Deming. In the Do phase, the team executes what was planned in the Plan phase — running the experiment to find out how the plan performs against reality. In Evo, Do corresponds to step implementation: carrying out the increment that was planned. The Do phase is not the end; its purpose is to generate the data and experience that the Study phase (*171) will analyse. Without Do, the PDSA cycle has no empirical content.

concepts.name: Document

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: related — a Specification is a specific kind of document; not all documents are specifications

concepts.definition: A document is a readable instrument for containing and conveying ideas of any kind.
concepts.overview: **Document** (*180) is any readable instrument — paper, digital, or machine-intelligible — that contains and conveys ideas of any kind. The definition is deliberately broad: a document is not limited to paper, not limited to human-readable text, and not limited to conventional "documentation." Computer source code, test scripts, and machine-intelligible artefacts are all documents under this definition. The keyed icon is `[]`, representing an upright page. Critically, a document is not necessarily documentation (a specification or instructional artefact), and not all documentation takes the form of documents — a real machine or prototype can serve as documentation of a system without being a document.

concepts.name: Documentation

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Documentation is a class of Specification; it specifies system use for people

relatedConcepts.name: Infoware
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Documentation is a class of Infoware (information intended for use)

relatedConcepts.name: Planware
relatedConcepts.note: sibling via Infoware — Planware covers human intentions (design, requirements); distinct from Documentation

relatedConcepts.name: Dataware
relatedConcepts.note: sibling via Infoware — Dataware is for computer consumption, not human instruction; contrasts with Documentation

relatedConcepts.name: Data
relatedConcepts.note: related — Data is any sensible signal; Documentation is a subclass of Data intended specifically for human instruction

concepts.definition: Documentation is written information that teaches people how to use systems.
concepts.overview: **Documentation** (*579) is written information specifically aimed at teaching people how to use systems. It includes analytical documentation (describing how a system works), instructional documentation / courseware (teaching users to operate it), and operational documentation (supporting day-to-day use). In Planguage's information classification, Documentation is a class of both Specification (*137) and Infoware (*578): it specifies a system for humans and is information intended for use. Its siblings in the information hierarchy — Planware (*577) and Dataware (*576) — serve different audiences and purposes: Planware records human intentions (requirements, designs), while Dataware is produced for computer consumption, not human instruction.

concepts.name: Domain

relatedConcepts.name: Scope
relatedConcepts.note: complement — Scope defines what is included in a system; Domain defines the field of influence or responsibility assigned to a subject

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: usage — Qualifiers can scope a Domain to a particular context or condition

relatedConcepts.name: Authority
relatedConcepts.note: overlap — Authority (*005) is one reason domains are declared; a domain identifies who has decision-making power over a subject

concepts.definition:
A domain is a major field of influence or responsibility for a defined subject.
**Standards comparison (Webster's):** "A field or sphere of activity or influence."
concepts.overview: **Domain** (*374) is a Planguage **System Boundary** concept that defines the field of influence or responsibility assigned to a subject — whether a person, team, system, or specification. Declaring domains serves three main purposes: assigning specification responsibility to appropriate stakeholders, identifying who has authority to approve or change something, and focusing attention on a coherent set of ideas. Domain is closely related to Scope (*419) but is broader — it names the territory of responsibility rather than just the boundary of inclusion. The concept also maps to Authority (*005): a domain tells you whose court something is in.

concepts.name: Downstream
concepts.keyedIcon: <~  (A <~ B means A is downstream of B)

relatedConcepts.name: Upstream
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — Upstream is the earlier process; Downstream is the later process that is impacted by what happens upstream

relatedConcepts.name: Process
relatedConcepts.note: host — Downstream is a partitioning concept applied to sequences of Processes

relatedConcepts.name: Parallelity
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Parallelity describes concurrent processes; Downstream describes sequential dependency

concepts.definition:
Relative to a given process, 'downstream' refers to any processes which are carried out later, and implies that they are impacted in some way by that upstream process.
**Usage:** 'Customer use' is downstream from 'pilot testing'.
**Parameter:** Downstream. Long form = Downstream From.
**Keyed icon:** `<~` — "A <~ B means A is downstream of B. Notice similarity with source arrow. Upstream is source or downstream pollution."
concepts.overview: **Downstream** (*052) is a Planguage **Partitioning** concept that locates a process *later* in a process sequence relative to a reference point, with the implication that the downstream process is impacted by what happens upstream. The concept carries a critical quality-economics insight: defects injected upstream become one to two orders of magnitude more expensive to fix by the time they surface downstream during testing or in the field. This makes Downstream not merely a directional label but a cost-amplification warning — the further downstream a defect travels, the more expensive it becomes. The keyed icon `<~` mirrors the flow direction, making process-sequence notation compact and unambiguous.

concepts.name: Drawn Icon

relatedConcepts.name: Keyed Icon
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Keyed Icon is constructed entirely from keyboard characters; Drawn Icon requires drawing tools. Both are sub-classes of Icon.

relatedConcepts.name: Icon
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Icon (*161) is the broader class; Drawn Icon is the non-keyboard variant

relatedConcepts.name: Symbol
relatedConcepts.note: sibling class — Symbol is the broader category of graphic representations; Icon (and Drawn Icon) is a specific sub-type

concepts.definition:
A drawn icon is a defined graphic symbol, or pictorial representation of a Planguage concept, constructed by drawing, rather than keying.
**Note:** Keyed Icons are a sub-class of icons constructed entirely by keying keyboard symbols. Drawn Icons require drawing tools rather than a keyboard.
concepts.overview: **Drawn Icon** (*085) is the graphical, non-keyboard form of a Planguage Icon (*161) — a pictorial representation of a concept that must be created with drawing tools rather than typed characters. The contrast with Keyed Icon (*144) is the defining distinction: Keyed Icons (e.g., `<~` for Downstream) can be typed inline anywhere text appears, making them portable and tool-agnostic; Drawn Icons require a diagram editor or drawing application and cannot be embedded in plain text. In Planguage documentation, two canonical drawn icon examples are a filled rectangle with an upward arrow (representing a process) and a circle with entering and exiting arrows (representing a system). Drawn Icons are most useful in visual reference materials, printed documentation, and modelling diagrams.

concepts.name: Due

relatedConcepts.name: During
relatedConcepts.note: sibling temporal parameter — During specifies concurrent scheduling; Due specifies a deadline

relatedConcepts.name: Before
relatedConcepts.note: sibling temporal parameter — Before specifies a temporal ordering constraint; Due specifies an absolute deadline

relatedConcepts.name: After
relatedConcepts.note: sibling temporal parameter — After specifies ordering relative to a prior event; Due specifies absolute timing

concepts.definition:
'Due' is a specification parameter indicating when some aspect of a specification is due.
**Historical note:** "The idea of 'Due' as a parameter was from an unpublished note by Jens Weber, Daimler Chrysler, Frankfurt."
concepts.overview: **Due** (*554) is a Planguage **Temporal Sequence Parameter** that attaches a deadline to any aspect of a specification — a deliverable, a constraint, a goal, or a test. Where Before (*312) expresses a relative ordering ("this must happen before that"), Due expresses an absolute endpoint: "this must be completed by this date or event." The parameter can carry a source citation (e.g., a contract section or supplier agreement), making the obligation traceable to its origin. This traceability is what distinguishes a Planguage Due parameter from a project plan date: it is a specification commitment with an auditable source, not a schedule estimate.

concepts.name: During
concepts.keyedIcon: ||  as in A||B  (A is done in parallel with B)

relatedConcepts.name: Before
relatedConcepts.note: sibling temporal parameter — Before specifies sequential ordering (A before B); During specifies concurrency (A and B simultaneously)

relatedConcepts.name: After
relatedConcepts.note: sibling temporal parameter — After specifies ordering after a prior event; During specifies concurrency

relatedConcepts.name: Due
relatedConcepts.note: sibling temporal parameter — Due specifies an absolute deadline; During specifies concurrent scheduling

relatedConcepts.name: Parallelity
relatedConcepts.note: related concept — Parallelity (*104) is the broader property of running things in parallel; During is the parameter that specifies parallelism for a specific event

relatedConcepts.name: Parallel Development
relatedConcepts.note: application — Parallel Development (*363) is a strategy that makes use of the During parameter to schedule concurrent Evo steps

concepts.definition:
'During' is a specification parameter used when specifying events (including Evo steps and tasks) to indicate a time dependency for events that must be carried out concurrently (that is, done in parallel).
**Keyed icon:** `||` as in `A||B` — "A is done in parallel with B."
concepts.overview: **During** (*314) is a Planguage **Temporal Sequence Parameter** that specifies concurrency: it marks two or more events, tasks, or Evo steps as occurring simultaneously rather than sequentially. The keyed icon `||` (double pipe) is borrowed from the parallel-composition notation used in process algebras — visually suggesting two streams running side by side. During can be expressed either as the keyword or as the `||` icon; the choice is purely stylistic. The concept also supports conditional concurrency: a step can be specified to run only if a parallel event did *not* actually occur during a specified concurrent window, making During a tool for both planning and contingency specification.

concepts.name: Dynamic

relatedConcepts.name: State
relatedConcepts.note: parent — State (*174) is the parent class; Dynamic is one of the states a system or process can be in

relatedConcepts.name: Statistical Process Control
relatedConcepts.note: application context — SPC (*466) monitors dynamic process behaviour over real time

concepts.definition:
Dynamic means something happening in real time.
**Antonyms:** Passive · Static
concepts.overview: **Dynamic** (*465) is a Planguage **State** concept that characterises something as happening in real time — as opposed to being static (fixed, unchanging) or passive (not self-initiated). In specification terms, a dynamic system or process is one whose behaviour unfolds over time and must be observed or controlled during operation, not just at a fixed point. The concept appears in Planguage primarily to distinguish between system states that require real-time measurement and control (dynamic) from those that can be assessed from a snapshot (static). Its antonyms — Passive and Static — are the defining contrast: a static specification is a point-in-time snapshot; a dynamic specification covers evolving behaviour.

concepts.name: Edit Audit [SQC]

relatedConcepts.name: Edit [SQC]
relatedConcepts.note: parent process — Edit Audit is the supervisory review that verifies the Edit sub-process was completed properly

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: parent system — Edit Audit is a sub-process within the SQC quality control cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Editor Advice Log
relatedConcepts.note: input — Edit Audit checks that the Editor Advice Log was properly heeded during editing

relatedConcepts.name: Team Leader
relatedConcepts.note: actor — the Team Leader carries out the Edit Audit

concepts.definition:
Edit Audit is an SQC sub-process, carried out by a team leader, to verify that reasonable and complete editing has been done.
**Note:** Edit Audit will try to make sure that valid main specification rules, the editor advice log, relevant editing and specification procedures, and main specification sources have been reasonably heeded when editing the specification.
concepts.overview: **Edit Audit** (*289) is the supervisory closure step of the Planguage SQC (Specification Quality Control) process: after the Editor (*277) has applied corrections from the Editor Advice Log (*296), the Team Leader (*281) performs an Edit Audit to verify that the editing was reasonable and complete. It is the quality-control check on the quality-control process itself — a meta-review that ensures the editor did not ignore valid issues, skip required procedures, or deviate from specification rules. Without Edit Audit, the Edit sub-process (*288) is self-certifying, which defeats the independence principle at the heart of SQC.

concepts.name: Edit [SQC]

relatedConcepts.name: Edit Audit [SQC]
relatedConcepts.note: downstream — Edit Audit is the supervisory review that follows and verifies the Edit sub-process

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: parent system — Edit is the correction sub-process within the SQC quality control cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Editor Advice Log
relatedConcepts.note: primary input — the Edit process is driven by issues recorded in the Editor Advice Log

relatedConcepts.name: Editor
relatedConcepts.note: actor — the Editor (usually the specification writer) performs the Edit sub-process

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Meeting
relatedConcepts.note: upstream — the Specification Meeting produces the Editor Advice Log that feeds the Edit process

concepts.definition: The Edit sub-process of SQC primarily attempts to correct a specification by removing identified defects. The Edit process includes any defined Edit process activity, such as sending messages to other specification owners about possible problems with their specification.
concepts.overview: **Edit [SQC]** (*288) is the correction phase of the Planguage SQC (Specification Quality Control) cycle: after checkers have identified defects in a Specification Meeting and a scribe has recorded them in the Editor Advice Log (*296), the Editor (*277) — usually the specification writer — reads the log and corrects the specification. The edit is not limited to the issues reported: the editor is free to correct additional defects found in any part of the specification and is also free to decline corrections they judge not to be major defects. The Edit sub-process is followed by Edit Audit (*289), in which the team leader verifies that editing was reasonable and complete.

concepts.name: Editor Advice Log

relatedConcepts.name: Edit [SQC]
relatedConcepts.note: consumer — the Editor Advice Log is the primary input to the Edit sub-process

relatedConcepts.name: Edit Audit [SQC]
relatedConcepts.note: audit target — Edit Audit verifies that the Editor Advice Log was properly heeded

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: parent system — the Editor Advice Log is produced within the SQC process

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Meeting
relatedConcepts.note: production context — the log is written during or after the SQC Specification Meeting

relatedConcepts.name: Scribe
relatedConcepts.note: author — the Scribe writes the Editor Advice Log based on oral checker reports

relatedConcepts.name: Editor
relatedConcepts.note: recipient — the Editor reads and acts on the Editor Advice Log

concepts.definition:
An Editor Advice Log is written formally by a scribe at an SQC Specification Meeting. It is based on oral reports from checkers.
**Contents:** issues · improvement suggestions · questions of intent for the specification writer.
**Writing mode:** brainstorming — volume now, analysis later. Written without debate, discussion, or consensus.
concepts.overview: **Editor Advice Log** (*296) is the formal record of issues, suggestions, and questions produced during an SQC Specification Meeting (*120) — written by a Scribe (*410) based on oral reports from checkers, without debate or consensus. It is the primary input to the Edit sub-process (*288): the Editor (*277) — usually the specification writer — reads each item and decides whether and how to correct the specification. The log is written in brainstorming mode (capture volume now; analyse later), and its existence depends on the Specification Meeting finding a worthwhile number of defects: too few or too many defects, or improperly performed checking, may mean no formal log is produced. When no log is written, the checkers' informal "scratchings" may be passed directly to the writer as a lighter-weight substitute.

concepts.name: Editor

relatedConcepts.name: Edit [SQC]
relatedConcepts.note: process — the Editor performs the Edit sub-process (*288); the role is defined by this activity

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: parent system — the Editor role exists within the SQC quality control cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Editor Advice Log
relatedConcepts.note: primary input — the Editor reads and evaluates the Editor Advice Log, then takes appropriate action

relatedConcepts.name: Edit Audit [SQC]
relatedConcepts.note: oversight — the Edit Audit (*289) reviews whether the Editor completed the Edit properly

relatedConcepts.name: Team Leader
relatedConcepts.note: oversight role — the Team Leader performs Edit Audit to verify the Editor's work

concepts.definition:
During the Edit sub-process of SQC, an 'editor' is a person who evaluates issues (and other Editor Advice Log information) and takes appropriate action on them.
**Note:** The appropriate action might include correcting something if the issues are defects, or sending change requests to other document owners if action needs to be taken at that level.
concepts.overview: **Editor** (*277) is the Planguage SQC role responsible for evaluating and acting on the items in the Editor Advice Log (*296) during the Edit sub-process (*288). The editor is usually the specification writer — the person who knows the specification best and is best positioned to judge whether each logged issue represents a real defect requiring correction. The editor is not a passive fixer: they evaluate each item independently, may correct far more defects than were reported (by searching the full specification), and may decline to fix items they judge are not major defects. Their work is subsequently reviewed by the Team Leader (*281) in the Edit Audit (*289).

concepts.name: Effect
concepts.keyedIcon: any benchmark or generic level of performance, e.g. O----|----> or O-----<-----<<----->

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: cause — a system performance attribute produces the Effect on a stakeholder

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: recipient — Effect is the differential value experienced by a defined stakeholder

relatedConcepts.name: System
relatedConcepts.note: host — Effect is produced by a performance attribute of a system acting on a second system or process

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: reference — Effect is measured relative to a stakeholder benchmark of prior experience

relatedConcepts.name: Sum of Performance
relatedConcepts.note: aggregate — the sum of performance attributes that produce aggregate effects

concepts.definition:
The result ('the effect') of using a system performance attribute (the 'cause').
Formally: the differential value to a defined stakeholder, caused by a defined level of a defined system attribute, acting on a defined stakeholder, in a defined stakeholder environment.
More simply and less formally: an **Effect** is the stakeholder joy from a system performance attribute.
concepts.overview: **Effect** (*441) is the downstream result — the actual value experienced by a stakeholder — produced when a system delivers a defined level of a performance attribute. An Effect is always relative: it is the *differential* value compared to what the stakeholder experienced before (their benchmark), in their specific environment. The same performance attribute (e.g., 99.98% availability) can produce a large Effect for one stakeholder and no Effect at all for another, depending on their circumstances and needs. Effect is therefore not a property of the system alone, but of the relationship between the system's performance and the stakeholder's context. Origin: concept by HumanAgent Gilb, end 2000.

concepts.name: Effectiveness

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: Effectiveness measures how good current performance attributes are at meeting stakeholder demands

relatedConcepts.name: Measure of Effectiveness
relatedConcepts.note: a specific metric for quantifying Effectiveness; see also SPROLES02

relatedConcepts.name: Benefit
relatedConcepts.note: actual achievement of benefits vs. expected is one measure of Effectiveness

relatedConcepts.name: Measure of Performance
relatedConcepts.note: a MOP considers only the effectiveness of a set of performance attributes; see also SPROLES02

relatedConcepts.name: Sum of Performance
relatedConcepts.note: a sum of performance for a delivered Evo Step can serve as a Measure of Performance and thus Effectiveness

relatedConcepts.name: Efficiency
relatedConcepts.note: Efficiency extends Effectiveness by incorporating cost; Effectiveness is raw impact, Efficiency is impact per resource

concepts.definition:
**Effectiveness** is a measure of how good the current attributes of a system are at delivering the stakeholders' current demands of the system.
Effectiveness is a raw measure of impact, and does not contain information about the costs of making that impact (performance *in relation to cost* is the role of an *efficiency* measure).
concepts.overview: **Effectiveness** (*053) asks a single focused question: is the system delivering what stakeholders actually need? It is a raw measure of impact — how closely the system's current performance attributes match stakeholder demands — without regard to the resources consumed. This makes Effectiveness the natural complement to Efficiency (*054): Effectiveness tells you whether you are achieving the right result; Efficiency tells you how cheaply you are doing so. ISO 9000:2000 defines Effectiveness as "the extent to which planned activities are realised and planned results achieved" — consistent with the Planguage view. Several different Measures of Effectiveness (*486) can be defined; actual vs. expected Benefit (*009) is one common form.

concepts.name: Efficiency (noun adjective)

relatedConcepts.name: Efficiency
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — this entry defines the noun-adjective usage of the Efficiency concept

concepts.definition: The noun adjective 'Efficiency' can be used to refer to any set of Performance to Cost Attribute ratios. For example: 'Efficiency Attributes, Efficiency Requirements, Efficiency Benchmarks, Efficiency Targets, and Efficiency Records.'
concepts.overview: **Efficiency (noun adjective)** (*394) is a grammatical clarification within Planguage: the word "Efficiency" can function as a noun adjective — a qualifying prefix applied to any specification parameter that deals with Performance-to-Cost ratios. This entry does not introduce a new concept; it documents how the word "Efficiency" can legally and usefully modify Planguage vocabulary items such as Attributes, Requirements, Benchmarks, Targets, and Records. It is a child entry of *054 Efficiency; understanding the parent concept is a prerequisite.

concepts.name: Efficiency

relatedConcepts.name: Effectiveness
relatedConcepts.note: Efficiency is Effectiveness in relation to cost; Effectiveness is the raw impact; Efficiency adds the cost dimension

relatedConcepts.name: Performance to Cost Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: a benefit-to-cost or performance-to-cost ratio is a measure of Efficiency

relatedConcepts.name: Efficiency (noun adjective)
relatedConcepts.note: child usage entry — how 'Efficiency' functions as a noun adjective prefix in Planguage specifications

concepts.definition:
**Efficiency** is 'effectiveness' in relation to cost.
A benefit to cost ratio or a performance to cost ratio would be a measure of efficiency.
concepts.overview: **Efficiency** (*054) is the cost-aware extension of Effectiveness (*053): it asks not just whether the right result is being achieved, but how cheaply. A performance-to-cost ratio — or benefit-to-cost ratio — is the canonical measure. The Specification Quality Control (SQC) example makes the concept vivid: SQC finds about one major defect per engineering hour; downstream testing and debugging are roughly ten times less efficient; field rework is roughly one hundred times less efficient. Efficiency is the concept that makes cost-of-quality reasoning precise. ISO 9000:2000 defines Efficiency as "relationship between the result achieved and the resources used." The synonym "Cost Effectiveness" is in wide use; Planguage treats it as equivalent.

concepts.name: Effort
concepts.keyedIcon: resource icon with benchmark and target icons

relatedConcepts.name: Work Hours
relatedConcepts.note: a measure of Effort — politically correct form of 'man hours'; the common unit on the Effort scale

relatedConcepts.name: Efficiency
relatedConcepts.note: Effort is the cost denominator in Efficiency (Performance-to-Cost) ratios

concepts.definition:
Human-energy task cost. The human resources needed to accomplish something.
Scale of measure: the defined [type of effort, default = engineering hours] needed to accomplish a defined [task].
concepts.overview: **Effort** (*368) is intentionally narrow: it covers human resource cost only — not money, compute, or materials. The default unit is engineering hours (or work-hours, the politically neutral equivalent of man-hours), though any human-energy unit can be defined. Effort is a resource scale that carries its own benchmark, fail limit, and constraint, exactly like any other Planguage quantified attribute. HP's "target effort savings" — a platform commitment to reduce product investment by X engineering months — is the canonical example in the source. ISO 9000:2000 notes Efficiency as "relationship between the result achieved and the resources used," confirming Effort as the denominator in Performance-to-Cost ratios.

concepts.name: Elementary

relatedConcepts.name: Compound
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — a Compound concept IS decomposed into sub-components; Elementary is NOT decomposed

relatedConcepts.name: Element
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — an Element can be complex; Elementary is the specific property of having no further decomposition

concepts.definition:
An 'elementary' component is not decomposed into sub-components.
A component can be elementary because it is unable to be decomposed into sub-components, or because there is no declared intent to decompose it.
concepts.overview: **Elementary** (*055) is a partitioning concept, not a complexity concept: a component is elementary not because it is simple, but because it has no declared sub-decomposition. The decision to treat something as elementary is practical and economic — driven by project size, complexity, risk, culture, and the granularity needed for precise control. Elementary concepts have exactly one scale of measure, are directly testable and measurable, and can be developed, tested, costed, and quality-controlled relatively independently. Their antonym is Compound (*023). This concept was revised in August 2014.

concepts.name: End

relatedConcepts.name: Means
relatedConcepts.note: complement — Means is the way to reach the Ends; End is the desired destination, Means is how to get there

relatedConcepts.name: Objective (noun)
relatedConcepts.note: canonical *100 entry — End is defined as a generic synonym for Objective *100

concepts.definition:
Future requirement or objective. Desired end state.
Generic synonym for *100.Objective.
concepts.overview: **End** (*100) is the Planguage concept for a future requirement or objective — a desired end state that a system or project is working toward. It is explicitly defined as a generic synonym for *100 Objective; the two terms are interchangeable. The conceptual pair is End/Means: Ends are what you are trying to achieve; Means (*047) are how you plan to achieve them. The keyed icon is "@" — the same as Objective. For more-specific goal or target concepts, the set of target icons (e.g., `------|->>----->----->`) applies. Note: *100 is shared across multiple related files (End, Objective-noun, Performance-Requirement, Objective-and-Performance-Requirements) as a polysemous concept number.

concepts.name: Ends

relatedConcepts.name: Starts
relatedConcepts.note: complement — Starts (*) marks the beginning; Ends (•) marks completion; together they bound an Evo step or event

relatedConcepts.name: Before
relatedConcepts.note: sequencing — used with Ends to specify 'X must start Before A Ends

relatedConcepts.name: After
relatedConcepts.note: sequencing — used with Ends to specify 'XX starts After A Ends

relatedConcepts.name: In Process
relatedConcepts.note: intermediate state — In Process (^) is the state between Starts (*) and Ends (•)

concepts.definition:
'Ends' is a Planguage parameter that specifies a condition that a defined term has completed successfully (is true).
Usage: to indicate sequential priority in planning time-consuming events such as Evo steps.
concepts.overview: **Ends** (*316) is a scheduling and sequencing parameter in Planguage, primarily used in Evo step planning. Its keyed icon is "•" (bullet). "A Ends" (written A•) means: A has completed successfully — its implementation is correct and complete. Ends pairs with Starts (*315, icon "*") and In-Process (*113, icon "^") to form the three-state lifecycle of any Evo step or planned event. The Before (*312) and After (*313) parameters are used together with Ends to express ordering dependencies: "X must start Before A Ends" or "XX starts After A Ends." A correct and complete implementation of a specification is the necessary condition for Ends.

concepts.name: Engineering Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Product Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — Product Constraint constrains the product; Engineering Constraint constrains the engineering process

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Engineering Constraint is a specialisation of Constraint, scoped to the engineering process

concepts.definition: An engineering constraint is a constraint on the engineering process itself, rather than on the product.
concepts.overview: **Engineering Constraint** (*473) is a specialisation of Constraint (*218) that targets the engineering process — the methods, tools, timelines, resources, and practices used to build and deliver the product — rather than the product's own properties or behaviour. Its antonym is Product Constraint (*474): a product constraint limits what the product may be; an engineering constraint limits how the product may be built. This concept is a derived stub: no standalone alphabetical entry for *473 was found in the source PDF. The definition is derived from its reference in Product-Constraint.474, which lists Engineering Constraint as the contrasting concept. This derivation was performed by VANeo.

concepts.name: Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: supertype — Engineering is the general discipline; Systems Engineering is its systems-focused specialisation

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary
relatedConcepts.note: core character — Engineering is described as an Evolutionary Process in Planguage

relatedConcepts.name: Principle
relatedConcepts.note: instrument — Engineering uses heuristics and Principles as its core operational tool

relatedConcepts.name: Risk
relatedConcepts.note: environment — Engineering operates in conditions of uncertainty and manages risk through heuristics

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: goal — optimal Stakeholder satisfaction is the stated goal of Engineering

concepts.definition: Engineering is an Evolutionary Process, using practical Principles, in order to determine, and identify the Means to deliver, the best achievable Performance and Cost levels balance, for optimal Stakeholder satisfaction, in a complex risk-filled environment.
concepts.overview: **Engineering** (*224) is, in Planguage, a fundamentally **evolutionary, heuristic, and quantitative** discipline — not a step-by-step algorithmic procedure. It uses Principles (rules of thumb from accumulated experience) to navigate uncertainty, balance Performance and Cost, and deliver the best achievable Stakeholder satisfaction. The defining characteristic is quantification: wherever the term "engineering" is used in Planguage, it implies measurement as the basic tool rather than intuition. Engineering is inherently a risk-taking activity; engineers manage that risk by making small changes, maintaining reversibility, and feeding back past results.

concepts.name: Entity

relatedConcepts.name: Attribute
relatedConcepts.note: property — entities are chosen and described by their performance and cost Attributes

relatedConcepts.name: System
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Systems can be imagined/conceptual; Entities must have provable real existence

relatedConcepts.name: Function
relatedConcepts.note: operation — every Entity appears to have a Function; what the entity does

relatedConcepts.name: Design Ideas
relatedConcepts.note: specification — the description of an Entity is its design or architectural specification

concepts.definition: Entities exist. An entity is a real thing. An entity is real in the sense that it has provable existence, and it has performance and cost attributes. An entity can be natural or human made. It can be conceptual or physical.
concepts.overview: **Entity** (*645) is, in Planguage, anything that has **provable existence** and possesses performance and cost Attributes — whether physical (a server), conceptual (a policy), or social (a law). The key distinction from System (*145) is that Systems can be imagined or conceptual in nature, whereas Entities must have real, demonstrable existence. Designers choose Entities because of their Attributes; the written description of an Entity is its design or architectural specification. Crucially, if all specifications were destroyed, the Entity itself would continue to exist — the specification is not the thing.

concepts.name: Entry Condition
synonyms: Gate (generic term covering both Entry and Exit conditions — McConnell)

relatedConcepts.name: Entry Process
relatedConcepts.note: execution — the Entry Process evaluates the relevant set of Entry Conditions

relatedConcepts.name: Exit Condition
relatedConcepts.note: counterpart — Entry Conditions gate entry; Exit Conditions gate completion

relatedConcepts.name: Exit Process
relatedConcepts.note: counterpart process — evaluates Exit Conditions at the end of a task

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: application — SQC uses Entry Conditions to gate inspection readiness

concepts.definition: An entry condition is a written part of a work-process standard. Entry conditions are usually found in sets. The relevant set of entry conditions is evaluated in an entry process. They are used to determine if there is entry permission to a task process.
concepts.overview: **Entry Condition** (*056) is a written gate criterion that must be met before a task process may officially commence. Entry Conditions prevent entry into failure-prone work, surface obstacles that must be removed, and encode organisational learning — any experience that warns of impending problems can be formalised as an Entry Condition and made available to everyone, including those who have not personally encountered the problem. All Entry Conditions in a set must normally be met for permission to enter; failed conditions must either be resolved or consciously waived with determinable risk. The generic term "Gate" (McConnell) covers both Entry and Exit conditions.

concepts.name: Entry Process

relatedConcepts.name: Entry Condition
relatedConcepts.note: content — the Entry Process evaluates the set of applicable Entry Conditions

relatedConcepts.name: Exit Condition
relatedConcepts.note: counterpart concept — Exit Conditions are evaluated by the Exit Process at task completion

relatedConcepts.name: Exit Process
relatedConcepts.note: counterpart process — evaluates Exit Conditions at the end of the task

concepts.definition: An entry process involves evaluating any applicable entry conditions for a process. The process itself is defined by a main task. When *all* entry conditions are met, the main process task may officially commence.
concepts.overview: **Entry Process** (*057) is the formal gate activity that precedes every main task process: it evaluates the set of applicable Entry Conditions and, only when all are satisfied, grants permission to begin. Its purpose is to avoid failed, uneconomic, or time-wasting execution of the main task. The Entry Process is identified by the abbreviation "E" (IBM convention, Radice/Humphrey) and the keyed icon `→[…]`. The full ETVX or ETX process control cycle — Entry, Task, Validation, eXit — places the Entry Process as the mandatory first step of any disciplined work process.

concepts.name: Environment Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Environment System
relatedConcepts.note: source — Environment Constraints are constraints on or from the Environment System

relatedConcepts.name: Focus System
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Environment Constraints apply to non-focus systems; Focus System Constraints apply to the focus

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: supertype — Environment Constraint is a subtype of Constraint, classified by target

relatedConcepts.name: Binary Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: expression form — Environment Constraints can be expressed as Binary Constraints

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: expression form — Environment Constraints can be expressed as Scalar Constraints

relatedConcepts.name: Demand Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: related constraint type — demand-style constraint form

relatedConcepts.name: Veto Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: related constraint type — veto-style constraint form

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: related constraint type — one of the four basic constraint types alongside Environment Constraints

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: related constraint type — one of the four basic constraint types alongside Environment Constraints

relatedConcepts.name: Function Constraints
relatedConcepts.note: related constraint type — one of the four basic constraint types alongside Environment Constraints

concepts.definition: An Environment Constraint is any system constraint that is not a focus system constraint. Environment constraints are particularly intended to describe constraints on the life cycle of a product or system, such as design and architecture phases, construction and acquisition phases, implementation phases, operational use phases, and shut down phases. Environment constraints can be expressed as binary constraints or as scalar constraints.
concepts.overview: **Environment Constraint** (*491) is a Constraint classified by its target: it applies to the Environment System (*493) rather than to the Focus System (*492). While a Focus System Constraint governs what the designed system must do or achieve, an Environment Constraint governs the conditions, lifecycle phases, and non-focus contexts within which the system must operate or be developed. There are four basic constraint types: function, performance, resource, and environment — and Environment Constraints can be expressed as either Binary Constraints (yes/no compliance) or Scalar Constraints (numeric range).

concepts.name: Environment System

relatedConcepts.name: Focus System
relatedConcepts.note: pair — the Environment System is everything related to the defined Focus System; the two together define the system boundary

relatedConcepts.name: Environment Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: constraint type — Environment Constraints originate from or apply to the Environment System

concepts.definition: An environment system is any system related to a defined Focus System. For example it could be a development process or development tool for a product (designated as the defined focus system).
concepts.overview: **Environment System** (*493) is the set of all systems related to a defined Focus System — everything outside the boundary of the system being designed. While the Focus System (*492) is the subject of the engineering effort, the Environment System is the context within which it must operate, be developed, and be maintained. This pairing — Focus System and Environment System — defines the scope boundary of any Planguage specification. The military standard MIL-STD-499B calls them "Enabling Systems." Environment Constraints (*491) govern what the Environment System requires.

concepts.name: Error

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Issue
relatedConcepts.note: downstream — a human Error in a specification process produces a Specification Issue (suspected violation logged during SQC)

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Defect
relatedConcepts.note: downstream — unresolved Specification Issues become Specification Defects

relatedConcepts.name: Fault (Bug, System Defect)
relatedConcepts.note: downstream — Specification Defects propagate into the system as Faults (Bugs)

relatedConcepts.name: Malfunction
relatedConcepts.note: downstream — Faults in execution produce Malfunctions (observable failures)

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: detection — SQC is the process that discovers whether errors have been made in specifications

relatedConcepts.name: Statistical Process Control
relatedConcepts.note: theory — SPC theory explains that errors are usually forced by bad work processes, not personal carelessness

concepts.definition: An 'error' is something done incorrectly by a human being. Errors are usually committed unintentionally; they are often forced to happen by 'bad' work processes (Statistical Process Control Theory [DEMING86, JURAN64 &74]).
concepts.overview: **Error** (*274), synonymous with Slip, is the human act that originates the defect chain — the moment a human being does something incorrectly, typically unintentionally. In Planguage's defect taxonomy, Error is the root cause: an Error produces a Specification Issue (a suspected violation caught in SQC), which may become a Specification Defect, which propagates into the system as a Fault (Bug), which in execution produces a Malfunction. Critically, Statistical Process Control theory (Deming, Juran) holds that errors are usually forced by bad work processes, not by individual carelessness — making process improvement, not blame, the correct corrective response.

concepts.name: Essential Objective

relatedConcepts.name: Fundamental Objective
relatedConcepts.note: relationship — Essential Objectives are those capable of influencing a Fundamental Objective; they feed into it

relatedConcepts.name: Controllable
relatedConcepts.note: pair — the test for a Fundamental Objective is that it must be both Essential *and* Controllable; these two criteria intersect

concepts.definition: Essential objectives are the ones which are capable of influencing the Fundamental objective when they are reached or implemented. Compare with 'Controllable'.
concepts.overview: **Essential Objective** (*231) is one of the two tests that a candidate Fundamental Objective must pass to be accepted as a true Fundamental Objective. An objective is *essential* if achieving it can actually influence the Fundamental Objective — it is a real driver of the terminal value, not a means or an irrelevant side-goal. The complementary test is *controllable* (*232): the decision-maker must be able to affect it. Fundamental Objectives that are both essential and controllable occupy the intersection; those that are essential but not controllable are out of the decision-maker's reach; those that are controllable but not essential are merely means. The framework is due to Keeney (1992).

concepts.name: Estimate, To

relatedConcepts.name: Estimate
relatedConcepts.note: product — 'to estimate' is the verb process; Estimate *058 is the noun result of that process

relatedConcepts.name: Quantify To
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Quantification uses more rigorous derivation; Estimation is a judgment where measurement is not practical

relatedConcepts.name: Measure To
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Measurement is direct observation; Estimation is a judgment used when measurement is impossible, impractical, or uneconomic

relatedConcepts.name: Specify To
relatedConcepts.note: upstream — specification of a numeric attribute precedes the need to estimate its level

concepts.definition:
In Planguage, 'to estimate' is the process of arriving at a judgement, by guessing the probable numeric value, of a numeric attribute level, using other methods than immediate measurement. Estimation is not to be confused with Quantification or Measurement.
Webster's: "to judge or determine generally but carefully (size, value, cost, requirements, etc.); calculate approximately."
concepts.overview: **Estimate, To** (*059) is the verb form of estimation — the process of forming a numeric judgement about an attribute level when direct measurement is unavailable or impractical. Planguage is precise about what estimation is not: it is not Quantification (*385) and it is not Measurement (*386). Estimation is the deliberate, principled exercise of judgement to arrive at a numeric value — a "careful guess" — used when the future has not yet happened, the past is not recorded, or measurement would be uneconomic. The noun result of this process is an Estimate (*058). The synonym "Predict, To" emphasises the forward-looking orientation of estimation.

concepts.name: Estimate

relatedConcepts.name: Estimate To
relatedConcepts.note: verb form — 'to estimate' is the process; Estimate is the noun result of that process

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: related parameter — Benchmarks record known past data; Estimates are used when Benchmark data is not available

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar
relatedConcepts.note: target type — Estimates are made about scalar (numeric) system attributes

concepts.definition: An estimate is a numeric judgment about a future, present or past level of a scalar system attribute. This includes all performance and cost attributes. Estimates are usually made where direct measurement is impossible (future), impractical (past), or uneconomic (current levels). An estimate is usually derived from available information, and past experience.
concepts.overview: **Estimate** (*058), qualified as 'derived,' is the noun form of estimation — a numeric judgement about the level of a scalar system attribute when direct measurement is not available. Estimates cover performance attributes, cost attributes, and any other numeric dimension of a system, for past periods with incomplete data, present conditions that are uneconomic to measure directly, and future states that have not yet occurred. The keyed icon `#` (the number symbol in the US; also the Impact Estimation table icon) signals an Estimate parameter in a Planguage spec. The synonym "predict" emphasises the forward-looking application. The companion verb concept is Estimate, To (*059).

concepts.name: Estimated Remaining Defects

relatedConcepts.name: Major Defect
relatedConcepts.note: unit of measurement — Estimated Remaining Defects is expressed in Major defects per Logical Page

relatedConcepts.name: Logical Page
relatedConcepts.note: unit of density — defect density is expressed per Logical Page

relatedConcepts.name: Defect Detection Process
relatedConcepts.note: input — the detection effectiveness rate is used to estimate total defects from those found

relatedConcepts.name: Cumulative Defect Removal Effectiveness
relatedConcepts.note: related metric — measures the total proportion of defects removed across the process

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: process — SQC is the primary process that generates defect-find data used to compute this estimate

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Level
relatedConcepts.note: target — the quality level goal expressed as remaining defects per page

concepts.definition:
This is an estimate of defect density remaining in a specification at any given time.
The estimate is based on defects found (using knowledge of % defect-finding effectiveness) and defects attempted removed (using knowledge of % effectiveness of the correction process). The defect density is usually expressed in Major defects per Logical Page.
concepts.overview: **Estimated Remaining Defects** (*060) is a computed metric that tells you how many Major defects are still lurking in a specification after an inspection round — even after you have tried to fix everything you found. It accounts for two compounding inefficiencies: the fact that defect-detection processes miss some fraction of defects, and the fact that correction processes fail to fix some fraction of what they find. The result is a probabilistic density figure — not a count of known defects, but an estimate of unknown ones. This makes it uniquely valuable: it is the number that tells you whether you are done, not the number of defects already fixed.

concepts.name: Evaluation Effort

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: process — SQC is the assumed evaluation process; Evaluation Effort is the cost of conducting it

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Level
relatedConcepts.note: output — the quality level (remaining Major defects per page) is what Evaluation Effort buys

relatedConcepts.name: Logical Page
relatedConcepts.note: density denominator — quality level is expressed per Logical Page

relatedConcepts.name: Major Defect
relatedConcepts.note: unit — quality level is measured in Major defects, so Evaluation Effort funds their discovery

concepts.definition:
This is the cost (in work hours) of determining the quality level (Remaining major defects per page) of a specification.
The process to do the evaluation is assumed to be SQC, but other processes to determine the quality level could be used. Use of sampling will dramatically reduce the evaluation cost, time and effort, at the expense of a mild decrease in accuracy and credibility.
concepts.overview: **Evaluation Effort** (*061) is the measured cost — in work hours — of running a Specification Quality Control process to establish the current quality level of a specification in terms of remaining Major defects per Logical Page. It is not the effort of fixing defects; it is the effort of *knowing* how many defects remain. The concept exists to ensure that SQC is managed as a cost-justified activity: the effort spent evaluating must be justified by the downstream savings from shipping higher-quality specifications. Sampling is the primary lever for reducing Evaluation Effort without sacrificing much accuracy.

concepts.name: Event

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: context — an event can be used as a qualifier condition to scope when a specification applies

relatedConcepts.name: Condition
relatedConcepts.note: relationship — an event condition is a qualifier condition; the event must have happened for the condition to be true

relatedConcepts.name: Status
relatedConcepts.note: effect — an event usually results in a measurable change in a status

concepts.definition:
An event is a specified occurrence.
An event must be clearly distinguishable from the non-occurrence of the event. It must be reliably observable, testable, or measurable in the real world. Consequently, events must be precisely defined — unambiguously. An event usually results in some measurable change in a status. An 'event condition' can be defined as a qualifier condition — the event must have happened for the qualifier condition to be true.
concepts.overview: **Event** (*062) is, in Planguage, a precisely defined and testable occurrence — a point in space-time that either has happened or has not. It is not an activity (like performing a task), nor an ongoing state, nor a social occasion. Its defining characteristic is binary observability: the event either occurred or it did not, and that fact must be verifiable in the real world. Events play two roles in Planguage: as qualifier conditions (scoping when a specification applies) and as progress indicators (the occurrence of an event changes a status and triggers subsequent activity). The precision requirement is non-negotiable — a vaguely defined event cannot be reliably detected.

concepts.name: Evidence

relatedConcepts.name: Claim
relatedConcepts.note: upgrade path — Claims that are proven out by real-world results become Evidence-backed; Evidence is the upgrade target for a Claim

relatedConcepts.name: Credibility
relatedConcepts.note: quality of evidence — Evidence has Credibility; stronger evidence carries higher Credibility Rating

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation
relatedConcepts.note: context — Evidence is required for each impact estimate in Impact Estimation

relatedConcepts.name: Assertion
relatedConcepts.note: relationship — Evidence is the historic-facts support for an Assertion; Assertions require Evidence to be credible

concepts.definition:
Evidence is the historic facts which support an assertion. The evidence usually will have been the basis for making an assertion.
In Impact Estimation, evidence is required for each impact estimate. Where there is no evidence, it should be clearly stated that there is none.
**Keyed icon:** `#<-` meaning "source (`<-`) of the estimate (`#`)."
concepts.overview: **Evidence** (*063) is the factual foundation that supports an assertion or impact estimate — the historic, real-world data that either backs up or undermines a claim about system performance. In Planguage, Evidence is not optional decoration: it is a required field for every impact estimate, and its absence must be explicitly stated ("no evidence"). The keyed icon `#<-` — combining the estimate marker `#` with the source arrow `<-` — signals that what follows is not a guess but a fact-backed figure. Evidence is the upgrade target for a Claim (*553): a claim that is validated by real-world results transforms into Evidence, giving it weight in future specifications. Evidence without a stated Credibility level is incomplete.

concepts.name: Evo Level
concepts.definition: Evo Level is the smallest unit of value-delivering work, sized to fit a single evolutionary delivery cycle (typically 1-2 weeks). Multiple Evo deliveries integrate to form a Solution. Evo deliveries are the operational, day-to-day cause whose accumulated effect is Solution.
concepts.overview: **Evo Level** (*805) is part of HumanAgent Gilb's Value Delivery framework, an extension to Tom Gilb's original Planguage. It is not in the source PlanguageGlossary.pdf — it has been authored to capture concepts the framework needs but the PDF did not name.

concepts.name: Evo Plan

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: context — an Evo Plan is the planning artefact of Evolutionary Project Management

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary
relatedConcepts.note: principle — the Evo Plan embodies the evolutionary principle of dynamic re-sequencing based on feedback

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: unit — an Evo Plan is a set of sequenced (and yet-to-be-sequenced) Evo Steps

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step Specification
relatedConcepts.note: detail — the Evo Plan holds tag names; detailed content is held in Evo Step Specifications

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation Table
relatedConcepts.note: tool — an Impact Estimation Table may be included in an Evo Plan to track step impacts and feedback

concepts.definition:
An Evo plan is a set of sequenced and/or a set of yet-to-be sequenced Evo steps. The current planned sequence of delivery of any of the steps should be reconsidered after each Evo step has actually been delivered, and the feedback has been analyzed. Many factors, internal and external, can cause a re-sequencing of steps and/or the insertion of previously unplanned additional step(s) and/or the deletion of some step(s).
It is the identification of the *next* Evo step for delivery that should be our focus for detailed practical planning. After all, at an extreme, the other planned steps may never be implemented in practice.
concepts.overview: **Evo Plan** (*322) is the strategic planning artefact of Evolutionary Project Management — a living sequence of Evo Steps that is continuously revised in the light of feedback after each delivery. Unlike a waterfall project plan, an Evo Plan is not committed in detail from the start: it identifies the *next* step clearly and holds the remaining steps in loose sequence, knowing that feedback from each delivery may change the order, add new steps, or eliminate planned ones. The Evo Plan is the highest-level scheduling instrument in the Evo process, but its power lies precisely in its flexibility — it is designed to change, not to be executed mechanically.

concepts.name: Evo Step Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Design Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: origin — outline Evo Step Specifications are produced at the end of Design Engineering, before Evo begins

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: context — Evo Step Specifications are produced and refined within the Evo process

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: subject — the Evo Step Specification is the formal written definition of an Evo Step's planned content

relatedConcepts.name: Actual Step Content
relatedConcepts.note: counterpart — the Evo Step Specification is the planned content; Actual Step Content records what was actually delivered and may differ

concepts.definition:
An Evo step specification is the formal written definition of the content of an Evo step.
An Evo step specification can differ from the reality of the delivered step content.
concepts.overview: **Evo Step Specification** (*370) is the planned, written definition of what a single Evo Step is intended to deliver — the design ideas it contains, the requirements it targets, and the conditions under which it will be executed. It is produced in two phases: as an outline during initial Design Engineering (to support step selection), and in full detail within Evo once a step has been selected as next. Critically, an Evo Step Specification is a *plan*, not a record — the actual delivered content is captured separately in Actual Step Content (*369). The gap between specification and actuality is expected, informative, and managed.

concepts.name: Evo Step

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step Specification
relatedConcepts.note: plan — the Evo Step Specification is the formal written definition of the step's planned content

relatedConcepts.name: Actual Step Content
relatedConcepts.note: record — what the Evo Step actually delivered is recorded as Actual Step Content

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Plan
relatedConcepts.note: schedule — the Evo Plan is the sequenced collection of Evo Steps

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary
relatedConcepts.note: principle — the Evo Step is the delivery unit that makes Evolutionary progress tangible

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: framework — Evo Steps are the atomic delivery units of Evolutionary Project Management

relatedConcepts.name: PDSA Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: lifecycle — each Evo Step follows the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Result Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: container — each step is developed and delivered within a result cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Development Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: phase — step development occurs in the development cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Production Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: phase — step production occurs in the production cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Delivery Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: phase — step delivery occurs in the delivery cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Result
relatedConcepts.note: synonym context — Step Result is a synonym for Result in the context of Evo

concepts.definition:
An Evo step ('evolutionary step' or, simply 'step') is a 'package of change', containing a set of design ideas, that on delivery to a system, is intended to help move the system towards meeting the yet-unfulfilled system requirements.
Evo steps are assumed to be small increments, typically a week in duration or 2% of total budget. There are two purposes for Evo steps: to move us towards the long-range requirements, and to learn early from stakeholder experience (with a view to changing plans and designs early).
concepts.overview: **Evo Step** (*141) is the atomic delivery unit of Evolutionary Project Management — a deliberately small package of change, containing a set of design ideas, delivered to real stakeholders in a real system. Its smallness is not an accident: 2%–5% of total project budget per step is the risk-calibrated size limit, chosen because it is a reasonable amount to gamble on any single learning cycle. Each Evo Step follows the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle: planned in the Evo Step Specification (*370), delivered as Actual Step Content (*369), studied via stakeholder feedback, and used to determine the next step. The two purposes — making progress and learning early — are inseparable: a step that makes progress without enabling learning is not an Evo Step.

concepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary
relatedConcepts.note: principle — Evolutionary Project Management is the method embodiment of the Evolutionary principle

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: unit — Evo Steps are the atomic delivery units of Evolutionary Project Management

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Plan
relatedConcepts.note: artefact — the Evo Plan is the scheduling instrument of Evolutionary Project Management

relatedConcepts.name: PDSA Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: lifecycle — each Evo Step follows the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Incremental Development
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Evolutionary differs from Incremental Development in that design changes over time, not just grows

relatedConcepts.name: Evo
relatedConcepts.note: alias — Evo is the standard abbreviation for this concept

concepts.definition:
A project management process delivering 'high-value-first' progress towards the *currently defined and approved requirements*, and then seeking to obtain, and use, realistic, early feedback.
Key components include: frequent delivery of system changes (steps); steps delivered to stakeholders for real use; feedback obtained from stakeholders to determine *next* step(s); the existing system is used as the initial system base; small steps (ideally between 2%–5% of total project financial cost and time); steps with highest value and benefit-to-cost ratios given highest priority for delivery; feedback used 'immediately' to modify future plans and requirements; total systems approach ('anything that helps'); results-orientation ('delivering the results' is the prime concern).
concepts.overview: **Evolutionary Project Management** (*355), abbreviated Evo, is Tom Gilb's iterative, feedback-driven project management process built on nine principles: frequent delivery, real stakeholder use, immediate feedback, small steps, value-first sequencing, dynamic plan adaptation, total systems orientation, and results focus. It is distinguished from Incremental Development (*318) by the fact that the design itself changes and adapts over time — it does not merely grow. Each Evo Step follows the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle; the Evo Plan is re-sequenced after every delivery based on what was learned. Evo had large-scale early use in IBM's Cleanroom techniques (Harlan Mills, 1970s) and has near-synonyms across the industry — Agile, Scrum, Lean, and Synch-and-Stabilize all share overlapping features, none perfectly.

concepts.name: Evolutionary

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: method — Evolutionary Project Management is the process expression of the Evolutionary principle

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Plan
relatedConcepts.note: artefact — the Evo Plan embodies the evolutionary principle of dynamic re-sequencing

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: unit — the Evo Step is the delivery unit through which evolutionary progress is made

relatedConcepts.name: Plan Do Study Act Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: mechanism — the PDSA Cycle is the iterative learning loop that makes a process evolutionary

concepts.definition: The 'evolutionary' concept implies association with Evolutionary Project Management; an iterative process of change, feedback, learning and consequent change. Evolutionary processes need to be carefully distinguished from other processes — those that do not iterate, do not learn from experience, and do not cater for change.
concepts.overview: **Evolutionary** (*196) is the underlying principle that defines a whole class of processes: iterate, learn from real feedback, and change consequentially. It is not a method — it is the criterion that distinguishes a genuine evolutionary process from one that merely delivers in phases. A process is evolutionary only if it iterates (cycles back), learns (uses feedback to update understanding), and changes (modifies plans, designs, or requirements based on that learning). Processes that phase-deliver without feedback loops are incremental, not evolutionary. Tom Gilb explicitly uses "Evo" as an abbreviation for both this principle (*196) and for Evolutionary Project Management (*355) — because he regards them as the same underlying concept expressed at different levels of abstraction.

concepts.name: Except

relatedConcepts.name: If
relatedConcepts.note: sibling logical-structure parameter — If includes conditionally; Except excludes explicitly

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: parent mechanism — Except is a qualifier that restricts the scope of a preceding term or expression

concepts.definition: 'Except' is a parameter which means that the following term or expression is an exception from the previous term or expression.
concepts.overview: **Except** (*389) is a **Logical Structure Parameter** in Planguage that carves exclusions out of a preceding scope expression. Where a term or qualifier establishes a set of targets or conditions, `Except` removes specific members from that set — making the exclusion explicit and unambiguous in the specification. It is the linguistic inverse of inclusion: rather than listing what applies, you state what does not. Except prevents scope creep and removes the ambiguity that arises when engineers assume a broad term covers everything.

concepts.name: Exit Condition

relatedConcepts.name: Entry Condition
relatedConcepts.note: pair — Entry Condition gates entry to a process; Exit Condition gates exit from it

relatedConcepts.name: Exit Process
relatedConcepts.note: executor — the Exit Process evaluates all applicable Exit Conditions

relatedConcepts.name: Work Process Standard
relatedConcepts.note: container — Exit Conditions are written into Work Process Standards

relatedConcepts.name: Downstream
relatedConcepts.note: recipient — work products are released to downstream processes only when Exit Conditions are satisfied

relatedConcepts.name: Exit [SQC]
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — Exit [SQC] is the SQC-domain application of Exit Condition evaluation

concepts.definition: An exit condition is a written part of a work-process standard. Exit conditions are usually found in sets. The relevant set of exit conditions is evaluated in an exit process. They are used to determine if there is exit permission from a task process. All the generic and specific exit conditions must normally be met, in order to exit from a process, thus releasing work products to the other 'downstream' processes.
