concepts.overview: **Exit Condition** (*064) is a formally written criterion — part of a [[Work-Process-Standard.138b]] — that must be satisfied before a process is permitted to conclude and release its output to downstream processes. Exit Conditions come in sets; all of them, generic and specific, must be met. They are evaluated during the [[Exit-Process.065]] and together form the quality gate that separates a process from what comes after it. The paired concept [[Entry-Condition.056]] governs entry to a process; Exit Condition governs departure.

concepts.name: Exit Process

relatedConcepts.name: Exit Condition
relatedConcepts.note: input — Exit Process evaluates the full set of Exit Conditions to determine release permission

relatedConcepts.name: Entry Process
relatedConcepts.note: pair — Entry Process gates process start; Exit Process gates process completion and release

relatedConcepts.name: Work Process Standard
relatedConcepts.note: container — Exit Conditions evaluated by this process are written into Work Process Standards

relatedConcepts.name: Downstream
relatedConcepts.note: recipient — work products are released to downstream processes upon successful Exit Process completion

relatedConcepts.name: Exit [SQC]
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — Exit [SQC] is the SQC-domain instantiation of the Exit Process

concepts.definition:
An exit process involves evaluating any applicable exit conditions for a process. Only when *all* exit conditions are met, can the main process task officially terminate and any process output be released to the next process.
*Note:* If any conditions fail, the exit process includes work to improve exit condition status to the required level. If all conditions are OK, then a process product can be released to its customer, and the process is officially completed.
Abbreviation [Exit Process *065]: X "As in 'eXit.'"
concepts.overview: **Exit Process** (*065) is the formal sub-process that evaluates the complete set of [[Exit-Condition.064]] criteria for a given lifecycle stage and decides whether the main process may officially conclude and release its output to [[Downstream.052]] processes. It is the paired counterpart of the [[Entry-Process.057]]: where Entry Process determines if work may start, Exit Process determines if the completed work may be released. If any Exit Condition fails, the Exit Process does not simply block — it includes the remediation work necessary to bring the work product up to the required level before release is permitted.

concepts.name: Exit [SQC]

relatedConcepts.name: Exit Condition
relatedConcepts.note: foundation — Exit [SQC] applies a defined set of Exit Conditions to determine SQC release permission

relatedConcepts.name: Exit Process
relatedConcepts.note: parent process — Exit [SQC] is the SQC-domain instantiation of the Exit Process

relatedConcepts.name: Entry Condition
relatedConcepts.note: pair — Entry Condition gates SQC entry; Exit Condition gates SQC exit

relatedConcepts.name: Entry Process
relatedConcepts.note: pair — Entry Process governs SQC start; Exit [SQC] governs SQC completion

relatedConcepts.name: Team Leader
relatedConcepts.note: decision-maker — the SQC Team Leader checks exit conditions and decides whether to allow exit

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: context — Exit [SQC] is a named sub-process of SQC (Specification Quality Control)

concepts.definition: Exit is the name of an SQC sub-process. The SQC team leader checks a set of defined SQC exit conditions, and decides whether to allow the specification to exit, based on the exit condition status; or whether to take other action, as a result of unsatisfied exit conditions.
concepts.overview: **Exit [SQC]** (*290) is the named exit sub-process within Specification Quality Control ([[SQC.051c]]). It is the SQC-domain instantiation of the general [[Exit-Process.065]]: the [[Team-Leader.281]] evaluates a defined set of [[Exit-Condition.064|Exit Conditions]] — including the key metric of estimated remaining major defect density — and either grants the specification permission to exit (releasing it to downstream processes) or initiates remediation. The decision is made by the Team Leader, not by consensus, and is based on objective condition status, not schedule pressure. Exit [SQC] is one half of the SQC gate pair, paired with Entry Condition *056 and Entry Process *057.

concepts.name: Expert

relatedConcepts.name: Source
relatedConcepts.note: generalisation — Expert is a Source that specifically knows the state of the art and how to achieve it

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: subject matter — an Expert knows the state-of-the-art benchmark levels in a discipline

relatedConcepts.name: Credibility
relatedConcepts.note: quality — the value of an Expert is measured partly by the Credibility of their claims

relatedConcepts.name: Credibility Rating
relatedConcepts.note: mechanism — Expert claims may carry a Credibility Rating to indicate confidence level

relatedConcepts.name: Knowledge
relatedConcepts.note: core attribute — an Expert is distinguished by actionable Knowledge of state-of-the-art and how to achieve it

concepts.definition:
A source that knows the state of the art levels in a defined discipline, and how to make them happen in practice.
*Note on 'Source':* 'Source' is used to include the idea that 'it does not matter if the expertise comes from a person, a group, or a written source such as a book, a paper, presentation, video, or internet.'
*Note on 'State of the art':* is the border between what we, in a given domain, have actually achieved in reality, and beyond that border, where 'no man has gone before us'. We 'know we don't know' how to go beyond that border. So the Expert knows what is 'possible, for sure'; and which might therefore be 'impossible for now', costly, risky, or challenging.
concepts.overview: **Expert** (*678) in Planguage is not simply someone with deep knowledge — it is a **[[Source.135]]** that knows both the state-of-the-art levels in a defined discipline *and* how to achieve those levels in practice. The "how" is the critical distinction: knowing what records exist is the entry-level of expertise; knowing what architecture, design, or strategy was used to achieve them is what makes expertise actionable. An Expert may be a person, a group, or a written source. Expertise without the "how" has almost no value in engineering — it produces aspirational goals with no path to achievement.

concepts.name: Explicit Parameters

relatedConcepts.name: Default Value
relatedConcepts.note: alternative — a Default Value defines a parameter implicitly; Explicit Parameters define it by direct naming

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: alternative mechanism — Scale Qualifiers define parameters by positional sequence rather than explicit name

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier Definition
relatedConcepts.note: alternative mechanism — Scale Variable (positional) vs. explicit parameter name

relatedConcepts.name: Generic Term
relatedConcepts.note: complement — Explicit Parameters are named using Generic Terms defined in the specification

concepts.definition: Parameters in a specification that are defined by *direct use* of their defined parameter name.
concepts.overview: **Explicit Parameters** (*378) are specification parameters that are introduced by directly writing their defined name — as opposed to being implied by position (Scale Qualifiers), inherited from a default (Default Value), or inferred from uniqueness. When a parameter name like `Scale`, `Goal`, or `Fault` appears verbatim in a specification, it is being used explicitly. Explicit Parameters make specifications easier to read, review, and maintain because the reader does not need to infer which parameter is being set from context or convention — the name is right there. They represent the most transparent form of parameter use in Planguage.

concepts.name: Explosion

relatedConcepts.name: Integration
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — Integration (implosion/synthesis) combines; Explosion decomposes

relatedConcepts.name: Level
relatedConcepts.note: result — Explosion creates hierarchical Levels; each decomposition step adds a Level

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter
relatedConcepts.note: host family — Explosion is a Logical Structure Parameter, a member of the Parameter family

concepts.definition: Explosion is a 'dramatic' word for 'hierarchical decomposition of complex specifications into useful, more elementary, detail'.
concepts.overview: **Explosion** (*066) is Planguage's term for hierarchical decomposition: the structured process of breaking a complex specification concept into progressively more elementary sub-components. The word is deliberately dramatic — to capture the contrast with the reductive, linear thinking that treats complexity as something to be avoided rather than something to be structured. Explosion is also known as Cartesian Analysis, attributable to René Descartes' method of dividing difficult problems into as many parts as needed to resolve them. Its antonyms — Integration, synthesis, aggregation — describe the reverse process of combining. In Planguage, explosion is the primary tool for managing specification complexity without losing traceability.

concepts.name: Expression Quotes

relatedConcepts.name: Expression
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — Expression Quotes delimit a single Expression, making its boundaries explicit

relatedConcepts.name: Data
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — double quotes delimit Data and Comments; single quotes delimit Expressions

relatedConcepts.name: Comment
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Comments use double quotes; Expression Quotes use single quotes — distinct syntactic roles

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: alternative — a complex expression can be named as a Tag and used by reference, instead of using Expression Quotes

concepts.definition:
Expression quotes are 'single quotes' at the beginning and end of an expression. They are used to make it clear that this is a *single* expression, using a set of related terms.
*Rationale:* They are useful when the expression is complicated and some doubt could arise as to the expression.
*Note:* These are quite distinct from the "double quotes" used to place comments anywhere in Planguage, and to express Data.
concepts.overview: **Expression Quotes** (*329) are the Planguage convention of using single quotes (`'…'`) to delimit a multi-term expression, signalling that the enclosed terms form a single unified unit rather than a sequence of independent elements. They solve a specific parsing ambiguity: when an expression is complex enough that its boundaries are unclear, wrapping it in single quotes makes the grouping explicit and unambiguous. The critical syntactic distinction is that **double quotes** (`"…"`) serve a different role — they mark Comments and Data. Single-quoted Expression Quotes and double-quoted Comments are not interchangeable.

concepts.name: Expression

relatedConcepts.name: Statement
relatedConcepts.note: container — an Expression is part or all of a Statement; a Statement is made up of one or more Expressions

relatedConcepts.name: Term
relatedConcepts.note: constituent — Expressions are composed of Terms; a Term is the smallest meaningful unit in Planguage

relatedConcepts.name: Definition
relatedConcepts.note: host — a Definition comprises one or more Statements, each made up of Expressions

relatedConcepts.name: Expression Quotes
relatedConcepts.note: delimiter — complex Expressions can be wrapped in single-quote Expression Quotes to make their boundaries explicit

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: naming — a complex Expression can be named as a Tag and referenced by that name in subsequent Expressions

concepts.definition:
A Planguage 'expression' is part or all of a Planguage 'statement': it is one or more related Planguage components of any kind.
Expressions are defined by one or more Planguage terms.
Expressions are comprised of Planguage language concepts. These concepts include: {parameters, icons, tags, qualifiers, sources, fuzzy terms}.
concepts.overview: **Expression** (*302) is the intermediate structural unit of Planguage, sitting between the atomic [[Term.151]] and the complete [[Statement.140]]. An Expression is one or more related Planguage components — parameters, icons, tags, qualifiers, sources, or fuzzy terms — that together form a meaningful unit within a statement. A [[Definition.044]] consists of one or more Statements; each Statement uses one or more Expressions; each Expression is composed of Terms. Once a complex Expression is defined (as when a Tag like `Adaptability` is assigned a full definition), it can itself become a Term in subsequent Expressions — enabling structured, hierarchical specification.

concepts.name: External Stakeholder

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — External Stakeholder is a subtype of Stakeholder, distinguished by direct impact or use of the Focus System

relatedConcepts.name: Internal Stakeholders
relatedConcepts.note: complement — Internal Stakeholders are within the organisation developing the system; External Stakeholders are outside it

relatedConcepts.name: Focus System
relatedConcepts.note: reference system — an External Stakeholder is defined by their relationship to a specific, named Focus System

relatedConcepts.name: User
relatedConcepts.note: example — a product user is a canonical External Stakeholder

relatedConcepts.name: Client
relatedConcepts.note: example — a product customer is a canonical External Stakeholder

relatedConcepts.name: Client Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Client Stakeholder is another defined stakeholder role; may overlap with External Stakeholder

concepts.definition:
External stakeholders are stakeholders which are directly impacted by, or which use, a defined focus system.
For example: a product customer or user is an external stakeholder in relation to that product (a defined focus system).
concepts.overview: **External Stakeholder** (*495) is a subtype of [[Stakeholder.233]] defined by the relationship of impact or use: an External Stakeholder is directly impacted by, or directly uses, a named [[Focus-System.492]]. The "external" in the name refers to position relative to the organisation developing the system — customers, users, regulators, and affected communities are external stakeholders. They are contrasted with [[Internal-Stakeholder.494|Internal Stakeholders]], who are within the developing organisation. The definition is relative to a specific Focus System: the same person may be an External Stakeholder for one system and an Internal Stakeholder for another.

concepts.name: External

relatedConcepts.name: Internal
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — External is outside scope; Internal is inside scope of the given object

relatedConcepts.name: Focus System
relatedConcepts.note: frame — what is External is defined relative to the boundary of the Focus System

relatedConcepts.name: Environment System
relatedConcepts.note: container — External entities belong to the Environment System surrounding the Focus System

relatedConcepts.name: External Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: application — stakeholders who are External to the Focus System boundary

concepts.definition: When describing the relationship amongst objects, **External** is an adjective which applies to any object outside the scope of a given object.
concepts.overview: **External** (*497) is a spatial boundary adjective that classifies an object as lying outside the scope of a given reference object — typically the [[Focus-System.492]]. It is a *place*-scope concept: it asks "where" an object stands relative to the reference system, not "when" or "under what conditions." An external object is not under the direct control of the given object; any influence it exerts is indirect or unpredictable. Degrees of externality exist — some objects are more remote than others.

concepts.name: Facilitator

relatedConcepts.name: Inspection
relatedConcepts.note: context — the Facilitator is particularly associated with quality control processes such as Inspection

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Assurance
relatedConcepts.note: domain — Facilitators support quality assurance processes

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: domain — Facilitators guide quality control processes

concepts.definition: A person or group who assists others in carrying out a work process, such as quality control or setting objectives; by virtue of their being especially trained, qualified, and knowledgeable in that process.
concepts.overview: **Facilitator** (*236) is a Review Role in Planguage — a person or group who enables others to perform a structured work process by virtue of specialised training, qualification, and process knowledge. The Facilitator does not own the work product being reviewed, nor make content decisions; instead, they ensure the process itself is executed correctly. This role is most prominent in quality control processes such as [[Inspection.051b]], but extends to any process where structured guidance is needed — including objectives-setting workshops, design reviews, and requirements reviews. The Facilitator's value lies precisely in being process-expert, not product-expert.

concepts.name: Failure Range

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: boundary — Fail marks the upper bound of the Failure Range (the point where acceptable ends)

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe Range
relatedConcepts.note: below — Catastrophe Range lies below (worse than) the Failure Range

relatedConcepts.name: Acceptable Range
relatedConcepts.note: above — Acceptable Range lies above (better than) the Failure Range; Fail is the shared boundary

relatedConcepts.name: Success Range
relatedConcepts.note: above — Success Range is within or above the Acceptable Range; Failure Range is its opposite

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: structure — Failure Range is a specific instance of the Range concept applied to scalar constraints

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: lower boundary — Survival marks the bottom of the Failure Range, below which is Catastrophe

concepts.definition:
A failure range is a scalar range where some stakeholders will not tolerate the attribute levels. They find the levels unacceptable.
A failure range lies between Acceptable Ranges and Catastrophe Ranges.
concepts.overview: **Failure Range** (*546, icon `!!`) is a Scalar Constraint defining the zone of attribute values that stakeholders find unacceptable but that does not yet constitute total system collapse. It is bounded above by [[Fail.098b]] — the level at which the [[Acceptable-Range.545]] ends — and below by [[Survival.440]] or the [[Catastrophe-Range.603]]. The Failure Range is the engineered warning zone: the system still operates, but it is delivering a degree of failure to some stakeholder. Delivering into the Failure Range is a specification violation and a design obligation to escape. The concept was substantially shaped by HumanAgent Gilb (May 2002) who observed that ranges can be defined either by stakeholders directly, or as compromise requirements aggregating multiple stakeholder ranges.

concepts.name: False

relatedConcepts.name: State
relatedConcepts.note: host — False is a predefined State value in Planguage

concepts.definition: Predefined State. Same as Off.
concepts.overview: **False** (*626) is a predefined [[State.174]] value in Planguage — the binary complement of True (On), equivalent to Off. It is used wherever a specification or evidence parameter needs to represent a binary negative condition: a function is off, a constraint is not met, a boolean attribute holds the negative value. As a predefined State, False reduces ambiguity in specifications that must distinguish between "absent," "zero," "null," and "explicitly off" — False is a named, defined state, not an absence of value.

concepts.name: Feature

relatedConcepts.name: Function
relatedConcepts.note: subset — not all Functions are worth listing as Features; only those perceptible and useful for comparison

relatedConcepts.name: Design Ideas
relatedConcepts.note: subset — not all Designs would be intelligible to stakeholders as Features (too technical); only notable designs qualify

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: subset — Performance attributes become Features only when their levels are noteworthy compared to benchmark systems

relatedConcepts.name: Quality
relatedConcepts.note: subset — Quality attributes become Features when their levels are differentiated from competitive benchmarks

relatedConcepts.name: Prototype
relatedConcepts.note: source anomaly — *187 is listed in the source as 'Cost Attribute'; the vault file at *187 is Prototype.187; no Cost-Attribute file exists — see Anomalies

concepts.definition:
A feature is a class of stakeholder perceptible characteristics of a system, which are useful for comparing against competitive product, service or system benchmarks.
The point being to help stakeholders see that this system is equal, better or different from others. A feature can be performance attributes (easy to learn), cost attributes (cheap to acquire), functions (can send SMS), or designs (uses titanium cover). Features for one set of stakeholders (like repair services) will be different for another set of stakeholders (like consumers).
concepts.overview: **Feature** (*519) is a Component & Object concept identifying a stakeholder-perceptible characteristic of a system that is useful for competitive comparison against benchmark products, services, or systems. A Feature can come from any class of system property — [[Performance.434]], cost, [[Function.069]], or design — but only those characteristics that stakeholders can perceive *and* find relevant for comparison qualify. The concept has a positive connotation: Features are what you highlight to stakeholders when arguing that your system is equal, better, or different from alternatives. Critically, Features are stakeholder-relative: what is a Feature for a consumer is not necessarily a Feature for a repair service.

concepts.name: Feedback

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: source — Feedback is generated from each Evo Step delivery and informs the next

relatedConcepts.name: Evo
relatedConcepts.note: cycle — Feedback is a core component of the Evo cycle: Deliver → Measure → Learn → Next Step

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Plan
relatedConcepts.note: application — Feedback drives decisions in the Evo Plan about next step priorities and scope

relatedConcepts.name: System
relatedConcepts.note: host — Feedback is a System Property; it characterises the information flow around a target system

concepts.definition:
Any form of information, about a defined event, which could potentially be used by any stakeholder, for any set of defined purposes.
**Form of Information:** defined: any sound, picture, text, event, etc., related to the 'Defined Feedback Causal Event', which can be captured, analyzed, and subsequently used, for any purpose, by any stakeholder, or witness.
**Captured:** in any form of 'memory' which allows it to be analyzed.
**Analyzed:** 'made sense of' for any Defined Purpose.
**Used:** applied in a Defined Application, by a Stakeholder, for a Defined Purpose.
concepts.overview: **Feedback** (*693) is a System Property in Planguage — the structured information signal generated by a defined event that can be captured, analyzed, and used by stakeholders for defined purposes. It is not merely a response or a reaction; it is a four-stage process: information is generated by a causal event, captured in some memory form, analyzed for meaning, and used by a stakeholder in a defined application. In the Evolutionary Delivery ([[Evo.355b]]) context, Feedback is the mechanism by which each [[Evo-Step.141]] delivery informs the next: the system is delivered, the Feedback is captured and analyzed, and the next step is shaped by what was learned. As one of the newest Planguage concepts (*693, added August 2024 for the Startup book), it formalises what was previously implicit in Evo thinking.

concepts.name: Fix Probability

relatedConcepts.name: Defect Specification
relatedConcepts.note: target — Fix Probability measures the success rate of attempts to correct Specification Defects

relatedConcepts.name: Fault
relatedConcepts.note: target — Fix Probability also applies to attempts to correct system Faults (bugs)

relatedConcepts.name: Inspection
relatedConcepts.note: context — Fagan Inspection data provides the primary empirical benchmark for Fix Probability

relatedConcepts.name: Error
relatedConcepts.note: root — Fix Probability addresses the probability of successfully removing the consequences of a human Error

concepts.definition: The Fix Probability is the probability that an attempt to correct (fix) a specification defect, or system fault, will succeed.
concepts.overview: **Fix Probability** (*067) is a Defect Metric that quantifies the likelihood that an attempt to correct a [[Defect-Specification.043]] or a system [[Bug.339|Bug / Fault *339]] will actually succeed — without reintroducing a defect or creating a new one. It is an empirical, data-driven metric: Fix Probability should be based on past data about an organisation's ability to remove defects, not assumed to be 1.0. IBM reported a baseline Fix Probability of 5/6 (approximately 83%) for defects found by [[Inspection.051b]] in software engineering documents; with rigorous quality control of each fix, rates approaching 99.9% have been recorded at NASA and IBM. The concept exists to make the risk of defective fixes explicit and measurable.

concepts.name: Focus System

relatedConcepts.name: Environment System
relatedConcepts.note: complement — all systems related to the Focus System but outside its boundary are Environment Systems

relatedConcepts.name: External
relatedConcepts.note: definition — External is defined relative to the Focus System boundary; anything outside is External

relatedConcepts.name: Internal
relatedConcepts.note: definition — Internal is defined relative to the Focus System boundary; anything inside is Internal

relatedConcepts.name: External Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: application — External Stakeholder is defined as a stakeholder outside the Focus System boundary

relatedConcepts.name: Internal Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: application — Internal Stakeholder is defined as a stakeholder inside the Focus System boundary

concepts.definition:
A focus system is the system, or product, we have decided to focus our attention on. All other systems related to it are 'Environment' systems.
The purpose of this concept is to allow us to define a focus on one particular element of a set of related systems.
For example if we are doing a project to develop a product, then that product is likely to be a focus system. All other related engineering and management processes and tools needed to do the project are the environment systems for the focus system.
concepts.overview: **Focus System** (*492) is a System Boundary concept that designates *which system we are currently specifying and designing* — the one system (or product) at the centre of our attention. Everything related to it but outside its boundary is an [[Environment-System.493]]. The Focus System concept is the reference point for all boundary distinctions in Planguage: [[External.497]] is defined as "outside the Focus System boundary"; [[External-Stakeholder.495]] is defined as "a stakeholder outside the Focus System." The Focus System is not fixed — it is a deliberate, context-dependent choice that can shift as the scope of a project or analysis changes. In MIL-STD-499B it is called "System of Interest."

concepts.name: Form

relatedConcepts.name: Template
relatedConcepts.note: close sibling — a Template is a reusable structural scaffold; a Form is a fixed-format data-collection document

relatedConcepts.name: Standard
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Form is a Standard specialised for data collection

relatedConcepts.name: Procedure
relatedConcepts.note: implicit sibling — a Form is an implicit Procedure for data collection

concepts.definition: A **form** is a written document (electronic or paper) that guides people to give specific data with specific content in specific formats, in specific presentation sequences. It is a 'work process standard' for data collection. It is also an implicit 'procedure' for data collection.
concepts.overview: **Form** (*068) is a fixed-format document — electronic or paper — that acts simultaneously as a Standard for data collection and an implicit Procedure for the sequence in which data is gathered. Unlike a Template, which provides a reusable scaffold that may be heavily adapted, a Form enforces a fixed presentation and constrains the responder to provide specific data in a specific order. When an electronic Form acquires user dialogue, conditional branching, and dynamic presentation, it crosses a threshold and becomes a human-computer dialogue rather than a Form in the Planguage sense.

concepts.name: Frontroom

relatedConcepts.name: Backroom
relatedConcepts.note: counterpart — Backroom is what stakeholders do NOT see; Frontroom is what they DO see

relatedConcepts.name: Recipients
relatedConcepts.note: target audience — Frontroom activity is visible to and for Evo step Recipients

relatedConcepts.name: Evo
relatedConcepts.note: methodology context — Frontroom and Backroom are Evo project management concepts

relatedConcepts.name: Result Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: containing cycle — Frontroom is the delivery cycle part of the Evo Result Cycle

concepts.definition: **Frontroom** is an adjective or noun, referring to a conceptual place, used to describe any project management processes or activities, in Evo, that are visible to the Evo step recipients.
concepts.overview: **Frontroom** (*343) is the visible half of an Evo project — the delivery cycle where incremental results are handed to stakeholders, demonstrated, reviewed, and measured. Its counterpart, the [[Backroom.342|Backroom]] (*342), holds the engineering work stakeholders do not see. The Frontroom is where the step is delivered to recipients, where stakeholder-level results are tested and measured, and where the real-world impact of each Evo increment becomes evident. Without a well-managed Frontroom, the engineering discipline of the Backroom has no measurable connection to stakeholder value.

concepts.name: Function Baseline

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Function Baseline is a Benchmark applied to the function dimension

relatedConcepts.name: Baseline
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — Function Baseline is the function-dimension form of Baseline

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar Baseline
relatedConcepts.note: analogue — Function Baseline is analogous to Scalar Baseline but for binary function, not scalar attributes

relatedConcepts.name: Function
relatedConcepts.note: subject — the Function dimension being baselined

relatedConcepts.name: Function Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: complement — a Function Baseline can be integrated with Function Requirements to show proposed changes

concepts.definition: A **function baseline** is an analytical statement of system functionality.
concepts.overview: **Function Baseline** (*489) is a structured statement of the functions that currently exist in a system — a snapshot of the functional capability at a specific point in time (e.g., a product version or a year). It serves two analytical purposes: it documents what an existing system does, and it provides a comparison baseline against which proposed functional changes (in [[Function-Requirement.074|Function Requirements]]) can be evaluated. It is the functional counterpart of the [[Scalar-Baseline.490|Scalar Baseline]] — applied to binary function existence rather than scalar attribute levels.

concepts.name: Function Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Function Constraint is one of the five Constraint sub-types (Function, Performance, Resource, Design, Condition)

relatedConcepts.name: Function
relatedConcepts.note: subject — Function Constraint restricts the function dimension

relatedConcepts.name: Function Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: umbrella class — Function Constraint is the stricter sub-type of Function Requirement (vs. Function Target)

relatedConcepts.name: Function Target
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Function Target is the default, less strict sub-type of Function Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: ancestor class — Function Constraint is ultimately a Requirement

concepts.definition:
A **function constraint** is a requirement which places a restriction on the functionality that may exist in a system.
A function constraint is binary: it specifies that a specific function must be, or must not be, present. The implication is that some kind of failure will result if a function constraint is not met (such as contract penalties).
concepts.overview: **Function Constraint** (*469) is the stricter sub-type of [[Function-Requirement.074|Function Requirement]] — a binary restriction specifying that a function MUST be present or MUST NOT be present, with a named consequence (penalty, breach, failure) if the constraint is not met. Unlike its sibling, the [[Function-Target.420|Function Target]], which expresses a desired function without an associated penalty, a Function Constraint is enforced: non-compliance is not an option. It is one of the five sub-types of [[Constraint.218|Constraint]] (*218), alongside Performance, Resource, Design, and Condition Constraints.

concepts.name: Function Design

relatedConcepts.name: Function
relatedConcepts.note: target dimension — Function Design primarily aims to satisfy Function requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Function Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: requirement counterpart — Function Design is selected to satisfy Function Requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Design Process
relatedConcepts.note: process context — Function Design is produced through the Design Process

relatedConcepts.name: Design Specification
relatedConcepts.note: parent form — Function Design is a specialised Design Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Cost Design
relatedConcepts.note: sibling design type — same multiple-impact principle; Function Design also affects cost

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint Design
relatedConcepts.note: sibling design type — any Function Design also impacts Constraint requirements as a side effect

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Design
relatedConcepts.note: sibling design type — Function Design also affects Performance as a side effect

concepts.definition:
**Function design** is a design primarily aimed at satisfying specified function requirements.
A specified function design has two characteristics, which we primarily select it for:
- function requirement satisfaction, and
- satisfactory consequent levels of performance and cost attributes.
concepts.overview: **Function Design** (*521) is a [[Design-Specification.586|Design Specification]] whose primary purpose is to satisfy [[Function-Requirement.074|Function Requirements]] — the *what* a system must do. But no design is purely functional: any Function Design, once implemented, simultaneously affects Performance, Cost, and Constraint requirements, whether intended or not. This **multiple-impact principle** is the defining insight of the Function Design concept: you select a design on its function-satisfying properties, but you must verify its consequent performance and cost impacts before committing. Function Design sits alongside [[Cost-Design.522|Cost Design]], [[Performance-Design.520|Performance Design]], and [[Constraint-Design.523|Constraint Design]] as one of the four design-type siblings in the Planguage design taxonomy.

concepts.name: Function Requirement
concepts.keyedIcon: (Function Tag) — parentheses symbolise the oval icon; alternative O.@

relatedConcepts.name: Function
relatedConcepts.note: subject — Function Requirement specifies the Function dimension

relatedConcepts.name: Function Target
relatedConcepts.note: default sub-type — specific, testable Function Requirement without a penalty clause

relatedConcepts.name: Function Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: strict sub-type — Function Requirement with a penalty clause (must/must not)

relatedConcepts.name: Function Design
relatedConcepts.note: design counterpart — Function Design satisfies Function Requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Function Baseline
relatedConcepts.note: analytic complement — Function Baseline states current state; Function Requirement states future state

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Function Requirement is a binary Requirement

concepts.definition:
A **function requirement** specifies that the presence or absence of a defined function is required.
A function requirement is binary, and can either be a specific function target or a generic function constraint.
concepts.overview: **Function Requirement** (*074) is the umbrella class for all binary requirements on the [[Function.069|Function]] dimension — specifying that a defined function must or must not be present in a system. It has two sub-types: [[Function-Target.420|Function Target]] (*420), which is the default (specific, testable, no penalty clause), and [[Function-Constraint.469|Function Constraint]] (*469), which is the strict form (must/must not, with a failure consequence). A Function Requirement is satisfied by *any* design that meets the function description — the specific design is separate from the requirement. Design ideas should not appear in a Function Requirement; if a design is mandatory, it is a [[Design-Constraint.181|Design Constraint]], not a Function Requirement.

concepts.name: Function Target

relatedConcepts.name: Function Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: umbrella class — Function Target is the default sub-type of Function Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Function Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Function Constraint is the strict sub-type of Function Requirement (with penalty clause)

relatedConcepts.name: Target
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — Function Target is a Target applied to the Function dimension

relatedConcepts.name: Function
relatedConcepts.note: subject — the Function being targeted

relatedConcepts.name: Function Design
relatedConcepts.note: design counterpart — Function Design is selected to satisfy a Function Target

concepts.definition:
A **function target** is a specific qualified function requirement type.
A function target is a specific testable function; it is not generic, nor is it a function constraint.
concepts.overview: **Function Target** (*420) is the default sub-type of [[Function-Requirement.074|Function Requirement]] — the specific, testable, qualifier-scoped form of a binary function specification. Unlike its sibling [[Function-Constraint.469|Function Constraint]] (*469), a Function Target carries no explicit penalty clause: it is desired, it is testable, it can be qualified with conditions, but its absence does not automatically constitute a breach. By default, any Function Requirement without an explicit constraint declaration is assumed to be a Function Target. The keyed icon `O.@` (oval with qualifier tag) signals specificity: this is not a generic function concept but a qualified, testable instance.

concepts.name: Function, To

relatedConcepts.name: Function
relatedConcepts.note: noun counterpart — Function *069 is what a system does; 'to function' is the verb form expressing active performance of it

relatedConcepts.name: Function (adjective)
relatedConcepts.note: grammatical sibling — Function-adjective *556 is the modifier form of the same root concept

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: scalar mechanism — 'to function' requires at least Survival-level performance and cost

concepts.definition: 'To **function**' means to carry out the defined functions of a system under the defined conditions, at least at survival level or better, for performance and cost.
concepts.overview: **Function, To** (*557) is the verb form of the [[Function.069|Function]] concept — expressing what it means for a system to *actively perform* its defined functions. It completes a grammatical triple with [[Function.069|Function]] (*069, noun) and [[Function-adjective.556|Function (adjective)]] (*556, modifier). The critical qualifier in the definition is "at least at survival level or better": a system does not "function" in the Planguage sense if it merely executes its defined activities while performing at an unacceptable level. To function is to execute the defined functions *and* maintain minimum acceptable performance and cost — the [[Survival.440|Survival]] threshold.

concepts.name: Function (adjective)

relatedConcepts.name: Function
relatedConcepts.note: noun counterpart — Function *069 is the noun form; Function (adjective) *556 is the modifier form restricting a noun to the function domain

relatedConcepts.name: Function, To
relatedConcepts.note: grammatical sibling — Function-To *557 is the verb form of the same root concept

relatedConcepts.note: primary example — 'Function' as an adjective modifying 'Constraint' restricts it to the function domain

relatedConcepts.name: Function Requirement

relatedConcepts.note: primary example — 'Function' as an adjective modifying 'Design' restricts it to the function domain

concepts.definition: A **function adjective** is used to restrict the modified noun (constraint as in function constraint) to the function area.
concepts.overview: **Function (adjective)** (*556) is the modifier form of the [[Function.069|Function]] concept — the adjective "function" placed before a noun to restrict that noun to the function domain. It completes a grammatical triple with [[Function.069|Function]] (*069, noun) and [[Function-To.557|Function, To]] (*557, verb). Examples of the adjective in use: [[Function-Constraint.469|Function Constraint]] (*469), [[Function-Requirement.074|Function Requirement]] (*074), [[Function-Design.521|Function Design]] (*521), [[Function-Baseline.489|Function Baseline]] (*489), [[Function-Target.420|Function Target]] (*420). Note that Tom explicitly chose "function" (not "functional") as the adjective form, for the same reason he chose "quality" rather than "qualitative" — the adjective should express the requirement *for* the noun, not make the noun "functional."

relatedConcepts.name: Attribute
relatedConcepts.note: peer relationship — Function is one of the four system attributes (alongside Performance, Resource/Cost, and Design)

relatedConcepts.name: Design Idea
relatedConcepts.note: distinguished from — Function is abstract ('what'); Design Idea is concrete ('how')

relatedConcepts.name: Mission

relatedConcepts.name: Function Design

relatedConcepts.note: requirement form — Function Requirement specifies that a Function must be present or absent

concepts.definition:
A **function** is 'what' a system does.
A function is a binary concept, and is always expressed in action ('to do') terms (for example, 'to span a gap' and 'to manage a process').
concepts.overview: **Function** (*069) is the binary, abstract specification of *what* a system does — expressed always in action terms, never in terms of design. Function is one of the four system attributes in Planguage (alongside Performance, Resource/Cost, and Design); it is the only one that is binary: a function is either implemented or not. Every function implies a purpose ([[Mission.097|Mission]]), and every implemented function carries associated Performance and Cost attributes — whether planned or not. Function must be clearly distinguished from [[Design-Ideas.047c|Design Ideas]]: the design is *how* the system delivers the function; the function is *what* it delivers. Function is the root concept for a family of related terms: [[Function-Requirement.074|Function Requirement]] (*074), [[Function-Target.420|Function Target]] (*420), [[Function-Constraint.469|Function Constraint]] (*469), [[Function-Design.521|Function Design]] (*521), [[Function-Baseline.489|Function Baseline]] (*489), [[Function-adjective.556|Function (adjective)]] (*556), and [[Function-To.557|Function, To]] (*557).

concepts.name: Fundamental Constraints

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Fundamental Constraints are the highest-authority subset of all Constraints

relatedConcepts.name: Generic Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: Strategic Constraints support Fundamental Constraints; set at the organisational responsibility level

relatedConcepts.name: Level
relatedConcepts.note: Fundamental Constraints come from a higher level than the receiving unit

relatedConcepts.name: Local
relatedConcepts.note: Means Constraints — set by instances supporting the strategic/fundamental level

relatedConcepts.name: Limit
relatedConcepts.note: keyed icon identical — a Limit is the canonical expression of a Fundamental Constraint on a scalar attribute

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Constraints
relatedConcepts.note: Strategic Constraints support Fundamental Constraints one level down

relatedConcepts.name: Fundamental Objective
relatedConcepts.note: structural parallel — Fundamental Objectives are the objective-side equivalent of Fundamental Constraints

concepts.definition: A 'given'. Fundamental Constraints are constraints that are handed down to us from higher authority. They are fundamental if we choose not to question them, but to heed them without question or alteration.
concepts.overview: **Fundamental Constraints** (*426) are the highest-authority constraints in a requirements hierarchy — given to a team or organisation from above and accepted without negotiation or alteration. They define the outer boundary within which all other design, planning, and specification must occur. Their canonical graphic expression is the Limit icon `----[----]----`, which is identical to the keyed icon for *606 Limit. They contrast with Strategic Constraints (*427), which a team *sets* at its own level of responsibility, and Local/Means Constraints (*376), which are set by subordinate instances. A Fundamental Constraint may not be the only constraint in force — conflicting authorities can issue different fundamental constraints, potentially without knowing of each other's existence.

concepts.name: Fundamental Objective

relatedConcepts.name: Means Objective
relatedConcepts.note: Means Objectives support Strategic Objectives in order to reach Fundamental Objectives — the bottom of the design hierarchy

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Objective
relatedConcepts.note: Strategic Objectives are strategies for reaching Fundamental Objectives — set by the receiving unit itself

relatedConcepts.name: Essential Objective
relatedConcepts.note: Essential Objective (*231) is a separate Gilb concept — not the same as Fundamental Objective (*229)

relatedConcepts.name: Fundamental Constraints
relatedConcepts.note: structural parallel — Fundamental Constraints are the constraint-side equivalent of Fundamental Objectives

relatedConcepts.name: Fundamental Objective
relatedConcepts.note: coined by Keeney [KEENEY92]

concepts.definition: Fundamental Objectives are 'givens'. They are what we are trying to support and impact by reaching 'strategic objectives'. They form the top level of a relative hierarchy of objectives. They are the given objectives handed down to 'us' from above.
concepts.overview: **Fundamental Objective** (*229) is the highest level in a relative hierarchy of objectives — the goals handed down from above that a team or unit must serve without questioning them. Fundamental Objectives define *why* we are doing the work at all; they cannot be justified by appeal to any higher internal objective because, as Keeney puts it, "it is important simply because it is important." All Strategic Objectives and Means Objectives exist only as design choices to reach the Fundamental Objectives. The term was coined by Keeney (1992) and adopted into Planguage; it should not be confused with Gilb's separate concept of Essential Objective (*231).

concepts.name: Funder

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Funder is a Stakeholder role defined by providing financial or other resources

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: Funders provide Resources (money or other) that make projects possible

relatedConcepts.name: Priority
relatedConcepts.note: Funders typically have strong Priority influence — they control whether the project continues

concepts.definition: One who provides money, or other resources, for a project.
concepts.overview: **Funder** (*344) is a Stakeholder role defined entirely by the act of providing Resources — money or other tangible resources — to make a project possible. The Funder holds significant implicit authority over project continuation, scope, and priority, because withdrawal of funding ends the project. In Planguage, a Funder is a Stakeholder whose interests and constraints must be formally specified: they are not merely a budget source but a party with Objectives, Constraints, and priority influence on the system being designed.

concepts.name: Fuzzy

relatedConcepts.name: Generic
relatedConcepts.note: Generic specifications use fuzzy brackets as fill-in-the-blank template placeholders

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: Fuzzy is a status marker on a Specification — flagging a known defect in the spec text

relatedConcepts.name: Authority
relatedConcepts.note: A fuzzy specification lacks the Authority to be treated as final or binding

concepts.definition: A specification, which is known to be somewhat unclear, potentially incorrect or incomplete, is called 'fuzzy'. It should be clearly declared as 'fuzzy'. The keyed icons '< >' are used to explicitly mark any fuzzy specifications.
concepts.overview: **Fuzzy** (*080) is a Status and Maturity Parameter — a declaration by a specification author that a particular statement is known to be unclear, potentially incorrect, or incomplete. The `< >` angle-bracket icons mark the problematic text so that readers are not misled and authors are not allowed to forget. A fuzzy specification is not a placeholder to be ignored; it is an explicit quality debt marker that demands resolution. In templates, fuzzy brackets serve double duty as fill-in-the-blank hints to future editors. The obligation to mark dubious content as fuzzy is typically adopted as a generic specification rule across an entire project or organisation.

concepts.name: Gaming

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: Gaming is a Stakeholder behaviour — the manipulating party is a Stakeholder with misaligned incentives

relatedConcepts.name: Measure
relatedConcepts.note: Gaming targets Measures — it is the manipulation of measurements or the requirements they derive from

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: Gaming subverts Requirements by manipulating how they are set or evaluated

concepts.definition: Conscious manipulation of requirements or evaluations so as to achieve special aims.
concepts.overview: **Gaming** (*241) is the deliberate, self-interested manipulation of requirements, measurements, or evaluation criteria to achieve outcomes that serve the manipulating party rather than the system's actual objectives. It is classified as a System Property — a behavioural property of the human/social system that surrounds and operates on a technical system. Gaming is not accidental misunderstanding; it is conscious distortion. In Planguage, precise, quantified requirements with independent measurement are the primary countermeasure: it is far harder to game a requirement that specifies a measurable scale, a defined benchmark, and an explicit acceptance test than one expressed in vague qualitative terms.

concepts.name: Gap

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: A Gap is a Range — specifically from a current level or impact estimate to a target or constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Design Problem
relatedConcepts.note: A Gap defines a new Design Problem — the need to close it drives design activity

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: The Gap typically runs from the Benchmark (current level) to the Goal or Fail level

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: The target end of a Gap is often a Goal level — closing the Gap means reaching the Goal

relatedConcepts.name: Priority
relatedConcepts.note: Gap size is a primary input to Priority — the larger the Gap, the higher the general claim on project resources

concepts.definition: For a scalar attribute, a Gap is the range from either an impact estimate, or a specific Benchmark (usually the current level), to a specific target (or occasionally, to a specific constraint).
concepts.overview: **Gap** (*359) is the quantified distance on a scalar attribute scale between where a system currently is (or where it is estimated to be) and where it needs to be (a Goal, a Fail level, or a Constraint). A Gap is not merely an observation — it is a claim on project resources: the larger the Gap, the higher the general priority to address it. When a Gap reaches zero, the attribute ceases to have priority and makes no further claim on resources. The synonym 'Residue' captures the same idea from a progress perspective — the residue is what remains of the Gap after some design progress has been made.

concepts.name: Generate

relatedConcepts.name: Combine
relatedConcepts.note: Antonym — Combine/Condense/Reduce To/Simplify/Summarize; icon '}' (many→one); Generate is one→many

concepts.definition: 'Generate' is a relationship concept. It relates things that produce other things. Keyed icon: 'A { B' means 'A Generates B'. There is an implication that the Generator (A) continues to exist after it has generated ({) something (B).
concepts.overview: **Generate** (*392) is a directional relationship concept meaning 'one thing produces one or more other things, while continuing to exist itself.' The keyed icon is `{` (left curly brace), read as 'generates' or 'spawns.' It is the antonym of Combine (*393), which uses `}` (right curly brace) for many-to-one condensation. The distinction from `=>` (Before/Sequence) is precise: `A => B` means A precedes B in time, without implying A created B or that A still exists. `A { B` means A actively generates B, and A persists. The curly brace set notation `{b, c}` naturally extends to express one generator producing multiple outputs.

concepts.name: Generic Attribute Level Icon

relatedConcepts.name: Attribute Level Icon Point
relatedConcepts.note: The Generic Attribute Level Icon (--|--) is drawn at an Icon Point (*252) on the attribute arrow

relatedConcepts.name: Attribute

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Goal (---->---) is another specific variant; the Generic icon is used when Goal vs. Benchmark is unspecified

concepts.definition: A neutral graphic symbol, `(---|---)`, for a numeric level of a performance or cost attribute. The Generic symbol is used in place of unknown, undetermined or uninteresting specific symbols of attribute priority or character; such as any Benchmark (example `---<<--`) or Target (example `---->---`).
concepts.overview: **Generic Attribute Level Icon** (*251) is the neutral `--|--` mark drawn at an Icon Point (*252) on a Planguage attribute scale arrow to indicate *some* numeric level of the attribute without committing to what *type* of level it is. It is the visual placeholder used when the level is known but its classification (Benchmark? Goal? Fail? Wish?) is either unknown, undetermined, or irrelevant in context. The vertical bar `|` is the minimal keyed form; the fuller `--|--` is the iconic form. Both are drawn at one or more positions along the attribute arrow `---->O------>` to indicate where levels fall on the scale.

concepts.name: Generic Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — 'applies to defined scope, and will be tailored locally

relatedConcepts.name: Generic
relatedConcepts.note: defined scope, reusable, tailored, local interpretation

relatedConcepts.name: Fundamental Constraints
relatedConcepts.note: Of basic unquestionable authority and priority — a Generic Constraint may also be Fundamental

relatedConcepts.note: Derivative Source (*450) is a Generic Constraint's generic name — the authority name from which local constraints are derived

concepts.definition: A Generic Constraint applies to a defined scope. It is tailored in interpretation or specification at the detailed level.
concepts.overview: **Generic Constraint** (*245) is a constraint that applies across a defined scope — such as a product line, a contract, or a legal jurisdiction — and requires local tailoring when applied to a specific project, product, or component. It "draws a border" around what is permissible, but allows more specific requirements to be defined inside that border. Generic Constraints typically originate from powerful stakeholders (regulators, corporate policy, large customers) and are generally non-negotiable; however, they must be analysed for conflicts and consequences. A Generic Constraint may simultaneously be a Fundamental Constraint (received from a higher authority) and a Global Constraint (applying across the entire system scope). Note: concept number *245 is shared with Global Constraint — a polysemy case.

concepts.name: Generic Qualifier

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: Scale Qualifiers are a specific type of Generic Qualifier — for use with Scale definitions.

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: The root parameter: a qualifier restricts the scope under which a specification applies.

relatedConcepts.name: Generic
relatedConcepts.note: The root adjective: applicable across a broad class of things, intended for decomposition into specific instances.

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier Conditions
relatedConcepts.note: Scale-Qualifier-Conditions (*666) are the result of decomposing generic qualifier sets.

concepts.definition: A Generic Qualifier is a set of higher level concepts, which are going to be decomposed into specific subsets and combinations, for use as qualifiers for any Planguage statement. Scale Qualifiers are a particular type (for Scale) of Generic Qualifiers.
concepts.overview: **Generic Qualifier** (*668) is a named set of higher-level qualifier dimensions that will be decomposed into specific combinations when applied to particular Planguage statements. It functions like a decomposition framework: the first declaration of a generic qualifier announces *which axes of variation* will be used (e.g. Country, City, Product Line, Service Level), and subsequent specifications then fill in specific combinations of values along those axes. [[Scale-Qualifier.381|Scale Qualifiers]] (*381) are the specific type of Generic Qualifier used with Scale definitions; the broader concept applies to any Planguage statement. Generic Qualifiers make decomposition strategies explicit and traceable.

concepts.name: Generic Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Generic Objectives
relatedConcepts.note: Polysemy — same concept number *216 is shared with Generic Objectives (Generic-Objectives.216). 'Generic Objective' was coined by Keeney (KEENEY92). Both concepts describe reusable generic requirements; separate files per concept-number-reuse rules.

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: Generic Requirement is a type of Requirement — one intended for reuse across many systems.

relatedConcepts.name: Generic
relatedConcepts.note: The root adjective: applicable across a broad class of things, reusable with tailoring.

relatedConcepts.name: Template
relatedConcepts.note: A generic requirement can be expressed as a template — a model to be filled in for a specific system.

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: Scale Qualifiers are a powerful tactic for specifying generic requirements — they provide the parameterisable dimensions.

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: Generic requirements can be of type Constraint — one of the noted sub-types.

concepts.definition: A generic requirement is one intended for potential use in many systems or sub-systems. It is always reusable, and often tailorable.
concepts.overview: **Generic Requirement** (*216) is a requirement written at a level of generality that makes it applicable — as-is or with local tailoring — across many systems or sub-systems. Rather than specifying a requirement tightly to one project, a generic requirement provides a reusable template that any relevant project can adopt. The term 'Generic Objective' (coined by Keeney, KEENEY92) is a close synonym, and both share concept number *216 in the Planguage source. The key enabling mechanism is the use of [[Scale-Qualifier.381|Scale Qualifiers]] — bracketed generic terms that stand for parameterisable dimensions, making the requirement a structured template rather than a fixed specification.

concepts.name: Generic Standard

relatedConcepts.name: Template
relatedConcepts.note: A generic standard can be expressed as a template — a model to be copied and filled out. Not all generic standards are templates (some are forms, lists, or models).

relatedConcepts.name: Work Process Standard
relatedConcepts.note: A work process standard is an 'official' written specification guiding engineers in a process. A generic standard is a reusable form of such a standard.

relatedConcepts.name: Generic
relatedConcepts.note: The adjective 'generic' means applicable across a broad class of things — the root property that makes a standard 'generic'.

relatedConcepts.name: Generic Term
relatedConcepts.note: Generic standards often contain generic terms — bracketed placeholders that must be defined when the standard is applied.

concepts.definition: A 'generic' standard is an example, model, specification, form, or template of a work process standard, which can then be tailored, or applied without tailoring, by their user to suit their purposes.
concepts.overview: **Generic Standard** (*150) is a reusable specification artefact — a standard expressed at the generic level so that it can be adopted by an organisation, team, or project either directly or with local tailoring. A generic standard is the master template from which many specific process standards are derived. It differs from a mere [[Template.254|Template]] in that it may take any form (a form, a list, a model, a procedure) — not just a fill-in document. The Planguage glossary itself contains generic standards: forms for Meters, Policies, and other artefacts that practitioners are explicitly intended to use, read, or teach from directly.

concepts.name: Generic Term

relatedConcepts.name: Specific
relatedConcepts.note: Specific' means applicable to a limited, specified set of things.

relatedConcepts.name: Generic
relatedConcepts.note: Generic means applicable to a large group or set of things — the root adjective.

relatedConcepts.name: Defined Term
relatedConcepts.note: A set of words and/or symbols (including icons) with a Planguage-defined meaning.

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: Scale Qualifiers are one example of generic terms — placeholders in a Scale definition.

relatedConcepts.name: Generic Standard
relatedConcepts.note: A generic standard (e.g. a template for a 'User Reaction' definition) uses generic terms as placeholders.

concepts.definition: A generic term is a Term in a Specification that needs further definition, there or elsewhere.
concepts.overview: **Generic Term** (*377) is a placeholder in a Planguage specification — a bracketed label that stands for a class of values that must be defined either locally (in the same spec) or globally (in a project glossary or generic standard). The most common examples are the bracketed labels in Scale Qualifier definitions, such as `[People]`, `[Faults]`, and `[Time Limits]` in a User Reaction scale. A generic term separates the *structure* of a specification from its *particular instance values*, enabling a single generic template to be applied to many specific contexts by substituting each generic term with concrete definitions. Until a generic term is defined, the specification is incomplete.

concepts.name: Generic

relatedConcepts.name: Specific
relatedConcepts.note: The opposite: applicable to a limited, specified set of things.

relatedConcepts.name: Generic Term
relatedConcepts.note: A term in a specification that is generic and needs further definition.

relatedConcepts.name: Generic Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: A requirement that is generic — intended for reuse across many systems.

relatedConcepts.name: Generic Standard
relatedConcepts.note: A standard expressed as a generic template for tailoring.

concepts.definition: Generic means *applicable to any individual component* of a group of components within a defined scope. Generic means general, as opposed to specific. 'Generic' things are often 'reusable' (with local tailoring that makes them more specific) in a variety of situations.
concepts.overview: **Generic** (*081) is the Planguage adjective applied to any specification element — rule, process, requirement, standard, term — that is designed for reuse across multiple systems, situations, or contexts rather than being tied to a single specific instance. The opposite of Generic is [[Specific.136|Specific]]. The key motivation is reuse: one well-crafted generic rule or requirement, applied (with local tailoring) across many contexts, is far preferable to duplicating nearly-identical definitions and then struggling to keep them consistent. Generic is a *characterisation* of scope, not a weakness of precision.

concepts.name: Gist

relatedConcepts.name: Ambition
relatedConcepts.note: When summarising a *scalar* specification, use Ambition rather than Gist. Ambition is the scalar-specific version of Gist.

concepts.definition: A Gist parameter is used to state the essence, or main point, of a specification. A Gist is a summary of the detailed specification.
concepts.overview: **Gist** (*157) is a Planguage description parameter that captures the essence of a specification in a single compact statement — before or alongside the full detail. It serves two engineering purposes: first, it enables a planning group to agree on *what the specification is about* before investing effort in precise detail; second, it gives readers a navigable summary that allows them to decide whether to read further. The keyed icon is `∑` (Greek sigma — the mathematical summation symbol, used as 'summary'). For *scalar* specifications, the more specific parameter [[Ambition.423|Ambition]] (*423) should be used instead of Gist.

concepts.name: Global

relatedConcepts.name: Local
relatedConcepts.note: The opposite: applies to a specific, limited set of components within the scope.

relatedConcepts.name: Inherited
relatedConcepts.note: A Global specification is inherited by all sub-components within its declared scope — Inherited (*516) is the result.

relatedConcepts.name: Attached Specification
relatedConcepts.note: Attached-Specification (*517) distinguishes Global, Local, and Inherited as three modes of specification attachment.

relatedConcepts.name: Global Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: A Constraint declared as Global — the most common use of the Global adjective in practice.

concepts.definition: 'Global' is an adjective used to specify that something applies to all (each individual component) of the set of components within the specified scope.
concepts.overview: **Global** (*375) is the Planguage scope adjective indicating that a specification applies across *every individual component* within a declared scope — not just a selected subset. It is the complement of [[Local.376|Local]] (*376), which applies to a specific limited set. When a specification is declared Global, it is automatically [[Inherited.516|Inherited]] (*516) by all sub-components within that scope — each component must satisfy the global requirement unless a higher-priority specification overrides it. Global is not absolute ('applies to the whole universe') but *scope-wide* ('applies to everything within the declared scope boundary'). The most common practical form is the [[Global-Constraint.245b|Global Constraint]] (*245).

concepts.name: Goal Step

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: An Evo Step is the incremental delivery unit. A Goal Step is the intermediate target level to be reached at or after that step.

relatedConcepts.name: Incremental Impact
relatedConcepts.note: The change in a scalar attribute produced by an Evo Step — the measured difference between Now and the Goal Step target.

relatedConcepts.name: Now
relatedConcepts.note: The current measured level of the attribute — the starting point from which Goal Steps progress.

relatedConcepts.name: Delivered Level
relatedConcepts.note: The measured level after an Evo Step is complete — what actually resulted, compared against the Goal Step target.

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: The ultimate committed target on the performance axis. Goal Steps are intermediate waypoints toward the Goal.

concepts.definition: A goal step is an intermediate target level on the way to an agreed goal level.
concepts.overview: **Goal Step** (*620) is a scalar target that marks a planned intermediate level of performance to be achieved at the end of a specific [[Evo-Step.141|Evo Step]] — a waypoint on the path from the current [[Now.513|Now level]] (*513) to the ultimate [[Goal.109|Goal]] (*109). In incremental development, it is rarely feasible or economical to jump directly from the current level to the final committed Goal in one delivery step. Goal Steps divide the journey into measurable, achievable increments. The keyed icon `')'` visualises this as an intermediate arrow point in the progress diagram (e.g. `-----')--->)`), showing the system advancing in stages. After each Evo Step, the [[Delivered-Level.533|Delivered Level]] (*533) is measured against the Goal Step to determine whether the step succeeded.

concepts.name: Goal

relatedConcepts.name: Acceptable Range
relatedConcepts.note: Goal is the upper bound of the Acceptable Range (Tolerable Range in STG) — the committed level that, when reached, constitutes success.

relatedConcepts.name: Tolerable
relatedConcepts.note: Tolerable is the lower STG threshold (project-viability); Goal is the upper STG threshold (success). The Tolerable Range spans between them.

relatedConcepts.name: StatusToGoal
relatedConcepts.note: the gap from current Status to this Goal level — measures the remaining distance to declared success

relatedConcepts.name: Success Range
relatedConcepts.note: Success Range begins at Goal level — reaching Goal declares success and places the attribute in the Success Range with no further improvement priority

concepts.definition: A Goal is a primary numeric target level of performance.
concepts.overview:
A **Goal** is the *committed* performance level a system will deliver.
It sits between `Fail` (must clear) and `Stretch` (would be nice) on the performance axis.

concepts.name: Grammar

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: Grammar is the rule system of Planguage — the language whose rules Grammar defines

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Language
relatedConcepts.note: Grammar operates within the broader specification language context

relatedConcepts.name: Symbol
relatedConcepts.note: Symbols are elements governed by Grammar rules

concepts.definition: Implicit: Planguage grammar. The system of rules used by Planguage users to form statements and larger constructions or relations from Planguage elements. The rules for Planguage.
concepts.overview: **Grammar** (*160) is the rule system governing how Planguage elements may be combined into valid statements, specifications, and constructions. It defines the legal syntax of Planguage — what can be said, how parameters relate to each other, and how elements may be nested or sequenced. Grammar is implicit in most Planguage use: practitioners follow its rules without necessarily naming the parameter. When referenced explicitly, Grammar names the governing syntactic framework of the Planguage specification language itself. Knowing the Grammar is the prerequisite for writing unambiguous, parseable specifications.

concepts.name: Guideline

relatedConcepts.name: Standard
relatedConcepts.note: Standard is stronger than a Guideline — Standards are mandatory; Guidelines are advisory

relatedConcepts.name: Note
relatedConcepts.note: Note is weaker than a Guideline — Guidelines carry more authority than Notes

relatedConcepts.name: Priority
relatedConcepts.note: Priority parameter can qualify the relative importance of a Guideline

relatedConcepts.name: Authority
relatedConcepts.note: Authority parameter specifies whose guidance a Guideline carries

concepts.definition:
A guideline is a specific written piece of advice, a recommendation, a tip, a hint, a suggestion, or a warning. It can be found in a specification, but is often placed into a set of guidelines, which are more widely available (sometimes held alongside the standards documentation).
Guidelines are not standards; they do not have absolute power. Their qualifiers and other parameters, such as 'Authority' and 'Priority' can give more information as to their individual priority.
concepts.overview: **Guideline** (*460) is the Planguage advisory concept that sits between a Note (*018) and a Standard (*138) in strength. It is written advice, a recommendation, a tip, a hint, a suggestion, or a warning — strong enough to deserve formal documentation but not strong enough to be mandatory. Guidelines often appear in separate guideline sets alongside standards documentation, giving practitioners easy access to advisory content without conflating it with binding requirements. The Authority and Priority parameters allow individual Guidelines to be graduated: some carry more weight than others, and their source can be explicitly identified.

concepts.name: Handbook Variant

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: Handbook Variant is a customised version of the Planguage Handbook for a particular context

relatedConcepts.name: Grammar
relatedConcepts.note: A Handbook Variant may extend or restrict standard Planguage Grammar

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Language
relatedConcepts.note: The Handbook Variant defines the local specification language variant in use

concepts.definition: A variation of the Planguage Handbook made for a particular organization, or language.
concepts.overview: **Handbook Variant** (*201) is an organisation-specific or language-specific adaptation of the standard Planguage Handbook. Where the canonical Planguage Handbook defines the full language for general use, a Handbook Variant tailors it — restricting, extending, or localising — for a specific organisational context, industry domain, or natural language. This is the formal mechanism by which organisations adopt Planguage without being forced to use every feature of the full language, and by which teams working in non-English environments can document the local terminology. A Handbook Variant is a legitimate, designed artefact, not an informal deviation.

concepts.name: Hierarchical

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: Hierarchical Tag Names use dot-separated Tag sequences to locate items in a specification hierarchy

relatedConcepts.name: High-Level
relatedConcepts.note: High-Level describes position in a Hierarchical structure

relatedConcepts.name: System
relatedConcepts.note: Systems are commonly described using Hierarchical decomposition structures

concepts.definition: Hierarchical is an adjective used to describe 'belonging to a hierarchy'. The elements of a hierarchy can be organized by some classification into distinct levels, where there is a relationship between the levels. Either the higher levels have some kind of authority or control over lower levels, or decomposition occurs down the hierarchy (the higher levels can be broken down into their lower-level sub-components).
concepts.overview: **Hierarchical** (*083) is the Planguage adjective for anything that belongs to a hierarchy — a structure organised into distinct levels where higher levels either have authority over lower levels, or decompose into them. In systems engineering, hierarchical structures appear in three important forms: organisational hierarchies (management authority), process hierarchies (sub-process decomposition), and specification hierarchies (from system name down to individual attributes). Planguage uses hierarchical tag names to locate specifications in these structures. The concept cautions that "higher level" is relative to a specific hierarchy — there is no universal notion of what is high or low without naming the hierarchy.

concepts.name: High-Level

relatedConcepts.name: Upstream
relatedConcepts.note: Upstream is often used as a more precise alternative — specifying that something is earlier in the process chain

relatedConcepts.name: Downstream
relatedConcepts.note: Downstream is the complementary directional concept — further along in the process or hierarchy

relatedConcepts.name: Priority
relatedConcepts.note: High-Level does not imply high Priority — the two must not be conflated

relatedConcepts.name: Authority
relatedConcepts.note: High-Level is often mistakenly used to mean high Authority — use Authority parameter instead

relatedConcepts.name: Hierarchical
relatedConcepts.note: High-Level describes a position near the top of a Hierarchical structure

concepts.definition:
'High-level' refers to a position that is 'high' (that is, closer to the top than the bottom) in any specified hierarchy of system components.
Since a given hierarchy can be made using any arbitrary top and bottom notions, the reference applies only to a given hierarchy, and is not universal for the system.
concepts.overview: **High-Level** (*082) describes a position near the top of a specified hierarchy. It is a relative term — what is "high-level" in one hierarchy may be "low-level" in another, because hierarchies can be constructed with arbitrary top and bottom notions. Tom Gilb explicitly discourages use of "high-level" in specifications: it is too imprecise, and specific reference to the actual component or person is always preferable. "High-level" does not automatically mean high priority in implementation terms. The concept exists to give practitioners a vocabulary for the term so they can identify and eliminate it from specifications where precision is required.

concepts.name: Historic Level

relatedConcepts.name: Past
relatedConcepts.note: Past is one of the two sub-concepts of Historic Level — the previously measured value of an attribute

relatedConcepts.name: Record
relatedConcepts.note: Record is one of the two sub-concepts of Historic Level — the best-ever measured value of an attribute

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: Historic Level is a type of Benchmark — a reference point from measured history

relatedConcepts.name: Trend
relatedConcepts.note: Trend is a forward-looking benchmark excluded from Historic Level — Historic Level is past-only
