concepts.definition:
A joint term for the two Benchmark level specifications of attributes, Past and Record.
Note: this does not include Trend and Future, which are benchmarks related to the future and are not in themselves historic.
Source notation: `*084 = {*<Past>. *<Record>}`
concepts.overview: **Historic Level** (*084) is a collective term for the two backward-looking scalar benchmarks used to contextualise attribute specifications: **Past** (*106) — the previously measured level of an attribute — and **Record** (*127) — the best-ever measured level. Together they provide the historical reference frame for understanding current performance and setting meaningful targets. Historic Level explicitly excludes forward-looking benchmarks (Trend, Future), which are predictions or projections rather than facts from history. The notation `*084 = {*Past. *Record}` treats Historic Level as a set of two sub-concepts rather than a concept with sub-types.

concepts.name: Host System

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: Host System receives the evolutionary delivery steps — it is the target of Evo Step deployments

relatedConcepts.name: Focus System
relatedConcepts.note: Focus System is the system being developed; Host System is the system receiving it

relatedConcepts.name: Environment System
relatedConcepts.note: Environment System is the wider context; Host System is the specific receiving system within that environment

relatedConcepts.name: System
relatedConcepts.note: Host System is a role a System plays — the receiving system in an evolutionary delivery context

concepts.definition: A host system receives the evolutionary *delivery steps*.
concepts.overview: **Host System** (*348) is the existing system into which evolutionary delivery steps (Evo Steps) are deployed. Where the Focus System (*492) is the system being designed and built, the Host System is the live environment that receives each incremental delivery. The distinction matters because the Host System has its own constraints, existing users, operational state, and dependencies — all of which constrain what can be delivered in each Evo Step and how. The Host System is not passive: it shapes what is feasible to deploy, and its characteristics must be specified as constraints on the delivery plan.

concepts.name: Icon

relatedConcepts.name: Keyed Icon
relatedConcepts.note: Keyed Icon is a sub-type of Icon — a textual/keyboard-typeable icon representing a concept

relatedConcepts.name: Drawn Icon
relatedConcepts.note: Drawn Icon is a sub-type of Icon — a graphical/pictorial icon representing a concept

relatedConcepts.name: Symbol
relatedConcepts.note: Symbol is the broader category — an Icon is a Symbol with a primarily pictorial convention

relatedConcepts.name: Symbology
relatedConcepts.note: Symbology is the complete system of Symbols and Icons used in Planguage

concepts.definition: In Planguage, an icon is a symbol, keyed (Keyed Icon) or drawn (Drawn Icon), that represents a concept. All Icons are graphic or pictorial in nature — they should not use words or national languages. But they can be annotated by words or symbols. They refer specifically to defined concepts, such as those in the Planguage Glossary.
concepts.overview: **Icon** (*161) is a Planguage Symbol (*162) that is graphic or pictorial in nature — it represents a defined concept without using words or national language. Icons exist in two forms: Keyed Icons (*144), which are keyboard-typeable representations, and Drawn Icons (*085), which are graphical/pictorial representations. Crucially, Icons refer specifically to *defined concepts* — they are not decorative; each icon maps unambiguously to a concept in the Planguage Glossary. The synonym "Plicon" (© Tom Gilb 2004) is a portmanteau of "Planguage Icon," used informally. An Icon is distinguished from a Symbol in that it emphasises pictorial convention over other semiotic mechanisms.

concepts.name: Idea

relatedConcepts.name: Design Idea
relatedConcepts.note: Design Idea is the primary Planguage specialisation of Idea — an idea for satisfying a design requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Process Improvement Suggestion
relatedConcepts.note: Process Improvement Suggestion is the process-focused specialisation of Idea

relatedConcepts.name: Plan
relatedConcepts.note: A Plan is a more developed form — an Idea that has been structured into a course of action

concepts.definition:
An 'idea' is an intellectual concept of any kind.
*Webster's Dictionary:* A plan, scheme, project, aim.
*American Heritage Dictionary:* A plan, scheme, or method.
concepts.overview: **Idea** (*086) is the most general design concept in Planguage: an intellectual concept of any kind that has relevance to the system being specified. In practice, Planguage is primarily interested in three classes of idea: attribute ideas (new ways of measuring or characterising system performance), design ideas (*047, new ways of satisfying design requirements), and project delivery cycle ideas (new approaches to Evo Steps and delivery planning). An Idea is the raw intellectual input to the design process — undeveloped relative to a Plan (*108), but worth capturing, tagging, and tracking. Ideas are not noise; they are early-stage solutions.

concepts.name: Ideal

relatedConcepts.name: Stretch
relatedConcepts.note: immediate predecessor — Stretch is the committed-but-ambitious level; Ideal lies beyond it

relatedConcepts.name: Target
relatedConcepts.note: generic class — Ideal is one kind of Target (or Benchmark, depending on use)

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: alternate classification — Ideal used for comparison is a Benchmark level

relatedConcepts.name: Perfect
relatedConcepts.note: distinction — Ideal can be reached and reset; Perfect is by definition unreachable

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Goal balances all constraints; Ideal ignores them

relatedConcepts.name: Wish
relatedConcepts.note: sibling non-commitment level — Wish is below Goal; Ideal is above Stretch

concepts.definition: An **Ideal** specification represents a hypothetical, and perhaps only theoretical, best level for stakeholders, irrespective of considerations such as cost, available technology, or culture. An Ideal parameter specifies an ideal level, on a defined Scale, under specified conditions for a scalar attribute. An Ideal level is *never* a *committed target* level — it is a *benchmark* level. We might want to move towards it, hold it out as motivation, but we do not expect to reach it in practice. It could conceivably be reached in the real world; in which case we may have to reset our 'ideal' notion towards a *new* level of ideal. In this sense Ideal differs from 'Perfection', which by definition cannot be improved.
concepts.overview: **Ideal** (*328) is a non-committed, aspirational scalar level that sits beyond Stretch on the performance axis — imagining the best possible outcome unconstrained by economics, available technology, or culture. It is not a target we promise to hit; it is a beacon that focuses effort and reveals direction. If Ideal is reached, a new Ideal must be set — this distinguishes it from Perfect (*648), which is by definition the ceiling that cannot be surpassed. Ideal can function as either a Benchmark (for comparison against Goal and Stretch levels) or a motivational target (when seriously pursued long-term). The keyed icon `>++` places it explicitly "more positive than Stretch `>+`" on the scalar axis.

concepts.name: If

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: context — If appears inside qualifier brackets [...]

relatedConcepts.name: Condition
relatedConcepts.note: subject — If introduces a Condition inside a qualifier

relatedConcepts.name: And
relatedConcepts.note: sibling logical operator — And combines multiple conditions

relatedConcepts.name: Or
relatedConcepts.note: sibling logical operator — Or introduces alternatives

concepts.definition: **If** is a logical operator parameter used in qualifiers to explicitly specify conditions. The `If` is *implied* for all terms in a qualifier — however, `If` may be used to communicate a condition more explicitly to the novice reader. The keyed icon `?` may be used before a condition (with a space between them) as an alternative notation.
concepts.overview: **If** (*399) is Planguage's explicit conditional operator, used inside qualifier brackets `[...]` to state conditions under which a requirement applies. Every term inside a qualifier already carries an implied `If` — the explicit keyword exists to make conditions unambiguous for less experienced readers. The keyed icon `?` provides a shorter notation for the same purpose: `[? USA]` reads identically to `[If USA]`. Synonyms `Where` (suggested by Don Mills, NZ) and `IF` (capitalised) are interchangeable. If is a sibling of `And` (*045) and `Or` (*514) in the Planguage logical operator family.

concepts.name: Illuminate

relatedConcepts.name: Illumination
relatedConcepts.note: the state produced by Illuminate

concepts.definition: (verb) A process that provides increased understanding of a concept, for a set of defined and purposeful conditions. To create Illumination (*833).

concepts.name: Illumination

relatedConcepts.name: Illuminate
relatedConcepts.note: the process that produces Illumination

concepts.definition: (noun) The degree to which a named object understands a defined artifact for a defined purpose.

concepts.name: Impact Estimate

relatedConcepts.name: Impact
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Impact is the general noun (estimated or actual); Impact Estimate is the parameter when estimated

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation
relatedConcepts.note: process — Impact Estimation is the process that produces Impact Estimates

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation Table
relatedConcepts.note: container — Impact Estimates live inside cells of the IE Table

relatedConcepts.name: Cell
relatedConcepts.note: record — each Cell in an IE Table holds one Impact Estimate

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Impact
relatedConcepts.note: component — the absolute numeric part of a full Impact Estimate

relatedConcepts.name: Percentage Impact
relatedConcepts.note: component — the % improvement part of a full Impact Estimate

relatedConcepts.name: Side Effect
relatedConcepts.note: related output — unintended impacts discovered during estimation

relatedConcepts.name: Credibility
relatedConcepts.note: qualifier — every Impact Estimate should carry a Credibility rating

concepts.definition: An **impact estimate** is an evaluated guess as to the result of implementing a design idea. In other words, it is a considered, quantified guess of the effect on a specific scalar requirement attribute (performance or resource) of implementing a design idea (or set of design ideas) in a system (or system subset) under stated conditions. A full impact estimate includes: a scale impact, a percentage impact, and uncertainty data (known error margins). The additional related information required to support an impact estimate includes the evidence, source(s), and credibility.
concepts.overview: **Impact Estimate** (*433) is the Planguage parameter that records a considered, quantified estimate of how much a design idea will move a scalar requirement attribute. It is the *estimated* form of the more general **Impact** (*087) — when an impact is measured rather than estimated, it becomes an actual measurement, not an Impact Estimate. A full record includes three elements: a Scale Impact (absolute numeric value), a Percentage Impact (% movement from baseline to target), and Uncertainty bounds (known error margins) — plus supporting Evidence, Source, and Credibility. The keyed icon `->.#` is a composite: `->` (impact) + `.` (made of) + `#` (estimate). Impact Estimates are recorded in Cells of the Impact Estimation Table (*638) as the primary output of Impact Estimation (*283).

concepts.name: Impact Estimation Table

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation
relatedConcepts.note: parent process — the IE Table is the main output of Impact Estimation

relatedConcepts.name: Cell
relatedConcepts.note: constituent — each row × column intersection is a Cell holding one Impact Estimate

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimate
relatedConcepts.note: content — Impact Estimates are recorded in Cells of the IE Table

relatedConcepts.name: Impact
relatedConcepts.note: subject — the table records impacts (estimated or measured) of designs on requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Uncertainty
relatedConcepts.note: cell field — each Impact Estimate in a Cell includes Uncertainty bounds

relatedConcepts.name: Credibility
relatedConcepts.note: cell field — each Cell records the Credibility of its Impact Estimate

relatedConcepts.name: Evidence
relatedConcepts.note: cell field — each Cell records supporting Evidence for its estimate

relatedConcepts.name: Design Ideas
relatedConcepts.note: column axis — Design Ideas form the column dimension of the IE Table

concepts.definition: An **impact estimation table** (IE table) is the main output specification of an Impact Estimation process. An IE table shows estimates or actual measurements of the effect of any set of designs (architecture, strategy, solution) on any set of requirements. The emphasis is on the impact of designs on the performance and resource targets.
concepts.overview: **Impact Estimation Table** (*638) is the central artefact of the Impact Estimation (*283) process — a matrix whose rows are requirements and whose columns are design ideas, with each intersection (Cell, *308) holding an Impact Estimate (*433) or actual measured impact. The table is simultaneously a design comparison tool, a completeness check (are all requirements covered?), a progress monitor for Evo steps, and a presentation aid for stakeholders. It is a "snapshot in time": the same table updated across Evo steps shows how actual measurements replace estimates as reality progressively confirms (or refutes) the design choices. The acronym is **IE Table**.

concepts.name: Impact Estimation

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimate
relatedConcepts.note: output — Impact Estimates are the per-cell results of the process

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation Table
relatedConcepts.note: artefact — the IE Table is the main output specification of this process

relatedConcepts.name: Impact
relatedConcepts.note: subject — Impact Estimation evaluates the quantitative impacts of designs

relatedConcepts.name: Design Ideas
relatedConcepts.note: input — Design Ideas are the column axis of the IE Table

relatedConcepts.name: Cell
relatedConcepts.note: record unit — each row × column intersection in the IE Table

relatedConcepts.name: Uncertainty
relatedConcepts.note: required component — every estimate must carry Uncertainty bounds

relatedConcepts.name: Credibility
relatedConcepts.note: required component — every estimate carries a Credibility rating

concepts.definition: **Impact Estimation** is a Planguage method/process to evaluate the quantitative impacts of design ideas on requirements.
concepts.overview: **Impact Estimation** (*283) is the Planguage process for systematically estimating — and later measuring — how much each design idea moves each scalar requirement attribute. It is Chapter 9 of Tom Gilb's *Competitive Engineering* and the analytical engine that turns design intuition into quantified, comparable data. The process produces an **Impact Estimation Table** (*638) whose cells record Impact Estimates (*433) for every design idea × requirement pair, with Uncertainty bounds and Credibility ratings. The keyed icon `->.#` is shared with Impact Estimate (*433) by design — the process and its per-cell output are inseparable. IE converts "we think this will help" into a structured, reviewable, updatable record.

concepts.name: Impact

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimate
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — Impact Estimate is Impact in the estimated (pre-measurement) case

relatedConcepts.name: Impacts
relatedConcepts.note: companion parameter — Impacts *334 records the relationship; Impact *087 records the numeric value

relatedConcepts.name: Impacted By
relatedConcepts.note: inverse — 'A Impacts B' is the same fact as 'B Impacted By A

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation
relatedConcepts.note: process — Impact Estimation is the systematic process for evaluating Impacts

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation Table
relatedConcepts.note: container — Impacts (estimated or actual) are recorded in the IE Table

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Impact
relatedConcepts.note: component — absolute numeric value on a Scale; part of a full Impact record

relatedConcepts.name: Percentage Impact
relatedConcepts.note: component — percentage movement; part of a full Impact record

concepts.definition: An **impact** is the estimated or actual numeric effect of a design idea (or set of design ideas or Evo step) on a requirement attribute under given conditions. Full impact information includes: a scale impact, a percentage impact, and uncertainty data (known error margins). The additional related information required to support an impact includes the evidence, source(s), and credibility. If an impact is estimated, it is an Impact Estimate (*433).
concepts.overview: **Impact** (*087) is the Planguage parameter for the numeric effect — estimated or measured — of a design idea on a scalar requirement attribute. It is the general form: when the effect is estimated (pre-implementation), it becomes an **Impact Estimate** (*433); when measured (post-delivery), it is simply an Impact with actual data. The keyed icon `->@` symbolises "impact (`->`) on a target (`@`)," reflecting that design ideas *do things to* requirement targets. A full Impact record contains three components — Scale Impact (absolute numeric), Percentage Impact (% from baseline to target), and Uncertainty (error margins) — plus supporting Evidence, Source, and Credibility. Impact is the currency of design evaluation in Planguage.

concepts.name: Impacted By

relatedConcepts.name: Risk
relatedConcepts.note: application — Impacted By is the primary mechanism for risk identification and analysis

relatedConcepts.name: Threat
relatedConcepts.note: application — Threats are one class of item that Impacted By captures (corrected from source: source listed *309 for Threat, but Threat is *671)

relatedConcepts.name: Dependency
relatedConcepts.note: sibling relationship — Dependencies are listed via Impacted By to make them explicit

relatedConcepts.name: Impacts
relatedConcepts.note: inverse — Impacts A -> B is the same fact as B Impacted By A; opposite subject

relatedConcepts.name: Supports
relatedConcepts.note: stronger variant — Supports (->>) is the primary intended positive impact; Impacted By covers all impacts including negative

relatedConcepts.name: Impact
relatedConcepts.note: subject — Impacted By documents the sources of Impact on a specification

concepts.definition: **Impacted By** is used to indicate any *other* specified items, (such as requirements, objectives, designs, policies, or conditions), which affect, or might affect, a defined specification itself, or what it refers to.
concepts.overview: **Impacted By** (*412) is a Planguage relationship parameter that maps the *sources of influence* on a specification — listing other requirements, designs, policies, risks, or conditions that could affect its outcome. Its primary engineering purpose is risk identification: by making influences explicit and documented, the team can design specific mitigations and track those influences through configuration management, quality control, estimation, and prioritisation. The keyed icon `->` is shared with Impacts (*334) — `A -> B` reads as "A impacts B" (Impacts subject) or equivalently "B is impacted by A" (Impacted By subject). Unlike Risk (*309) and Threat (*671), Impacted By is neutral — it captures both positive and negative influences.

concepts.name: Impacts

relatedConcepts.name: Supports
relatedConcepts.note: stronger variant — Supports (->>)  is the primary intended positive impact; Impacts covers all including side effects

relatedConcepts.name: Impacted By
relatedConcepts.note: inverse — Impacts A -> B is the same fact as B Impacted By A

relatedConcepts.name: Impact
relatedConcepts.note: numeric subject — Impacts *334 lists which things are affected; Impact *087 records how much

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation Table
relatedConcepts.note: pre-population — Impacts can be used to pre-populate IE Table structure before numeric estimates are ready

relatedConcepts.name: Side Effect
relatedConcepts.note: content — Impacts captures side effects (including negative) as well as intended positive impacts

concepts.definition: The **Impacts** parameter is used to identify the set of attributes that are considered likely to be impacted by a given attribute (usually another requirement attribute or a proposed design idea).
concepts.overview: **Impacts** (*334) is a Planguage relationship parameter that lists *which* requirement attributes or specifications a given design idea or attribute is expected to affect — without yet committing to numeric estimates. It is the *pre-numeric* companion to Impact Estimation: you record `Impacts {Learning, Development Cost}` to enumerate the scope of effect before filling in the Impact Estimation Table (*638) with quantities. The keyed icon `->` is identical to the Impacted By (*412) arrow — `A -> B` means "A impacts B" — but the same icon is also used by Until (*551) in numeric contexts (e.g., `30 ->60`); Tom explicitly disambiguates these by context. Impacts covers *both* intended positive impacts and unintended side effects, making it broader than Supports (`->>` for primary intended delivery).

concepts.name: Implementation Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Result Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Implementation Cycle is part of a Result Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Development Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: constituent — Development Cycle (R&D focus) is one of three cycles inside Implementation Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Production Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: constituent — Production Cycle (manufacture focus) is one of three cycles inside Implementation Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Delivery Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: constituent — Delivery Cycle (distribution focus) is one of three cycles inside Implementation Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Evo
relatedConcepts.note: parent methodology — Implementation Cycle is a structural element of Evolutionary Project Management

relatedConcepts.name: Act-PDSA
relatedConcepts.note: PDSA parallel — Implementation Cycle is comparable to the 'Do' and 'Act' phases of the Shewhart PDSA cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Statistical Process Control
relatedConcepts.note: framework — PDSA cycle is the operational core of Shewhart's Statistical Process Control

concepts.definition: An **implementation cycle** is part of a result cycle. It consists of the (Evo) development cycle, production cycle and delivery cycle. Implementation means 'taking a plan, or an idea, and turning it into reality'.
concepts.overview: **Implementation Cycle** (*123) is the Evo sub-cycle that converts plans into real delivered systems. It is one component of the Result Cycle (*122) and itself contains three sub-cycles: Development Cycle (*413, research and development), Production Cycle (*407, manufacture or code production), and Delivery Cycle (*049, distribution to customers). The emphasis is on "contact with reality" — implementation is not just execution; it generates feedback that enables adjustment in subsequent Evo steps. Tom draws an explicit parallel to the 'Do' phase of Shewhart's PDSA (Plan-Do-Study-Act) cycle: implementation is where designed plans meet physical or digital reality and produce measurable outcomes.

concepts.name: Implementation Instance

relatedConcepts.name: Implementation
relatedConcepts.note: the abstract role of which this is one particular realisation

relatedConcepts.name: Component
relatedConcepts.note: an Implementation Instance is one concrete Component in the deployed system

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: each Evo step may produce one or more Implementation Instances

relatedConcepts.name: Idea
relatedConcepts.note: the original idea upstream of this instance

concepts.definition: An Implementation Instance is a particular real-life representation of an idea. Possibly one of many planned, implemented, or obsolete.
concepts.overview: **Implementation Instance** (*684) is one concrete occurrence of an [[Implementation.683]] — the individual, traceable realisation of an idea as it exists (or existed) in the real world. While Implementation (*683) describes the abstract role of "the real-world form of an idea," an Implementation Instance is the specific artefact, deployment, or object at a specific time and place. Multiple instances may co-exist (e.g., a service running in three regions), may be planned but not yet built, or may be obsolete versions superseded by later increments. The concept enables precise tracking across the lifecycle of a system.

concepts.name: Implementation

relatedConcepts.name: Implementation Instance
relatedConcepts.note: a single concrete realisation of this Implementation

relatedConcepts.name: Component
relatedConcepts.note: an Implementation may correspond to a Component or set of Components in the system

relatedConcepts.name: Design Ideas
relatedConcepts.note: an Implementation is the real-life realisation of a Design Idea

relatedConcepts.name: Idea
relatedConcepts.note: the abstract upstream concept; Implementation is its real-world form

concepts.definition: An implementation is the real-life representation of an idea.
concepts.overview: **Implementation** (*683) is the real-world realisation of an idea — a plan, design, or concept that has been given concrete form. It was added to Planguage so that changes to real instances of a design or plan can be documented and tracked. Crucially, an Implementation normally references the plan or design that spawned it, but implementations without known corresponding plans are also possible. Tom Gilb envisaged applying this concept within a Needs and Means tracking tool to bridge the gap between intended design and actual delivered system.

concepts.name: Includes

relatedConcepts.name: Consists Of
relatedConcepts.note: stronger: exhaustively lists all components; Includes allows partial lists

relatedConcepts.name: Component
relatedConcepts.note: each item listed in an Includes set is a Component of the parent

relatedConcepts.name: Consists Of
relatedConcepts.note: inverse structural view — Consists Of asserts completeness; Includes does not

concepts.definition: 'Includes' expresses the concept of inclusion of a set of components within a larger set of components. 'A Includes B.' means that B is a sub-component of the component A.
concepts.overview: **Includes** (*391) is a Planguage logical structure parameter that asserts part-whole membership: if A Includes B, then B is a sub-component of A. The keyed icon `{ }` (set braces) expresses this structurally — `A: {B, C, D}` is shorthand for `A Includes {B, C, D}`. Crucially, Includes is weaker than [[Consists-Of.616]]: it admits a *partial* list — there may be more sub-components than the ones named. Consists Of, by contrast, claims exhaustiveness. This distinction matters for specification completeness: Includes says "at least these"; Consists Of says "exactly these."

concepts.name: Incremental Development

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: Evo is a subclass of incremental development that adds measurement, learning, and value-priority ordering

relatedConcepts.name: Incremental Development
relatedConcepts.note: self — see polysemy note; type field was truncated in source

concepts.definition: Incremental development means designing a system largely up-front, and then dividing its construction, and perhaps handover, into a series of cumulative increments.
concepts.overview: **Incremental Development** (*318) is a software and systems engineering approach where design is done mostly up-front and construction is then divided into cumulative, sequential increments. It is defined in Planguage primarily in *contrast* to Evolutionary Project Management (Evo) — all Evo processes are incremental, but not all incremental processes are Evo. The critical distinctions: Incremental Development lacks Evo's per-step measurement of delivered performance, its feedback-driven learning loop, its intent to change requirements and design based on feedback, and its discipline of delivering the highest value-to-cost increments first. Confusing "incremental" with "evolutionary" is, in Tom's words, a "sure sign of people who do not have deep understanding" of the value of feedback.

concepts.name: Incremental Scale Impact

relatedConcepts.name: Incremental Impact
relatedConcepts.note: the general concept; Incremental Scale Impact is the scalar, numeric form

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Impact
relatedConcepts.note: Scale Impact is the absolute delivered level; subtract Baseline to get Incremental Scale Impact

relatedConcepts.name: Baseline-To-Target Pair
relatedConcepts.note: anchors Baseline (0%) and Target (100%) against which the increment is measured

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: each Evo step produces one Incremental Scale Impact measurement per scalar requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation
relatedConcepts.note: Impact Estimation estimates Incremental Scale Impact before delivery

concepts.definition:
For a scalar requirement, this is the numeric impact of a design idea *relative* to the specified baseline level. If there is a negative impact, then the numeric value will be negative.
**Scale Impact − Baseline = Incremental Scale Impact**
concepts.overview: **Incremental Scale Impact** (*307) quantifies the contribution of a single design idea or Evo step to a scalar requirement, measured as the delta from the baseline. The formula is `Scale Impact − Baseline = Incremental Scale Impact`. If the baseline (Past) is 20 minutes and the Scale Impact (delivered result) is 12 minutes, the Incremental Scale Impact is 8 minutes improvement. The sign matters: a negative value means the design idea made things worse relative to baseline. This concept is the numeric precision instrument of Evo — without it, "impact" remains vague. A key insight: the impact of a design idea is **not constant**; it depends on the circumstances (what was already in place), making Incremental Scale Impact path-dependent.

concepts.name: Indicator

relatedConcepts.name: Metric
relatedConcepts.note: an Indicator often derives from a metric — a defined measurement procedure

relatedConcepts.name: Measure
relatedConcepts.note: a Measure produces the value compared in an Indicator

relatedConcepts.name: Sign
relatedConcepts.note: polysemy — Sign.195 is the alias file sharing this concept number

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: an Indicator compares a measure against an expected result — which is a form of Benchmark

concepts.definition:
An **indicator** is the result of a comparison of a measure or metric with a baseline quantity or expected result.
A Planguage parameter defining an indicator type, and its condition: Example {red light, flashing}.
concepts.overview: **Indicator** (*195) is a Scalar Benchmark concept that represents the *result of comparing* a measure or metric against a baseline or expected value — expressed in a defined, observable form. In Planguage, an Indicator is specified as a type (what kind of indicator) together with its condition (what states it can take), such as `{green light, red light, flashing}`. The archetypal use case is the IEEE Technical Interface Recommendation example: a specification goal of >90% Clarity, with the Indicator defined as any green or flashing panel light confirming that status. Synonym: Sign (same concept number *195; alias file Sign.195.md exists).

concepts.name: Indirect Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Direct Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: the contrast concept — explicitly formatted as a constraint; Indirect Constraint is any other spec that has constraining effect

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Indirect Constraint is one category of Constraint by source

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: a Goal is an Indirect Constraint — it restricts the range of acceptable design choices

relatedConcepts.name: Wish
relatedConcepts.note: a Wish is an Indirect Constraint — prioritisation pressure without formal constraint syntax

relatedConcepts.name: Stretch
relatedConcepts.note: a Stretch is an Indirect Constraint — motivating target that shapes design without formal constraint form

relatedConcepts.name: Authority
relatedConcepts.note: an Authority statement attached to a specification acts as an Indirect Constraint on how the spec is interpreted and changed

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: a Stakeholder designation indirectly constrains priorities and acceptable trade-offs

concepts.definition:
Any *other specification, except a direct constraint,* which indirectly has the effect of constraint.
This can include any other requirement {function, Goal, Wish, Stretch}, and previous and pre-emptive level of architecture or design, and any statement of priority attached to a specification (such as Authority, Source, Stakeholder).
concepts.overview: **Indirect Constraint** (*511) is any specification that is not written in constraint syntax but has the practical effect of constraining design choices. While a Direct Constraint (*510) explicitly names a constraint (Limit, Fail, Constraint, qualifier) and is formatted as one, an Indirect Constraint is any other requirement — a Goal, a Wish, a Stretch, an architectural pre-decision, or a priority assignment such as Authority, Source, or Stakeholder — that narrows the space of acceptable design solutions. The concept is important for complete constraint analysis: systems are constrained not only by what is labelled "Constraint" but by everything that makes certain design options impossible or unacceptable.

concepts.name: Indirect Costs

relatedConcepts.name: Cost
relatedConcepts.note: Indirect Costs are a sub-category of Cost — the costs of producing inputs rather than of producing the output directly

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: Indirect Costs consume Resources (money, time, work-hours)

relatedConcepts.name: Performance-to-Cost Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: Indirect Costs reduce the P/C ratio by increasing the denominator without directly producing output

concepts.definition: A resource (money, time, work-hours) needed to produce an *input* to a system.
concepts.overview: **Indirect Costs** (*250) are the costs of producing the inputs that a system requires — not the costs of producing the system's output directly. They are "invisible" costs in the sense that they do not appear in the direct bill-of-materials but are nonetheless real and often underestimated. In engineering, high-quality drawings, specifications, training materials, and data preparation are classic indirect costs: essential inputs, but costs incurred before the main process even begins. Ignoring Indirect Costs leads to systematically underestimated budgets and schedules.

concepts.name: Information

relatedConcepts.name: Agent
relatedConcepts.note: An Agent gives interpretation to Data to produce Information

relatedConcepts.name: Data
relatedConcepts.note: Data is the raw material; Information is what an Agent derives from it by interpretation

relatedConcepts.name: Infoware
relatedConcepts.note: Infoware is the carrier medium for Information — any device for informing people about ideas

concepts.definition: Information is the interpretation an agent gives to data.
concepts.overview: **Information** (*320) is not data. Data are raw facts; Information is what an Agent produces by *interpreting* those facts in a context and for a purpose. Information includes interpretation, conclusions, signals to act, and bases for decisions — it is data made meaningful. Planguage plays a dual role: as a language structure it organises data to make it useful, and as a set of processes (Impact Estimation, SQC) it interprets data into actionable Information. The Baudrillard paradox — "information can tell us everything... answers to questions we have not asked" — highlights that raw data abundance does not equal useful Information.

concepts.name: Infotect

relatedConcepts.name: Systect
relatedConcepts.note: An Infotect is a subordinate design function to Systects; information systems architecture is a sub-domain of systems architecture

relatedConcepts.name: Software Engineer
relatedConcepts.note: A parallel discipline subsidiary to systems engineering; primarily concerned with providing computer instructions — not the full breadth of an Infotect's scope

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Engineer
relatedConcepts.note: The broader engineering discipline of which Infotecture is a specialisation

relatedConcepts.name: Softcrafter
relatedConcepts.note: A related engineering role in the software domain

relatedConcepts.name: Architect
relatedConcepts.note: An Infotect is an information system Architect — a specialised kind of Architect

concepts.definition: The Infotect is: (1) Information systems architect. (2) Responsible for all aspects of the system — manual procedures, people, training, documentation, motivation — and if they are used at all, both hardware and software, including dataware. (3) Goal oriented: the infotect's job is to design a way to reach the stated objectives, measurably. (4) Discipline synchronizer; design and plan control for all specialty engineers and planners. *[Gilb88, p351]*
concepts.overview: **Infotect** (*568) is the engineering role responsible for the complete architecture of an *information system* — a Architect specialised to information systems. Crucially, the Infotect's scope is not limited to software or hardware: it encompasses manual procedures, people, training, documentation, and motivation, as well as any technical components. The Infotect is goal-oriented (designing to reach measurable objectives) and a discipline synchronizer (coordinating all specialty engineers). An Infotect is subordinate to the Systect (*565), since information systems architecture is a sub-domain of systems architecture.

concepts.name: Infotecture

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architecture (Systecture)
relatedConcepts.note: Systems architecture (Systecture) has Infotecture as a subset — along with Software Systecture

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: Infotecture is a specialised architecture discipline for information systems — a kind of Architecture

relatedConcepts.name: Infotect
relatedConcepts.note: Infotecture is the discipline; Infotect is the role that practises it

concepts.definition: Infotecture is a discipline practised by Infotects (*568). It is information systems architecture. Infotecture is a specialised architecture discipline limited to information systems of any kind, and not necessarily including computers or software!
concepts.overview: **Infotecture** (*569) is the architecture discipline for information systems — practised by the Infotect (*568) role. Its scope is all information systems of any kind, including purely manual or human-based information systems that involve no computers or software whatsoever. Infotecture is a sub-domain of Systecture (*564), the broader systems architecture discipline. The defining boundary is *information systems*, not *technology systems* — a filing cabinet system, a hospital records workflow, or a military briefing process are all within Infotecture's domain.

concepts.name: Infoware

relatedConcepts.name: Dataware
relatedConcepts.note: Dataware is one sub-type of Infoware — structured data stores for computers

relatedConcepts.name: Planware
relatedConcepts.note: Planware is plans (information, data) for humans — another sub-type of Infoware

relatedConcepts.name: Documentation
relatedConcepts.note: Documentation is primarily for human instruction about system operation — another sub-type of Infoware

relatedConcepts.name: Logicware
relatedConcepts.note: Logicware is active logic directing computers — not primarily Infoware except where humans read it directly

relatedConcepts.name: Information
relatedConcepts.note: Information is the interpretation humans get from analysing Infoware

concepts.definition: Infoware encompasses any *devices* for informing *people* about *ideas*. Infoware is information carriers in the widest sense of the word. This includes anything people can read (text, diagrams, pictures) and any real artefacts which people can learn something from such as: models, prototypes, real systems, people, groups, organisations, any observable part of the universe.
concepts.overview: **Infoware** (*578) is the broadest possible category of information carrier — any device, artefact, or observable thing that informs a person about an idea. It includes written documents, diagrams, pictures, models, prototypes, real systems, and even other people and organisations. The defining criterion is whether the thing is *used to inform a person* — not what it is made of or whether it is digital. Infoware is the carrier; [[Information.320]] is what the Agent extracts from it. Sub-types include [[Dataware.576]] (data for computers), [[Planware.577]] (plans for humans), and [[Documentation.579]] (operational instruction).

concepts.name: Inherited

relatedConcepts.name: Global
relatedConcepts.note: Global specifications become Inherited specifications where they apply — Global is a source mechanism for Inheritance

relatedConcepts.name: Local
relatedConcepts.note: Local specifications at a high level can become Global to lower levels and therefore Inherited — Local is the contrast (directly stated)

relatedConcepts.name: Attached Specification
relatedConcepts.note: Attached is directly and visibly present; Inherited is implicitly applied from elsewhere — the complementary contrast

relatedConcepts.name: Inherited Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: Inherited Architecture is the architectural application of the Inherited parameter — design constraints that apply implicitly from supra-specifications

concepts.definition: A specification element is termed 'inherited' if it applies *implicitly* to a specific specification. Inherited specification elements are not *directly* specified in a statement (that is, they are not local to a given specification), but they are inherited from related specifications, usually those at a higher level (a supra-specification).
concepts.overview: **Inherited** (*516) is a Relationship Parameter that marks specification elements which apply to a given specification *implicitly* — not because they are stated locally, but because they are carried in from related specifications, typically at a higher level (supra-specifications). Inherited elements contrast with Local elements (directly stated in a given spec) and Attached elements (physically present in the spec document). A specification element can be inherited from a Global specification, from a parent specification, or from any supra-level source. Inherited elements can be explicitly overridden by local specifications — but only where an override is specifically stated; otherwise the inherited value governs.

concepts.name: Innovation

relatedConcepts.name: Improvement
relatedConcepts.note: Improvement is the broader category; Innovation is Improvement of order-of-magnitude or greater scale

relatedConcepts.name: Creativity
relatedConcepts.note: Creativity is a related concept — the generative process that produces novel ideas; Innovation is the outcome when those ideas deliver measurable step-change value

relatedConcepts.name: Value
relatedConcepts.note: Innovation is measured in stakeholder-valued system attributes — Value is the denominator of what matters

relatedConcepts.name: Performance-to-Cost Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: Innovation is operationalised as a major improvement in the ratio of performance to cost — the P/C efficiency frontier

concepts.definition: Order of magnitude, or better, improvement in performance/cost efficiency, in stakeholder-valued system attributes.
concepts.overview: **Innovation** (*679) is not a process, a mindset, or a culture value — it is a measurable outcome: a 10:1 or better improvement in the ratio of performance to cost across stakeholder-valued system attributes. Tom's definition deliberately includes both the performance *and* the cost dimensions, and explicitly includes simultaneous improvement across *multiple* attributes. A 10× performance improvement at ten times the cost is not innovation in this sense. The benchmark is "order of magnitude" as a useful starting point, but the definition allows context-specific arguments: some domains will accept less (25%), others may require more. The key discipline is that the degree of innovation is argued, not assumed.

concepts.name: Input/output axis

relatedConcepts.name: Control Axis
relatedConcepts.note: The Control Axis *261 is the horizontal axis of a process rectangle (CE enter, CX exit); the Input/output axis *260 is the vertical axis (DE top, DX bottom) — the two axes define the process rectangle together

relatedConcepts.name: Input
relatedConcepts.note: Input *331 corresponds to DE (Data Entry) — the top of the I/O Axis

relatedConcepts.name: Output
relatedConcepts.note: Output *636 corresponds to DX (Data Exit) — the bottom of the I/O Axis

relatedConcepts.name: PDSA Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: The top of the I/O Axis corresponds to the Do phase of PDSA; the bottom corresponds to the Act phase

relatedConcepts.name: Process
relatedConcepts.note: The process rectangle is the graphical model that the I/O Axis describes

concepts.definition: The vertical axis of a process rectangle. The top represents inputs to the process (data and/or material) — *DE* (Data Entry) below. The bottom represents outputs from the process (data and/or material) — *DX* (Data Exit) below. Abbreviation: I/O Axis. Not coincidentally, the top side also represents the 'Do' part of the PDSA cycle, and the bottom part represents the 'Act' part of the cycle.
concepts.overview: **Input/output axis** (*260) is the vertical axis of the Planguage process rectangle model. It defines where inputs enter a process (top — DE, Data Entry) and where outputs leave it (bottom — DX, Data Exit). The I/O Axis pairs with the [[Control-Axis.261]] (the horizontal axis, CE–CX) to fully define the process rectangle's geometry. The alignment with the PDSA cycle is deliberate and structural: the top (input / Do) is where work enters; the bottom (output / Act) is where results are evaluated and acted upon.

concepts.name: Input

relatedConcepts.name: Process Input
relatedConcepts.note: the specific process-context form of Input — enters a Process rectangle from the top

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: function input is a resource attribute — money, effort, other resources entering a function

relatedConcepts.name: Process Output
relatedConcepts.note: the complementary concept — what exits the process after the input has been transformed

concepts.definition: Input (or System Input) is anything which enters a system.
concepts.overview: **Input** (*331) is a Process I/O Parameter in Planguage that describes anything entering a system — whether a resource attribute flowing into a function, or a resource asset flowing into a process. Two distinct uses of the term are carefully separated: a function input (a resource attribute such as money or effort) and a process input (a resource asset that triggers or feeds a process step). Understanding which sense is meant depends on whether the enclosing icon is an oval (function) or a rectangle (process). Both senses share the fundamental idea that systems consume something to produce something, and that consumption must be explicitly specified.

concepts.name: Integration

relatedConcepts.name: Deployment
relatedConcepts.note: follows Integration — Deployment moves integrated system upgrades out to result stakeholders

relatedConcepts.name: Production Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: container — Integration is part of the Production Cycle within an Evo step

relatedConcepts.name: Development Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: upstream of Integration — developed or acquired components arrive from the Development Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Delivery Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Delivery Cycle follows Production Cycle; Integration feeds into Deployment which feeds into Delivery

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: the unit being assembled — Integration inserts Evo step components into the target system

concepts.definition: Integration is the process of inserting Evo step components into a system. It is part of the production cycle (which is one of the three major sub-processes for implementation of an Evo step: development, production, and delivery). Integration works with developed or acquired step components, and does whatever it takes to integrate them into a system. Deployment within the delivery cycle then moves the system upgrades out to the result stakeholders.
concepts.overview: **Integration** (*357) is the Evo process that assembles developed or acquired step components into a running system — the "insert" step that turns independently developed pieces into a cohesive, deployable increment. It sits inside the Production Cycle, between the Development Cycle (which creates the components) and the Delivery Cycle (which deploys them to stakeholders via Deployment *358). Integration is the technical join point of evolutionary delivery: it is where partial implementations become usable system states. Its success or failure determines whether a planned Evo step increment can actually be delivered.

concepts.name: Intelligible

relatedConcepts.name: Complicated
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — Complicated describes a system that is difficult or impossible to understand; Intelligible is the opposite state; scope differs (Intelligible applies to specifications; Complicated covers all systems)

relatedConcepts.name: Complex
relatedConcepts.note: orthogonal — Complex is structural (has interconnected parts); a Complex system can still be Intelligible

relatedConcepts.name: Clarity
relatedConcepts.note: specification property — Clarity is the prerequisite for Intelligibility of a specification; a Clear spec can be Intelligible to its readers

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: primary subject domain — Intelligible is most precisely a property of a Specification relative to a defined readership

concepts.definition: Capable of being understood.
concepts.overview: **Intelligible** (*675) is a System Property in Planguage meaning "capable of being understood." As a specification concept, it is most precisely a property of a **written specification** relative to a defined readership — not a binary absolute but a testable question: can the people who need to use this specification actually understand it? Tom raises the key design question: should we distinguish between a well-articulated specification that some readers find difficult, and a badly-articulated specification that causes even less understanding? Both are failures, but of different kinds — one attributable to the reader, the other to the writer. The antonym Unintelligible frames the defect side. Intelligible is narrower in scope than [[Complicated.676\|Complicated *676]] — Complicated covers all systems including physical and behavioral systems; Intelligible focuses on the specification and communication layer.

concepts.name: Interface

relatedConcepts.name: Component
relatedConcepts.note: the elements being connected — an Interface is the agreed connection between two or more Components

relatedConcepts.name: System Container
relatedConcepts.note: synonym added March 10 2023 — same concept, new name

concepts.definition: An interface is an agreed connection and boundary between system components.
concepts.overview: **Interface** (*194) is a Component & Object in Planguage that defines the agreed connection and boundary between system components. It is not a component itself but the contract and medium that enables two or more components to communicate or transfer anything useful — a device, a definition, a language, a protocol, a physical connector. The key word is *agreed*: an Interface is a specification-level concept, not merely a technical artifact. It requires mutual commitment from both sides to a defined connection form. In 2023 the synonym "System Container" (*691) was added, recognising that an Interface can also be understood as the container that holds the space between components.

concepts.name: Internal Stakeholder

relatedConcepts.name: Focus System
relatedConcepts.note: the system that Internal Stakeholders directly impact — they are defined by their direct impact on the Focus System

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Internal Stakeholder is a Stakeholder whose impact is direct and inside the system boundary

relatedConcepts.name: External Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: sibling and contrast — External Stakeholders are in the External Environment and impact the system indirectly

relatedConcepts.name: Environment System
relatedConcepts.note: context — Internal Stakeholders are related to the environment systems supporting the Focus System

concepts.definition: Internal stakeholders are stakeholders that directly impact a defined focus system. They are related to the environment systems supporting the focus system. For example, a tester is an internal stakeholder for a test process supporting the development of a product (defined as a focus system).
concepts.overview: **Internal Stakeholder** (*494) is a Stakeholder who directly impacts a defined Focus System — occupying the Internal Environment alongside the system itself. Unlike External Stakeholders (*495), who reside in the External Environment and influence the system indirectly, Internal Stakeholders are directly involved in or directly affected by the system's operation or development. They include both system-level roles (Client, User, Sponsor, System Owner) and project-level roles (Project Team, Project 'Customers'). The boundary between internal and external is always relative to a specific, defined Focus System — what is internal to a test process may be external to the larger product system it supports.

concepts.name: Internal

relatedConcepts.name: External
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — External applies to any object outside the scope of a given object; together Internal/External partition the Place scope

relatedConcepts.name: Internal Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: primary application — the Internal Stakeholder is classified as such because they are inside the Focus System's scope boundary

relatedConcepts.name: Focus System
relatedConcepts.note: the reference object — 'internal' is defined relative to a specific Focus System or other declared boundary

concepts.definition: When describing the relationship amongst objects, 'internal' is an adjective which applies to any object inside the scope of a given object.
concepts.overview: **Internal** (*496) is a System Boundary adjective in Planguage that classifies any object as being *inside* the scope of a given reference object. It operates on the *Place* scope dimension — not time or event — and asks: where does this object stand relative to another? Within its extent of influence (internal) or outside it ([[External.497\|external *497]])? An internal object may literally be a physical part of a larger object, or it may be inside the logical, organisational, or authority boundary of that object. Internal/External together form a complementary pair that partitions any system's environment relative to a declared boundary.

concepts.name: Is Part Of
concepts.keyedIcon: X {y}.    meaning y Is Part Of X

relatedConcepts.name: Consists Of
relatedConcepts.note: inverse — 'X consists of y' is the same relationship viewed from the containing side; Is Part Of views it from the component side

relatedConcepts.name: Includes
relatedConcepts.note: similar but weaker — Includes can give a partial list of contents; Is Part Of asserts a complete containment membership

relatedConcepts.name: Generate
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Generate/Spawns implies active generation, not containment or membership

relatedConcepts.name: Component
relatedConcepts.note: the thing that Is Part Of something — a Component is a part; the Is Part Of parameter names its containing whole

relatedConcepts.name: Element
relatedConcepts.note: synonym for Component in this context — Element is also named in source as a use of Is Part Of

concepts.definition: A Parameter which indicates that a specification is a component or element of something else.
concepts.overview: **Is Part Of** (*621) is a Logical Structure Parameter in Planguage that declares, from the component's perspective, that a specification belongs to a larger containing whole. It is the inverse of [[Consists-Of.616\|Consists Of *616]] — where Consists Of says "X is made of y," Is Part Of says "y is part of X." The keyed icon `X {y}` expresses this as a containment set: y is inside X. Unlike [[Includes.391\|Includes *391]], which may list only some contents, Is Part Of expresses complete membership — the specification asserting it belongs to the named container. This makes it the appropriate parameter for bottom-up structural reasoning: "given this specification, what larger whole does it belong to?"

concepts.name: Issue

relatedConcepts.name: Resolution
relatedConcepts.note: every Issue must be Resolved — declared either a Defect or requiring no further action

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Issue
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — a Specification Issue is an element of written specification suspected of violating a specification rule

relatedConcepts.name: Risk
relatedConcepts.note: predecessor in the defect chain — a Risk that materialises becomes an Issue (no longer probabilistic); as per Risk.309 claims log

relatedConcepts.name: Bug
relatedConcepts.note: step in the defect chain — an Issue sits between Error and Defect; a Bug is in the live deployed system (post-Integration)

relatedConcepts.name: Error
relatedConcepts.note: origin — Error/Slip is the human mistake that precedes Issue in the defect chain

relatedConcepts.name: Malfunction
relatedConcepts.note: endpoint — Malfunction is the observable system failure when a Bug is provoked; Issue is the earlier detection point

concepts.definition: An issue is any subject of concern that needs to be noted for analysis and resolution.
concepts.overview: **Issue** (*276) is a Defect Concept in Planguage that captures any subject of concern requiring notation, analysis, and resolution — before a final determination of its status. In SQC, a Specification Issue is specifically a suspected rule violation noted for later resolution: it will be declared either a Defect (if the rule is actually violated) or closed (if not). In the broader defect chain, Issue marks the detection point — the moment a problem is noticed — sitting between Error (the originating human mistake) and Defect (confirmed rule violation in a specification). Once a Risk materialises it becomes an Issue (no longer probabilistic). Once a Bug is provoked in a deployed system, it may also surface as a detected Issue. Resolution is mandatory: every Issue must be resolved.

concepts.name: Item

relatedConcepts.name: Issue
relatedConcepts.note: primary sub-type — an Issue is the main class of Item (super-major, major, minor, or new); most Items are Issues

relatedConcepts.name: Process Improvement Suggestion
relatedConcepts.note: second sub-type — an Item may be a PIS noted for later process improvement; not a spec defect

relatedConcepts.name: Question of Intent
relatedConcepts.note: third sub-type — an Item may be a Question directed to the specification Author for intent clarification

relatedConcepts.name: Checker
relatedConcepts.note: source — Checkers report Items during the SQC logging session

relatedConcepts.name: Scribe
relatedConcepts.note: logger — Scribe logs Items as they are reported by Checkers

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: context — Item is the unit of logging within Specification Quality Control

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Meeting
relatedConcepts.note: resolution venue — Items logged during SQC are resolved in the Specification Meeting

concepts.definition: An item is a term for whatever gets reported by checkers and then logged by a Scribe during SQC logging.
concepts.overview: **Item** (*300) is the unit of SQC logging — the generic term for anything that a Checker reports and a Scribe records during a Specification Quality Control session. Items form a taxonomy with three primary members: Issues (the defect-detection class, with four severity sub-types), Process Improvement Suggestions (process-level observations not tied to a specific spec defect), and Questions of Intent (directed to the author to clarify ambiguous specification intent). The Item concept exists to give SQC's logging process a single, neutral label that covers all three types equally — a Checker does not pre-classify everything before reporting it; the Scribe logs it as an Item and classification follows.

concepts.name: Keyed Icon

relatedConcepts.name: Drawn Icon
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Drawn Icon is realised graphically; Keyed Icon is realised as typed characters

relatedConcepts.name: Icon
relatedConcepts.note: parent category — a Keyed Icon is one kind of Icon

relatedConcepts.name: Symbol
relatedConcepts.note: ancestor — an Icon is one kind of Symbol

relatedConcepts.name: Symbology
relatedConcepts.note: collection — the full set of Keyed Icons forms the Planguage Symbology

concepts.definition: A keyed icon is a non-alphabetic and non-mnemonic set of one or more key-able characters that make up a keyed icon symbol, with defined interpretation. The choice of keyed characters is as closely related as possible to the corresponding icon, and ideally is acceptable to all language cultures. The keyed icon will normally be combined with tags and other Planguage terms to give complete statements or expressions. Some keyed icons, like many words, are ambiguous in isolation, but are unambiguous in context of other specifications.
concepts.overview: **Keyed Icon** (*144) is Planguage's primary notation mechanism: typed characters (not drawings) that visually suggest the concept they denote — `>` for a forward-pointing goal, `|` for a level position on a scale, `<->` for a baseline-to-target pair. They are chosen to be short, cross-cultural, and independent of any natural language, which allows Planguage specifications to be read consistently across language barriers. A Keyed Icon is always combined with tags and other Planguage terms in context; in isolation some icons are ambiguous, but context disambiguates. The four design rationales — brevity, language-independence, graphical appeal, and pedagogical utility — make Keyed Icons the workhorse of every Planguage specification.

concepts.name: Kickoff

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: parent process — Kickoff is the first named sub-process of SQC

relatedConcepts.name: Checking
relatedConcepts.note: downstream step — Checking follows Kickoff in the SQC sequence

relatedConcepts.name: Checker
relatedConcepts.note: key participant — Checkers are recruited and briefed at Kickoff

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: subject — the Specification to be reviewed is established at Kickoff

concepts.definition: Kickoff is an SQC sub-process. It usually involves a team meeting to agree on the master plan, and to commit to doing the planned SQC work.
concepts.overview: **Kickoff** (*286) is the first active sub-process of a [[SQC.051c|Specification Quality Control]] session — the planning and commitment gate before any checking begins. It is not a mere procedural formality: without an explicit Kickoff, SQC sessions drift into ad-hoc inspection without agreed scope, assigned Checkers, scheduled effort, or committed exit criteria. Kickoff establishes who will check what, against which rules, at what rate, by when — turning a wish to review into a structured, auditable process. It is the moment the team transitions from passive reading to active, accountable quality control.

concepts.name: Kid

relatedConcepts.name: Parent
relatedConcepts.note: inverse relationship — a Parent *267 has one or more Kids; a Kid has one Parent

relatedConcepts.name: Supra
relatedConcepts.note: lateral hierarchy concept — Supra is an ancestor-level concept; Kid is a descendant-level concept

relatedConcepts.name: Descendant
relatedConcepts.note: extension — a Descendant *268 is a Kid or any further sub-Kid in the hierarchy

concepts.definition: The kid is the immediate offspring or subset of any component type with any sub-components (for example, function, process, plan, step or system).
concepts.overview: **Kid** (*266) is Planguage's term for the immediate child of any decomposable entity — a function, a process, a plan step, or a system component. The Kid/Parent pair (*266/*267) is Planguage's primary hierarchy-navigation vocabulary, expressing the one-level-down relationship without implying any specific decomposition method. Because Planguage operates across multiple levels of system abstraction, the Kid relationship is the structural glue that connects a specification at one level of perception to its sub-components at the next level down. The Descendant (*268) generalises Kid to any depth below the current node.

concepts.name: Kin

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: application domain — Kin specifications are cross-checked in SQC for defects

relatedConcepts.name: Checking
relatedConcepts.note: technique — Kin cross-checking is a Checking strategy within SQC

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: common shared source — requirements are the typical origin from which Kin documents are derived

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: the entities that stand in the Kin relationship

concepts.definition: Kin specifications are specifications which derive from an identical set of source specifications. For example, test plans, source code and user handbooks could all be derived from the same requirements or the same design.
concepts.overview: **Kin** (*353) is a Planguage relationship parameter that identifies a set of specifications that share an identical origin — derived from the same upstream source. Because Kin documents were all generated from the same requirements or design, inconsistencies between them reveal defects in one or more of the Kin set. This makes Kin a powerful cross-checking strategy in [[SQC.051c|Specification Quality Control]]: two documents that should agree (because they were both derived from the same source) are checked against each other, exposing defects that would be invisible if each document were checked only against its own rules. The United Defense Minnesota case study reported that code-against-test-case Kin checking found major defects in both documents.

concepts.name: Knowledge

relatedConcepts.name: Data
relatedConcepts.note: lower tier — Data is the base layer below Information below Knowledge in the DIKW pyramid

relatedConcepts.name: Information
relatedConcepts.note: intermediate tier — Information is analyzed Data; Knowledge is contextualized Information

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: access subject — Knowledge is accessible by a system stakeholder

concepts.definition: Facts, information, and skills *accessible* by a system *stakeholder* by any *means*; for the theoretical or practical understanding of a subject.
concepts.overview: **Knowledge** (*686) is the Planguage term for contextualised information that a [[Stakeholder.233|system stakeholder]] can access by any means for the theoretical or practical understanding of a subject. It occupies the third tier of the DIKW pyramid (Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom), distinguishing it from raw Data (*319) and analytically-structured Information (*320). The Planguage definition emphasises *access* and *purpose* (understanding a subject) rather than any storage medium — Knowledge can be in a document, a person's head, or a system's output. This makes Knowledge a system property: it can be specified, measured for accessibility, and designed for.

concepts.name: Landing Zone

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — a Landing Zone is a named kind of Range

relatedConcepts.name: Acceptable Range
relatedConcepts.note: component — the Acceptable Range (Fail to Goal) is one part of the Landing Zone

relatedConcepts.name: Acceptable Level
relatedConcepts.note: any level within the Landing Zone is an Acceptable Level

relatedConcepts.name: Tolerable
relatedConcepts.note: qualifier — levels within the Landing Zone are tolerable outcomes

relatedConcepts.name: Success Range
relatedConcepts.note: component — the Success Range (above Goal) is the upper part of the Landing Zone

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: boundary marker — the Goal level divides Acceptable Range from Success Range within the Landing Zone

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: lower boundary — just better than Fail marks the lower edge of the Landing Zone

relatedConcepts.name: Stretch
relatedConcepts.note: upper boundary — the Stretch level marks the upper extent of the Landing Zone

concepts.definition: A landing zone is a target range that stretches from just better than a Fail level through the Goal/Budget level to the Stretch Level.
concepts.overview: **Landing Zone** (*605) is a target range concept that replaces the naive idea of a single exact Goal with a realistic zone of acceptable outcomes spanning from just above [[Fail.098b|Fail]] (*098) through [[Goal.109|Goal]] (*109) to [[Stretch.404|Stretch]] (*404). The metaphor is a parachute landing zone: you aim for the centre, but a landing anywhere within the zone is a success. For a set of requirements, the overall Landing Zone is multi-dimensional — a "space" across all requirement dimensions simultaneously — which reflects the engineering reality that sub-par performance in one dimension is acceptable when offset by superior performance elsewhere. The concept was contributed by Intel Oregon via Erik Simmons (2002).

concepts.name: Language

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — Planguage is the specific engineered Language for systems engineering and management

relatedConcepts.name: Basic Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: core form — Basic Planguage is the un-tailored kernel of the Planguage Language

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage Term
relatedConcepts.note: vocabulary — Planguage Terms are the atomic vocabulary elements of the Planguage Language

relatedConcepts.name: Project Language
relatedConcepts.note: tailored instance — a Project Language is a Planguage tailored for a specific project

relatedConcepts.name: Language
relatedConcepts.note: self-reference used as parent class

concepts.definition: An {agreed, understood, defined} {written, graphical or oral} means of expressing any ideas, concepts or notions. We are particularly interested in a specialised language for systems engineering and management, which we call "Planguage" here.
concepts.overview: **Language** (*373) is Planguage's foundational concept for any agreed, understood, and defined means of expressing ideas — written, graphical, or oral. It is the parent class for [[Planguage.030|Planguage]] itself and for all project-tailored languages derived from it. Three properties — *agreed* (shared convention), *understood* (shared meaning), and *defined* (explicit rules) — distinguish a Language from informal discourse. Without all three, specification statements lose their engineering force: they become ambiguous prose rather than testable requirements. The Planguage project exists to create and maintain a Language that meets all three criteria for systems engineering and management.

concepts.name: Level of Perception

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: context-dependent — what counts as a Requirement vs. Design Idea depends on the Level of Perception

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: carries the Level of Perception as a qualifier for its parameters

relatedConcepts.name: Kid
relatedConcepts.note: hierarchy navigation — Kid/Parent relationships are relative to the Level of Perception

relatedConcepts.name: Parent
relatedConcepts.note: hierarchy navigation — Parent is the node one level above in the current Level of Perception

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: mechanism — Level of Perception is typically expressed as a Qualifier in square brackets

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: example — a Goal level may differ by Level of Perception (Architecture Level vs. Test Level)

concepts.definition: The 'Level of Perception' is the organisational or process level which a specification is at or related to. For example, the architectural level is downstream of system level requirements level but is upstream of specialist engineering levels.
concepts.overview: **Level of Perception** (*590) is the organisational or process level from which a specification is written — the vantage point that determines what counts as a requirement, what counts as a design idea, and which components are "Kids" or "Parents" at that level. Without a defined Level of Perception, fundamental Planguage concepts become undefined: a component that is a requirement at the system level becomes a design idea at the stakeholder level, and a design idea at the system level becomes a requirement at the implementation level. Naming the Level of Perception in a qualifier (e.g., `[Architecture Level]`) grounds the specification in a specific vantage point and prevents the most common form of requirements confusion — arguing about whether something is a "requirement" or a "design" without specifying *at what level of abstraction*.

concepts.name: Level

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — a Level is a defined position within a Range

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: named Level — the committed target level on a performance or resource scale

relatedConcepts.name: Budget
relatedConcepts.note: named Level — the committed resource target level

relatedConcepts.name: Stretch
relatedConcepts.note: named Level — the motivating level beyond Goal

relatedConcepts.name: Wish
relatedConcepts.note: named Level — the aspirational level beyond Stretch

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: named Level — the minimum acceptable; below is a defect

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: named Level — the existence-threatening boundary

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe
relatedConcepts.note: named Level — alias for Catastrophe Limit; extreme boundary

relatedConcepts.name: Past
relatedConcepts.note: named Level — the measured historical benchmark level

relatedConcepts.name: Record
relatedConcepts.note: named Level — the best-ever observed level

relatedConcepts.name: Trend
relatedConcepts.note: named Level — the projected future level based on current trajectory

relatedConcepts.name: Limit
relatedConcepts.note: extreme boundary Level — the outer edge of the scale range

concepts.definition: A level is a defined numeric position on a scale of measure.
concepts.overview: **Level** (*337) is the atomic quantification concept in Planguage — a single defined numeric position on a [[Scale-of-Measure.132|Scale of Measure]]. Every named Planguage target (Goal, Fail, Stretch, Wish, Survival, Catastrophe) and every benchmark (Past, Record, Trend) is a Level. The Keyed Icon `|` represents the generic attribute level — a vertical marker on the scale bar — and can substitute for any of the more specific level icons. A Level indicates one of four roles: a benchmark (what was measured), a target (what is required), a constraint (a limit), or an impact estimate (what a design idea is predicted to achieve). Understanding Level is understanding the foundation of all quantified specification in Planguage.

concepts.name: Life Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: System
relatedConcepts.note: subject — Life Cycle is the total duration of existence of a defined System

relatedConcepts.name: Development Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: subset — the Development Cycle is the portion of the Life Cycle concerned with building and releasing the system

relatedConcepts.name: Delivery Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: subset — the Delivery Cycle covers the delivery portion of the Life Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: method — Evo uses the Life Cycle framework; Evo steps happen within the Life Cycle but affect its slope and timing

concepts.definition: The life cycle is the entire duration of existence of a defined system — from inception to retirement or disposal, independently of the specific methods used for development and maintenance.
concepts.overview: **Life Cycle** (*600) is the total span of a [[System.145|system's]] (*145) existence, from inception through to retirement or disposal. Its defining characteristic is *method independence*: the Life Cycle is a property of the system, not of the development process chosen. Whether a system is built using Waterfall, Evo, Agile, or any other method, it still has a Life Cycle. The development process determines the *shape* of the curve (how quickly value is delivered, how often production phases recur), but it does not alter the fact that the system begins, exists, and ends. This distinction prevents the common confusion between a project's delivery plan and the system's actual duration of existence.

concepts.name: Limit

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: structural parent — a Limit lives at the border of a Range

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: Fail Limit — the lower commitment constraint; below = defect

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: Survival Limit — the lower hard constraint; below = catastrophe

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe
relatedConcepts.note: Catastrophe Limit — equivalent to Survival; alternate naming

relatedConcepts.name: Tolerable
relatedConcepts.note: Tolerable Limit / Worst Acceptable Case — synonym framing

relatedConcepts.name: Commitment Parameters
relatedConcepts.note: Limit is one of the three Commitment parameters (Fail, Goal, Limit)

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Goal is the second Commitment parameter; Limit is the third

concepts.definition: A limit is a numeric level at a border — that is, at an edge of a scalar range (a success range, an acceptable range, a failure range, or a catastrophe range). It is specifically used at the edges of ranges associated with constraints: the fail limit and the survival limit / catastrophe limit.
concepts.overview: **Limit** (*606) is a Planguage Range & Level concept that names the numeric level sitting at the boundary of a scalar range.
