Where a Goal marks a desired target and a Fail marks the boundary of acceptable performance, a Limit marks the hard constraint edge — the line that must not be crossed without consequence. Together with Fail (*098) and Goal (*109), Limit is one of the three Commitment Parameters (*027): values that carry a binding engineering promise. The most common Limits in practice are the Fail Limit (lower acceptable boundary) and the Survival / Catastrophe Limit (the hard-crash boundary below which the system is non-viable).

concepts.name: Local

relatedConcepts.name: Global
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — Global applies across a declared scope; Local is restricted to a subset

relatedConcepts.name: Inherited
relatedConcepts.note: Inherited applies implicitly from supra-specifications; Local is explicitly stated in the given spec

relatedConcepts.name: Attached Specification
relatedConcepts.note: an Attached Specification is physically present and always Local; Local is the broader adjective

relatedConcepts.name: Local
relatedConcepts.note: see also four-scope axis: Local · Global · Inherited · Attached

concepts.definition: 'Local' is an adjective used to specify that something applies only to a restricted subset of a defined scope.
concepts.overview: **Local** (*376) is a Planguage scope-partitioning adjective that restricts the applicability of a specification element to the immediately enclosing context: a single requirement, a single component, or a single named block. Its counterpart is Global (*375), which declares system-wide or project-wide applicability. Local is the default when no explicit scope qualifier is stated and nothing in the surrounding structure implies otherwise. Understanding Local is essential for reading hierarchical Planguage specifications correctly: a Note, Rationale, or Design Idea that is Local applies exactly where it appears — no further, no inference needed.

concepts.name: Locus

relatedConcepts.name: Units Context
relatedConcepts.note: primary component of the Locus — holds place, space, event, authority, source, priority

relatedConcepts.name: Units of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: the measurement unit that gives the numeric level its meaning

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: the Scale on which the level is defined (canonical file: Scale-of-Measure.132)

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: qualifiers can carry Locus information — time, place, event — directly in the Scale

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier Definition
relatedConcepts.note: scale variable; can carry Locus context in a target or constraint specification

concepts.definition: A 'locus' is the integration of all factors/elements that define a scalar level. A locus consists of: a specified scalar level; a specified unit of measure; a units of measure context. The objective of all additional information is to improve the clarity and reality of the specification for purposes of getting control over it, and for contracting purposes.
concepts.overview: **Locus** (*524), formally the Scalar Level Locus, is the complete set of information required to define a scalar specification level without ambiguity. A bare number such as "60 minutes" is almost never sufficient: you need the scale, the unit, the context (who, where, under what conditions), and the authority behind it. The Locus bundles all of these into one related set — a number plus its full specification universe. Without a complete Locus, a requirement level is a promise with no meaning; with a complete Locus, it becomes a testable, contractable, engineering commitment.

concepts.name: Logging

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: Logging is a sub-activity within SQC — occurs at Specification Meetings and Process Meetings

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Meeting
relatedConcepts.note: issues, PISs, and QOIs are logged during the Specification Meeting

relatedConcepts.name: Process Meeting
relatedConcepts.note: process defect causes and PISs are logged during the Process Meeting

relatedConcepts.name: Item
relatedConcepts.note: an Item (Issue, PIS, QOI) is the unit of SQC logging

relatedConcepts.name: Scribe
relatedConcepts.note: the Scribe is the role responsible for Logging during SQC

concepts.definition: 'Logging' is the writing of notes (logs) according to defined standards with the intention of their later use.
concepts.overview: **Logging** (*089) is the SQC sub-activity of capturing specification findings in a structured, standards-conformant form during formal review sessions, so that the findings can be acted upon later. It is not informal note-taking or personal annotation — Logging is a defined process step, performed by the Scribe role (*410) during Specification Meetings (*120) and Process Meetings (*119), producing Items (*300) that become the input to subsequent SQC sub-processes (resolution, process improvement, and retrospective analysis). The standard distinguishes Logging from voluntary personal note-taking precisely because the resulting log must be usable by others who were not present.

concepts.name: Logical Page

relatedConcepts.name: Background
relatedConcepts.note: non-background words are counted; Background words are excluded from the Logical Page count

relatedConcepts.name: Checking Rate
relatedConcepts.note: measured in Logical Pages per hour; Logical Page is the volume unit for Checking Rate calibration

relatedConcepts.name: Major Defect
relatedConcepts.note: defect density is measured in Majors per Logical Page; Logical Page is the denominator

concepts.definition: A logical page is defined as a defined number of *non-background* words. Default Logical Page volume: If no other definition is given, use '300 non-background words' per logical page as default.
concepts.overview: **Logical Page** (*103), abbreviated LP, is the standard unit of specification volume used in SQC to make Checking Rate (*015) and defect density calculations independent of physical page format. Because physical pages vary in size, font, margin width, and content density, counting "pages" gives misleading volume measures. A Logical Page is always exactly the same thing: a defined count of non-background words. The default is 300 non-background words per LP. Background text (*507) — rationale, commentary, descriptive context — is excluded because defects found in Background are almost always minor, not major; the risk-bearing specification content is Non-Commentary, and that is what Logical Pages measure.

concepts.name: Logicware

relatedConcepts.name: Dataware
relatedConcepts.note: Dataware does not necessarily control computer logic — structured data for computers, not instructions

relatedConcepts.name: Planware
relatedConcepts.note: Planware is plans for humans, not computers — not Logicware

relatedConcepts.name: Infoware
relatedConcepts.note: Infoware is information of any kind; a small subset might be Logicware when humans read it for information

relatedConcepts.name: Documentation
relatedConcepts.note: Documentation is primarily for human consumption — contrast with Logicware (for computer consumption)

relatedConcepts.name: Software
relatedConcepts.note: Software is the human-facing term for computer instructions; Logicware is the Planguage system-classification term

concepts.definition: Any information which is intended to control the logical action of a computer. This includes the obvious — computer programs (logic itself) — including any data that in fact controls the computer logic, such as user parameters which control computer logic, and data integrated into the programmed logic itself. It would also include any logic at any level such as operating systems, software layers, and even hardware-based firmware. It includes logic written by people, or generated by other logicware.
concepts.overview: **Logicware** (*575) is the Planguage system-material classification for any information whose function is to control the logical action of a computer. It is broader than "software" in the everyday sense: it includes operating systems, firmware, data tables that act as control structures, configuration parameters that alter computational paths, and logic generated by other Logicware (e.g., compiled output, generated code). The key criterion is not the form of the information but its purpose — if it controls computer logic, it is Logicware. Logicware sits in the Software & Technology Material family alongside Dataware (*576), Planware (*577), Infoware (*578), and Documentation (*579), each distinguished by its intended consumer and function.

concepts.name: Logistics

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: Logistics manages the flow of Resources — materiel and personnel are Resources in the system context

relatedConcepts.name: Component
relatedConcepts.note: materiel managed by Logistics is a Component of the system it supports

relatedConcepts.name: Delivery Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: Logistics supports the distribution and deployment phases of the Delivery Cycle

concepts.definition: The procurement, distribution, maintenance, and replacement of materiel and personnel.
concepts.overview: **Logistics** (*242) is the Planguage-adopted term for the complete set of activities that keeps materiel and personnel flowing correctly through a system: acquiring them, distributing them, maintaining them, and replacing them when needed. Tom Gilb adopts the American Heritage Dictionary definition directly — Logistics is not a Planguage-invented concept but a well-established operational discipline that Planguage incorporates into system specifications wherever the system's performance depends on the management of physical or human resources over time. In a system specification, Logistics is typically a non-functional requirement domain: the system must support, or be supported by, a logistics capability.

concepts.name: Lower Level

relatedConcepts.name: High Level
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — High Level is a position in a hierarchy that is 'high' relative to a defined set; Lower Level is the counterpart below

relatedConcepts.name: Kid
relatedConcepts.note: a Kid is a Lower-Level element relative to its Parent in the Planguage hierarchy

relatedConcepts.name: Supra
relatedConcepts.note: Supra is the ancestor-level direction; Lower Level is the descendant direction

relatedConcepts.name: Level of Perception
relatedConcepts.note: which element is Lower Level depends on the Level of Perception — the observer's vantage point

concepts.definition: Something lower in a hierarchy than high-levels.
concepts.overview: **Lower Level** (*090) is a Planguage partitioning adjective that identifies an element's position in a hierarchy as being below a reference set of high-level elements. It is the counterpart to High Level (*082): where High Level identifies positions of broader scope or greater abstraction, Lower Level identifies positions of narrower scope or greater detail. Crucially, "lower" is always relative — there is no absolute lower level; the designation depends on the hierarchy being traversed and the Level of Perception (*590) of the observer. In Planguage specifications, Lower Level elements are typically sub-components, sub-requirements, or implementation details that elaborate a higher-level specification.

concepts.name: Major Defect

relatedConcepts.name: Defect Specification
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — a Major Defect is a specific class of Specification Defect

relatedConcepts.name: Minor Defect
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Minor Defect is the contrasting lower-impact class

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: SQC is the process in which Major Defects are found, classified, and logged

relatedConcepts.name: Checker
relatedConcepts.note: the Checker classifies each Issue as Major or Minor during SQC

relatedConcepts.name: Logical Page
relatedConcepts.note: defect density is measured in Majors per Logical Page

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rule
relatedConcepts.note: a Major Defect is a violation of a Specification Rule with high downstream cost potential

concepts.definition: A Major defect is a specification defect (a rule violation), which if not fixed at an early stage of specification, then its consequences will possibly grow substantially, in cost-to-fix and/or damage potential. A Major defect has on average approximately an order of magnitude more downstream cost potential than its cost to remove immediately.
concepts.overview: **Major Defect** (*091), abbreviated **M**, is the primary defect classification in SQC: a specification rule violation whose downstream cost potential is approximately ten times its immediate cost to fix. The classification is an engineering economics concept, not an aesthetic judgement. Major Defects must be found and fixed early in the specification process; if allowed to propagate into design, code, and testing, the same defect will cost an order of magnitude more to correct — and may cause damage that exceeds even that. Without the Major/Minor distinction, SQC effort is wasted: up to 90% of checking time may be consumed by low-impact Minor Defects while high-impact Majors remain undetected.

concepts.name: Malfunction

relatedConcepts.name: Error
relatedConcepts.note: Error / Slip is the human mistake that originates the defect chain — the upstream trigger

relatedConcepts.name: Issue
relatedConcepts.note: Issue is the observable symptom in the specification; sits between Error and Defect in the chain

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Issue
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Issue is the SQC specialisation of Issue — suspected spec rule violation

relatedConcepts.name: Defect Specification
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Defect is the confirmed rule violation; precedes Bug/Fault in the chain

relatedConcepts.name: Bug
relatedConcepts.note: Bug / Fault is the latent defect in the deployed system; Malfunction is what happens when a Bug is provoked

relatedConcepts.name: Malfunction
relatedConcepts.note: Malfunction is the observable, realised endpoint of the defect chain

concepts.definition:
A system has a 'malfunction' when it does something not intended, or not desired, according to its design/construction specification, or according to reasonable stakeholder expectations (even though there may be no official specification about that expectation). *Malfunctions are undesired outputs (including no outputs) from a 'real' system.*
**Defect chain:** Error/Slip → (Specification Issue) → Specification Defect → Fault/Bug → Malfunction
concepts.overview: **Malfunction** (*275) is the observable, realised failure endpoint of the Planguage defect chain. It is what happens in the real deployed system when a Bug (*339) is provoked by an agent or a data condition: an undesired output, a missing output, or a behaviour that violates either the formal specification or reasonable stakeholder expectation. A Malfunction is the defect chain made visible — it is the event that stakeholders, users, and operators experience. Unlike a Bug (latent, invisible until provoked) or an Issue (a specification-stage suspicion), a Malfunction has occurred: it is a completed, observable, negative system event. Severity ranges from catastrophic and permanent to barely noticeable, depending entirely on what the violated specification governs.

concepts.name: Master Definition

relatedConcepts.name: Master Term
relatedConcepts.note: a Master Term is the primary reference tag pointing to a Master Definition

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: a Master Definition is an authoritative element within a Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Source
relatedConcepts.note: a Master Definition should record Source, authority, version, and status

relatedConcepts.name: Authority
relatedConcepts.note: a Master Definition names the Authority whose reading is canonical

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: a Master Term (Tag) points to its Master Definition

concepts.definition: The **Master Definition** of a specification, or specification element, is the primary and authoritative source of information about its meaning. The master definition overrides any other (informal, not master) definition that is in conflict with it.
concepts.overview: **Master Definition** (*303) is the single, authoritative definition of a term or concept — the one source of meaning that overrides all others if they conflict. Every important term in a Planguage specification should have at most one Master Definition; everything else is commentary or informal shorthand. The Master Definition should record its Source, Authority, version, and status, so that readers can trace where the definition came from and who is responsible for it. Only one Master Definition per term is permitted within a given scope: multiple competing "master" definitions are a contradiction in terms.

concepts.name: Master Term

relatedConcepts.name: Master Definition
relatedConcepts.note: a Master Term is the primary reference tag pointing to a Master Definition — the two are inseparable

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: a Master Term is a Tag — the canonical capitalised identifier for a defined concept

concepts.definition: A **Master Term** is the primary, or only, reference tag to a master definition (*303).
concepts.overview: **Master Term** (*159) is the canonical Tag that serves as the unique reference handle for a [[Master-Definition.303|Master Definition]]. Where Master Definition (*303) is the authoritative statement of what a concept means, Master Term (*159) is the name you look it up by. Every Master Definition should have exactly one Master Term; the Master Term is what you write when you reference the definition elsewhere in a specification. Together, Master Term and Master Definition form the minimal unit of precise language in a Planguage specification.

concepts.name: Materials

relatedConcepts.name: Process Input
relatedConcepts.note: Materials enter a process as Process Inputs

relatedConcepts.name: Process Output
relatedConcepts.note: Materials may exit a process as Process Outputs

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: Materials are a sub-class of Resource — physical, non-information resources

relatedConcepts.name: Component
relatedConcepts.note: Materials are Components of a process or system when they are consumed or transformed

concepts.definition: **Materials** are non-information process-inputs and process-outputs.
concepts.overview: **Materials** (*326) is the Planguage term for physical, non-information inputs and outputs of a process — the raw materials, parts, goods, and physical objects that flow into or out of a system or process. This distinguishes them from information-based inputs and outputs, which are handled by separate concepts. In a manufacturing context, Materials are clearly physical; in a service context, they include tangible objects handled (documents, samples, packages) — but not the information content of those objects. Materials are a sub-class of Resource that is consumed or transformed, rather than merely used.

concepts.name: Maximum

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: Fail specifies the delivered performance floor; Maximum specifies the operational ceiling — distinct axes of constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: Survival is the extreme lower limit; Maximum is the extreme upper operational limit

relatedConcepts.name: Minimum
relatedConcepts.note: Minimum is the lower operational constraint; Maximum is the upper — together they define the operational band

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe
relatedConcepts.note: Catastrophe is the level beyond which system survival fails; Maximum prevents reaching such extremes operationally

concepts.definition: A **Maximum** specification is a constraint citing the highest allowable numeric level of a scalar variable in the operational variations of a system.
concepts.overview: **Maximum** (*537) is a scalar constraint that defines the upper operational bound — the highest level a scalar attribute is permitted to reach during normal system operation after handover. It is distinct from [[Fail.098b|Fail]] (*098): Fail constrains the *delivered* performance level at handover, while Maximum constrains the *operational variation* of that attribute during use. A system may be delivered well above the Fail level and still, in operation, exceed a Maximum constraint due to circumstances unknown at handover time. Together with [[Minimum.536|Minimum]] (*536), Maximum defines the permitted operational band, and the concept is particularly valuable in contracts that must distinguish between handover levels and operational levels.

concepts.name: Means Constraints

relatedConcepts.name: Means Objective
relatedConcepts.note: Means Constraints are at the same level as Means Objectives — both define the means-level requirement set and both can be overruled

relatedConcepts.name: Means Concept
relatedConcepts.note: Means Constraints constrain the means (design ideas, strategies) at the means level

relatedConcepts.name: Fundamental Constraints
relatedConcepts.note: Fundamental Constraints are above us and outside our control — the level above Means Constraints; we cannot override them

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Constraints
relatedConcepts.note: Strategic Constraints are self-imposed in our planning — above Means Constraints; we own and can change them

concepts.definition: **Means Constraints** are constraints imposed at levels 'below' and supporting us. This means that we can therefore overrule means constraints, if we need to in order to better satisfy our strategic requirements.
concepts.overview: **Means Constraints** (*428) are constraints that originate from the means level — from below our planning horizon. They are imposed by sub-systems, sub-teams, or lower-level design decisions that support our strategic objectives, rather than by overarching principles or our own strategic planning. The critical property of Means Constraints is **overridability**: because they come from a level we have authority over, we can override them when our strategic requirements demand it. This is the key distinction from [[Fundamental-Constraints.426|Fundamental Constraints]] (*426) — which come from above and cannot be overridden — and from [[Strategic-Constraints.427|Strategic Constraints]] (*427) — which are self-imposed and can be changed through our own planning process. The three Means-cluster concepts — [[Means-Concept.047d|Means Concept (*047)]], [[Means-Objective.215|Means Objective (*215)]], and **Means Constraints (*428)** — together define the means level of a system hierarchy.

concepts.name: Means Objective

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Objective
relatedConcepts.note: the Ends we are responsible for; Means Objectives exist only to serve Strategic Objectives

relatedConcepts.name: Means Concept
relatedConcepts.note: Means Objectives are one kind of Means — a variable performance objective formulated as a strategy

relatedConcepts.name: Means Constraints
relatedConcepts.note: Means Constraints are at the same level as Means Objectives; together they define the means-level requirement set

relatedConcepts.name: Measure of Effectiveness
relatedConcepts.note: Means Objectives are measured by Measures of Effectiveness at the means level

relatedConcepts.name: Measure of Performance
relatedConcepts.note: Means Objectives are operationalised via Measures of Performance

relatedConcepts.name: Abstract Strategy
relatedConcepts.note: a Means Objective is a kind of Abstract Strategy — a qualitative intermediate objective

concepts.definition: **Means objectives** are a 'strategy', in the format of a performance objective, to meet strategic objectives. They exist only to support meeting strategic objectives.
concepts.overview: **Means Objective** (*215) is a performance objective formulated as a strategy — it looks like a requirement (it is quantified, with a Scale, Meter, and Goal) but functions like a design choice (it is selected as the best means to reach a Strategic Objective). A Means Objective is always relative to a defined stakeholder level: your Means Objective can become your subordinate's Strategic Objective. This relativism is intentional — it enables a hierarchy of objectives where each level sees its objectives as ends and its chosen means as subordinate. The classification is temporary: as soon as a better means exists, the Means Objective should be replaced. The three Means-cluster concepts — [[Means-Concept.047d|Means Concept (*047)]], **Means Objective (*215)**, and [[Means-Constraints.428|Means Constraints (*428)]] — together describe the means level of a system hierarchy.

concepts.name: Measure, To

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: measurement is performed on a defined Scale; the Scale provides the units and context

relatedConcepts.name: Meter
relatedConcepts.note: the Meter is the defined measuring process or instrument used to obtain the numeric value on the Scale

relatedConcepts.name: Quantify To
relatedConcepts.note: Quantify is defining an attribute with a scale and benchmarks — distinct from measuring a real system

relatedConcepts.name: Estimate To
relatedConcepts.note: Estimate is predicting future results from past data — distinct from measuring a real system

concepts.definition: To **measure** is to determine the numeric level of a scalar attribute under specified conditions, using a defined process, by means of examining a real system.
concepts.overview: **Measure, To** (*386) is the *verb* concept — the act of measuring. It is distinct from [[Measure-noun.132b|Measure (noun) *132]], which is the *Scale of Measure* — the dimensional framework on which measurement happens. To measure is to obtain an actual numeric reading from a real system, on a defined [[Scale-of-Measure.132|Scale]] (*132), using a defined [[Meter.093|Meter]] (*093), under specified conditions. This distinguishes measuring from [[Quantify-To.385|Quantifying]] (*385) — which merely defines an attribute with a scale — and from [[Estimate-To.059|Estimating]] (*059) — which predicts future values from past data. Measuring is done on reality; quantifying is done on paper; estimating is done about the future.

concepts.name: Measure of Effectiveness

relatedConcepts.name: Measure of Performance
relatedConcepts.note: MoP is the direct performance measure; MoE is the downstream knock-on effect of that MoP in another system

relatedConcepts.name: Means Objective
relatedConcepts.note: Means Objectives are MoPs; their downstream strategic impacts are MoEs

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Objective
relatedConcepts.note: Strategic Objectives are what MoPs impact — they are the MoE side of the pair

concepts.definition: A **Measure of Effectiveness** is the quantified impact of a defined Measure of Performance (*482, MoP) on a defined system under defined environmental conditions.
concepts.overview: **Measure of Effectiveness** (*486) is the downstream, cross-system impact of a performance attribute — what happens in another system (or at a higher strategic level) as a consequence of achieving a particular MoP level. Where a MoP measures an attribute of a system in isolation, an MoE measures what that achievement *causes* elsewhere. MoE and MoP are always a pair: every MoP implies one or more MoEs, and every MoE traces back to at least one MoP. The distinction matters because optimising the MoP without tracking the MoE can produce locally excellent but strategically irrelevant performance.

concepts.name: Measure of Performance

relatedConcepts.name: Measure of Effectiveness
relatedConcepts.note: MoE is the downstream cross-system impact of a MoP; the two always form a pair

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: MoP is the quantified, measurable expression of a Performance attribute

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: Scale defines what is being measured; MoP is expressed on a Scale

relatedConcepts.name: Effectiveness
relatedConcepts.note: Effectiveness is the parent quality; MoE operationalises it at the cross-system level

concepts.definition: A **Measure of Performance** is a quantitative expression of performance or effectiveness attributes of a system. The Measure of Performance expresses the isolated measurable performance of a system, without respect to its knock-on effects (Measures of Effectiveness *486) in other systems.
concepts.overview: **Measure of Performance** (*482) is the numeric, internally-scoped measurement of a system attribute — how fast, how reliable, how usable — measured within the system's own boundary, under defined conditions. A MoP is always isolated: it does not include second-order effects in other systems. Its paired concept, the Measure of Effectiveness (*486), captures those downstream consequences. The distinction is essential: optimising a MoP without tracking the corresponding MoE can produce a technically excellent system that fails to deliver strategic value. MoP is the engineer's measurement; MoE is the stakeholder's reality.

concepts.name: Mechanism

relatedConcepts.name: Agent
relatedConcepts.note: Agents are one defined kind of Mechanism — the human or automated actor that executes processes

relatedConcepts.name: Process
relatedConcepts.note: a Process is (part of) HOW the Mechanism does a function — the activity that the Mechanism performs

relatedConcepts.name: Function
relatedConcepts.note: a Mechanism answers HOW a Function is performed — the means of execution

relatedConcepts.name: Procedure
relatedConcepts.note: a Procedure describes in writing how a Mechanism executes its Process

concepts.definition:
"A system of mutually adapted parts working together as … a means by which a particular effect is produced."
In Planguage: a **Mechanism** is HOW the system does a function ("means"). Don Mills (NZ, 2002) articulated the four-level WHY/WHAT/HOW/HOW structure: *Providing the service is WHY a system does a function. The function is WHAT the function does. A mechanism is HOW the system does a function ("means"). A process is (part of) HOW the mechanism does a function ("activity").*
concepts.overview: **Mechanism** (*527) is the *means* by which a system performs a function — the component, device, agent, or assembly of parts that makes a function happen. It sits between the Function (what the system does) and the Process (how the mechanism executes its activity). Agents (*163) are the canonical Planguage sub-type of Mechanism: the human or automated actor that follows a procedure to run a process. The concept is borrowed from the Oxford English Dictionary's definition and extended by Don Mills in 2002 into a WHY/WHAT/HOW/HOW hierarchy that gives each system element a precise analytical role.

concepts.name: Mega-step

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: an Evo Step is the atomic delivery unit; a Mega-step contains two or more of them

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: Evo is the process framework in which Mega-steps organise multiple delivery steps

relatedConcepts.name: Goal Step
relatedConcepts.note: a Goal Step is a milestone-defined Evo step; Mega-steps can be used to compose milestone-level groupings

relatedConcepts.name: Milestone
relatedConcepts.note: a Mega-step is one form of milestone — a grouping of delivery steps treated as a coherent delivery unit

concepts.definition: A **Mega-step** is an evolutionary 'step', or step plan, which includes two or more delivery steps.
concepts.overview: **Mega-step** (*345) is a composite Evo planning unit: a named grouping of two or more delivery steps (*141) that is treated as a single coordinated release or milestone. Mega-steps can nest — a Mega-step may contain other Mega-steps, all of which ultimately resolve to delivery steps at their leaves. The concept is the Planguage equivalent of what Microsoft called a "milestone" in their large-scale incremental development practice (Cusumano 1995): a 25–33% project chunk of 6–10 weeks containing everything needed, in theory, to ship to customers. Mega-steps give programme managers a planning layer above individual steps without abandoning the incremental discipline that makes Evo work.

concepts.name: Meter

relatedConcepts.name: Meter
relatedConcepts.note: Meter (parameter) *093 is the Planguage keyword; a Meter (noun) *094 is any artefact defined using that parameter

concepts.definition: A **Meter** (noun) is anything defined with the Meter parameter (*093). It is the concrete artefact — a measurement device, test process, or counting procedure — that results from writing a `Meter:` specification block.
concepts.overview: **Meter (noun)** (*094) is the artefact class produced by the Meter parameter (*093). Where *093 is the Planguage keyword — the specification instruction that says "describe how you will measure" — *094 is the *thing you get* when you follow that instruction: the specific measuring device, test process, survey, or accounting procedure selected for use on a given Scale. The distinction parallels "Process" (the parameter) versus "a process" (any instantiated process): *093 is the generic concept; *094 is the instance class. These two entries appear on the same page (p. 218) of Tom's source because they are inseparable: every Meter (noun) is created by a Meter (parameter) specification, and every Meter parameter specification creates a Meter (noun).

concepts.name: Meter

relatedConcepts.name: Meter (noun)
relatedConcepts.note: a Meter (noun) is any concrete artefact defined using this parameter — the specific measurement device or process selected

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: Scale defines WHAT is measured; Meter defines HOW — they are always paired

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Goal is one of the target values measured via the Meter; Meter gives feedback on whether Goal is being approached

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: Fail is the constraint level against which Meter results are compared to determine defect status

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: Benchmarks (Past, Record, Trend) are typically collected using a Meter; the Meter sub-parameter supports qualifier-scoped Benchmark values

relatedConcepts.name: Past
relatedConcepts.note: Past benchmarks are often collected with a specific Meter — the Meter [Past] sub-parameter captures this

relatedConcepts.name: Record
relatedConcepts.note: Record benchmarks similarly use a Meter — the Meter [Record] sub-parameter captures the instrument used

concepts.definition: A **Meter** parameter is used to identify, or specify, the definition of a practical measuring device, process, or test that has been selected for use in measuring a numeric value (level) on a defined Scale. *(Keyed icon: `-|?|-` — a `?` on top of the Scale icon `-|-|-`.)*
concepts.overview: **Meter** (*093) is the Planguage parameter that specifies *how* a scalar attribute is measured. Where the Scale (*132) determines *what* is being measured and gives meaning to the numbers, the Meter determines the practical measurement method — the survey, test script, APM agent, or accounting procedure used to produce those numbers. The Meter delivers feedback about real-system variation on the Scale, at timely intervals, at the lowest cost consistent with the quality of measurement needed for confident engineering decisions. Deming said it best: "There is nothing more important for the transaction of business than use of operational definitions." A Meter is the Planguage operationalisation of that imperative.

concepts.name: Method

relatedConcepts.name: Process
relatedConcepts.note: a Process is a defined activity envelope (Entry→Do→Exit); a Method is a discipline-bound family of techniques that may invoke many Processes

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: Planguage is both a specification language and a set of Methods (Impact Estimation, SQC, Evo, etc.)

relatedConcepts.name: Procedure
relatedConcepts.note: a Procedure is the written description of how one Process runs; a Method is a higher-level systematic body of Procedures and Processes

concepts.definition: A **Method** is a body of systematic techniques used by a specific discipline.
concepts.overview: **Method** (*547) is a discipline-level collection of systematic techniques — a coherent body of practices that a field uses to achieve its goals. Where a Process (*113) is a defined activity envelope for one sequence of steps, and a Procedure (*115) is the written description of how one Process runs, a Method is the broader systematic framework that a discipline relies on: a family of Processes, Procedures, and heuristics unified by a common purpose and theoretical basis. Planguage (*030) is itself a Method — it is a specification language *and* a set of methods (Impact Estimation, SQC, Evo, VDT) used by systems and requirements engineers.

concepts.name: Metric
concepts.keyedIcon: -|-|-> (Scale with units) or ---> (Scalar Arrow, simplified without explicit units)

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: a Scale parameter (or set of Scales) is the Planguage way of specifying a Metric; Scale is the vocabulary of Metric

relatedConcepts.name: Meter (noun)
relatedConcepts.note: the Meter noun is the measurement instrument; the Metric is the system of measures the Meter produces values on

relatedConcepts.name: Level
relatedConcepts.note: a Level is a specific value on a Scale; a Metric enables the quantification of such Levels

concepts.definition: A **Metric** is a system of related measures that facilitates the quantification of an attribute. The metric may be composed of one or more measure dimensions or characteristics. A *complex* attribute specification — one defined with a set of several Scales of Measure — is *also* a metric expression. There is no implication that a metric is 'elementary' (having only a *single* Scale).
concepts.overview: **Metric** (*095) is the system of measures used to quantify an attribute — the vocabulary and structure that makes a quality expressible as a number (or set of numbers). A Metric may be simple (one Scale, one unit) or complex (a multi-dimensional composite of Scales). In Planguage, Metrics are specified using the `Scale:` parameter or a set of Scales. The purpose is not measurement for its own sake: Metrics increase clarity, enable logical design thinking, support legal contracting, and drive evolutionary tracking of engineering progress. The word "metric" has been heavily abused; in Planguage it means specifically: a defined system of quantification for an attribute, not a KPI dashboard column.

concepts.name: Milestone

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: in Evo, successful Evo Step completion is the normal milestone; a Milestone is any defined measure of project progress

relatedConcepts.name: Mega-step
relatedConcepts.note: a Mega-step (set of Evo steps) is one way to define a more complex Milestone

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: Evo is the framework in which Milestones mark incremental delivery progress

relatedConcepts.name: Milestone
relatedConcepts.note: self — see note on domain

concepts.definition: A **Milestone** is any defined measure of project progress. In Evolutionary Project Management, the successful completion of Evo steps is the normal milestone concept. But any set of Evo steps (Mega-steps) can be used to define interesting milestones.
concepts.overview: **Milestone** (*372) is the most general concept for marking project progress: any defined, verifiable point in a project that signals that a specified state has been reached. In Planguage, Milestones are not fixed time-boxes — they are defined by content and conditions, not by calendar. An Evo Step's successful exit is the natural atomic Milestone in Evo. A Mega-step (*345) groups multiple steps into a higher-level Milestone. The Microsoft case (Cusumano 1995) illustrates industrial-scale Milestone practice: 25–33% project chunks treated as shippable units — what Planguage would call Mega-step Milestones.

concepts.name: Minimum

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: Fail is the delivered-level constraint (at handover); Minimum is the post-handover operational-variation constraint — distinct axes

relatedConcepts.name: Maximum
relatedConcepts.note: Maximum is the sibling upper-bound operational constraint; together Minimum and Maximum define the operational range

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: Survival is the Scalar Constraint below which the system ceases to function; Minimum is a less severe lower bound for operational control

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe
relatedConcepts.note: Catastrophe is the limit below which the system cannot recover; Minimum defines an earlier, operational warning boundary

concepts.definition: A **Minimum** is a constraint specification citing the lowest allowable level of a scalar variable in the operational variations of a system. It is used to define operational characteristics of a system after handover to stakeholders.
concepts.overview: **Minimum** (*536) is a Scalar Constraint that specifies the lowest allowable value of an attribute *during ongoing operation* — after the system has been handed over to stakeholders. It is deliberately distinct from Fail (*098), which constrains the *delivered* level at handover. The distinction matters because a system can be delivered above the Fail threshold but subsequently drop below the Minimum during operation due to conditions unknown at delivery time. Minimum enables post-handover process control and operational contracts. Its sibling, Maximum (*537), defines the upper operational bound.

concepts.name: Minor Defect

relatedConcepts.name: Major Defect
relatedConcepts.note: sibling pair — Major is the opposite severity class; downstream removal cost is significantly higher

concepts.definition: A minor defect is a non-major defect. It has no major downstream cost potential.
concepts.overview: **Minor Defect** (*096) is the lower-severity class of specification defect in Planguage's SQC framework — the complement to Major Defect (*091). A minor defect can be deferred and fixed later at approximately the same cost; it does not trigger compounding downstream costs if left unresolved in the current phase. The distinction is not about the *size* of the defect but about its *potential consequences downstream*. Minor defects can be left to chance or collected and resolved in a later phase without significant penalty.

concepts.name: Mission

relatedConcepts.name: Function
relatedConcepts.note: Mission is the highest-level Function of a system — an un-dramatic statement of main function

relatedConcepts.name: Core Ideology
relatedConcepts.note: Core Ideology (Collins/Porras) is the broader strategic context; Mission is the 'What

relatedConcepts.name: Core Purpose
relatedConcepts.note: Core Purpose is the 'Why'; Mission is the 'What' — a complementary but distinct concept

relatedConcepts.name: Scope
relatedConcepts.note: Mission is one type of scope delineator — it bounds the system's purpose domain

concepts.definition:
A mission specifies who we are (or what we do) in relation to the rest of the world. It is the highest level of function of a system. The mission should not contain 'vision' description ('We make the best planes in the world'). It is an un-dramatic statement of the main function of a business or organization.
Mission, like function, intentionally excludes specific levels of attributes in its description.
concepts.overview: **Mission** (*097) is the highest-level Function of a system or organisation — a plain, un-dramatic statement of *what* the system does in relation to the rest of the world. It is a Requirement, not an aspiration: it excludes performance levels, quality claims, and Vision-language. Mission is deliberately paired with Core Purpose (*662, the *Why*) — Mission says *What* we do; Core Purpose explains *Why* that matters. A well-formed Mission is unambiguous, testable, and narrow enough to exclude what the organisation does *not* do.

concepts.name: Mitigation

relatedConcepts.name: Risk
relatedConcepts.note: Mitigation reduces Risk by lowering P(Attack→Damage); residual Risk remains unless Mitigation is provably 100% effective

relatedConcepts.name: Threat
relatedConcepts.note: Threat is the latent source; Threat Mitigation strategies reduce the existence of Threats in type and volume

relatedConcepts.name: Attack
relatedConcepts.note: Attack is a Threat activated; Attack Mitigation reduces the existence of Attacks in type and volume

relatedConcepts.name: Damage
relatedConcepts.note: Post-Attack Mitigation reduces Damage after a successful Attack

concepts.definition: Mitigation is any Strategy which is intended to deal with a Threat (potential Attack), or an actual Attack, within the system, or by being added on after the Threat has successfully penetrated the system (Attack has occurred).
concepts.overview: **Mitigation** (*670) is the Planguage risk-analysis parameter for any Strategy that deals with Threats, Attacks, or resulting Damage. It operates at three distinct intervention points: before an Attack (Threat Mitigation), during an Attack (Attack Mitigation), and after damage has occurred (Post-Attack / Post-Damage Mitigation). Mitigation is not a single action but a layered set of defensive strategies, each of which may partially or fully reduce Risk — while acknowledging that no Mitigation is guaranteed to be 100% effective, meaning residual Risk always requires specification. The synonym "Security *670" reflects the close relationship between Mitigation and security engineering.

concepts.name: Mode

relatedConcepts.name: Condition
relatedConcepts.note: a Mode of operation can be described by many variable, possible, and impossible States/Conditions

relatedConcepts.name: State
relatedConcepts.note: a Mode is characterised by a set of possible and impossible States; State and Condition are the finer-grained context within a Mode

concepts.definition: A mode is a defined type of operation of a system.
concepts.overview: **Mode** (*485) is a Planguage Temporal Sequence Parameter that names a defined type of operation of a system. A Mode provides a structured context for requirements: different Modes may allow or prohibit different Functions, impose different Performance Constraints, or trigger different Conditions and States. Specifying Modes makes implicit operational context explicit — enabling engineers to write requirements that are clearly scoped to a named operational regime (e.g., "normal operation," "emergency mode," "maintenance mode").

concepts.name: Model

relatedConcepts.name: Template
relatedConcepts.note: Template's purpose is to give ideas about possible patterns or ideas; Model's purpose is to convey information about one or more aspects of a system or product

concepts.definition:
A model is an artificial representation of an idea or a product. The representation can be in any useful format including specifications, drawings and physical representations.
Rationale: to convey information about an idea without having to deal with a full scale and real version of it.
concepts.overview: **Model** (*448) is a Planguage Software and Technology Material concept: an artificial representation of an idea or product, in any useful format — specifications, drawings, physical mock-ups, simulations. The defining purpose is to convey information without requiring the full-scale real version. A Model can have all the attributes of a real system — Function, Design, Performance, Cost, and Constraints — but at reduced scale, fidelity, or completeness. This is what distinguishes a Model from a Template (*254): a Template provides a pattern or starting point for generating something; a Model represents something that already exists or is being designed.

concepts.name: Monster

relatedConcepts.name: Symmetry
relatedConcepts.note: Monster is part of a symmetric extension of the Planguage target axis — Symmetry *695 is the companion concept enabling 'open to rare monster success' alongside Downside limits

relatedConcepts.name: Trigger
relatedConcepts.note: Trigger *696 is the detection signal for when Monster-level conditions are approaching; early detection signal for the Monster

relatedConcepts.name: Stretch
relatedConcepts.note: Monster sits above Stretch on the ambition axis; Stretch is the conventional motivating level; Monster is a conditional extreme-upside capture level

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Goal is the committed level; Monster is an extreme optional target far above Goal and Stretch, conditional on demand and supply both exceeding forecasts

concepts.definition:
A new ambition level above Stretch. Syntax: `Monster: Scale 100 × Goal { if available, then capture }`
Example: Goal: 5,000 Model 3 / week · Stretch: 7,500 / week · Monster: 20,000 / week `{ if demand and supply both exceed forecasts by 3σ }`.
**Suggested by Grok for the *Precise Heresies* book.**
concepts.overview: **Monster** (*694) is the most recent Planguage target level — a conditional extreme-upside ambition level positioned above Stretch on the scalar performance axis. It is not a commitment (unlike Goal); it is an explicitly conditional capture target: "if exceptionally favourable conditions materialise, we will seize this level." Monster extends the Planguage target family symmetrically upward, paired with the Symmetry (*695) concept that argues systems should be as open to extreme upside as they are protected against extreme downside. The concept was suggested by Grok during Tom Gilb's development of the *Precise Heresies* book (2025-11-26) and is among the newest Planguage concepts.

concepts.name: Motivating

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: Stakeholders are the defined parties whose motivation the systems engineer must identify; Motivating components cause defined Stakeholders to act

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: Motivating Needs translate into formal Requirements — identifying what motivates Stakeholders is the upstream step before requirements are written

relatedConcepts.name: Need
relatedConcepts.note: Motivating Needs are the specific sub-class of Need that cause Stakeholders to fund or support a project

relatedConcepts.name: Action
relatedConcepts.note: Motivating components cause defined Stakeholders to perform defined Actions

concepts.definition:
A 'motivating' systems component is one which causes people to act.
**Formally:** Motivating [defined Systems Component] is a cause of defined [Stakeholders] for doing defined [Actions].
**Usage 1. Motivating Needs:** the stakeholder needs which cause them to fund or otherwise support a project or any effort to achieve those needs.
Rationale: if a systems engineer can correctly identify the motivating components, they can derive relevant requirements and designs; and as a result get better funding and support for their efforts.
concepts.overview: **Motivating** (*443) is a Planguage adjective classifying any system component — need, requirement, function, design idea — that *causes* defined Stakeholders to act. The formal definition captures the causal structure: a motivating component → Stakeholders → Actions. The most practically important use is **Motivating Needs** — the specific stakeholder needs that cause them to fund, support, or engage with a project. Systems engineers who correctly identify motivating components can write requirements that stakeholders actually care about, and as a result secure the funding and cooperation the project requires. The concept encodes Jack Welch's measurement observation: what you don't measure and reward, you don't get.

concepts.name: Must Avoid

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: POLYSEMY — Fail.098 is the preferred current name for the same scalar constraint concept; Must Avoid.098 is the legacy synonym maintained for backward compatibility. Both files share concept number *098.

relatedConcepts.name: Must Do
relatedConcepts.note: Must Do *539 (synonym: Tolerable *539) is the level just slightly better than the Must Avoid level — the minimum performance that is still acceptable

concepts.definition:
Must Avoid is a parameter, an abbreviation for the concept 'Fail limit' (*098). It is defined as a level that must be avoided if possible because there is some type and degree of failure at that level and at numerically worse levels.
*See also:* Fail (-ure) Limit *098 — preferred use.
concepts.overview: **Must Avoid** (*098) is a legacy Planguage scalar constraint parameter — the earliest name for what Tom Gilb now calls the Fail limit (Fail.098). Both names share concept number *098 in standard Planguage polysemy. Must Avoid is maintained in the glossary for backward compatibility with organisations and literature that have used the term since 1988. The preferred modern parameter is **Fail** (also *098), with keyed icon `!`. Must Avoid uses icon `>>` — which Tom himself notes is less intuitive than `!` for a warning limit. The concept defines the level at which some degree of failure begins, and at all numerically worse levels.

concepts.name: Need

relatedConcepts.name: Problem Definition
relatedConcepts.note: Problem Definition is the upstream source of a Need; a Need is often the stakeholder's expression of a stated Problem

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: a Need may or may not be agreed as a formal Requirement; Requirements are the formalised, prioritised subset of Needs

relatedConcepts.name: Design Ideas
relatedConcepts.note: a Need might not be acted upon through a Design; Design Ideas are the implementation response to formally prioritised Needs

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: a Need is always a Need of a defined Stakeholder — the concept is only meaningful relative to a stakeholder who holds it

relatedConcepts.name: Change Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: a single Need can generate multiple Change Requirements; Need is the underlying motivation, Change Requirement is the formalised specification

concepts.definition:
A 'need' is something desired by a defined stakeholder.
The implication is that satisfying that need would have some value for some stakeholder.
A need might not be agreed as a formal requirement, and it might not be prioritized such that it is actually acted upon (designed and implemented).
It is a term often used as a stakeholder view of a problem before requirements specification is carried out.
concepts.overview: **Need** (*599) is a pre-requirements concept in Planguage — the raw stakeholder-level expression of desire or problem, prior to formal specification. A Need is always held by a defined Stakeholder; satisfying it would have value. But a Need is not automatically a Requirement: it may not be formally agreed, not be prioritised, and never be implemented. This looseness is intentional: Need belongs at the problem-exploration stage, before the discipline of requirements specification has filtered, formalised, and committed to specific obligations. Need is the upstream input to Problem Definition, which feeds Requirements, which are then acted upon through Design Ideas.

concepts.name: Non-Commentary

relatedConcepts.name: Implementable-Specification
relatedConcepts.note: polysemy — *294 is shared; Implementable Specification is the spec-architecture framing of the same binding content

relatedConcepts.name: Commentary
relatedConcepts.note: dual — Commentary is the non-binding wrapper; Non-Commentary is the binding core

relatedConcepts.name: Background
relatedConcepts.note: one kind of Non-Commentary — framing context that is still binding (not mere comment)

relatedConcepts.name: Core-Specification
relatedConcepts.note: the most critical subset of Non-Commentary — the five core parameters

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: the whole; Non-Commentary is the binding half

relatedConcepts.name: Major-Defect
relatedConcepts.note: a defect in Non-Commentary is, by definition, a major defect

concepts.definition: 'Non-commentary' refers to written specification that is not commentary: it is either core specification or background specification. All major specification defects are found in non-commentary. But, not all specification defects in non-commentary specifications are major. By definition, major defects *cannot* be found in 'commentary'.
concepts.overview: **Non-Commentary** (*294) is the binding half of any Planguage specification — the 'meat' as opposed to the 'fat'. It encompasses both Core Specification (*633, the five essential parameters: Scale, Meter, Goal, Constraint, Definition) and Background Specification (*507, the supporting context such as Source, Risk, Assumption, Past). Non-Commentary is where major defects live: a defect in Core Specification or Background is a major defect by category, whereas a defect in Commentary is almost always minor. Quality controllers performing SQC should concentrate their rigorous checking effort on Non-Commentary territory, scanning commentary only quickly. Concept *294 is polysemic with [[Implementable-Specification.294b]] — Tom Gilb's alternative framing of the same idea as "the part of the spec that can actually be implemented."

concepts.name: Status

relatedConcepts.name: Past
relatedConcepts.note: sister concept — Past is a previous Status (historical snapshot); Status is the current snapshot; same measurement structure at different temporal positions

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: Status is one form of Benchmark — the current-state reference level from which progress is measured

relatedConcepts.name: Goal-Step
relatedConcepts.note: Goal Step is the planned increment; Status reports the current level against which Goal Steps are calibrated

relatedConcepts.name: Level
relatedConcepts.note: Status is a named kind of scalar Level — a defined position on a Scale at the present point in time

relatedConcepts.name: Scale-of-Measure
relatedConcepts.note: Status is always expressed on a Scale — it reports the current position on that Scale

relatedConcepts.name: Tolerable
relatedConcepts.note: Status is compared to Tolerable to determine if the project is in the Intolerable Range (below Tolerable) or alive (at or above Tolerable); see StatusToTolerable *699

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Status is compared to Goal to determine if the attribute is in the Success Range (Status ≥ Goal) or still needs work (Status < Goal); see StatusToGoal *700

relatedConcepts.name: Status
relatedConcepts.note: Polysemy disambiguation: Status *174 is Condition Status (evaluation outcome of a condition check); Status *513 is Scalar Status (current measured numeric value on a scale)

relatedConcepts.name: StatusToTolerable
relatedConcepts.note: the gap from current Status to the Tolerable threshold — measures distance to project-viability line

relatedConcepts.name: StatusToGoal
relatedConcepts.note: the gap from current Status to the Goal level — measures distance to declared success

concepts.definition: A **Status** level is the current scalar value of an attribute being tracked as a system evolves — the last known measured level on a defined Scale of Measure, at a defined point in time, space, and event condition.
concepts.overview: **Status** (*513) is the current measured value of a scalar attribute — the present-moment anchor for tracking progress during system evolution. Compare Status to [[Tolerable.539|Tolerable]] to determine which range the project is in. Compare Status to [[Goal.109|Goal]] to know how far success is. The keyed icon `----(----` marks the current position on the attribute level axis.

concepts.name: Numeric Tag

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: parent — a Numeric Tag is one specific form of Tag; Tag is the general identification concept

relatedConcepts.name: Abbreviation
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Abbreviation is a language-dependent short form; Numeric Tag is language-neutral

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage-Term
relatedConcepts.note: context — the Planguage Term is the natural-language name; the Numeric Tag is its language-neutral identifier

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage-Concept
relatedConcepts.note: subject — every Planguage Concept has exactly one Numeric Tag

concepts.definition:
A term beginning with the 'asterisk *' sign, and immediately followed by a number. The Numeric Tag is the human-language-neutral unique tag for each Planguage Glossary-defined term.
**Rationale:** This *Tag is intended to help identify Planguage concepts unambiguously regardless of local natural language, local business type terminology, company terminology, dialect, spelling, translations, changes in terminology, or any other reason for variation. It is applied to all glossary defined terms and to related symbols, icons and Planguage constructs.
concepts.overview: **Numeric Tag** (*110) is the stable, language-neutral unique identifier for every concept in the Planguage glossary — written as an asterisk followed immediately by a number (e.g., `*110`). Where natural-language names are vulnerable to translation, dialect variation, corporate renaming, and spelling inconsistency, the Numeric Tag is invariant. A concept can acquire new names, synonyms, or translations without changing its *NNN identity. This makes Numeric Tags essential for cross-language communication, glossary maintenance, and unambiguous cross-referencing in multi-organisation engineering projects. The same mechanism applies to concept polysemy: when two concepts genuinely share a concept number (Tom Gilb's convention for closely related synonyms), they share a Numeric Tag — which is itself a documented claim about their relationship.

concepts.name: OK

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: lower boundary — the Fail level is just below OK; once above Fail, the system enters the OK range

relatedConcepts.name: Scale-of-Measure
relatedConcepts.note: context — OK is a level position on a Scale of Measure

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: upper boundary — the OK range runs from just above Fail up to just below Goal

relatedConcepts.name: Acceptable-Range
relatedConcepts.note: container — the Acceptable Range is the band from OK to Goal; OK is its lower boundary

relatedConcepts.name: Success-Range
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — the Success Range begins above Goal; OK is the lower complement below Goal

relatedConcepts.name: Tolerable
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Tolerable is the level just above Catastrophe; OK is the level just above Fail — different positions on the axis

relatedConcepts.name: Level
relatedConcepts.note: parent — OK is a named Level on a scalar attribute axis

concepts.definition:
The OK point is the level which is, barely, no-longer considered Failure. The OK Range starts just above the Fail level, at the OK Point; and continues until the Goal point level. The dictionary definition of '*satisfactory, but not especially good*', is suitable.
The OK concept is designed so that it allows us to specify a 'positive' point (Tolerable, OK, Goal, Stretch), rather than 'negative points' (Catastrophe, Fail). OK is the lower (worst) boundary of the OK area, where the upper boundary of the OK range is just below the Goal level.
concepts.overview: **OK** (*669) is the named scalar level that marks the minimum acceptable performance — the lowest point at which a system is no longer in Failure. It sits just above Fail (*098) and defines the bottom of the Acceptable Range (*545): from OK up to (but not including) Goal (*109). The dictionary sense — "satisfactory but not especially good" — captures it well. OK was introduced as a *positive* label for the minimum acceptable state, complementing the negative labels (Catastrophe, Fail). Its synonym, Satisficed (*669), is credited to Erik Simmons (Intel, 2014) drawing on Herbert Simon's satisficing concept: reaching the minimally acceptable level in a complex system where optimality is unverifiable. Per the Goal *109 claims log, OK is "minimum acceptable performance; just inside the Success Range" — more precisely, just inside the Acceptable Range, below the Success Range.

concepts.name: Object

relatedConcepts.name: Artifact-Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: hierarchy — Entity → Object → Artifact; Artifact is a man-made Object

relatedConcepts.name: Entity
relatedConcepts.note: hierarchy — Entity is the broadest category; Object is a tangible Entity

relatedConcepts.name: System
relatedConcepts.note: synonym / scale — an Object is a small System; a System is a large Object; distinction is relative scope

relatedConcepts.name: Component
relatedConcepts.note: role — an Object is typically a Component of a larger Object or System

relatedConcepts.name: Attribute
relatedConcepts.note: characterisation — Objects are described by their Performance, Function, Resource, and Design attributes

concepts.definition:
An object is any system component that can be described in terms of its attributes; functions, *performance, and cost*; as well as past, present or future attribute states.
An object can be real or conceptual. It is a term we use for systematic building blocks of larger systems — which themselves might be viewed as more-complex objects. Any object can be composed of sub-objects. It is a matter of taste, and relative scope whether we use the term object or system to describe something.
concepts.overview: **Object** (*099) is the Planguage concept for any system component that can be fully described by its Attributes — Performance, Function, Cost, and Design — plus its attribute states across time. Objects can be real or conceptual, small or large; the distinction between Object and System (*145) is one of relative scope, not structural type. A watch is an Object when viewed as a component of a larger system; it is a System when viewed as the focus of analysis. The key Planguage departure from software engineering's use of "object" is explicit: Objects include *performance and cost* attributes — the central systems-engineering idea that the software field routinely overlooks.

concepts.name: Objective Function

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: output — Goals are derived from an Objective Function by identifying highly desirable states

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: subject — the Objective Function is defined relative to specific stakeholders' utility

relatedConcepts.name: Value
relatedConcepts.note: substance — the Objective Function maps states of the world to their value (utility) for stakeholders

relatedConcepts.name: Aim
relatedConcepts.note: upstream — an Aim is qualitative; the Objective Function formalises and maps the utility that an Aim points toward

relatedConcepts.name: Vision
relatedConcepts.note: upstream — Vision provides qualitative direction; the Objective Function operationalises it as a utility-valued mapping

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: downstream — Requirements are formal expressions of desirable states identified through the Objective Function

concepts.definition:
"An objective function maps future sequences of states of the world to the value they have for specific stakeholders, in utility terms. Objective functions have various inputs from which to derive an overall utility value. The inputs can be called the dimensions of the objective function.
The assumed aim is to maximise the utility we get.
Applying our objective function (which could well be no more than a judgment) helps us identify particular sets of states that look highly desirable to us and which we may choose to take as goals. Goals (also known as objectives, targets, 'a vision', and so on) are a mental device for creating and communicating plans."
— Matthew Leitch, *Dynamic Management for an Uncertain World*, 23 July 2002.
concepts.overview: **Objective Function** (*619) is the stakeholder-relative mapping from system states to utility — the formal description of what a stakeholder *values* and how much. It is a View & Stakeholder Parameter: it is always defined relative to specific stakeholders, and it expresses their values as a utility function over possible futures. Its inputs are the *dimensions* of the objective function — the attributes, conditions, and outcomes that the stakeholder cares about. Its output is a scalar utility value for any given future state. Goals (*109) are then chosen as the states that score highly on this mapping. The Objective Function is thus the bridge between qualitative Visions (*422) or Aims (*001) and quantitative Goals (*109) — it is the formal articulation of "what we are trying to maximise."

concepts.name: Objective

relatedConcepts.name: Subjective
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — Subjective depends on a specific observer's value judgement; Objective does not

relatedConcepts.name: Objectivity
relatedConcepts.note: noun form — Objectivity is the property; Objective (adj) is the descriptor applied to a measurement or specification

relatedConcepts.name: Scale-of-Measure
relatedConcepts.note: enabler — a measurement is Objective when it is expressed on an agreed Scale independent of observer values

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: context — Performance levels are the canonical example of Objective quality specification in Planguage

relatedConcepts.name: Objective-Function
relatedConcepts.note: contrast — Objective Function (noun) is a utility mapping; Objective (adjective) is an orthogonal concept about value-independence

concepts.definition:
Independent of a given set of values. Not 'Subjective'.
**Objective Quality:** Quantifiable quality levels independent of the value judgement (good or bad levels) of defined stakeholders. Example: "The mean time to repair an average fault is less than 24 hours."
concepts.overview: **Objective** (*656, adjective) means *independent of a given set of values* — specifically, independent of the value judgements of any particular observer or stakeholder group. An objective measurement or specification is one that any suitably equipped observer can verify without needing to share a particular value system. In Planguage, this is operationalised through Scale of Measure: a specification that states "mean time to repair < 24 hours" is objective because it can be verified by anyone with a clock, regardless of whether they think 24 hours is *good* or *bad*. The adjective is distinct from *Objective Function* (*619, a noun) and from *Objective* as a noun (*100, a requirement type). The antonym is Subjective (*657): a judgement that depends on the observer's value framework.

concepts.name: Objectivity
concepts.definition: **Objectivity** means being independent of subjective influences — a reality outside individual minds, closer to some real truth independent of the observer's person or culture.
concepts.overview: **Objectivity** (*388) describes the degree to which an analysis, measurement, or specification is free from the distortions of individual perspective, culture, or personal bias. Planguage does not treat objectivity as binary — all work exists on a spectrum between full objectivity and full subjectivity. Understanding that spectrum, naming it, and quantifying it is central to credible engineering. Planguage supplies dozens of parameters and devices — Scales, Meters, Confidence levels, Source citations — to move specifications toward the objective end of that spectrum.

concepts.name: Observability
concepts.definition: **Observability** is the property of a system component (a state variable) such that it is possible to compute or estimate that component's state from a finitely long observation of the system's outputs. The generic term "observable" covers any means of observing a system: testing, measuring, seeing, sensing, feeling, hearing, and so on.
concepts.overview: **Observability** (*176) is a system property borrowed from feedback control theory: a system is observable if you can determine its full internal state by watching its external outputs over a finite time. In Planguage, observability is a prerequisite for measurable specifications — if you cannot observe a quality attribute, you cannot verify that it has been achieved. The companion concept is [[Controllability.175]]: a component is controllable if a signal can drive it to a desired state, and observable if its state can be inferred from outputs. Both are required for a closed-loop engineering discipline.

concepts.name: On
concepts.definition: **On** is a predefined State value. **On** is the same as True (*625). It represents the binary "active / true" condition of a two-state system attribute.
concepts.overview: **On** (*625) is a synonym entry for True (*625) — a predefined, named value for a two-state (Boolean) attribute in Planguage. When a Scale of Measure uses discrete binary states, Planguage provides the paired values On/True (*625) and Off/False (*626) as standard named constants. The concept sits within the State (*174) family. For the canonical definition, see [[True.625b]].

concepts.name: Open-Ended
concepts.definition: **Open-Ended** means that a system's architecture — its interfaces and basic structure — is of such a nature that most system changes, no matter how unexpected, are relatively easy to handle without major effort. The more open-ended, the easier the change will probably be.
concepts.overview: **Open-Ended** (*101) is a system property describing the degree to which a system's architecture can absorb unexpected changes with minimal effort. It is the qualitative parent concept for a family of measurable Adaptive attributes including Portability, Improvability, Extendability, and Connectability. A system that is highly open-ended does not merely tolerate planned extensions — it handles changes that were not foreseen at design time. Open-endedness is not a vague aspiration; it is quantifiable through the Adaptive attribute metrics described in CE Section 5.6.

concepts.name: Operational
concepts.definition: **Operational** refers to a state of defined systems in defined states of operation. It is used as a qualifier for Requirements, Attributes, and Functions: Operational Requirements, Operational Attributes, Operational Functions — each referring to the set that applies to the system while it is in a defined, active operating state.
concepts.overview: **Operational** (*562) is an adjective that scopes a requirement, attribute, or function to the system's defined operational states — the conditions under which the system is actively fulfilling its purpose. It contrasts with Adaptive attributes, which describe how easily the system can be changed or ported. An Operational Requirement specifies the behaviour the system must exhibit while running; an Adaptive requirement specifies how easy it is to change that behaviour. Together, Operational and Adaptive (*563) cover the full lifecycle of system quality.

concepts.name: Optimize
concepts.definition: To **optimize** a design ("design optimization") is to reduce one or more resources needed to achieve specified levels of performance or stakeholder values — or to improve the impact of designs in the direction of specified performance targets.
concepts.overview: **Optimize** (*417) is a design process activity: the deliberate search for designs that either reduce the resources required to achieve a specified performance level, or improve performance for a given resource budget. Optimization is not vague "making things better" — it is targeted improvement against explicit Scales and Meters, working toward Design Targets. It applies equally to development-process efficiency (reducing time, people, money to meet specs) and to product design (reducing lifecycle costs at a specified quality level). The core engineering measure of optimization success is an improved value-to-cost ratio.

concepts.name: Optimum Checking Rate
concepts.definition: The **Optimum Checking Rate** is the average rate of checking a specification that gives the highest productivity (effectiveness). It is usually measured as the number of pages or lines per hour at which the peak ability to identify major defects per page is achieved.
concepts.overview: **Optimum Checking Rate** (*126) is the specific Checking Rate (*015) at which a specification review yields the most major defects per page. It is a calibrated SQC parameter, not a universal constant — the optimum varies by document type, checker experience, and domain. Its practical importance is severe: organisations that allow checkers to read at their natural "comfortable" pace almost always exceed the optimum rate, producing the illusion of a thorough review while finding far fewer defects than a slower, more deliberate pace would yield. The Optimum Checking Rate is the antidote to fast, cheap-feeling, defect-missing inspections.

concepts.name: Option
concepts.definition: An **Option** is a short form of "template option." It defines optional parameters or qualifiers in a model or a template for Planguage. An Option is indicated by placing the parameter name in parentheses `( )` in the template definition — showing that it may be omitted in any given specification instance.
concepts.overview: **Option** (*432) marks a parameter or qualifier within a Planguage template as non-mandatory — it may be included or excluded in any specific specification that uses the template. The keyed icon is parentheses around the parameter name: `(ParameterName: ...)`. This is in contrast to mandatory template parameters, which appear without parentheses. Option keeps templates flexible without losing the discipline of a defined structure: readers know exactly which fields are required and which are permissible additions.

concepts.name: Or Better

relatedConcepts.name: Or Worse
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — marks the lower boundary of an unacceptable range, opposite of Or Better

relatedConcepts.name: Until
relatedConcepts.note: sibling range qualifier — marks an upper bound on a level

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — Or Better defines one edge of a range

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar Target
relatedConcepts.note: context — Or Better is typically attached to a Target level

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar
relatedConcepts.note: context — Or Better applies within a scalar specification

concepts.definition: **Or Better** is an expression used within a scalar specification to explicitly emphasise that the specified level has a range of acceptable values, rather than being just a fixed, single value. In other words, **Or Better** helps identify the specified level as the beginning of a desired range.
concepts.overview: **Or Better** (*550) makes explicit that a specified numeric level is the *minimum* acceptable value — anything exceeding it is also acceptable. It is implied by any scalar Target specification, but stating it removes all ambiguity for readers who might otherwise treat a Target as a hard exact value. The keyed icon `-> +` visually signals that the range extends toward higher (more positive) numbers. Its antonym is [[Or-Worse.549|Or Worse]], which opens the unacceptable range in the opposite direction.

concepts.name: Or Worse

relatedConcepts.name: Or Better
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — marks the lower boundary of an acceptable range, opposite of Or Worse

relatedConcepts.name: Until
