relatedConcepts.note: sibling range qualifier — marks an upper bound on a level

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — Or Worse defines one edge of an unacceptable range

relatedConcepts.name: Fail / Must Avoid
relatedConcepts.note: context — Or Worse is typically attached to a Fail or Must Avoid level

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar
relatedConcepts.note: context — Or Worse applies within a scalar specification

concepts.definition: **Or Worse** is an expression used within a scale specification to explicitly emphasise that the specified level has a range of unacceptable values, rather than being just a fixed, single value. In other words, **Or Worse** helps identify the beginning of a 'no go' range.
concepts.overview: **Or Worse** (*549) makes explicit that a specified numeric level is the *maximum* acceptable boundary for a failure or constraint — anything at or below it is unacceptable. It is implied by a Constraint or Fail-type specification, but stating it removes ambiguity for readers who might treat the figure as a precise threshold rather than the opening of a prohibited range. The keyed icon `-> -` signals that the range extends toward lower (more negative/worse) numbers. Its antonym is [[Or-Better.550|Or Better]], which opens the acceptable range in the opposite direction.

concepts.name: Or

relatedConcepts.name: And
relatedConcepts.note: sibling logical operator — conjunction, pairs with Or for compound qualifiers

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: primary context — Or appears inside qualifier brackets

relatedConcepts.name: Or
relatedConcepts.note: self (keyed icon form: |)

concepts.definition: **Or** is a logical operator used in qualifiers, or other appropriate specifications, to indicate alternative conditions. If any one **Or** condition is true, then the set of conditions is true.
concepts.overview: **Or** (*514) is the Planguage logical disjunction operator: when multiple conditions are joined by Or, the compound is true if *any one* of the conditions is true. It appears most commonly inside qualifier brackets to specify that a requirement applies under any of several alternative circumstances. The terse keyed form is `|` — the same pipe symbol used in many programming languages. Parentheses may be used to group and clarify compound logical expressions combining Or with [[And.045|And]].

concepts.name: Output

relatedConcepts.name: Process Output
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — the output of a process (data or material); shares number *179 with Product

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: context — function outputs are performance attributes (qualities, resource savings, workload capacities)

relatedConcepts.name: Process Input
relatedConcepts.note: complement — inputs enter a process; outputs leave it

relatedConcepts.name: Result
relatedConcepts.note: synonym — Result (*130) is an alternate name for Output in some contexts

concepts.definition: An **output** (or system output) is the result of a system.
concepts.overview: **Output** (*636) describes what a system or process produces. It has two primary forms in Planguage: a *function output* (a performance attribute such as quality, resource saving, or workload capacity), and a *process output* (a resource asset — always data for intellectual processes, but extensible to materials for physical processes). Understanding which form is intended is critical because function outputs are measured as [[Performance.434|Performance]] attributes, while process outputs are tracked as resource results. The complement is [[Process-Input.178|Input (*178)]].

concepts.name: Owner

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: parent — an Owner is a Stakeholder with specific authorisation rights over an object

relatedConcepts.name: Plan Parameter
relatedConcepts.note: context — Owner is a plan parameter that can be specified for any object

concepts.definition: An **Owner** is a person or group responsible for an object, and for authorising any change to it.
concepts.overview: **Owner** (*102) is the Planguage authority role that designates who is responsible for a given object — a system, specification, standard, process, or any other defined artifact — and who must authorise any change to it. Every object that can be changed should have an identified Owner. The Owner maintains the object's control information (Status, Version, Quality Level, Location) and ensures it conforms to relevant standards. An Owner is a specialised [[Stakeholder.233|Stakeholder]] with binding authority over the object's lifecycle.

concepts.name: Parallel Development

relatedConcepts.name: Parallelity
relatedConcepts.note: specialisation — Parallelity is the parameter that quantifies the degree of parallel development

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: context — Parallel Development applies when multiple Evo Steps run concurrently

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: parent methodology — Parallel Development is a strategy within Evo

relatedConcepts.name: Feedback
relatedConcepts.note: trade-off — concurrent steps reduce the feedback available between steps

relatedConcepts.name: Platform Management
relatedConcepts.note: same concept number *363 — polysemy; see Platform-Management.363 for that distinct concept

concepts.definition: **Parallel Development** is any development of more than one Evo step that takes place at the same time.
concepts.overview: **Parallel Development** (*363) is the Evo strategy of running multiple Evolutionary steps concurrently rather than sequentially. It trades some of the learning advantage of sequential delivery — where each step's feedback informs the next — against the scheduling advantage of reduced elapsed time between successive deliveries. With intelligent step planning, the loss of inter-step feedback can be minimised. The parameter [[Parallelity.104|Parallelity (*104)]] quantifies how many concurrent Evo cycles are operating at any moment.

concepts.name: Parallelity

relatedConcepts.name: Parallel Development
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept — Parallelity quantifies the degree of Parallel Development

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: unit — Parallelity counts how many Evo Steps run concurrently

relatedConcepts.name: Backroom
relatedConcepts.note: context — Parallelity applies to both Backroom and Frontroom Evo cycles

relatedConcepts.name: Frontroom
relatedConcepts.note: context — Parallelity applies to both Frontroom and Backroom Evo cycles

concepts.definition: **Parallelity** is having a number of parallel Evolutionary cycles. These can be any type of Evo cycles — frontroom or backroom (concurrent engineering).
concepts.overview: **Parallelity** (*104) is the Planguage relationship parameter that specifies or measures the count of concurrent Evolutionary cycles in operation at any given time. It quantifies [[Parallel-Development.363|Parallel Development (*363)]] — making explicit what is otherwise left as an informal arrangement. Both [[Frontroom.343|Frontroom]] and [[Backroom.342|Backroom]] cycles count toward the Parallelity measure, so concurrent engineering in the backroom and parallel user-facing increments in the frontroom are both captured by the same parameter.

concepts.name: Parameter Definition

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter Specification
relatedConcepts.note: parent — Parameter Definition is one form of Parameter Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter Value
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — Parameter Value is the other form of Parameter Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Parameter Definition describes what a Parameter means

concepts.definition: A **parameter definition** is a set of words defining the parameter. It is a parameter specification.
concepts.overview: **Parameter Definition** (*323) is the descriptive component of a [[Parameter-Specification.325|Parameter Specification (*325)]]: a set of words that defines what a parameter means, as opposed to assigning it a numeric value. It typically appears as the content of a `Scale:` or `Meter:` parameter — for example, "Up-time of [defined components] in [defined places] at [defined times]" defines what the Scale measures. Together with [[Parameter-Value.324|Parameter Value (*324)]], it forms the complete Parameter Specification. Parameter Definitions make the meaning of measurement unambiguous before any numeric target is stated.

concepts.name: Parameter Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter Definition
relatedConcepts.note: component — one of the two forms of Parameter Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter Value
relatedConcepts.note: component — the other form of Parameter Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Parameter Specification is the content of a Parameter

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: syntax position — Parameter Specification comes after the parameter name and any [qualifier]

concepts.definition: A **parameter specification** is either the 'Parameter Definition', or the 'Parameter Value'. It generally comes after the parameter name, after any [qualifier], and before any source information.
concepts.overview: **Parameter Specification** (*325) is the umbrella term for the content of a Planguage parameter — everything that follows the parameter name and any optional qualifier bracket, up to the source pointer (`<-`). It has exactly two forms: a [[Parameter-Definition.323|Parameter Definition (*323)]] (a set of words describing what the parameter means) or a [[Parameter-Value.324|Parameter Value (*324)]] (a numeric or categorical level). Understanding this two-form structure clarifies the syntax of every Planguage specification line: name + [qualifier] + *specification* + source.

concepts.name: Parameter Value

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter Definition
relatedConcepts.note: A Parameter Value is one kind of Parameter Specification *325, alongside Parameter Definition *323 — together they constitute all content that can follow a parameter name

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter Specification
relatedConcepts.note: Parameter Value is a sub-type of Parameter Specification — every Parameter Value is also classified as a Parameter Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter
relatedConcepts.note: Parameter Value specifies the meaning of a given Parameter — it is the numeric content of a parameter usage

concepts.definition: The parameter value is a numeric value, which varies along a defined scale, and which specifies the meaning of a given parameter.
concepts.overview: **Parameter Value** (*324) is the numeric content that gives a Planguage parameter its quantitative meaning — the actual number on the scale. Every parameter value is a specific position along a defined Scale of Measure, stated under qualifying conditions. Crucially, every parameter value is also classified as a Parameter Specification (*325): the two concepts overlap because a numeric value both specifies and defines the parameter's intent. The distinction from Parameter Definition (*323) is that definitions are textual/descriptive, while values are numeric. Without parameter values, Planguage specifications remain qualitative — parameter values are what make requirements testable.

concepts.name: Parameter

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter Definition
relatedConcepts.note: Parameter Definition *323 specifies the meaning of a Parameter in textual/descriptive form — one of two kinds of Parameter Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter Value
relatedConcepts.note: Parameter Value *324 specifies the meaning of a Parameter in numeric form — the other kind of Parameter Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter Specification
relatedConcepts.note: Parameter Specification *325 is the supertype covering both Parameter Definition and Parameter Value — what follows a parameter name in a Planguage tag

relatedConcepts.name: Term
relatedConcepts.note: A Parameter is a Planguage-defined Term — distinguishable from user-defined terms by its leading capital letter

relatedConcepts.name: Project Language
relatedConcepts.note: Projects may extend the core Parameter set by defining tailored parameters in a Project Language *247

relatedConcepts.name: User-Defined Term
relatedConcepts.note: User-Defined Terms *530 describe the target system; Parameters describe the specification language — the two are distinct

concepts.definition: A parameter is a Planguage-defined term. Parameters are always written with at least a leading capital letter, to signal the existence of a formal definition.
concepts.overview: **Parameter** (*105) is a formally defined term within the Planguage specification language — the named slots that give a specification its structure. Parameters include concepts such as Goal, Scale, Past, Meter, Survival, Risk, and dozens more: each is a Planguage keyword, capitalised to signal its formal status. Parameters are not user-defined terms (which describe the target system); they are parts of the specification language itself. A parameter is brought to life in a tag by appending a Parameter Specification (*325) — either a textual Parameter Definition (*323) or a numeric Parameter Value (*324). Projects may extend the core parameter set by declaring tailored parameters in a Project Language (*247).

concepts.name: Parent

relatedConcepts.name: Kid
relatedConcepts.note: Kid *266 is the immediate inferior component — Parent and Kid are the two sides of the same hierarchical relationship

concepts.definition: A parent is the *immediate superior* component to a kid.
concepts.overview: **Parent** (*267) designates the immediate superior component in a Planguage specification hierarchy. Every specification element that has sub-elements has a Parent relationship — it is the structural backbone of decomposition in Planguage. Parent and Kid (*266) are a conjugate pair: you cannot have a parent without at least one kid, and every kid has exactly one immediate parent. The Parent relationship is what makes it possible to trace a specific requirement or design decision back through successively higher levels of abstraction until the root business objective is reached. Without this hierarchical linkage, a specification is a flat list; with it, it is a traceable tree.

concepts.name: Participant
concepts.definition: A person or group who participates actively in a defined process.
concepts.overview: **Participant** (*238) is the Planguage review-role term for any person or group who takes an active part in a defined process — typically a specification review, inspection, or quality gate. The definition is deliberately broad: a Participant is not a passive observer, but an active contributor to the process. In structured reviews (such as Planguage Inspections), roles are assigned to ensure that participation is purposeful and accountable — a Participant who is named for a review is expected to have read the material, assessed it against criteria, and be prepared to contribute findings. The concept applies whenever a defined process has named or typed participants whose involvement is tracked.

concepts.name: Past

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: Past is a form of Benchmark — a reference level stated on a defined Scale for comparison with targets

relatedConcepts.name: Status
relatedConcepts.note: Sister concept — Past is a previous Status (historical snapshot); Status *513 is the current snapshot; conceptually the same measurement at different temporal positions. In STG: Status = current measured level; Past = a prior Status reading used as benchmark.

relatedConcepts.name: Level
relatedConcepts.note: Past is a named kind of scalar Level — a defined position on a Scale at a specific historical point in time

relatedConcepts.name: Scale-of-Measure
relatedConcepts.note: Past is always expressed on a Scale — it reports a historical position on that Scale

concepts.definition: A Past parameter is used to specify historical experience, a 'benchmark'. A Past specification states a historical numeric level, on a defined Scale, under specified conditions [time, place, event] for a scalar attribute.
concepts.overview: **Past** (*106) is the Planguage parameter for recording historical measured levels of a scalar attribute — the starting point of calibrated improvement. It captures where a system (or predecessor system, or competitor) actually was on a defined Scale, at a specific historical time and place. Its sister concept is Now (*513), which records the current level rather than a historical one; conceptually both are the same kind of measurement, differing only in temporal position. Past levels are essential for setting rational targets: without knowing where you started, you cannot judge whether a Goal is ambitious, trivial, or impossible. The keyed icon `<` points backward along the scale arrow, signalling a historical reference point.

concepts.name: Path Plan

relatedConcepts.name: Step Level
relatedConcepts.note: Step Level *535 is the individual planned intermediate target within a Path Plan — the Path Plan is a series of Step Levels

relatedConcepts.name: Delivered Level
relatedConcepts.note: Delivered Level *533 records what was actually achieved at a step; Path Plan expresses what was planned

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: Path Plans incorporate Benchmark levels (Past, Past competitors) as contextual reference points within the path

relatedConcepts.name: Goal-Step
relatedConcepts.note: Goal Steps are incremental planned levels — the Path Plan aggregates them into a complete planned trajectory

concepts.definition: A Path Plan is a series of two or more specified levels on a defined scale of measure from defined optional Benchmark levels and including any interesting series of defined constraint and Target levels. The path plan can be used to specify any interesting planned set of intermediary targets before a major target such as a Goal level is reached, and it can include that major target level. Usage: it is particularly useful for describing our planned levels, and their benchmark/constraint context levels for a series of releases and for a set of evolutionary delivery steps.
concepts.overview: **Path Plan** (*534) is the Planguage mechanism for expressing a planned trajectory of improvement across multiple releases or evolutionary delivery steps — the full sequence of where you are going, not just the final destination. A Path Plan combines Benchmark reference levels (Past, competitor data), intermediate constraint and Target levels (Step Levels), and the major Goal or Stretch targets into a single coherent specification on one defined Scale. The abbreviation parameter is `Path`. The keyed icon `<-v->` represents the path as a trajectory along the scalar arrow. The Path Plan makes evolutionary delivery strategies explicit and testable: each step in the path has a committed level that can be measured at delivery.

concepts.name: Pattern

relatedConcepts.name: Generic Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: Generic Qualifier *668 is itself a Planguage pattern — a reusable structure for qualifying conditions

relatedConcepts.name: Qualified Conditions
relatedConcepts.note: Qualified Conditions *666 exemplify the pattern form: context + problem + solution, applied to qualifier specification

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier Definition
relatedConcepts.note: Scale Qualifier Definition *446 is a concrete Planguage pattern for defining qualifier semantics on a Scale

concepts.definition: A 'Pattern' is a general tool that defines any idea structure, or sets of structures, in any intelligible format, which can be exploited by tailoring it to, or copying it into, a specific domain. Patterns are a form of stored wisdom or knowledge. The main idea is to allow people to organize and reuse knowledge, rather than re-inventing it from scratch or memory.
concepts.overview: **Pattern** (*655) is the Planguage concept for reusable knowledge structures — formalised solutions to recurring problems in a specific context. The concept draws on both Christopher Alexander's architectural pattern language (context → problem → forces → solution) and James Coplien's software design pattern formulation. A Pattern is not a template to be followed blindly: it is a documented piece of wisdom that is exploited by tailoring or copying into a specific domain. Crucially, Planguage itself is a collection of patterns — Scale definitions, Principles, Entry and Exit Rules, Process descriptions, Glossary entries, and Standards are all patterns in the Planguage sense: reusable structures that can be adapted for specific projects and domains.

concepts.name: Percentage Impact

relatedConcepts.name: Incremental Scale Impact
relatedConcepts.note: Percentage Impact is Incremental Scale Impact *307 expressed as a percentage of the required improvement (benchmark→target distance)

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Impact
relatedConcepts.note: Scale Impact *403 is the broader category; Percentage Impact is the percentage-normalised form used in impact estimation tables

relatedConcepts.name: Percentage Uncertainty
relatedConcepts.note: Percentage Uncertainty *383 is always stated together with Percentage Impact — the ± deviation that expresses estimation risk on the same percentage scale

concepts.definition:
A percentage impact is an incremental scale impact expressed as a percentage of the required improvement (The required improvement being the scalar distance between a chosen benchmark (0%) and a chosen target (100%)).
A percentage impact is part of an impact estimate and is used in Impact Estimation tables.
concepts.overview: **Percentage Impact** (*306) is the normalised form of Incremental Scale Impact (*307) — it expresses how much a specific design idea contributes to the required improvement, as a percentage of the total gap from baseline to target. By mapping all design ideas onto a common 0–100% scale (where 0% = no improvement from benchmark and 100% = full achievement of target), the Percentage Impact makes different design ideas directly comparable regardless of the underlying measurement unit. Percentage Impact is always accompanied by Percentage Uncertainty (*383), which expresses the ±deviation around the estimate. Together, `%Impact ± %Uncertainty` forms the core metric of an Impact Estimation table — the primary tool for evaluating design ideas before committing to them.

concepts.name: Percentage Uncertainty

relatedConcepts.name: Percentage Impact
relatedConcepts.note: Percentage Uncertainty is always stated together with Percentage Impact *306 — it expresses the ±deviation around the central Percentage Impact estimate

relatedConcepts.name: Uncertainty
relatedConcepts.note: Percentage Uncertainty is a specific form of Uncertainty *310, quantified on the same percentage scale as Percentage Impact

relatedConcepts.name: Incremental Scale Impact
relatedConcepts.note: Percentage Uncertainty derives from Scale Uncertainty, which in turn is based on the Incremental Scale Impact *307 estimate range

concepts.definition:
Percentage uncertainty is calculated from the scale uncertainty, baseline and target data; and stated together with the percentage impact value.
Percentage Uncertainty can be used to identify risks in using specific design ideas: the numeric 'best case' and 'worst case' deviations from the Percentage Impact estimate provides important pointers towards the level of risk involved.
concepts.overview: **Percentage Uncertainty** (*383) is the ±deviation around a Percentage Impact estimate — it quantifies how uncertain the impact estimate is, expressed on the same percentage scale. Where Percentage Impact (*306) says "this design idea contributes approximately X% of the required improvement," Percentage Uncertainty says "that X% could in practice range from (X − U)% to (X + U)%." High Percentage Uncertainty signals high engineering risk: the design idea might do much more or much less than estimated. This risk profile directly drives engineering actions — more investigation, design refinement, early evolutionary step delivery, or contract conditions controlling impact. The keyed icon `%.±?` combines the percentage sign, the uncertainty ± symbol, and the question mark of open uncertainty.

concepts.name: Perfect

relatedConcepts.name: Ideal
relatedConcepts.note: Perfect implies Ideal, but Ideal does not imply Perfect

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: Perfect is a benchmark concept; used as a Benchmark parameter

concepts.definition: A 'perfect' level of an attribute is a level that is flawless, complete and without defect of any kind. It cannot ever be improved under any circumstances. It is a benchmark concept.
concepts.overview: **Perfect** (*648) is the absolute upper bound of any performance attribute — a level that is flawless, complete, and incapable of further improvement under any circumstances. Because perfection cannot be reliably attained or proven attained in real systems, it is never a valid *target*; it functions solely as a *benchmark*. The key distinction is that every Perfect level is Ideal, but not every Ideal level is Perfect — Ideal is context-sensitive (e.g. a market share of 51% may be Ideal precisely because 100% invites anti-monopoly action). Notably, the notion of perfect is also viewpoint-dependent: a component with apparent faults may be part of a larger system operating at a faultless level.

concepts.name: Performance Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Constraint is a sub-type of Performance specification

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Constraint is one component of a full Performance Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Target
relatedConcepts.note: Constraint limits lie 'outside' target levels on the scale

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Constraint is a scalar specialisation of Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: Fail is one of the two primary constraint parameters

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: Survival is one of the two primary constraint parameters

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Survival limit
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Survival limit is the Survival sub-type of Performance Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Design
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Design must satisfy Performance Constraints

concepts.definition: A performance constraint specifies some upper and lower limits for an elementary scalar performance attribute. These limits are either levels at which failure of some kind will be experienced, or levels at which the survival of the entire system is threatened. Fail and Survival parameters are sufficient to specify performance constraints.
concepts.overview: **Performance Constraint** (*438) defines the hard outer boundaries — the *Fail* and *Survival* limits — that a scalar performance attribute must not breach. Unlike performance targets (Goal, Stretch, Wish), which express aspirational levels, constraints express the edges of acceptable operation: cross a Fail limit and the system has failed in some defined sense; cross a Survival limit and the system's continued existence is at risk. Constraints are typically imposed by stakeholders with authority (law, contract, safety standards), and that authority should be documented alongside the constraint. A key nuance is that constraints apply in *both* directions — there are valid reasons to constrain performance from above as well as below.

concepts.name: Performance Design

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Design aims to satisfy Performance requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Function Design
relatedConcepts.note: Parallel design category: function vs. performance

relatedConcepts.name: Design Process
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Design is produced by the Design Process

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Cost Design
relatedConcepts.note: Parallel design category: performance vs. cost

relatedConcepts.note: Performance Design may have side effects on Function Requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Design Specification
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Design is a type of Design Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Design exists to satisfy Performance Requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Design
relatedConcepts.note: self

concepts.definition: Performance Design is design specification aimed at, or as a side effect, satisfying performance level requirements. By definition this includes capacity requirements, quality requirements and savings requirements.
concepts.overview: **Performance Design** (*520) is the category of design specification whose primary purpose — or significant side effect — is to satisfy performance-level requirements: quality, workload capacity, and resource saving. It is the performance-focused counterpart to Function Design (*521) and Cost Design (*522). The most important insight is that *no design is pure*: any design specification, however narrowly intended, will in reality affect multiple requirement dimensions simultaneously — performance, function, cost, and condition constraints all interact whether or not the designer plans for it.

concepts.name: Performance Survival limit

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: Survival is the parameter that expresses a Survival limit

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Survival limit constrains a scalar Performance attribute

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Fail

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Target
relatedConcepts.note: Target levels sit inside the Survival boundary on the performance scale

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Design
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Design must not breach the Survival limit

concepts.definition: A hard constraint on a scalar performance specified by the Survival limit parameter. Crossing a Performance Survival limit means the continued existence or viability of the entire system is threatened.
concepts.overview: **Performance Survival limit** (*477) is the hardest category of constraint in the Performance cluster — the level beyond which the system itself is at existential risk. While a Fail limit (*098) marks where a requirement is not met, a Survival limit marks where the *system* cannot continue to operate. It is expressed using the `Survival` parameter and applies to scalar performance attributes (quality, capacity, savings). Its parallel on the resource side is Resource Survival limit (*476). The Survival limit is the non-negotiable outer edge of acceptable operation; no performance design is valid if it permits the Survival limit to be breached.

concepts.name: Performance Target

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Target sets a desired level of a Performance attribute

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Target is one component of a Performance Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: Constraints bound the scale; targets sit inside those bounds

relatedConcepts.name: Target
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Target is a scalar specialisation of Target

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Goal is the committed performance target type

relatedConcepts.name: Stretch
relatedConcepts.note: Stretch is the uncommitted motivating target type

relatedConcepts.name: Wish
relatedConcepts.note: Wish is the uncommitted valued target type

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Survival limit
relatedConcepts.note: Survival limit is the outer boundary within which targets are set

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Design
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Design aims to achieve Performance Targets

concepts.definition: A performance target is a stakeholder-valued, numeric level of system performance. There are three types: a committed planned level (Goal), an uncommitted motivating level (Stretch), and an uncommitted valued level (Wish).
concepts.overview: **Performance Target** (*439) expresses *where we want to get to* on a performance scale — as distinct from a Performance Constraint (*438), which expresses *where we must not go*. Every performance target is numeric and stakeholder-valued, meaning it reflects something a stakeholder cares about enough to commit to (Goal), be challenged by (Stretch), or wish for (Wish). Performance targets are always set *inside* the constraint boundaries; a target that exceeds a Survival or Fail limit is definitionally invalid. Together, Performance Targets and Performance Constraints form a complete Performance Requirement (*100).

concepts.name: Performance to Cost Ratio

relatedConcepts.name: Sum of Performance
relatedConcepts.note: Numerator: Sum of Performance is the top of the ratio

relatedConcepts.name: Sum of Costs
relatedConcepts.note: Denominator: Sum of Costs is the bottom of the ratio

relatedConcepts.name: Value
relatedConcepts.note: Performance-to-Cost Ratio approximates value; Value-to-Cost is more precise

relatedConcepts.name: Benefit
relatedConcepts.note: Benefit-to-Cost is a more precise but more demanding variant

relatedConcepts.name: Quality to Cost Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: Polysemous sibling: Quality-to-Cost-Ratio.010 shares concept number *010

concepts.definition: For a design idea (or set of design ideas or an Evo step), the ratio of the performance improvements to the cost of the resources needed to implement them. For a selected set of requirements: **Performance to Cost Ratio = Sum of Performance / Sum of Costs**. Such ratios allow comparison of different design ideas to determine which is the most cost efficient. Popularly (USA): "Bang for the buck."
concepts.overview: **Performance to Cost Ratio** (*010) is a composite quantification parameter that compares how much performance gain a design idea delivers against how much it costs to implement — the Planguage formalisation of "bang for the buck." It is calculated as the Sum of Performance (*008) divided by the Sum of Costs (*128), and is used to rank competing design options during Evo steps. Its most important insight is that it is a *simpler* metric than a true Value-to-Cost or Benefit-to-Cost ratio: it measures how far a project is moving toward its goals per unit of expenditure, not the real-world value that stakeholders receive for that cost.

concepts.name: Performance

relatedConcepts.name: Quality
relatedConcepts.note: Quality is the 'how well' sub-type of Performance

relatedConcepts.name: Workload Capacity
relatedConcepts.note: Workload Capacity is the 'how much' sub-type of Performance

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Saving
relatedConcepts.note: Resource Saving is the 'how much saved' sub-type of Performance

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Requirement specifies desired Performance levels

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Target
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Target sets a desired Performance level

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Constraint sets hard limits on Performance levels

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Survival limit
relatedConcepts.note: Hardest constraint on Performance — system existence at risk

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Design
relatedConcepts.note: Performance Design is the solution mechanism for achieving Performance

relatedConcepts.name: Performance to Cost Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: Measures efficiency: performance gain per unit of cost

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: Benchmarks calibrate Performance levels against external references

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: Constraint is the parent class of Performance Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Measure of Performance
relatedConcepts.note: Measure of Performance is the quantification mechanism for Performance

concepts.definition: System performance is an attribute set that describes measurably 'how good' the system is at delivering *effectiveness* to its stakeholders. Each individual performance attribute level has a different 'effectiveness,' for different stakeholders, and consequently different value or utility. Performance attributes are scalar, and are of three types: Quality ('how well'), Workload Capacity ('how much'), and Resource Saving ('how much saved').
concepts.overview: **Performance** (*434) is the broadest Planguage concept for measuring *effectiveness* — everything about how well a system serves its stakeholders, expressed as scalar, measurable attributes. It encompasses three sub-types: Quality ('how well' something is done), Workload Capacity ('how much' can be handled), and Resource Saving ('how much' is saved compared to an alternative). The key distinction from conventional usage is that Performance in Planguage is not limited to throughput or speed — it explicitly includes all qualitative measures that stakeholders care about. The value of any given Performance level is stakeholder- and condition-specific.

concepts.name: Philosophy
concepts.definition: "A basic theory concerning a particular subject." (*The American Heritage Dictionary, Dell.*) In Planguage usage: "The set of values of an individual culture." Planguage is based on the central idea that quantification of multiple critical quality values is basic to controlling real systems.
concepts.overview: **Philosophy** (*217) is a system property that captures the foundational theory or set of values underlying a system, organisation, or culture. In Planguage, the concept is most often used as a documentation parameter to state the core belief system that drives a project or system's design choices. Its most important insight — and the philosophy of Planguage itself — is that precise quantification of multiple critical quality values is not optional: it is the *basic mechanism* by which real systems are controlled, improved, and verified.

concepts.name: Place

relatedConcepts.name: Time
relatedConcepts.note: Time is the temporal counterpart to Place's spatial/organisational scope

relatedConcepts.name: Event
relatedConcepts.note: Event is the third scope dimension alongside Place and Time

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: Place is used as a qualifier condition (e.g. [Place = USA])

relatedConcepts.name: Scope
relatedConcepts.note: Place is one of the non-temporal, non-event Scope dimensions

concepts.definition: 'Place' defines '*where*'. It relates to any notion of place, such as geographic location, stakeholder role, customer market, or system component. Place is used both as a parameter and in a qualifier condition.
concepts.overview: **Place** (*107) is the Planguage scope parameter that captures the non-temporal, non-event dimension of *where* a requirement, target, or constraint applies. It encompasses geography, organisation, user type, system component, and role — any useful dimension of 'where' that helps qualify a requirement. Alongside Time (*153) and Event (*062), it forms the three-dimensional qualifier space that makes Planguage requirements precise and condition-specific. A requirement that omits Place is implicitly universal — which is rarely the stakeholder's intent and often dangerously wrong.

concepts.name: Plan Do Study Act Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: PDSA-Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: polysemous alias — same number, same concept

relatedConcepts.name: Plan [PDSA]
relatedConcepts.note: first phase of the cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Do [PDSA]
relatedConcepts.note: second phase of the cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Study [PDSA]
relatedConcepts.note: third phase of the cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Act [PDSA]
relatedConcepts.note: fourth phase of the cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: parent domain in which PDSA cycles operate

relatedConcepts.name: Statistical Process Control (SPC)
relatedConcepts.note: analytical foundation for the Study phase

concepts.definition: The **Plan Do Study Act Cycle** (PDSA Cycle) is a process cycle — a method for changing a defined work process so that it measurably improves. The cycle requires standardizing and stabilizing the target process first, so that the effects of any change can be credibly observed. Developed by Walter Shewhart and taught by W. Edwards Deming.
concepts.overview: **Plan Do Study Act Cycle** (*168) is a four-phase iterative method for improving any work process through disciplined experimentation. Each pass through the cycle produces either an adopted improvement or a refined hypothesis to test next. The key distinction from ad-hoc change is the *Study* phase: data is collected and analyzed before any change is permanently adopted. The most important insight is that you cannot improve what you have not first stabilized — process control is the prerequisite for process improvement.

concepts.name: Plan

relatedConcepts.name: Plan Do Study Act Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: parent cycle of which Plan [PDSA] is the first phase

relatedConcepts.name: Do [PDSA]
relatedConcepts.note: immediately following phase

relatedConcepts.name: Plan
relatedConcepts.note: general concept of a plan; a lifecycle phase — distinct from this PDSA phase

relatedConcepts.name: Planned Level
relatedConcepts.note: scalar target parameter; shares the word 'plan' but unrelated in meaning

relatedConcepts.name: Planning
relatedConcepts.note: the broader human activity of visualizing the future

concepts.definition: **Plan [PDSA]** is the first phase of the Plan Do Study Act Cycle (*168). It involves specifying a theory or hypothesis — including a procedure for testing it — before any change is made to the process under improvement.
concepts.overview: **Plan [PDSA]** (*169) is the hypothesis-and-design phase that opens every PDSA improvement cycle. Without a clear, testable theory, the Study phase has nothing to confirm or refute. The key distinction from general planning (*108, *382) is that Plan [PDSA] is always paired with a specific measurement design: you declare in advance what you will observe and what outcome would count as confirmation. The most important insight is that the quality of the entire cycle depends on the precision of the hypothesis formulated here.

concepts.name: Plan

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Plan / Goal
relatedConcepts.note: scalar target parameter and Evo planning concept; same number, different concept

relatedConcepts.name: Plan [PDSA]
relatedConcepts.note: the Plan phase within a PDSA cycle; distinct from this lifecycle concept

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Plan
relatedConcepts.note: specific evolutionary project plan for implementing Evo steps

relatedConcepts.name: Planning
relatedConcepts.note: the broader human activity that produces Plans

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: a plan can contain requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement Specification
relatedConcepts.note: formal requirements within a plan

relatedConcepts.name: Planned Level
relatedConcepts.note: scalar target parameter; shares word 'plan' but is a numeric target, not an artifact

concepts.definition: A **Plan** (*108) is an idea, or more likely a set of ideas, created with a view to possible future implementation.
concepts.overview: **Plan** (*108) is a lifecycle artifact — a collection of ideas, requirements, design decisions, and project-management content created with the intent of guiding future action. It sits within the broader planning cluster alongside Planning (*382), Evo Plan (*322), and Plan [PDSA] (*169), but is specifically the *document or artifact* that results from planning activity. The key distinction from Plan [PDSA] (*169) is that Plan *108 is an artifact, not a process phase. The key distinction from Planned Level (*109) is that Plan *108 is a collection of ideas, not a single numeric target on a scale.

concepts.name: Planguage Concept

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: the specification language that defines and uses these concepts

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage Term
relatedConcepts.note: any name that points to a formally defined Planguage concept

relatedConcepts.name: User-Defined Term
relatedConcepts.note: project-local terms that are NOT Planguage concepts

concepts.definition: A **Planguage Concept** (*188) is a formally specified idea used in Planguage. Planguage is defined formally in Gilb: *Competitive Engineering* [2005, Elsevier]. www.Gilb.com contains samples and many related papers.
concepts.overview: **Planguage Concept** (*188) is the meta-level idea that makes Planguage reusable across projects and languages: a formally defined unit of meaning that is independent of the particular word, symbol, or language used to refer to it. A concept can be referenced by any synonym, icon, number, or foreign-language term — the underlying definition remains stable. The key distinction from a Planguage Term (*211) is that a concept is the *meaning*, while a term is one of possibly many *names* pointing to that meaning. The most important insight is that separating concept from term allows a specification to be taught in Norwegian, Japanese, or any other language without rewriting the definitions themselves.

concepts.name: Planguage Parameter
concepts.definition: Planguage Parameter is the taxonomy class for all Planguage keywords used in specifications (Goal, Fail, Meter, Source, Risk, etc.). It is a grouping concept: every Planguage keyword is a kind of Planguage Parameter, organised into 14 sub-groups (Identification, Description, Scope, Qualifier, Source, Logical-Structure, Relationship, Temporal, Status, Evidence, Risk-Analysis, Quantification, Process-I/O, View).
concepts.overview: **Planguage Parameter** (*830) is part of HumanAgent Gilb's Value Delivery framework, an extension to Tom Gilb's original Planguage. It is not in the source PlanguageGlossary.pdf — it has been authored to capture concepts the framework needs but the PDF did not name.

concepts.name: Planguage Term

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: the specification language that defines which terms belong to it

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage Concept
relatedConcepts.note: the meaning that a Planguage Term names; term and concept are distinct

relatedConcepts.name: User-Defined Term
relatedConcepts.note: project-local names that are NOT Planguage terms

concepts.definition: A **Planguage Term** (*211) is any concept name that is defined as being part of Planguage.
concepts.overview: **Planguage Term** (*211) is the linguistic face of a Planguage Concept — the specific word, symbol, or phrase by which a formally defined concept is accessed in a specification. A single concept (*188) may have many terms pointing to it (English, Norwegian, German, a keyed icon, an acronym), but each term, taken alone, is just a name. The key distinction from a Planguage Concept (*188) is that terms are project-level and language-level labels; concepts are the cross-project, language-independent definitions those labels point to. The most important insight is that Planguage terms are valid *across* projects and organizations — which is precisely what separates them from User-Defined Terms (*530).

concepts.name: Planguage

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage Concept
relatedConcepts.note: the formally defined ideas that make up Planguage's vocabulary

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage Term
relatedConcepts.note: any concept name defined as being part of Planguage

relatedConcepts.name: User-Defined Term
relatedConcepts.note: project-local terms that extend Planguage within a project

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement Specification
relatedConcepts.note: one of the key artifacts Planguage is used to produce

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: one of the key methods Planguage supports

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: SQC — one of the key methods Planguage supports

concepts.definition: **Planguage** (*030) is a specification language and a set of related methods for systems engineering. It specifically supports requirement specification, design specification, design impact analysis, specification quality control, and evolutionary project management.
concepts.overview: **Planguage** (*030) is the integrated specification language and methodology that Tom Gilb developed to make systems engineering quantified, testable, and evolutionary. Its name contracts "Planning Language" — a term Tom still uses before introducing "Planguage" to new audiences. The key distinction from informal specification languages is that Planguage is formally defined: every term maps to a concept (*188), every scalar specification uses a Scale (*132) and a target parameter (*109), and every project uses a PDSA-driven delivery cycle (*168). The most important insight is that Planguage is not merely a notation — it is a complete epistemology for engineering systems: you do not know what you mean until you can measure it.

concepts.name: Planning

relatedConcepts.name: Planning
relatedConcepts.note: the general human activity of visualizing the future; Planning [SQC] is a specific sub-process within SQC

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: the parent process of which Planning [SQC] is a sub-process

relatedConcepts.name: Review
relatedConcepts.note: SQC is a structured form of review; Planning [SQC] opens the review process

relatedConcepts.name: Plan
relatedConcepts.note: lifecycle artifact; shares the word 'plan' but Planning [SQC] is a process step, not an artifact

concepts.definition: **Planning [SQC]** (*284) is the opening sub-process of Specification Quality Control. An SQC team leader produces a 'master plan' for the quality control of a specific 'main specification.' The planning session lasts approximately one hour and involves completing a Master Plan form — assigning defect types to reviewers, specifying which document areas will be checked, and setting checking rates.
concepts.overview: **Planning [SQC]** (*284) is the structured preparation phase that makes Specification Quality Control efficient, targeted, and measurable. Rather than letting reviewers loose on a document without direction, Planning [SQC] divides the inspection work deliberately: who looks for which defect type, in which sections, at what checking rate. The key distinction from general Planning (*382) is that Planning [SQC] is entirely within the SQC process — it does not produce a project plan or a lifecycle artifact; it produces a one-page Master Plan form for a single review session. The most important insight is that without this planning step, SQC becomes uncoordinated reading, which wastes effort and misses systematic defect classes.

concepts.name: Planning

relatedConcepts.name: Plan
relatedConcepts.note: the artifact that Planning produces; Planning is the activity, Plan is the output

relatedConcepts.name: Plan [PDSA]
relatedConcepts.note: the hypothesis-and-design phase of a PDSA cycle; Planning *382 is broader and precedes it

relatedConcepts.name: Planning [SQC]
relatedConcepts.note: a specific bounded sub-process within SQC; a narrower instance of Planning

relatedConcepts.name: Goal / Planned Level
relatedConcepts.note: scalar target; a numeric output a Plan may contain

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: requirement specification is one of the key activities within Planning

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: Evo is a specific approach to Planning and execution

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: SQC is included within the scope of Planning

concepts.definition: **Planning** (*382) is a human activity of 'visualizing the future,' with the intents of being prepared for it and modifying future States to suit Stakeholder purposes. Its scope includes analysis, requirement specification, design, design analysis, quality control, and project management (with feedback to the planning process).
concepts.overview: **Planning** (*382) is the broadest concept in the planning cluster — the human activity that encompasses analysis, specification, design, quality control, and project management whenever these are done with the intent of shaping a future state. It produces Plans (*108) and encompasses specialized instances like Planning [SQC] (*284) and the Plan phase of PDSA (*169). The key distinction from Plan (*108) is that Planning is the activity while a Plan is the artifact that activity produces. The most important insight is that Planning is not a preliminary phase that ends before execution begins — it includes feedback from the delivery process, making it an ongoing, recursive activity throughout a project's life.

concepts.name: Planware

relatedConcepts.name: Dataware
relatedConcepts.note: any written planware can be computer held and is dataware

relatedConcepts.name: Infoware
relatedConcepts.note: Infoware is information of any kind; a small subset of which might be planware

relatedConcepts.name: Documentation
relatedConcepts.note: planware is probably largely documented, but some plans are in people's minds or agreed and presented orally, or made by default

relatedConcepts.name: Logicware
relatedConcepts.note: Logicware is the active logic directing computers; to some degree plans and intents can be described in logicware — which in that case is a form of planware

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: a specification is a primary form of written planware

concepts.definition: **Planware** is any specification, intent or agreement, which documents or reveals human intentions, and perhaps the background and status for those intentions. In simpler words, any plans of any kind. It does not have to be written.
concepts.overview: **Planware** (*577) is the Planguage system-material classification for anything that captures or communicates human intentions — plans, strategies, agreements, specifications, or informal understandings. Unlike [[Logicware.575]], which directs computers, Planware is directed at *people*: its consumer is a human who reads, hears, or otherwise apprehends an intention. Crucially, Planware does not have to be written — a verbal agreement, a shared mental model, or a default assumption all count. Planware sits in the Software & Technology Material family alongside [[Dataware.576]], [[Logicware.575]], [[Infoware.578]], and [[Documentation.579]], distinguished by its function: to carry human intention.

concepts.name: Platform Development

relatedConcepts.name: Platform Management
relatedConcepts.note: numerically adjacent and thematically paired — Platform Management governs the reuse strategy that Platform Development operationalises

relatedConcepts.name: Parallel Development
relatedConcepts.note: same concept number *363 used for a distinct concept (polysemy) — Platform Development involves parallel product variants, but this is distinct from Parallel Development as a concurrency strategy

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: the common cohesive underlying architecture is the foundation of Platform Development

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: Evo context — Platform Development is compatible with and often applied within Evo methodology

concepts.definition: A product development process based on products derived from a common cohesive, underlying architecture, and related synchronized development processes and organizational values [JANDOUREK96 (HP)]. **Platform Development** is an attempt to reuse 10% to 90% of the common elements when creating product variants. The 'Platform' refers to the base architecture and related common development processes for a set of related products.
concepts.overview: **Platform Development** (*362) is a lifecycle process strategy in which a family of related products is derived from a shared, coherent underlying architecture and synchronised development processes. Rather than building each product variant from scratch, Platform Development reuses 10% to 90% of common elements — architecture, components, process, and organisational conventions — across the product family. The 'Platform' is not just a technical base; it includes the aligned development processes and organisational values that make reuse consistent. Its thematically paired partner is [[Platform-Management.363b]], which governs the strategic management of that reuse across concurrent projects.

concepts.name: Pointer

relatedConcepts.name: Time
relatedConcepts.note: a Pointer may reference Time as part of a qualifier

relatedConcepts.name: Place
relatedConcepts.note: a Pointer may reference Place as part of a qualifier

relatedConcepts.name: Event
relatedConcepts.note: a Pointer may reference Event as part of a qualifier

relatedConcepts.name: Condition
relatedConcepts.note: a Pointer may reference Condition as part of a qualifier

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: Scale Qualifiers are a structured application of Pointer-based references

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier Definition
relatedConcepts.note: defines the meaning of a Scale Qualifier — a form of pointer target

relatedConcepts.name: Indicator
relatedConcepts.note: an Indicator is a pointer-based reference to a measurement of value

relatedConcepts.name: Status
relatedConcepts.note: Status is a current value that a Pointer may reference

relatedConcepts.name: Generic Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: Generic Qualifiers use pointer-based references to condition statements

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: Tags are the primary Pointer mechanism in Planguage — symbolic names that reference definitions

concepts.definition: A **Pointer** is a stable symbolic reference to a potentially evolving definition. There are several types of references (informally, "pointers") in Planguage: Tags (character strings that name a parameter or specification), Sources (references to the origin of a specification), External Identifiers (such as a Uniform Resource Identifier), and Defined Terms (entries from a Planguage glossary or project-specific terminology). Their key property is stability: the reference remains constant, while the underlying definition it refers to can evolve over time.
concepts.overview: **Pointer** (*698) is the Planguage concept for any stable symbolic reference to a potentially evolving definition. Pointers are the mechanism by which Planguage manages complexity and change: the symbol (Tag, Source, External Identifier, or Defined Term) stays constant while the thing it points to can be updated without breaking the reference. Pointers are *scale-free* — they work at any level of complexity and can reference a single value, a full specification, or an entire hierarchy of nested specifications. The primary Pointer type is the [[Tag.146]], which names a parameter or specification and can stand in for it anywhere in a Planguage document.

concepts.name: Policy

relatedConcepts.name: Standard
relatedConcepts.note: Policy is a sub-type of Standard in Planguage — a standard specifically governing decision-making

relatedConcepts.name: Priority
relatedConcepts.note: a Policy may be overridden by higher-priority considerations — priority tradeoffs determine when policies yield

relatedConcepts.name: Authority
relatedConcepts.note: Policy has an Authority parameter — the person or body that establishes and can override it

relatedConcepts.name: Decision-maker
relatedConcepts.note: Policy enables delegation of decision-making to other people at other times

relatedConcepts.name: Condition
relatedConcepts.note: unknown conditions at the time of writing the policy' are what Policies are designed to handle

concepts.definition: A **policy** is a set of principles for decision-making, which permit delegation of decision-making to other people, at other times, under 'unknown conditions at the time of writing the policy'. However, policy may be ignored for higher priority considerations. For example, because of a law or contract in conflict with the policy.
concepts.overview: **Policy** (*111) is a Planguage Standard that encodes decision-making principles in a form that allows safe delegation. The defining characteristic is that a Policy is written to handle *unknown future conditions* — situations and decisions that cannot be anticipated at writing time but that the Policy author wants to guide nonetheless. Rather than specifying actions directly, a Policy specifies principles that enable other people, at other times, to make decisions consistently with the policy author's intent. Policies are not absolute: they may be overridden by higher-priority considerations such as law, contract, or executive authority. The Planguage `Type: Policy` parameter makes this explicit in specifications.

concepts.name: Potential Consumer

relatedConcepts.name: Consumer
relatedConcepts.note: Consumer is the active/current version — a Potential Consumer is one who does not yet use or pay for the system but might

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: Potential Consumers are a category of Stakeholder — affected by the system but not yet engaged with it

relatedConcepts.name: Evo Step
relatedConcepts.note: Potential Consumers may become current consumers through Evo steps that extend the product's reach

concepts.definition: A **Potential Consumer** is an organization, or individual, which does not presently use or pay for a defined system {product, Evo step, service, process} but who might consider doing so.
concepts.overview: **Potential Consumer** (*354) is a Stakeholder category for any organisation or individual who does not currently use or pay for a defined system but who might do so in the future. The concept uses "consumer" deliberately rather than "client" or "customer" to avoid implying that direct payment is required — a Potential Consumer is anyone who *might use* something, regardless of whether they pay for it directly. This distinction matters in systems where usage is separate from payment (public services, free tiers, subsidised access) and in product strategy where expanding to new user groups is a planned Evo step.

concepts.name: Pragmatic

relatedConcepts.name: Rule
relatedConcepts.note: Rules are formal specifications; Pragmatics are informal but effective alternatives when rules do not exist or cannot be derived

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: Pragmatics can substitute for or complement formal Specifications when theory is unavailable or impractical

concepts.definition: A **'pragmatic'** is a device for getting something done, which is more *practical* than theoretical. We do not have to understand why or how it works, only know that it probably works. This would not satisfy a scientist, but is useful in engineering. Heuristics are pragmatics.
concepts.overview: **Pragmatic** (*230), used as a noun, names any device, rule-of-thumb, or technique that achieves a result in practice without requiring theoretical justification. The defining criterion is that it *probably works* — empirically, repeatedly — even when the underlying mechanism is not understood. This distinguishes pragmatics from theoretically derived rules: a Rule must follow from first principles; a Pragmatic need only be reliably effective. Heuristics are the canonical example. In engineering, pragmatics are indispensable when theory is absent, incomplete, or impractical to apply — but their provisional nature should always be acknowledged.

concepts.definition: **Pre-requisite Steps** are evolutionary steps that are defined as pre-requisite by some Planguage mechanism. Examples of mechanisms are use of parameters Starts, Before, During, Ends, After.
concepts.overview: **Pre-requisite Steps** (*317) are [[Evo-Step.141|Evo Steps]] that have been formally defined as required predecessors of other Evo steps using Planguage temporal parameters — specifically `Before`, `After`, `Starts`, `Ends`, and `During`. The concept names the *result* of applying those ordering constraints: any step that another step depends upon is a Pre-requisite Step. This is the Evo-specific sequencing mechanism, distinct from the more general [[Precedes.445]] (which applies to any Planguage specification) and from [[Pre-requisite-Conditions.024c]] (which specifies state gates, not step ordering).

concepts.definition:
**'Precedes'** gives information about required sequential *evaluation* of Planguage statements, terms or expressions, in relation to one another. It is implied that the result of the evaluation of any preceding statement or expression, must be applied to the following Planguage component evaluations.
Usage: `A Precedes B.`  or  `A: Precedes: B`
Iconic 'Use A (B)' means B Precedes A in evaluation as a Planguage statement, and the results of B should be applied to the understanding of A.
"Precedes" applies to any Planguage specification, and its *evaluation* sequence. Before/After are specifically limited to the *execution* sequence of Evo steps.
concepts.overview: **Precedes** (*445) is the Planguage temporal sequence parameter that specifies required *evaluation* ordering of any Planguage statement, term, or expression. Its keyed icon is `(….)` — parentheses indicating sequencing. The defining distinction: `Precedes` governs *evaluation* order and applies to *any* Planguage specification. `Before` and `After` govern *execution* order and are specifically limited to Evo steps. When `A Precedes B`, the result of evaluating A must be understood and applied before B can meaningfully be evaluated. The iconic form `B(A)` indicates that A must be evaluated before B — the containing specification depends on the result of its contained expression.

concepts.name: Precision

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: primary tool for improving Precision

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Quality-Control

relatedConcepts.name: Relative-Specification

concepts.definition: Precision is a general specification quality. It is the degree to which a specification points out exactly and accurately the system components (e.g. stakeholders, design functions, sub-systems) for which the specification is *intended* by the Author to apply. And consequently, it is also the degree to which a specification *avoids unnecessary generalization*, beyond the system components that it is *intended* to apply to, by the author of the statement (or by the objective intent of the system).
concepts.overview: **Precision** (*401) is a specification quality attribute that measures how accurately a specification targets exactly the system components it is meant to address — no more, no less. A specification is *subjectively* precise when its author intends it narrowly, but *objectively* imprecise when that narrow intent still fails to match what the broader system or higher-priority specifications require. The key tool for enforcing Precision in Planguage is the Qualifier, which makes scope, stakeholder applicability, and conditions explicit. Without Precision, requirements silently drift into unintended territory — or fail to reach the territory they were supposed to cover.

concepts.name: Price of Nonconformance

relatedConcepts.name: Process-Improvement
relatedConcepts.note: PONC reduction is a core driver of process improvement

relatedConcepts.name: Rework

concepts.definition: The **Price of Nonconformance (PONC)** is "What it costs to do things wrong" [CROSBY85]. PONC is the cost to find and fix defects between two defined points in a systems engineering development process — including reprocessing, rework, scrap, warranty, downtime, and all other costs incurred because requirements were not met the first time.
concepts.overview: **Price of Nonconformance** (*034) is the total financial and resource cost imposed by failure to conform to requirements — everything spent finding defects, fixing them, and dealing with their consequences. Coined by Philip Crosby, PONC is the counterpart to Price of Conformance (what it costs to *do* things right). A critical insight from systems engineering practice is that PONC escalates sharply the later in the development lifecycle a defect is found: roughly 20:1 from development to test, and 80:1 from development to field use. Measuring and minimising PONC is therefore a primary driver of early defect detection and process improvement.

concepts.definition: A **principle** is a short basic statement which summarizes and teaches basic philosophy or the pragmatics of a method.
concepts.overview: **Principle** (*208) is a concise foundational statement encoding the philosophy or pragmatic guidance of a method, discipline, or system. Principles are not requirements in the conventional sense — they do not specify measurable targets — but they shape the reasoning behind requirements and design decisions. In systems engineering, heuristics (empirically derived principles) are a recognised and powerful tool for navigating design complexity that cannot be fully formalised. Tom Gilb treats Principles and Heuristics as closely related, both serving the role of condensed wisdom that guides practitioners when rules and specifications alone are insufficient.

concepts.definition: **Priority Level** refers to the specified attribute level class {Wish, Stretch, Goal, Fail, Survival}. The final priority relationship is determined by other factors such as qualifier and Authority. Priority Level *471 is the parameter used to describe the attribute level's relative importance, ordered from least committed {Wish (5)} to hardest constraint {Survival (1)}.
concepts.overview: **Priority Level** (*471) is the Planguage parameter that classifies any quantified attribute target into one of five canonical level classes — Survival, Fail, Goal, Stretch, and Wish — ranked from inviolable constraint to aspirational desire. These labels are not just labels: they encode the stakeholder's commitment and the system's obligation at that value. A Goal is what you plan to achieve; a Fail is the minimum acceptable; a Survival is the hard floor or ceiling that, if breached, threatens system or project viability. Priority Level enables specification readers to understand not just *what* the target is but *how important it is relative to all other targets*.

concepts.definition: **Priority signals** are any specification attributes — local, in the environment, or inherited — which can be used to determine the priority (claim on limited resources) of one specification over others.
concepts.overview: **Priority Signal** (*515) is any attribute within or associated with a specification that carries information about the specification's relative claim on limited resources — its priority compared to other specifications. Priority Signals can be explicit (a declared Authority, a Priority Level label like Fail or Survival, a Qualifier condition) or implicit (a date, a stakeholder weight, an inherited property from a parent specification). The role of Priority Signals is to give specification readers and decision-makers the information they need to resolve conflicts between competing requirements without relying on informal negotiation. Understanding and making Priority Signals explicit is essential for disciplined requirements prioritisation.

concepts.definition: **Priority** is a parameter used to indicate the relative importance or ordering of requirements, design elements, or other specification items. The keyed icons `>`, `<`, `=` are used to express relative priority relationships: `>` means higher priority than; `<` means lower priority than; `=` means equal priority to.
concepts.overview: **Priority** (*112) is the Planguage parameter that expresses the relative importance — the claim on limited resources — of one specification compared to another. It is not a simple rank number: Planguage encodes priority through keyed icons (`>`, `<`, `=`), through Priority Level labels (Survival, Fail, Goal, Stretch, Wish), and through Priority Signals (any specification attribute that carries priority information). When two requirements conflict over the same limited resource, Priority determines which wins — and when Priority is not explicit, that determination defaults to informal negotiation, which is undocumented, inconsistent, and unauditable.

concepts.definition: A **problem definition** is a statement of a problem that implicitly needs one or more solution options.
concepts.overview: **Problem Definition** (*598) is a formal statement of a problem — a declaration of what must be solved, decided, or achieved — that inherently implies that one or more solution options are needed. In Planguage, a Problem Definition is not merely a complaint or observation; it is a structured specification of the problem space, complete enough that solution options can be evaluated against it. A well-formed Problem Definition may itself be expressed as a set of Requirements (including targets, constraints, assumptions, and conditions), making the transition from problem to solution tractable and auditable.

relatedConcepts.note: Evo is Tom Gilb's method for tackling complex real problems iteratively

concepts.definition: A question to be considered, solved or answered.
concepts.overview: **Problem** (*270) is the most general term in Planguage for any question that must be considered, solved, or answered. In systems engineering, problems arise in many domains — design, management, marketing, research, environment — and Planguage offers a general method for capturing and addressing any of them through specification. The crucial insight about real problems is their complexity: real problems have many performance and resource dimensions that cannot be resolved by pure design reasoning. They require incremental, feedback-driven solution — which is exactly what Evolutionary Project Management (Evo) provides.

concepts.definition: A **procedure** is a repeatable description to instruct people as to the best-known practice, or recommended way, to carry out the task, of a defined process.
concepts.overview: **Procedure** (*115) is a written, repeatable description of how a defined Process's Task should be performed — encoding the best-known practice at the time of writing. A Procedure is not the Process itself (which is the defined flow of Tasks from Entry to Exit conditions) but the human-readable instruction set for executing one of that Process's Tasks. Procedures are foundational to continuous process improvement: without a written Procedure, there is no stable baseline from which improvement can be measured, no consistency across practitioners, and no way to train new Agents in best-known practice.

concepts.definition: A Process Change Management Team is a team responsible for managing and governing changes to defined processes in an engineering or development organisation.
concepts.overview: **Process Change Management Team** (*118) is the authoritative body that evaluates, decides on, and implements changes to an organisation's defined work processes. It receives Process Improvement Suggestions (*088) generated during Process Meetings (*119) and by any stakeholder, analyses their value-to-cost impact, and — when justified — commissions changes to the relevant Process Descriptions (*177). The key distinction is that process change is not peer-level: it requires a team with formal authority over the process definitions. This concept is marked *provisional* — no standalone Tom Gilb definition was found in the source; the definition is derived from context.

concepts.definition: A process description is a process definition. It consists of the following components: {entry conditions, procedure, exit conditions}. The process description must also reference any rules that apply.
concepts.overview: **Process Description** (*177) is the formal, written definition of a process — the document that makes a process repeatable, teachable, and improvable. It specifies three required components: entry conditions (what must be true before the process starts), a procedure (the steps to execute), and exit conditions (what must be true for the process to be considered complete), plus any governing rules. The critical insight is that a Process Description *is* a standard: improving a process means changing the Process Description and then ensuring people follow the changed version. Without this, "process improvement" is informal and unverifiable.

concepts.definition: The Resources used to improve a work Process.
concepts.overview: **Process Improvement Effort** (*116) is the category of resources — primarily staff time and attention — consumed by the activity of improving work processes. It is the *cost side* of the process improvement equation: every Process Improvement Suggestion (*088) that gets analysed, trialled, and adopted consumes Process Improvement Effort, and that expenditure must be justified by a corresponding value gain. The concept is deliberately broad ("resources used") rather than narrowly defined as hours alone, because process improvement may also consume training budget, tooling, and organisational coordination. Tracking this effort is prerequisite to calculating the value-to-cost ratio of process improvement activity.

concepts.definition: A process improvement suggestion is an idea to change a process, in order to improve its performance and/or cost. Suggestions should be directed to the relevant process owner for evaluation (to see if they have sufficient value-to-cost impact).
concepts.overview: **Process Improvement Suggestion** (*088) is a structured idea for changing a process to improve its performance or reduce its cost, generated by anyone working with a process — especially SQC Checkers working with procedures, rules, and checklists. The suggestion is not a mandate: it must be directed to the Process Owner, analysed for value-to-cost impact, and trialled before adoption. The concept is notably stimulated by everyday engineering work: friction with standards during real work is the most reliable signal that a process could be better. The key distinction from a defect is that a defect is a violation of an existing rule; a suggestion is a proposal that the rule itself could be improved.

concepts.definition: The systematic activity of determining the root systemic causes of human work process problems, then changing defined and stable work processes, so as to eliminate, or reduce, the human tendency to commit errors; and to thus improve productivity or costs.
concepts.overview: **Process Improvement** (*114) is the formal, systematic activity of identifying *why* a process produces defects — not just what the defects are — and then changing the process definition so that the root systemic causes are eliminated or reduced. The critical distinction from defect removal is that Process Improvement targets the *source* in the process, not the individual error instances. Proof of improvement is empirical: a changed process must demonstrably produce better results. This is not an aspirational activity — it is a disciplined, quantified loop: identify root systemic cause → change the Process Description → verify the outcome.
