concepts.definition: A process input is any data and/or materials input into a process.
concepts.overview: **Process Input** (*178) is the Planguage parameter that names and specifies what enters a process — data, materials, or both. It is represented by the keyed icon `->` (right-pointing arrow) preceding the process icon, forming the standard Planguage notation `<process input> -> ^[<process>]`. Process Inputs are the counterpart to Process Outputs (*179): an output from one process commonly becomes an input to the next. Specifying inputs explicitly — including components and specifications — makes process interfaces visible, which is prerequisite to measuring and improving them. Examples of inputs include design specifications, requirements documents, and physical components entering a manufacturing or inspection process.

concepts.definition: The subset of Planguage (or of a specific Project Language), which describes work activities. It is used to specify the process descriptions that utilize, or produce, the information expressed when using the Specification Language and Product Language.
concepts.overview: **Process Language** (*246) is the defined subset of Planguage dedicated to describing *how work is done* — processes, procedures, rule evaluation, entry and exit condition evaluation. It is the writing medium for Process Descriptions (*177) and the vocabulary for specifying the activities that consume Specification Language outputs and produce Product Language outputs. Like all Planguage sub-languages, it is a *standard*: it can be taught, reused across projects, and continuously improved by an organisation. The key insight is that Planguage is not a single flat language — it has three domain-specific sublanguages (Specification Language for requirements, Process Language for activities, and an implied Product Language for products), and understanding which sublanguage governs a given concept prevents category errors in specification work.

concepts.definition: A process meeting is an SQC sub-process. It is part of the SQC Defect Prevention Process (DPP).
concepts.overview: **Process Meeting** (*119) is a structured 30-minute meeting held immediately after an SQC Specification Meeting (*120), attended by the same SQC participants, with the specific purpose of extracting grass-roots insights into defect root causes and collecting practical process improvement suggestions. About ten defects are selected and each receives exactly three minutes of attention — one minute to describe, one to identify causes, one to suggest prevention. The meeting operates in brainstorming mode: ideas are captured without criticism or finalisation. The Process Change Management Team (*118) receives the output and decides what to act on. The time-box and the separation of idea capture from decision-making are structural, not optional.

concepts.definition: Measures of attributes of a specific process 'output' (see process output attributes).
concepts.overview: **Process Output Metrics** (*121) are the quantitative measures applied to what a process produces — measuring attributes of the output to determine whether the output (and therefore the process) is performing to standard. Tom's canonical example: the requirements coming out of a requirements specification process can be measured for their Major Defect (*091) content — 20 Majors per page vs. 1 Major per page is a factual statement about process quality. The critical insight is that consistent quality in a process output is an *indirect* measure of the process itself: if the output is consistently clean, the process is consistently good. If the output is consistently defective, the process is consistently broken — regardless of effort applied.

relatedConcepts.note: metrics that measure the quality attributes of this Process Output

relatedConcepts.name: Process Description
relatedConcepts.note: exit conditions in the Process Description define what constitutes a valid Process Output

concepts.definition: A process output is any data or materials output from a process.
concepts.overview: **Process Output** (*179) is the Planguage parameter that specifies what a process produces — data, materials, or both — expressed in the notation `^[Process] -> <output tag>`. It is the right-hand side of the standard Planguage process I/O equation, with Process Input (*178) on the left. Process Outputs are measurable via Process Output Metrics (*121), which provide indirect evidence of the process quality that produced them. A Process Output from one process commonly becomes the Process Input to the next, making explicit output specification essential for verifiable process pipeline design. This concept is dual-polysemous with Product.179 — both file names share concept number *179, which is normal in Tom Gilb's glossary.

concepts.name: Process

relatedConcepts.name: Procedure
relatedConcepts.note: the formal description of how a process runs

relatedConcepts.name: Task
relatedConcepts.note: the unit of work within a process; all formal processes contain tasks

relatedConcepts.name: Entry-Condition
relatedConcepts.note: conditions that must be true before the process begins

relatedConcepts.name: Entry-Process
relatedConcepts.note: the opening phase of a process (setup, preconditions)

relatedConcepts.name: Exit-Condition
relatedConcepts.note: conditions that must be satisfied for the process to be complete

relatedConcepts.name: Exit-Process
relatedConcepts.note: the closing phase of a process (handoff, post-conditions)

relatedConcepts.name: In-Process
relatedConcepts.note: polysemy sibling at same number — the state of currently executing a process

relatedConcepts.name: Process-Improvement
relatedConcepts.note: the root activity for the CPI family this concept anchors

relatedConcepts.name: Process-Improvement-Effort
relatedConcepts.note: the organised effort to improve a process

relatedConcepts.name: Process-Change-Management-Team
relatedConcepts.note: the team responsible for managing process change

relatedConcepts.name: Process-Meeting
relatedConcepts.note: a meeting type within the process cluster

relatedConcepts.name: Sub-Process
relatedConcepts.note: a process nested inside another process

relatedConcepts.name: Process-Description
relatedConcepts.note: the written specification of a process

relatedConcepts.name: Work-Process
relatedConcepts.note: synonym family member — a process as seen from the work perspective

relatedConcepts.name: Process-Language
relatedConcepts.note: the language artefacts that define a project's processes

relatedConcepts.name: Supra-process
relatedConcepts.note: a process that contains other processes

relatedConcepts.name: Action
relatedConcepts.note: an action often invokes a process

relatedConcepts.name: Act-noun
relatedConcepts.note: an informal act; contrast with the formal definition of Process

concepts.definition: A process is the set of Entry Process, Task and Exit Process. A process is formally defined or definable. All formal processes contain tasks. A task alone is not a formal defined process.
concepts.overview: **Process** (*113) is the foundational structural concept in Planguage for describing organised work. It is the envelope that surrounds tasks: an Entry Process prepares conditions, one or more Tasks produce outputs, and an Exit Process verifies completion and hands off. The critical distinction is formality — a task alone is *not* a process; only a defined structure with entry, body, and exit qualifies. This makes Process the root node for an entire cluster of CPI (Continuous Process Improvement) concepts, from Sub-Processes to Process Improvement to Process Language.

concepts.name: Producer

relatedConcepts.name: Process
relatedConcepts.note: the process from which the Producer generates product

relatedConcepts.name: Product
relatedConcepts.note: the output that a Producer generates

relatedConcepts.name: Agent
relatedConcepts.note: broader category; Producers are a class of Agent

relatedConcepts.name: Author
relatedConcepts.note: sub-class of Producer: specifically generates written products

concepts.definition: A 'producer' is the agent or process, which generates product from a process. One class of producer is 'author', who is a producer of written products as opposed to non-written products. Producers make products for customers and users.
concepts.overview: **Producer** (*280) is the role — or process — that generates a Product from within a Process. It is the active, output-generating element in the production chain, bridging process execution and product delivery. A Producer may be a human agent (a developer, a writer, a designer) or an automated process. One well-known sub-class is the **Author** (*280), who produces specifically written products. The concept emphasises that products do not appear spontaneously — they require a committed, identifiable source of generation accountable to customers and users.

concepts.name: Product Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Engineering-Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: a constraint on the engineering process itself, rather than the product

relatedConcepts.name: Product
relatedConcepts.note: the target of a Product Constraint — the process output being constrained

relatedConcepts.name: Process
relatedConcepts.note: the engineering process whose output (Product) is being constrained

concepts.definition: Product Constraints are constraints that apply to the process output of an engineering process: the product or system being made by it.
concepts.overview: **Product Constraint** (*474) is a requirement that limits or bounds the characteristics of the output of an engineering process — the product or system itself, rather than the process that produces it. It is a member of the "Constraint by Target" family, distinguished from Engineering Constraint *473 by what it applies *to*: Product Constraints govern the artifact delivered to stakeholders, while Engineering Constraints govern how the engineering team works. The synonym "System Constraint" reflects the common case where the product is a system. Precise distinction between these two constraint types is essential for traceability: confusing them leads to requirements being written in the wrong specification layer.

concepts.name: Product Level
concepts.definition: Product Level is the layer where products and services are described as functions and qualities. Products are the output that stakeholders consume to satisfy their needs. Product requirements quantify the Functions and Qualities the Solutions must deliver.
concepts.overview: **Product Level** (*803) is part of HumanAgent Gilb's Value Delivery framework, an extension to Tom Gilb's original Planguage. It is not in the source PlanguageGlossary.pdf — it has been authored to capture concepts the framework needs but the PDF did not name.

concepts.name: Production Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Backroom
relatedConcepts.note: the Production Cycle is an optional Backroom cycle within the Result Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Result-Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: the parent cycle that contains the Production Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Implementation-Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: sibling Backroom cycle — handles implementation alongside Production

relatedConcepts.name: Development-Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: sibling cycle — the broader development envelope

relatedConcepts.name: Delivery-Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: the cycle for which the Production Cycle prepares products

concepts.definition: An optional backroom cycle, within the result cycle of Evo, concerned with product integration, or manufacturing and distribution of any products required for the delivery cycle.
concepts.overview: **Production Cycle** (*407) is one of the optional Backroom cycles inside the Evo Result Cycle. Its job is product integration, manufacturing, and distribution — the work needed to take outputs from the development and implementation cycles and prepare them for actual delivery to stakeholders. It is "optional" because not all Evo steps require a separate production phase; some can go directly from implementation to delivery. When it does exist, the Production Cycle operates in the Backroom (away from stakeholder-facing activity), coordinating whatever physical or digital assembly is needed before the Delivery Cycle can begin.

concepts.name: Productivity

relatedConcepts.name: Product
relatedConcepts.note: Productivity is about delivering Products (process outputs) that represent stakeholder value

relatedConcepts.name: Process
relatedConcepts.note: the engineering process whose output constitutes the Productivity measurement

relatedConcepts.name: Engineering-Productivity
relatedConcepts.note: Tom's simplified framing: the ability to deliver agreed requirements

concepts.definition: Productivity is **delivering promised value to stakeholders**. 'Deliver' means actually measurable handed over and available to stakeholders. 'Promised' means that clear written agreements, are made in contacts, requirements, documents and slides, or clear undeniable expectations are set. 'Value' means something of perceived use, to the stakeholder; they need it, they want it, they are willing to sacrifice resources to get it, they will be unhappy if it is late or lower in power than their expectations.
concepts.overview: **Productivity** (*659) is Tom Gilb's deliberately redefined concept of engineering productivity — not output per unit time, but *delivering promised value to stakeholders*. It has three testable components: *Deliver* (measurable handover), *Promised* (written or undeniable agreements), and *Value* (something stakeholders actually need, want, and will sacrifice resources for). The simplified engineering formulation is: Productivity = the ability to deliver agreed requirements. This reframes productivity from a resource ratio (outputs/inputs) into a stakeholder-value obligation, forcing engineers to ask not "how much did we produce?" but "did we deliver what we committed to?"

concepts.name: Profession

relatedConcepts.name: Producer
relatedConcepts.note: a Producer occupies a Profession (e.g., Author, Engineer)

relatedConcepts.name: Agent
relatedConcepts.note: an Agent operates within a defined Profession

concepts.definition: An individual activity specialization requiring considerable training and/or experience. Examples: planner, engineer, quality control manager, project manager, top manager, supervisor, field worker of various types.
concepts.overview: **Profession** (*207) is the Planguage concept for a specialised role that requires substantial training or experience to perform competently. It is an *individual* specialisation — a role held by a person, not by a team or organisation. In engineering contexts, Professions include planner, engineer, QC manager, project manager, and many others. The concept matters in Planguage because assigning a Task or Process to a Profession implies a quality expectation: the work will be done by someone with the competence that the role requires. A Profession is not just a job title — it is a claim about the level of skill and training the role demands.

concepts.name: Progress

relatedConcepts.name: Regress
relatedConcepts.note: the opposite of Progress — movement away from target levels

relatedConcepts.name: Incremental-Scale-Impact
relatedConcepts.note: the incremental change in scale that constitutes a unit of Progress

relatedConcepts.name: Scale-Impact
relatedConcepts.note: the overall scale movement within which Progress is measured

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: the scalar dimension along which Progress is measured

concepts.definition: Progress is scalar-requirement movement, from benchmarks towards desired and intended levels, like targets and constraints.
concepts.overview: **Progress** (*652) is the measurable movement of a scalar attribute from its current Benchmark level toward the desired levels specified by targets (Goals, Musts) and constraints. It is directional — toward the target — and quantified, not merely qualitative ("we feel we are getting better"). The opposite is Regress (*653), movement away from target. Progress is tracked using Planguage's keyed icon `<|`, and is central to Evo's step-by-step improvement model: each step should demonstrate measurable Progress on one or more scale requirements. Without this concept, it is impossible to objectively determine whether iterative engineering is actually moving in the right direction.

concepts.name: Project Language

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Language
relatedConcepts.note: sub-language of Project Language: the formal Planguage terms (Scale, Must, Plan, Defined)

relatedConcepts.name: Process-Language
relatedConcepts.note: sub-language of Project Language: the process definitions (Procedures, Exit Conditions) — also Process-Language.246 (batch 40)

relatedConcepts.name: User-Defined-Term
relatedConcepts.note: sub-language element: terms defined by the project team for their specific context

relatedConcepts.name: System-Description-Language
relatedConcepts.note: related language artefact for describing the system being built

concepts.definition: The set of all Process Language, Product Language and Specification Language artifacts used by a defined project.
concepts.overview: **Project Language** (*247) is the complete, project-specific linguistic system that a team uses to communicate precisely. It is the union of three sub-languages: the **Specification Language** (formal Planguage terms like Scale, Must, Plan), the **Product Language** (project-specific tags and attribute definitions for the product being built), and the **Process Language** (the defined procedures and exit conditions that govern how the team works). Together these three sub-languages form the team's shared vocabulary — neither Planguage alone nor their own jargon alone, but a combined, scoped, and project-tailored language. Project Language is what makes multi-person specifications unambiguous within the project boundary. It is closely related to Process Language *246 (rewritten in batch 40).

concepts.name: Project

relatedConcepts.name: Project-Language
relatedConcepts.note: the language artefact scoped to a defined Project

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary-Project-Management
relatedConcepts.note: Evo: the preferred method for managing a Project in Planguage practice

relatedConcepts.name: Evo-Step
relatedConcepts.note: the iterative unit within an Evo Project

relatedConcepts.name: Production-Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: one of the cycles within a Project

concepts.definition: A project is an activity to produce change to a defined system.
concepts.overview: **Project** (*649) is defined in Planguage with deliberate minimalism: it is an activity — organised work — directed at producing change in a *defined system*. The two load-bearing words are "change" (not maintenance of the status quo, but a directed transformation) and "defined system" (the target must be scoped and named, not vague). This definition is intentionally broad: a Project can be a software development effort, a process improvement initiative, an infrastructure upgrade, or an organisational restructuring — any purposeful activity aimed at transforming an identified system. In practice, Tom associates Projects with Evolutionary Project Management (Evo) as the preferred execution method, where change is delivered iteratively in measurable steps.

concepts.name: Proposal

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: a written format for a proposal or something more accepted and approved than a proposal

concepts.definition: A suggestion to be considered, evaluated, analyzed, estimated before becoming accepted, approved or considered valid. A proposal can be put forward orally, by specification, or be implied in some other formulation as a consequence ('let us stick with the current design' implies whatever that current design specifically is.)
concepts.overview: **Proposal** (*587) is a maturity status designating an idea or suggestion that has not yet been accepted or approved. It sits at the earliest stage of the specification life-cycle, before review, impact estimation, and formal agreement have occurred. Unlike a Specification, a Proposal is explicitly tentative — it invites scrutiny rather than demanding compliance. The most important insight is that labelling something a Proposal keeps stakeholders from treating an idea as a commitment before its consequences have been evaluated.

concepts.name: Prototype
concepts.definition: A **prototype** is any design implementation made with one primary objective: to get feedback from stakeholders, including collection of data about costs and quality levels, for that technology or design, for those stakeholders. A prototype reflects only conceptual design decisions, not decisions driven by implementation concerns.
concepts.overview: **Prototype** (*187) is a design implementation whose primary purpose is to generate learning — stakeholder feedback, cost data, and quality measurement — rather than to deliver a finished product. In Gilb's framework, Evolutionary Delivery (Evo) steps function as prototypes whenever their results are used to revise plans. The critical distinction is intent: a conventional prototype is typically discarded after learning; an Evo step prototype is kept if it succeeds, making the investment double-duty. Pilot implementations are a subclass — smaller-scale deployments intended to validate scalability before full rollout.

concepts.name: Purpose

relatedConcepts.name: Rationale
relatedConcepts.note: parameter for declaring information that justifies a specification

concepts.definition: **Purpose** is the reason something exists, has been done, or is made.
concepts.overview: **Purpose** (*528) is a Planguage parameter for declaring why a specification, requirement, design idea, or system exists. It answers the 'why' question that every other parameter in a spec implicitly depends on. When Purpose is missing, readers cannot evaluate whether a requirement is worth satisfying, whether a design achieves what was intended, or whether a constraint is still relevant. The most important insight is that an unstated Purpose is a hidden assumption — and hidden assumptions are the root cause of most requirements disputes.

concepts.name: QC Parameter
concepts.definition: QC Parameter is the taxonomy class for parameters used in Quality Control work (Defect, Sample, Major Defect, Root Cause, Inspection metrics, etc.). It groups the *language* side of Quality Control — the terms used to describe defect work — separate from the *enacted* QC Process.
concepts.overview: **QC Parameter** (*831) is part of HumanAgent Gilb's Value Delivery framework, an extension to Tom Gilb's original Planguage. It is not in the source PlanguageGlossary.pdf — it has been authored to capture concepts the framework needs but the PDF did not name.

concepts.name: Qualifier

relatedConcepts.name: View
relatedConcepts.note: Qualifiers can be used to specify a view of a system

relatedConcepts.name: Time
relatedConcepts.note: when' qualifier condition class

relatedConcepts.name: Place
relatedConcepts.note: where' qualifier condition class

relatedConcepts.name: Event
relatedConcepts.note: if' qualifier condition class

relatedConcepts.name: Condition
relatedConcepts.note: base concept for qualifier conditions

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier Condition
relatedConcepts.note: individual element within a qualifier

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier Conditions
relatedConcepts.note: the set of conditions used in a statement qualifier

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: individual condition qualifier within a scale definition; aka [Scale Parameter]

relatedConcepts.name: Generic Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: named, reusable qualifier defined from a set of conditions

concepts.definition: A **qualifier** is a defined set of conditions, embedded in or referenced by a specification. All of its conditions must be 'true' for that specification to apply. A qualifier defines any interesting set of specific time, location, and event conditions — sometimes classified as 'when', 'where', and 'if' conditions. Square brackets around the qualifier conditions are used to denote a qualifier.
concepts.overview: **Qualifier** (*124) is the Planguage construct that scopes a specification to a specific set of conditions — time, place, event — that must all be simultaneously true for the specification to apply. It is syntactically expressed as a comma-separated list inside square brackets, where AND logic is always implied. Qualifiers are not optional decoration; they are the primary mechanism for dividing a system into distinct, verifiable, potentially overlapping views, and they carry significant weight in determining the priority of a specification. The most important insight is that a requirement without a qualifier is a requirement that applies everywhere and always — which is almost never what is meant.

concepts.name: Quality Assurance

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control (SQC)
relatedConcepts.note: a specific QC process; a subset of QA

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation (IE)
relatedConcepts.note: a QA activity — estimating design impact on quality

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: QC is a subset of QA

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: QA activities help ensure quality constraints are met

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: QA activities produce evidence that quality requirements are satisfied

concepts.definition: **Quality Assurance (QA)** is the generic name for any set of activities which have as their primary or partial intent, or effect, to influence ('assure') the quality levels of a product or process. QA includes but is not limited to Quality Control — it also encompasses quality specification, design to reach quality levels, Impact Estimation of design impact on quality, evolutionary evaluation of quality levels, SQC, and cost management aspects such as cost of quality.
concepts.overview: **Quality Assurance** (*282) is the broadest category in the quality management family, encompassing every activity that influences product or process quality — from requirement specification through design, testing, inspection, and evolutionary measurement. Quality Control (*279) is a proper subset of QA: QC finds defects; QA also prevents them through better design and process improvement. The critical distinction is that QA includes activities that produce quality (design, specification, estimation), not just activities that detect its absence. The most important insight is that a team doing QC but not QA is playing defence; a team doing full QA has shaped the quality outcome from the start.

concepts.name: Quality Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Quality
relatedConcepts.note: Quality Constraint limits quality levels

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: Quality Constraint is a type of requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: sibling concept — targets 'how good'; constraint sets the floor/ceiling

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Assurance
relatedConcepts.note: QA activities ensure quality constraints are not violated

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: QC detects violations of quality constraints

concepts.definition: A **Quality Constraint** sets limits on how bad, or how good, a quality level is allowed to be — on 'how well' the system should perform. When analysing specific stakeholder situations and design costs, a quality constraint may need adjustment or exception when it is violated by the realities of what is buildable.
concepts.overview: **Quality Constraint** (*305) specifies the permissible range of a quality level — the floor (minimum acceptable quality) and ceiling (beyond which additional quality is not required). Unlike a Quality Requirement Goal that expresses an attractive target, a Quality Constraint is a brake: it says what the design must not fall below or exceed. Five specialisation types cover the full range from global policy constraints to specific failure-avoidance levels. The most important insight is that constraints are not negotiating positions — they define the boundary of acceptable design space, and a design that violates one requires either an exception or a constraint revision.

concepts.name: Quality Control

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control (SQC)
relatedConcepts.note: SQC is a specialised QC process for specifications

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Assurance
relatedConcepts.note: QC is a proper subset of QA

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: QC detects violations of quality constraints

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: QC checks work products against quality requirements

concepts.definition: **Quality Control (QC)** is the generic name for a set of processes that try to check the quality of a work product compared to applicable 'standards' — rules that define acceptable quality. QC includes testing, Specification Quality Control (SQC), and any other activity such as meetings, hearings, customer feedback and surveys that can result in discovery of defects in products. It does not include other forms of quality assurance such as 'design' and 'process' improvement.
concepts.overview: **Quality Control** (*279) is the defect-detection subset of Quality Assurance (*282). It covers every process that checks a work product against a quality standard — testing, inspection, SQC, surveys, hearings — but explicitly excludes activities that shape quality upstream, such as design improvement and process change. The critical distinction is that QC is reactive: it finds quality problems that already exist. Full QA also includes the proactive activities that prevent those problems from being created. The most important insight is that excellent QC on top of a poorly designed system is an expensive way to discover what a better design process would have prevented.

concepts.name: Quality Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Quality
relatedConcepts.note: the attribute that a quality requirement measures

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: Quality Requirement is a specialised type of Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Requirement (Objective)
relatedConcepts.note: Quality Requirement is a type of Performance Requirement — highlighted by Tom Gilb

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: sibling — constraints set the floor/ceiling; requirements express targets

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Assurance
relatedConcepts.note: QA provides evidence that quality requirements are satisfied

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: QC checks work products against quality requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Quality-to-Cost Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: related concept — the ratio of quality delivered to cost invested

concepts.definition: A **quality requirement** is a type of performance requirement that deals with 'how good' a system needs to be.
concepts.overview: **Quality Requirement** (*453) is a performance requirement whose subject is a quality attribute — availability, security, usability, maintainability, or any other dimension of 'how good'. It is expressed using a Scale (unit of measurement) and one or more target levels (Goal, Stretch, Wish) plus a floor level (Fail). Unlike a Quality Constraint (*305), which sets hard limits on permissible quality ranges, a Quality Requirement expresses an attractive target the design should aim for. The most important insight is that a quality requirement without a quantified Scale is not a requirement — it is a wish that cannot be verified, allocated to a design, or used to make trade-off decisions.

concepts.name: Quality Status

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Level
relatedConcepts.note: Quality Level is the numeric degree of quality; Quality Status is the categorical approval state

relatedConcepts.name: Status
relatedConcepts.note: Quality Status is a specialised form of Status applied to specifications

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Maturity
relatedConcepts.note: Maturity tracks developmental progress; Quality Status tracks approval and exit decisions

concepts.definition: The **Quality Status** parameter for a specification refers to the official determination of quality approval. Local concepts can be used. Generally the classes are {Not Exited, Exited}. Other possible categories include: Undetermined, Under Revision, Exited, Approved, 'initial, defined, agreed upon, released' (used by DaimlerChrysler 2002 for working state), Validated (passed Spec Concept Review), and *Verified* (proven to be present and correct by some form of test or observation). This can be used for a document, or any defined specification space, including a single requirement or design specification.
concepts.overview: **Quality Status** (*463) is a categorical benchmark that records the official approval or exit state of a specification — a document, a single requirement, or any defined specification space. Unlike the numeric Quality Level (*360), which measures *how well* written a specification is, Quality Status answers the binary-to-categorical question: has this specification been formally accepted? The core classes are {Not Exited, Exited}, though teams may adopt richer schemes (Undetermined, Under Revision, Validated, Verified) to match their own process milestones. Its most important insight is that quality level and quality status are independent: a specification can score well numerically yet still be "Not Exited" if it has not passed its formal exit gate.

concepts.name: Quality

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: Quality is a child of Performance; Performance also includes Workload Capacity and Resource Saving

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Saving
relatedConcepts.note: Sibling performance attribute — measures how much a system saves rather than how well it performs

relatedConcepts.name: Workload Capacity
relatedConcepts.note: Sibling performance attribute — measures how much a system can handle rather than how well it performs

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: A Quality Requirement specifies a target level for a Quality attribute

relatedConcepts.name: Value
relatedConcepts.note: Quality is a key driver of stakeholder value; higher quality is generally valued

relatedConcepts.name: Quality-to-Cost Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: Ratio of quality improvement to design cost — the efficiency metric for quality investments

relatedConcepts.name: Quantity
relatedConcepts.note: Quantity ('how much') is the sibling class distinguished from Quality ('how well')

concepts.definition: A **quality** is a scalar attribute reflecting 'how well' a system functions as viewed by a defined Stakeholder. Quality includes: {Availability, Usability, Integrity, Adaptability, and many others}. All qualities can be described numerically using a defined Scale, or set of Scales. Existing quality levels can be specified as benchmarks, and needed future quality levels can be specified as targets and constraints. Quality is distinct from the other performance attributes: Workload Capacity (*459) and Resource Saving (*429).
concepts.overview: **Quality** (*125) is the Planguage term for any scalar attribute that answers the question 'how well' a system performs a function, as judged by a defined stakeholder. It is one of three children of Performance (*434), the others being Workload Capacity (*459) and Resource Saving (*429). Every quality is quantifiable: it has a definable Scale, measurable levels, specifiable targets and benchmarks, and tradeable increments. The key distinction that makes quality Planguage-specific is that quality levels are always *articulable independently of design* — what level of availability you need is a separate question from how you intend to achieve it. The most important insight is that while more quality is generally valued, perfect quality (100%) is unattainable in practice and asymptotically expensive.

concepts.name: Quantify, To

relatedConcepts.name: Scale
relatedConcepts.note: Quantification begins with the definition of a Scale — the prerequisite act

relatedConcepts.name: Meter
relatedConcepts.note: A Meter is used in Measurement, which is distinct from but enabled by Quantification

relatedConcepts.name: Measure To
relatedConcepts.note: Measuring is the distinct act of determining where we are on the scale; quantifying defines the scale and levels

relatedConcepts.name: Estimate To
relatedConcepts.note: Estimation determines a particular past or future number on the scale; also distinct from quantification

concepts.definition: To **quantify** is to specify numerically. To articulate a variable attribute, using a defined scale of measure, and specifying one or more benchmark or target levels on the Scale. The resulting specification is 'quantified'. In Planguage, quantification begins with the definition of a Scale. Quantification continues and takes on more specific meaning by using benchmarks, targets, assumptions, and the many other specification parameters that relate to the defined scale of measure.
concepts.overview: **Quantify, To** (*385) is the act of specifying numerically: defining a scale of measure and placing one or more benchmark or target levels on it. It is the foundational specification act in Planguage, prerequisite to estimation, measurement, testing, and feedback control. The concept's most important and often-misunderstood distinction is that quantification is *not* the same as measurement and is *not* the same as estimation. Quantification defines what is being measured and what the targets are; measurement determines the actual current value; estimation predicts a future or past value. You can fully quantify without performing either measurement or estimation.

concepts.name: Quantity Goal

relatedConcepts.name: Workload Capacity
relatedConcepts.note: Workload Goals are a subclass of Quantity Goal — specifying how much volume a system must handle

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Saving
relatedConcepts.note: Savings Goals are a subclass of Quantity Goal — specifying how much resource must be saved

relatedConcepts.name: Objective
relatedConcepts.note: An Objective is complex and can have one or more Goals; a Goal is elementary with a single scale of measure

relatedConcepts.name: Quantity
relatedConcepts.note: Quantity Goal is the goal variant of the Quantity attribute class

relatedConcepts.name: Quality
relatedConcepts.note: Quantity Goals are distinguished from Quality Goals — the former answers 'how much', the latter 'how well

concepts.definition: **Quantity Goal** is an umbrella class of *performance* goals which covers just about all other goals than those we class as Qualities. Any goal which expresses 'how much' rather than 'how well' is a quantity goal. Quantity goals include {Workload (*459) Goals and Savings (*429) Goals}. Rationale: we needed a very general concept to distinguish Performance Quality goals from most others, and the common denominator they had was that they were conventionally and easily quantified.
concepts.overview: **Quantity Goal** (*464) is the umbrella category for performance goals that express 'how much' — covering workload capacity goals and resource saving goals — as distinct from Quality goals, which express 'how well.' It is a scalar target: an elementary requirement with a single scale of measure. The key conceptual function of Quantity Goal is to provide a clean separation between the two major kinds of performance goals in a specification, making it clear which goals concern the magnitude of system operation and which concern the manner of system operation. Its most important insight is that quantity attributes are 'conventionally and easily quantified' — they tend to already be in numeric form in stakeholders' minds, unlike quality attributes which often require more deliberate scaling work.

concepts.definition: A **Quantity** describes 'How much' a system performs or consumes. A quantity is an attribute measured in terms of Capacity (*459) or Resources (*199). A 'quantity' is a type of attribute which we would not normally call a 'quality' (*125). All system quantities can have quality attributes attached to them. For example, the quantity attribute 'responsiveness' can also be characterized by quality attributes such as reliability, variation, measurability, and testability.
concepts.overview: **Quantity** (*437) names the class of system attributes that answer 'how much' — speed, throughput, weight, time, money, space, effort — as opposed to Quality (*125), which answers 'how well.' Quantity covers two major sub-domains: performance attributes (what a system produces or handles) and resource attributes (what a system consumes). The most important insight is that the two categories are not mutually exclusive in specification: any quantity attribute can itself have quality attributes attached to it, creating a layered specification where both the magnitude and the manner of performance must be specified.

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: Question of Intent is raised during SQC — the Specification Quality Control process

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Meeting
relatedConcepts.note: The SQC Specification Meeting is where the Question of Intent is asked and answered orally

relatedConcepts.name: Editor Advice Log
relatedConcepts.note: The Question of Intent is immediately logged in the Editor Advice Log by the Scribe

relatedConcepts.name: Scribe
relatedConcepts.note: The Scribe logs the Question of Intent in the Editor Advice Log during the meeting

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Writer

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: The Question of Intent concerns the technical intention of a Specification

concepts.definition: A **Question of Intent** is a question concerning the technical intention of a Specification, directed to a Specification Writer. It is asked orally during the SQC Specification Meeting. It is immediately logged in the Editor Advice Log by the Scribe. It is answered orally by the Writer at the *end* of the Specification Meeting — so the question and answer are available to the editor during Edit. The 'Question of Intent' was invented at Douglas Aircraft Co. (now Boeing) in 1988. It was used as a diplomatic way for junior engineers to hint to senior engineers that their engineering specifications were not totally understood, without suggesting that there was any engineering defect involved.
concepts.overview: **Question of Intent** (*301) is a SQC process tool invented at Douglas Aircraft (Boeing) in 1988 to diplomatically surface ambiguity or lack of clarity in a specification without implying that a defect exists. It is raised orally during the Specification Meeting, logged by the Scribe in the Editor Advice Log, and answered by the Specification Writer at the meeting's close — giving the editor a prompt to consider whether clarification should be added to the written specification. Its most important insight is the separation of diplomatic intent from defect accusation: a junior engineer can question a senior's specification without the social cost of saying "this is wrong," while still generating a concrete action to improve it.

relatedConcepts.note: A Landing Zone is a defined target range — a bounded region on the scale where a result is acceptable

relatedConcepts.name: Gap
relatedConcepts.note: A Gap range is the unfulfilled distance between a benchmark and a target

relatedConcepts.name: Success Range
relatedConcepts.note: STG Success Range: at/above Goal — success declared, no further improvement priority

relatedConcepts.name: Tolerable Range
relatedConcepts.note: STG Tolerable Range (= Tom's Acceptable Range): between Tolerable and Goal — project alive, below target

relatedConcepts.name: Failure Range
relatedConcepts.note: In STG, the lower portion of the Tolerable Range (between Tolerable/Survival and Fail)

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe Range
relatedConcepts.note: STG Intolerable Range: below Tolerable/Survival — project fails

relatedConcepts.name: Tolerable
relatedConcepts.note: Tolerable *539 is the project-viability threshold that defines the STG three ranges

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Goal *109 is the success threshold that bounds the upper end of the Tolerable Range and starts the Success Range

relatedConcepts.name: Tolerable
relatedConcepts.note: Tolerable/Must-Do *539: the Tolerable (Acceptable) Range threshold

relatedConcepts.name: Incremental Scale Impact
relatedConcepts.note: Incremental Scale Impact *307 describes the change in attribute level from an Evo step — expressed as a range on the scale

concepts.definition: A **range** is the extent between and including two defined numeric levels on a scale of measure. Range, as used in the figure, captures a snapshot of some common scalar attribute ranges using the target and constraint levels. Examples of different range classifications include: Success Range — project or product success, from Goal Level and better; Failure Range — some degree of problems or failure; Catastrophe Range — beyond failure, no use and no hope; Tolerable Range / Acceptable Range — just above failure range, just worse than Goal Level.
concepts.overview: **Range** (*552) is the extent between and including two defined numeric levels on a scale of measure — the fundamental spatial concept of Planguage's scalar notation. Every scalar specification implicitly defines ranges: a Goal level creates a Success Range (Goal and better) and a Failure Range (below the Constraint); a Constraint creates a Catastrophe Range (below it). Ranges carry the same qualifier conditions as the levels that define them. The most important insight is that ranges are typically *implied* by level specifications rather than stated separately — but they are always present, always interpretable, and always relevant to design decisions that must satisfy multiple stakeholders with overlapping ranges.

concepts.name: Rate

relatedConcepts.name: Checking Rate
relatedConcepts.note: Checking Rate *015 is the most important specific instance of Rate in SQC — the speed of specification review

relatedConcepts.name: Optimum Checking Rate
relatedConcepts.note: Optimum Checking Rate *126 is the Rate level that maximises major defect-finding effectiveness

concepts.definition: **Rate** refers to the defined speed with which a defined task is carried out, per defined unit-of-volume worked on. Rates can be set as process standards. This implies that adjustment of rates of work towards more effective or optimum rate-levels is something that can be 'learned' statistically by an organisation in order to improve their own work processes. The most important rate, for effectiveness in identifying major defects, is the optimum checking rate — the best speed for checking a management or engineering specification, including the time needed to check it against all prior related specifications and all official standards. This rate can usually be observed to be in the range 1±0.9 Logical Pages (of 300 non-background words) per hour of analysis.
concepts.overview: **Rate** (*139) is the defined speed at which a defined task is executed per defined unit of volume — a process standard that can be statistically learned and optimised over time within an organisation. The concept exists to make work speed a first-class specifiable and improvable variable, not an incidental outcome. Its most important application is the Optimum Checking Rate (*126): the speed of specification review that maximises major defect-finding effectiveness, empirically observed to be approximately 1 Logical Page per hour (with a ±0.9 range). The key insight is that rate is a learnable, adjustable process characteristic — not a fixed property of the work or the people.

concepts.definition:
A rationale is the reasoning or principle that explains and thus seeks to justify a specification.
'Rationale' is a parameter for declaring information that justifies a specification.
concepts.overview: Rationale is a Planguage parameter that records the logic, politics, economics, or other reasoning behind a specification — the answer to "why does this spec exist?" Unlike Basis, which states the assumptions that must remain true for a specification to hold, Rationale explains the conditions that motivated the specification in the first place. Its primary jobs are to pre-answer reader questions, to motivate acceptance of the specification, and to surface information that enables risk analysis. When the rationale stated turns out to be false or obsolete, the specification itself becomes a candidate for revision.

concepts.name: Readership

relatedConcepts.name: Inspection
relatedConcepts.note: Readership is a key inspection artifact that guides the inspection process

relatedConcepts.name: Rationale
relatedConcepts.note: Rationale for term choices depends on knowing the intended readership

concepts.definition: The readership (or intended readership) of a specification is all the 'types of people' we intend shall read or use the specification.
concepts.overview: Readership is an Inspection Artifact parameter that declares, explicitly, which types of people are expected to read or use a given specification. Stating the readership prevents authors from writing for an assumed audience that may not represent the real one, and gives checkers a criterion by which to judge whether communication has been clear. Without a declared readership, both authors and reviewers must guess at the appropriate level of terminology, detail, and abbreviation — a guess that reliably produces gaps. The readership parameter is typically placed in a document header or in another prominent location.

relatedConcepts.name: Baseline

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation
relatedConcepts.note: Real Values are one of the two modes used in Impact Estimation

concepts.definition: Real values are estimates in impact estimation based on the 'real' defined Scale of measure.
concepts.overview: Real Values is the mode of expressing impact estimates using the actual units of the defined Scale of Measure — for example, "3 minutes", "99.7%", or "€14,000" — as opposed to expressing them as a percentage of the travel between a baseline and a target. The contrast is with Percentage Impact (*306), which normalises all progress onto a 0%–100% arc from baseline to goal. Real Values preserve the physical meaning of the measurement scale and are directly verifiable against instrument readings; Percentage Impact values sacrifice that grounding for cross-attribute comparability. Understanding which mode is in use is essential for interpreting any impact estimate correctly.

concepts.definition: An Evo delivery step recipient. A host system user, a customer, a client, a consumer, a stakeholder, a market or any people or instances that are the target, or potential target, of an Evo step delivery.
concepts.overview: Recipient is the Planguage stakeholder role that names who actually receives the output of an Evo delivery step. It is deliberately broad — any person, organisation, market segment, or system instance that is the target of delivery qualifies. In the Evo framework, identifying the recipient is essential because it anchors the question "did delivery succeed?" — success is defined by whether the recipient's needs were met, not by whether the implementation was completed. Recipients interact with the project through the Frontroom, while the Backroom performs the work that eventually reaches them.

concepts.definition:
A Record parameter is used to inform us about an interesting extreme of achievement.
A Record specification states a benchmark level, on a defined Scale, under specified conditions [time, place, event], for a scalar attribute that represents an impressively good level, or state-of-the-art.
concepts.overview: Record is a Scalar Benchmark that marks the known frontier of achievement — the best (or most extreme) level ever measured for a given attribute under specified conditions. Its primary purpose is not to set a target but to demonstrate that a level is technically possible, and to challenge teams to understand what would be required to approach, meet, or beat it. Because state-of-the-art levels tend to be costly and high-risk, specifying a Record early alerts stakeholders to the difficulty terrain. The keyed icon `<<` represents a doubled "past" arrow, emphasising that this is an extreme historical benchmark. Source citation is especially important for Record values.

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: Regress falls in the lower region of the scale range

concepts.definition: Regress refers to a scalar level that is worse than a defined benchmark.
concepts.overview: Regress is the counterpart to Progress: where Progress marks a scalar level better than a benchmark, Regress marks one that is worse. In the context of Evo step estimation and impact analysis, Regress means the step has moved the measured attribute in the wrong direction relative to the benchmark. The keyed icon `<!` combines the "past" benchmark arrow with an exclamation mark, flagging the deterioration as noteworthy — a warning signal rather than a neutral data point. Tracking Regress explicitly is essential for honest Evo step accounting: a step that causes deterioration on any attribute must be visible, not hidden.

concepts.definition:
A relationship is a connection between objects.
For example, A |-| B. "A is in a relationship to B. There is no notion of impact — just connectedness."
concepts.overview: Relationship is the foundational Planguage parameter for declaring that two or more Objects are connected in some way, without implying direction, impact, or causation. The keyed icon `|-|` is intentionally symmetric — the vertical bars on each side emphasise equality and mutual connection. Relationship is the generic superclass from which a rich taxonomy of specific relationship types descends: hierarchical relationships (Parent, Kid, Sibling, Kin), structural relationships (Set, Subset, Is-Part-Of, Consists-Of, Includes), directional relationships (Upstream, Downstream, Supra), and impact/support relationships (Impacts, Impacted-By, Supports, Supported-By, Dependency). Understanding which specific relationship type applies is critical for precise specification.

concepts.definition: A 'relative' specification is a Planguage specification where the exact interpretation is dependent on the meaning of one or more other specifications.
concepts.overview: Relative Specification names the class of specification statements whose meaning cannot be determined without reference to other specifications or external context. Words and phrases like "improved," "better," "world class," "faster," and "highly competitive" are relative — they declare a direction or aspiration without supplying a measurable definition. In Planguage, relative specifications are acceptable in summary statements (Gist, Ambition) as initial intent declarations, but they must eventually be resolved into testable form using a Scale of Measure, a benchmark (such as Past), and a target (such as Goal). A relative specification that is never resolved remains unjudgeable and untestable.

relatedConcepts.name: Add
relatedConcepts.note: the inverse operation — Add inserts a specification into a defined set

concepts.definition: Remove is a Planguage verb indicating the removal of some specification from a defined set of specifications.
concepts.overview: Remove is a Logical Structure Parameter that explicitly marks the deletion of one or more specifications from a defined set. In Planguage, specifications exist within structured sets — removing one must be declared, not assumed or left implicit. Remove pairs naturally with Add (*643) as the inverse operation, and both are combined in Replace (*641), which performs a Remove and Add in a single atomic operation. The keyed icon `-` in context signals that a specification is being subtracted from its container set.

concepts.name: Replace

relatedConcepts.name: Remove
relatedConcepts.note: the '-' component of Replace — Remove is performed first

relatedConcepts.name: Add
relatedConcepts.note: the '+' component of Replace — Add is performed second

concepts.definition: Replace is a Planguage verb indicating the replacement of some specification with another.
concepts.overview: Replace is a Logical Structure Parameter that atomically removes one specification from a defined set and inserts another in its place. The keyed icon `±` captures the operation precisely: the `-` indicates the old specification is removed, and the `+` indicates the new one is added. Replace is the combined form of Remove (*642) and Add (*643), and it is the appropriate parameter when a specification is being superseded rather than simply retired. Using Replace rather than separate Remove and Add operations makes the substitution relationship explicit and auditable — readers can see not just that something changed, but what replaced what.

concepts.definition: A 'report' is an *oral* statement made during SQC at a specification meeting or a process meeting.
concepts.overview: In Specification Quality Control (SQC) a Report is the brief spoken statement by which a checker flags a finding to the rest of the SQC team. Reports are always oral; writing comes later when the scribe logs them. The three valid report types at a specification meeting are Issues, Questions of Intent, and Process Improvement Suggestions; at a process meeting the subject matter shifts to defect causes and potential process cures. Economy of language is essential — Tom Gilb insists on seven words or fewer per report, keeping sessions fast and free of monologue. The Report is thus the atom of the SQC feedback loop.

concepts.definition: A requirement specification is a defined set of requirements. It also includes any relevant requirement background, such as benchmarks, and also any appropriate commentary.
concepts.overview: A Requirement Specification is the document-level artefact that collects and organises requirements into a coherent whole. It is not merely a list of requirements — it also carries background material (benchmarks, stakeholder context) and commentary that aids interpretation. The specification is the *output* of the Requirements Specification Process (*634), which is itself a subset of the broader Requirements Engineering (*614) discipline. Having a requirement (*026) is not the same as having a requirement specification; requirements can exist informally, but a specification formalises and bounds them.

concepts.definition: A 'requirement' is a **stakeholder-valued system state, under stated conditions.**
concepts.overview: A Requirement is the foundational concept of Planguage: it is any system state that a stakeholder cares about, expressed under the conditions in which that state must hold. The definition is deliberately narrow — it is not a feature, not a design decision, not a user story, but a *state* that can be tested for existence in a system. Requirements exist independently of solutions; they are inputs to design processes, not outputs. Crucially, requirements are conditional and priority-weighted: not every stated requirement will be implemented, and a requirement can be superseded, deprioritised, or never acted upon at all.

concepts.definition:
Requirements Engineering is a requirements process carried out with an engineering level of rigor.
Requirements Engineering includes all aspects of requirements gathering and maintenance, including but not limited to:
- requirements solicitation (including stakeholder analysis)
- requirements analysis
- requirements quality control
- requirements review
- requirements change management
- requirements specification (the process)
- contracting and bidding requirements
- requirements risk analysis
- requirements priority analysis
concepts.overview: Requirements Engineering is the disciplined, rigorously engineered form of the Requirements Process (*612): same activities, higher standards. The key differentiator is *engineering rigor* — quantification, testability, SQC, traceability, and systematic change management applied throughout. It encompasses everything from initial stakeholder solicitation through to change management and risk analysis. Requirements Engineering subsumes the Requirements Specification Process (*634) as one of its components, producing Requirement Specifications (*508) as its primary artefact. The distinction from the generic Requirements Process is one of degree: all Requirements Engineering is a Requirements Process, but not all Requirements Processes meet engineering standards.

concepts.definition:
The requirements process includes all aspects of requirements gathering and maintenance, including but not limited to:
- requirements solicitation (including stakeholder analysis)
- requirements analysis
- requirements quality control
- requirements review
- requirements change management
- requirements specification (the process)
- contracting and bidding requirements
- requirements risk analysis
- requirements priority analysis
concepts.overview: The Requirements Process is the generic label for all activities concerned with identifying, analysing, specifying, reviewing, and maintaining requirements throughout a project. It is broader than merely "writing a spec" — it spans solicitation from stakeholders through to priority analysis and change management. When the same process is executed with engineering-grade rigor (quantification, formal SQC, systematic traceability), it rises to Requirements Engineering (*614). The Requirements Process is also the parent process within which the more specific Requirements Specification Process (*634) operates.

concepts.definition: The process of specification of requirements.
concepts.overview: The Requirements Specification Process is the specific subprocess within the broader Requirements Process (*612) and Requirements Engineering (*614) that takes gathered, analysed requirements and transforms them into a formal Requirement Specification (*508). It is defined briefly in the Planguage glossary because its identity rests on its output — the specification — rather than on a proprietary method. The process is downstream of solicitation and analysis, and upstream of quality control review and baselining. Its output (the Requirement Specification) is the primary artefact consumed by design and architecture processes.

concepts.definition: The solution of a problem is a resolution.
concepts.overview: A Resolution is, simply put, what you call a solution when the context is a defined problem. The concept is brief by design — it names the relationship between problem and solution without prescribing how the solution is found. In Planguage, problems (*270) are stated precisely so that resolutions can be evaluated against them. Design problems (*654) in particular are resolved by design ideas (*047), making the Resolution concept the counterpart to the Problem concept in the design discourse. The term appears most naturally in SQC and design contexts where an issue or problem is formally "resolved."

concepts.definition:
The total quantity of a defined resource which has been allocated for defined purposes, at defined times, under defined conditions.
This is not just any budget, but some larger allocation for a company, division, project or phase from which individual budgets specifications may be made. It is the Limit for the sum of all budgets in a specified area and time.
concepts.overview: Resource Allocation is the authorised ceiling — the total quantity of a resource formally committed for defined purposes across a specified scope and time. It is explicitly *not* an individual budget; it is the meta-budget from which individual Resource Budgets (*430) are carved. The difference between Resource Allocation and what is actually consumed (Resource Observation, *502) or assumed to be consumed (Resource Assumption, *500) determines what Resource is Available (*504). In Planguage, Allocation is a formal state declaration, not a casual planning estimate.

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Allocation

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Available

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Observation

relatedConcepts.name: Resource

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Budget
relatedConcepts.note: budgets are set partly based on resource assumptions

concepts.definition:
A resource assumption is an estimate or guess about the total quantity of a defined resource which will be available under given conditions [when, where, if].
This is not the same as a specific resource allocation. But the assumption is a useful basis for deciding on the allocation.
concepts.overview: A Resource Assumption is the planning-phase estimate of how much of a defined resource will be available — before that availability has been formally allocated or empirically observed. It is explicitly acknowledged as an estimate or guess, not a confirmed fact. The Resource Assumption is the planning-mode counterpart to the Resource Observation (*502): where observations track what has actually been consumed, assumptions project what will be available. The key downstream use is deriving Resource Available (*504): in planning, Available = Allocation minus Assumption. The explicit naming of assumptions is a Planguage discipline that forces teams to surface and examine their planning premises.

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Observation

concepts.definition: The resource available is the remaining portion of the resource allocated that can be used to budget designs, tasks or Evo steps.
concepts.overview: Resource Available represents the unspent remainder of a previously allocated resource pool — the portion still free for assignment to designs, tasks, or incremental delivery steps. It is not the total resource ever granted to a project but only what has not yet been committed. Tracking what is available prevents over-commitment and gives planners a real-time picture of remaining capacity. The key distinction from Resource Observation is that Available is calculated from Allocation minus committed use, while an Observation is a direct measurement at a point in time. Together these two concepts close the resource accounting loop.

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: the Fail/Survival side of a Resource Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Budget

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Saving

concepts.definition:
A resource budget describes how much of a resource we plan to have available.
A resource budget is a target level (Goal, Wish, Stretch) of a specified resource, which is related to a specific system component, with defined qualifiers for 'where', 'when' and 'events'. This implies that one resource requirement can have many resource budgets.
It is quite different from a Cost Budget, which is a plan for how much of a resource we will use.
concepts.overview: A Resource Budget is a stakeholder-set target level that specifies how much of a defined resource should be made available — not how much will be consumed. It uses the positive target parameters (Budget, Wish, Stretch) rather than the warning parameters (Fail, Survival) and is attached to a specific component, location, and time qualifier. The critical distinction from a Cost Budget is intentional: a Resource Budget controls availability while a Cost Budget controls expenditure. Multiple Resource Budgets can be nested under a single Resource Requirement, making it the primary tool for allocating limited resources across sub-systems without unintentional excess. The term "budget" is preferred over "target" for resources precisely to signal this allocation-and-availability intent.

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Budget
relatedConcepts.note: the aspirational complement to this warning concept

relatedConcepts.name: Fail

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: secondary constraint parameter: unrecoverable threshold

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe

relatedConcepts.name: Range

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Survival limit
relatedConcepts.note: specific Survival-level instance of a Resource Constraint

concepts.definition:
A resource constraint is a resource requirement, which specifically *restricts*, or *serves as a warning* about, the level that can be used of a resource.
A resource constraint is specified as a scalar resource attribute level. It signals the level at which *some degree of system failure* will be experienced or, the level at which the entire system becomes threatened.
Two main parameters can be used to specify these constraint levels: Fail (Fail and worse might be recoverable) and Survival (worse is unrecoverable).
concepts.overview: A Resource Constraint is the warning and restriction component of a Resource Requirement — it names the resource levels at which the system starts to fail or can no longer survive. Unlike Resource Targets (which express aspirational allocation), Resource Constraints express the danger zone: the Fail level signals recoverable trouble, and the Survival level signals the point of no return. Planners and designers should aim to stay far away from these levels, not merely beneath them. The distinction from Performance Constraints is that Resource Constraints govern the consumption of inputs (time, money, energy, space) while Performance Constraints govern the quality of outputs (speed, accuracy, capacity). Both must be specified by stakeholders with documented authority and rationale.

concepts.name: Resource Efficiency

relatedConcepts.name: Resource

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Saving

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Efficiency

relatedConcepts.name: Productivity
relatedConcepts.note: productivity is output per unit resource; closely related

relatedConcepts.name: Performance

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: efficiency improvement can be expressed as a Resource Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Saving Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: a requirement to improve efficiency by a specific saving level

concepts.definition:
Resource efficiency is a system attribute describing how well resources are utilized when the system produces output.
For a given system output level, better resource efficiency means 'using less resources'.
concepts.overview: Resource Efficiency measures the ratio between the output a system produces and the resources it consumes to produce that output — the classic "doing more with less" metric. It is a system attribute (a quality of the system) rather than a requirement or a budget, though it can be quantified and specified using the Planguage scalar framework. The key insight is that efficiency is always relative: it is meaningful only when the output level is held constant, so that reductions in resource use are not disguised reductions in output. Resource Efficiency is closely related to Productivity (*659) and is the basis for Resource Saving (*429) and Resource Saving Requirements (*622). Distinguishing total resource cost (including platform overhead) from marginal cost (pure production cost, excluding sunk capital) is essential to valid measurement.

concepts.name: Resource Observation

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Allocation
relatedConcepts.note: the allocation that a Resource Observation measures against

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Available
relatedConcepts.note: the derived figure that an Observation should confirm

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Assumption
relatedConcepts.note: sibling state concept; an assumed rather than observed value

concepts.definition: A resource observation is a determination, by any means, of the quantity of a defined resource that is available, at a given time, location and conditions.
concepts.overview: A Resource Observation is a measurement act — the process of determining, by any valid means, how much of a defined resource actually exists at a specified time and place. It is the empirical counterpart to the planning concepts of Resource Allocation (*503) and Resource Available (*504): where those concepts express what *should* be available, an Observation reports what *is* available. The phrase "by any means" is deliberate — direct counting, sampling, estimation, sensor reading, and financial reporting all qualify. The key purpose is to feed reality back into resource planning: an Observation that disagrees with the Available figure reveals unrecorded commitments, leakage, or measurement error that needs investigation.

concepts.name: Resource Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: defines what kind of resource is being specified

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Target

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: the warning component: Fail, Survival

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Budget
relatedConcepts.note: a Resource Budget is a specific Resource Target within a Resource Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: analogous concept for quality outputs rather than resource inputs

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: self — anchor

concepts.definition:
A resource requirement specifies how much of a resource should be made available for later consumption.
A resource requirement is a scalar attribute with one or more resource targets and/or resource constraints specified.
concepts.overview: A Resource Requirement is the complete specification of how a defined resource is to be managed: it combines the aspirational targets (Resource Targets: Budget, Wish, Stretch) with the warning thresholds (Resource Constraints: Fail, Survival). A single Resource Requirement — one scale, one resource type — can carry multiple levels, each qualified by component, location, time, and event. This is the parent structure that holds Resource Budgets and Resource Constraints together. The canonical figure for this concept is a tree: Resource Requirement at the root, branching to Resource Target (Budget, Stretch, Wish) on one side and Resource Constraint (Fail, Survival) on the other.

concepts.name: Resource Saving Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Saving
relatedConcepts.note: the measure that a Resource Saving Requirement quantifies and mandates

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: a Resource Saving Requirement is a sub-type of Performance Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept; saving requirements are always resource-denominated

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Efficiency
relatedConcepts.note: savings requirements arise from wanting to improve efficiency

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: sibling concept; Resource Saving Requirement is requirement-side; Resource Requirement is allocation-side

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: resource saving is one dimension of system performance

concepts.definition:
A resource saving requirement is a 'resource reduction' performance requirement. It specifies the specific savings in resource utilization that are needed: 'how much' is to be saved.
The focus is that it is the specific level of *saving* that is the requirement (as opposed to the improvement in quality or workload capacity being the driving motivation).
concepts.overview: A Resource Saving Requirement is a Performance Requirement (*100) whose motivating purpose is to reduce resource consumption by a specified amount — not to improve output quality or increase workload capacity. The scale must be resource-denominated (cost, hours, energy, material), and the requirement is expressed either as a target level compared to a benchmark or as a direct saving ratio. The key distinction from a Resource Requirement (*431) is temporal and motivational: a Resource Requirement allocates resource for the current project; a Resource Saving Requirement mandates that the *system being built* will consume fewer resources than its predecessor does. It is about the system's future operational performance, not the project's own budget.

concepts.name: Resource Saving

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: resource saving is a dimension of system performance

relatedConcepts.name: Quality
relatedConcepts.note: resource saving is one of the three performance attribute types alongside quality and workload capacity

relatedConcepts.name: Workload Capacity

relatedConcepts.note: the requirement form: mandates that a specific saving level must be achieved

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Efficiency

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept; saving is always expressed in resource units

concepts.definition:
A resource saving is a performance attribute of a system. It expresses 'how much' better the system currently performs in terms of resources than it did at some previous benchmark time.
For example, a resource saving can express how much less resource in training effort or maintenance cost is needed in one system compared to another. This measure can be used for benchmarking or for setting requirements, or even for reporting on progress in design or actual measured implementation of new systems.
concepts.overview: Resource Saving is a scalar benchmark attribute that measures the improvement in a system's resource consumption compared to a defined previous state. It is one of the three performance attribute types — alongside Quality (*125) and Workload Capacity (*459) — that together constitute system Performance (*434). The "saving" is expressed as the difference between a past benchmark level and a current or target level on a resource-denominated scale. It can serve three distinct purposes: as a measurement tool for comparing system versions, as a planning tool for setting benchmarks, or as a basis for requirement-setting via a Resource Saving Requirement (*622). The critical qualifier is that "better" means using fewer resources to produce the same output — not merely consuming less by doing less.

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: the generic Survival parameter; Resource Survival limit is its resource-specific instance

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Survival limit

relatedConcepts.name: Fail

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Target
