relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept; the resource being constrained

concepts.definition: A Survival limit (*440) on a scalar resource use.
concepts.overview: A Resource Survival limit is the absolute floor for a scalar resource attribute — the level beyond which the system cannot recover. It is a specific instantiation of the generic Survival parameter (*440) applied to resource consumption rather than to output quality. Like all Survival-level constraints, it marks the point of no return: exceeding it means the system (or project) faces unrecoverable failure. The key distinction from the Fail level (*098) is severity: Fail signals trouble that may be managed or recovered from; Survival signals the end. The analogous concept on the performance side is Performance Survival limit (*477). A Resource Survival limit must always be specified by an authoritative stakeholder with explicit rationale, because it represents the hardest of all hard limits.

concepts.name: Resource Target

relatedConcepts.name: Budget
relatedConcepts.note: the primary Resource Target parameter: committed allocation level

relatedConcepts.name: Wish
relatedConcepts.note: a valued but uncommitted Resource Target level

relatedConcepts.name: Stretch
relatedConcepts.note: a challenging but uncommitted Resource Target level

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept; the resource being targeted

relatedConcepts.name: Target
relatedConcepts.note: the generic target concept; Resource Target is the resource-specific instance

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: the warning complement; constraints define danger, targets define aspiration

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: the parent; Resource Target is one component of a Resource Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: ancestor; a Resource Requirement is a Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Budget
relatedConcepts.note: a Resource Budget is a Resource Target using the Budget parameter

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Target
relatedConcepts.note: the analogous concept for output quality levels

concepts.definition:
A resource target is a qualified resource level we aim, or might possibly aim, towards keeping within, while working towards performance goal levels.
Three parameters are used to specify resource targets {Budget, Stretch and Wish}. A Budget level is the *primary* resource target type. A Stretch level represents a resource target that is *not* committed, but is a level of challenge and motivation. The Wish level represents a resource level that would have value to some stakeholder, but again is not committed.
Resource targets represent the reasonable, perhaps profitable, levels of cost, we must expect to pay to reach our performance and function targets within any constraints.
Resource targets differ from resource *constraints*, which are the levels that signal problems, danger, or lack of profitability. We do not plan and design to merely stay *within* resource constraints, but to *avoid* going anywhere near them at all!
concepts.overview: A Resource Target is the aspirational component of a Resource Requirement — the resource level that designers and planners aim to stay within while pursuing performance and function goals. It uses three parameters: Budget (the committed, primary level), Stretch (an ambitious non-committed challenge), and Wish (a stakeholder-valued but non-committed aspiration). The critical distinction from Resource Constraints is motivational: targets define where you want to be, constraints define the danger zone you must stay clear of. Resource Targets are also distinct from Performance Targets (*439): Resource Targets govern the input side (consumption of time, money, energy), while Performance Targets govern the output side (quality, speed, capacity). A Budget is simultaneously a Resource Target and a Resource Budget — the two concepts overlap at that parameter.

concepts.name: Resource Type Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Budget
relatedConcepts.note: Resource Type Constraint restricts which resource types may be used — distinguishable from a budget (a level limit on a specific resource)

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: Resource Type Constraint governs which resource classes are permissible inputs to a system

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — Resource Type Constraint is a specific kind of Resource Constraint applied to resource type/class

relatedConcepts.name: Restriction
relatedConcepts.note: Resource Type Constraint IS a restriction (*498 = Condition Constraint used as Restriction); it is not itself a budget

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Limit
relatedConcepts.note: Resource Type Constraint is distinct from a Resource Limit — a limit sets a ceiling on a specific resource; a type constraint restricts which types may be used

concepts.definition: A **Resource Type Constraint** puts an explicit generic restriction on use of resource types or classes to solve a problem. It is a restriction (*498) and not itself a resource budget.
concepts.overview: A **Resource Type Constraint** does not limit how *much* of a given resource may be used (that is a Resource Budget or Resource Limit); instead it restricts *which types or classes* of resource are permissible. Because it applies generically across resource categories rather than to a single named resource, it is dynamic — its interpretation shifts as the resource landscape changes. Typical uses include technology-class restrictions, environmental requirements ("no coal-powered alternatives"), and diversity rules on resource sourcing. Classifying a requirement as a Resource Type Constraint prevents it from being confused with a budget and ensures the multi-resource, dynamic nature of the restriction is visible in the spec.

concepts.definition: A **resource** is any potential system input. It is any kind of input 'fuel' necessary for building, operating or maintaining a given system. A resource is an asset or a supply that can be used to produce the functionality, or performance levels, of a system.
concepts.overview: **Resource** (*199) is the hub concept for all Resource-family specifications in Planguage. Any input that a system consumes — time, money, effort, space, data, energy, or otherwise — is a resource. Resources are distinguished from resource *savings* (a performance attribute measuring relative reduction in consumption) and from resource *levels* (planned budgets, targets, constraints). The key engineering insight is that resources must be viewed in terms of *total potential availability*, and requirements must be specified so that planned consumption never exceeds available supply at any point in time or circumstance. Resources in Planguage are quantified via scales, governed by targets and constraints, and monitored through observations.

concepts.name: Responsible

relatedConcepts.name: Authority

relatedConcepts.name: Role

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: the responsible party is typically a named stakeholder or organisational instance

concepts.definition: **Responsible** is the person or instance assigned formal responsibility for achieving a specified plan element.
concepts.overview: **Responsible** (*646) is a Planguage parameter that names the individual or organisational instance formally accountable for delivering a specified plan element — a requirement, a project step, a process, or any other specification node. Unlike Authority (*005), which defines *who may decide*, Responsible defines *who is answerable for the result*. Assigning Responsible to every specification element makes accountability traceable, inspectable, and non-deniable. Without a named Responsible, a plan element has no owner and therefore no enforcement path.

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Constraint

concepts.definition: A **Result Constraint** is a term for a requirements constraint used for any of the requirement types: quality, cost, or Function. It is used where we do not wish to be more specific about the specific type of constraint. The term 'result' refers to any combination of performance, cost, or function results.
concepts.overview: **Result Constraint** (*200) is the generic constraint term covering any combination of performance, cost, or function outcomes. When a constraint applies broadly across result types — or when the specifier does not need to distinguish whether the constraint is specifically about quality, cost, or function — "Result Constraint" is the right label. It is intentionally non-specific: not all constraints are result constraints (legal and cultural constraints are excluded), but all quality constraints, resource constraints, and function constraints are subtypes of Result Constraint. The concept provides a useful umbrella for cross-cutting constraints without forcing premature categorisation.

relatedConcepts.name: Result

concepts.definition: Within Evo, a **Result Cycle** is an entire Evo step cycle aimed at delivering a result that moves towards satisfying the overall requirements. A result cycle consists of Plan Do Study Act (PDSA) activities.
concepts.overview: **Result Cycle** (*122) is the fundamental unit of iterative delivery in Evolutionary Project Management (Evo). Each Result Cycle is a complete cycle of Plan, Do, Study, Act activities aimed at producing a measurable result — an outcome that moves the system closer to satisfying its overall requirements. A Result Cycle contains four component sub-cycles: a strategic management cycle, a development cycle, a production cycle, and a delivery cycle. The delivery cycle is the only "frontroom" activity (visible to users); the others are "backroom." Multiple Result Cycles may execute serially and in parallel. The distinguishing feature of Evo is the emphasis on contact with reality: each Result Cycle generates feedback that adjusts subsequent planning.

concepts.name: Result

relatedConcepts.name: Plan Do Study Act (PDSA) Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: a Result is the outcome of the 'Do' phase in a PDSA Cycle; it is analysed in the 'Study' phase

relatedConcepts.name: Evolutionary Project Management
relatedConcepts.note: within Evo, 'Result' specifically refers to outcomes of delivery cycles within Result Cycles

relatedConcepts.name: Delivery Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: a Result is produced by completing a delivery cycle in Evo

relatedConcepts.name: Result Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: a Result Cycle is the full PDSA step that produces a Result; the Result is the cycle's output

relatedConcepts.name: Result Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: a Result Constraint defines a binding acceptance criterion for a Result — they are normative counterpart to the empirical Result

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: an incremental Result can be expressed as a change relative to a benchmark — e.g., relative to Past

concepts.definition: A **Result** is an outcome for a system after — or the 'testable effect of' — the 'Do' phase of any Plan Do Study Act (PDSA) cycle. Results are analysed in the 'Study' phase. Within Evo, 'result' is specifically used to refer to any outcome of a delivery cycle within a result cycle.
concepts.overview: **Result** (*130) is what is left after you have done something to a system — the measurable, testable change in the system's state produced by a Do cycle. A Result can be expressed as an absolute level (the current system state) or as an incremental change relative to a benchmark (how much the system improved or regressed). Multiple attributes — performance levels, resource levels, functional capabilities — can be simultaneously impacted by a single system change, making a Result potentially multidimensional. Results are the empirical input to the Study phase of PDSA, where they are compared against requirements and used to calibrate the next planning iteration. Without measurable Results, Evo degenerates into assertion-based management.

concepts.name: Reuse Percentage

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: Reuse Percentage is a Scalar Benchmark — a measure of past or target reuse that serves as a comparative baseline

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: reuse of existing components reduces resource consumption (effort, time, cost) required for development

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: Reuse Percentage uses % of volume (or defined type) as its scale of measure

concepts.definition: **Reuse Percentage** is the [defined type of; default = % of volume] percentage of the product development which is accomplished by exploiting the existence of existing components' design or development effort.
concepts.overview: **Reuse Percentage** (*367) is a scalar benchmark metric that measures the degree to which a development process succeeded in leveraging existing components rather than re-inventing them from scratch. It is expressed as a percentage of total product volume (or another defined measure type) that derives from reuse. The metric captures reuse intent and achievement — from 10% (incidental reuse) to near 90% (platform-dominated product) — but does not by itself determine whether that reuse was economically justified. Reuse has costs; high reuse percentage is not automatically a good result. The measure is most meaningful when paired with a resource comparison (effort and time saved vs. cost of reuse infrastructure).

concepts.name: Review Criteria

relatedConcepts.name: Clarity Rules
relatedConcepts.note: an example of a standard for how well written a specification should be; used in Clarity Reviews *607

relatedConcepts.name: Design Rules
relatedConcepts.note: rules for how to design, as opposed to how to specify a design (*129); a type of Content Rule

relatedConcepts.name: Content Rules
relatedConcepts.note: a different type of standard focusing on how good ideas are in terms of meeting requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Review
relatedConcepts.note: Review Criteria are the standards and procedures that define and direct a Review (*197)

relatedConcepts.name: Review Focus

relatedConcepts.name: Checklists
relatedConcepts.note: checklists are one form of Review Criteria that operationalise the criteria for individual reviewers

relatedConcepts.name: Clarity Review

relatedConcepts.name: Spec Content Review
relatedConcepts.note: Spec Content Review uses Content Rules as its Review Criteria

concepts.definition: **Review Criteria** are the rules (and related checklists), the defined procedures, and any other standards or guidelines to be used to define and direct the analysis process, for a particular review activity. They are the questions the reviewers must ask and answer. They are the basis for determining the outcome of the review.
concepts.overview: **Review Criteria** (*541) is the umbrella concept for all the standards, rules, procedures, and guidelines that define what a review examines and how. Without Review Criteria, a review is an unstructured discussion; with them, it is an engineered quality-control process with defined questions, defined outcomes, and traceable results. Three major types of Review Criteria exist in Planguage: Clarity Rules (*129, governing specification intelligibility), Design Rules (*593, governing the quality of design ideas), and Content Rules (*543, governing the quality of requirements as ideas). Review Criteria are closely related to — but distinct from — Review Focus (*608): criteria are the *standards* used, while focus is the *primary purpose* the review pursues.

concepts.name: Review Focus

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rules
relatedConcepts.note: one device to determine the review focus, by choosing a particular set of rules

relatedConcepts.name: Checklists
relatedConcepts.note: an additional tactic for sharpening the focus within a given set of rules

relatedConcepts.name: Spec Content Review (SCR)
relatedConcepts.note: a content review is one general class of review focus

relatedConcepts.name: Clarity Review
relatedConcepts.note: another class of review focus which asks 'is the spec clear to readership?

relatedConcepts.name: Review Criteria
relatedConcepts.note: the many types of standards (rules being only one) used to define and direct the analysis process for a particular review activity

relatedConcepts.name: Review
relatedConcepts.note: Review Focus is a defining parameter of a Review — it names the primary purpose of the review

concepts.definition: A **Specification Review Focus** is the primary purpose of a review. It is in practice defined by the set of rules, checklists, process description, people participation, or other devices for analysing particular aspects of a specification. If the Spec QC process is used, then the primary tool for determining review focus is the set of rules that are used to detect defects in the spec.
concepts.overview: **Review Focus** (*608) names the primary purpose of a specification review and determines which aspects of the specification will be examined. Focus is operationalised through the choice of Review Criteria (*541): the rules, checklists, processes, and participation decisions that collectively direct reviewer attention toward specific aspects of the spec. Two major classes of review focus appear in Planguage: Clarity Review (*607), which asks "is the spec clear to its readership?", and Spec Content Review (*542), which asks "are the ideas in the spec actually good?" A review may have multiple foci, but naming the primary one ensures that reviewers know what they are looking for before they start looking.

concepts.name: Risk

relatedConcepts.name: Uncertainty
relatedConcepts.note: Uncertainty does not imply a negative result as clearly as 'risk' does

concepts.definition: A Risk is the **possibility** of [[Damage.673|Damage]] occurring.
concepts.overview:
A **Risk** is the *possibility* of Damage occurring.
It quantifies how likely a Threat is to activate as an Attack that defeats Mitigation.

concepts.name: Role

relatedConcepts.name: Role [SQC]
relatedConcepts.note: Role as used in Specification Quality Control (SQC)

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: Stakeholders are a related but distinct concept — not synonymous with Role

concepts.definition:
A **Role** is a defined responsibility, interest or scope for people. More fully, a Role is:
- A defined Process, carried out by Defined Actors, with Defined Skills, acting according to Defined Rules, for Defined Purposes, with a Defined Responsibility, and a Defined Duration, leading to a Defined Role Result.
concepts.overview: A Role in Planguage is not a job title or an organisational position — it is a structured specification of what a person or group is responsible for doing in a given process. Every Role has actors, skills, rules, purpose, responsibility, duration, and an expected result, making it a complete and auditable unit of accountability. The distinction from Stakeholder is crucial: a Stakeholder is someone with a stake in an outcome, while a Role is the functional capacity in which they act. Roles formalise process accountability so that specification and review activities have clearly owned participants. Role is used extensively in SQC (*411) to define who does what during quality control activities.

concepts.name: Root Causes

relatedConcepts.name: Common Cause
relatedConcepts.note: One category of root cause — systemic, always-present variation sources

relatedConcepts.name: Special Cause
relatedConcepts.note: Another category of root cause — assignable, episodic variation sources

relatedConcepts.name: Defect Prevention Process (DPP)
relatedConcepts.note: Process that acts on root causes to prevent recurrence

relatedConcepts.name: Process Improvement
relatedConcepts.note: Root cause identification drives process improvement

relatedConcepts.name: Statistical Process Control
relatedConcepts.note: SPC is used to distinguish common from special causes

relatedConcepts.name: Continuous Process Improvement
relatedConcepts.note: Root cause analysis is central to CPI

relatedConcepts.name: Systemic
relatedConcepts.note: Common causes are systemic in nature

concepts.definition: **Root Causes** are the ultimate upstream reason why an error/defect/fault/malfunction sequence occurs. Rationale: Root causes are interesting because by identifying them you will generally have identified the most efficient points for change to prevent downstream problems.
concepts.overview: Root cause analysis is the intellectual discipline of tracing defects and malfunctions upstream to their originating conditions rather than addressing only their surface symptoms. In Planguage, root causes are divided into two fundamental classes: Common Causes, which are systemic and present in all process outputs, and Special Causes, which are assignable to specific episodes or conditions. Identifying which class a root cause belongs to determines the appropriate response — systemic improvement for common causes, targeted correction for special causes. The Defect Prevention Process (DPP) uses root cause identification to feed permanent fixes back into the system, breaking the recurrence cycle. Root cause analysis is the engine of genuine process improvement rather than symptom management.

concepts.name: Rule

relatedConcepts.name: Standard

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rule

concepts.definition: A **Rule** is any statement of a standard on how to write or carry out some part of a systems engineering or business process.
concepts.overview: Rules in Planguage are the operational layer of the Standards hierarchy: they translate broad standards into actionable, checkable instructions for specific process activities such as specification writing and specification review. Unlike policies (which set intent) or glossary concepts (which define terms), Rules tell practitioners exactly what to do or not do in a given context. They exist at multiple levels — business rules, system rules, design rules — and are further specialised into classes such as Specification Rules and Specification Review Rules. The figure associated with *333 shows Rules sitting within a hierarchy under Standards, branching into Specification Rules, which branch further into Generic, Requirement, Design, Evo, and other sub-types. Rule *333 is the canonical prose-definition entry for the Rule concept; Rule *609 is a related entry extracted from the Standards hierarchy diagram in the source PDF.

Its sub-types include: Generic Specification Rule, Concept Rule, Policy Rule, Process Rule, Process Structure, Specification Rule, and Other Rules.
concepts.overview: Rule *609 is a specialisation-stub entry derived from the Standards hierarchy diagram at PDF page 379. It documents the structural role of Rule as a named component type within Standard *138, sitting at the same level as Concept *595, Policy *111, Process *113, and Specification *137. The concept number *609 is shared with Specification-Rule.609 and Specification-Rules.609 — an anomalous polysemy within the glossary numbering system, flagged for awareness rather than resolution here. The canonical, prose-defined Rule concept is Rule *333. This file preserves the corrected hierarchy from the 2026-05-04 VANeo extraction pass, which corrected an earlier error that had incorrectly described Rule *609 as the parent of Specification Rules and Design Content Rules.

concepts.name: Safety Deviation

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Factor
relatedConcepts.note: The prescribed ratio of over-design whose shortfall is expressed as Safety Deviation

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Margin
relatedConcepts.note: The required margin whose gap from actual is the Safety Deviation

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Impact
relatedConcepts.note: The % deviation from target; compared to safety margin to compute safety deviation

concepts.definition: A **Safety Deviation** is a measure of the estimated-or-observed difference between a required safety margin, and the estimated or actual system attribute level. It answers: 'How safe is the current design?' or 'How safe are we compared to plan?'
concepts.overview: Safety Deviation is the quantitative gap between where a design or project currently stands and where its required safety margin demands it should be. It is computed per scalar attribute — every performance goal and resource budget can have its own safety deviation value — making it a granular, attribute-level risk monitor. A negative safety deviation signals that the design has not yet achieved the required over-design; the larger the negative value, the greater the risk of failing to deliver the required level. Safety Deviation works in concert with Safety Factor (*131), Safety Margin (*637), and Safety Impact (*406): the Factor prescribes the required over-design ratio, the Margin translates that ratio into a level, and the Deviation measures the gap between the current estimate and that level. Used systematically, safety deviation gives technical management a real-time risk dashboard across all design attributes, enabling proactive intervention before problems compound.

concepts.name: Safety Factor
concepts.keyedIcon: nX  (where n is the numeric safety factor)

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Deviation
relatedConcepts.note: Measures the gap between current design and the level required by the safety factor

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Margin
relatedConcepts.note: The scalar level derived from applying the safety factor to a target or constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Impact
relatedConcepts.note: The % deviation from target levels; compared against the safety factor to assess adequacy

concepts.definition: A **Safety Factor** is the dimensionless ratio of 'conscious over-design' that is either required, or actually applied to some part of a system. It communicates and prescribes the degree of deliberate margin built into a design beyond the minimum required level.
concepts.overview: A Safety Factor is the dimensionless multiplier that translates a stated performance target or cost constraint into a harder, over-designed engineering level — the required safety margin. Historically rooted in mechanical engineering (load-bearing structures are designed to handle multiples of the expected load), Planguage extends this concept to any measurable system attribute. A safety factor of 2X on a response-time target means the design must achieve twice the required performance level to be considered safe. The safety factor is set either by an external standard (engineering codes, policy) or at project level. It is deliberately dimensionless so that it can be applied uniformly across attributes regardless of their units of measure. Safety Factor, Safety Margin (*637), Safety Deviation (*405), and Safety Impact (*406) form a four-concept cluster that together provide quantified risk monitoring at the attribute level.

concepts.name: Safety Impact

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Factor
relatedConcepts.note: The required over-design ratio; Safety Impact is compared against the safety factor to assess adequacy

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Margin
relatedConcepts.note: Safety Impact can serve as an estimated or actual safety margin when no specific safety factor is declared

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Deviation
relatedConcepts.note: Safety Deviation = Safety Impact − required Safety Margin

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation
relatedConcepts.note: Process that produces impact estimates from which Safety Impact is derived

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimate
relatedConcepts.note: The estimated impact value from which Safety Impact is computed

relatedConcepts.name: Impacts
relatedConcepts.note: Parameter grouping that includes Safety Impact

relatedConcepts.name: Percentage Uncertainty
relatedConcepts.note: Uncertainty range on the impact estimate affects safety impact reliability

relatedConcepts.name: Percentage Impact
relatedConcepts.note: Safety Impact is a specific form of percentage impact — deviation from target at 0% level

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Impact (Absolute Impact)
relatedConcepts.note: Absolute impact in scale units; complementary to percentage-based Safety Impact

relatedConcepts.name: Incremental Impact
relatedConcepts.note: The potential benefit or savings at each Evo increment; Safety Impact is computed per increment

concepts.definition: **Safety Impact** is the % deviation from target levels (targets = 0% level). It is an indirect measure of how well a required safety factor is met in theory or in practice. A positive safety impact for performance means the design exceeds the target; a positive safety impact for cost means the estimate is below budget.
concepts.overview: Safety Impact is the percentage by which an estimated or actual design outcome deviates from the stated target level — with the target defined as 0% and improvements measured outward in each attribute's favourable direction. For performance attributes, a positive safety impact means the design exceeds the target (good); for cost budgets, a positive safety impact means the cost is below budget (also good), but the sign convention is inverted. Safety Impact is independent of any declared safety factor: it reports where the design actually is, while the safety factor specifies where it needs to be. The gap between the two is Safety Deviation (*405). Together with Safety Factor (*131), Safety Margin (*637), and Safety Deviation (*405), Safety Impact forms the four-concept cluster that provides complete, quantified risk monitoring at the attribute level. The concept is tightly linked to Impact Estimation (*283) as the process that produces the estimates from which Safety Impact is calculated.

concepts.name: Safety Margin

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Factor
relatedConcepts.note: The dimensionless ratio from which the safety margin is derived

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Deviation
relatedConcepts.note: Measures the gap between current design level and the required safety margin

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Impact
relatedConcepts.note: The % deviation from target; can function as an estimated safety margin when no factor is set

concepts.definition: A **Safety Margin** is a scalar difference between a required defined target or constraint level, and its calculated safety level derived using the appropriate safety factor. It expresses how much over-design is required, in the attribute's own units or as a percentage.
concepts.overview: The Safety Margin is the concrete engineering target that a design must achieve in order to satisfy a declared Safety Factor. Where the safety factor is dimensionless (e.g., 2X), the safety margin is expressed in the attribute's own terms — either as the absolute difference on the scale, or as a percentage where the required target level is taken as 100% and the baseline as 0%. A safety margin is required (derived from the safety factor), but it can also be estimated or actual (derived from impact estimation or measured results). If no specific safety factor is specified, a safety margin can still be computed relative to the target or constraint level itself (equivalent to a factor of 1). The relationship between Safety Factor (*131), Safety Margin (*637), Safety Impact (*406), and Safety Deviation (*405) forms the complete four-concept cluster for quantified risk monitoring. Note: the figure referenced in the source PDF for this concept is blank — the diagram area was empty in the PDF at page 338.

concepts.name: Sample

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control (SQC)
relatedConcepts.note: SQC is the primary process that uses sampling to check specifications

relatedConcepts.name: Statistical Process Control
relatedConcepts.note: SPC uses sampling to monitor process behaviour

concepts.definition: In a quality control process, a **Sample** is a small part of a document, product or system, which is selected for checking. The intent of an SQC sample is that it will give *some* information about the specification without the *cost* of checking more of it — never to identify or remove *all* defects, even from the sampled portion.
concepts.overview: A Sample in SQC is a deliberate partial view: a selected excerpt of a specification reviewed in a quality control session instead of the full document. The rationale is economic — checking an entire document is expensive, and the marginal return diminishes rapidly. A sample gives diagnostic information about defect density and type at lower cost than full-coverage review, enabling statistical inference about the whole. Tom Gilb quantifies the consequence of this approach directly: SQC process effectiveness per single pass is in the range of 30% to 88%, meaning even 100% QC coverage of a document is still only a sample of all defects present. This means sampling is not a compromise — it is an honest acknowledgement of the nature of inspection. Testing also uses sampling. The concept belongs to the Inspection Artifact ancestry, connecting it to the wider SQC process (*051) and Statistical Process Control (*466).

concepts.name: Scalability

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: scalability is measured on defined scales for each scaling dimension

relatedConcepts.name: Attribute
relatedConcepts.note: scalability is a system quality attribute

relatedConcepts.name: Evo
relatedConcepts.note: scalability is a cross-cutting concern in evolutionary delivery

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar
relatedConcepts.note: scalability is expressed as scalar measurements on defined scales

concepts.definition: **Scalability** is a system quality that encompasses different types of scaling (such as volume, speed, backup activity, diagnosis activity, and security activity) and different degrees of scaling for defined stakeholders using a defined set of scaling strategies.
concepts.overview: **Scalability** (*685) is not a single quality but a family of related qualities, each corresponding to a distinct type of scaling and a distinct stakeholder need. A system may scale well on volume (handling more transactions) but poorly on security activity (maintaining protection as load grows). Planguage treats scalability as a scalar quality attribute: it must be specified on defined scales of measure for each scaling type, with explicit stakeholder scope and explicit scaling strategies. Tom Gilb's "Scale-Free" work (2016) argues that scalability principles should be embedded from the outset rather than retrofitted, making scalability a design-time constraint and target rather than an afterthought.

concepts.name: Scalar Baseline

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar
relatedConcepts.note: a scalar baseline is expressed on a scalar scale of measure

relatedConcepts.name: Baseline
relatedConcepts.note: scalar baseline is a specialised form of baseline

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: baseline and benchmark require clarification; see Notes

relatedConcepts.name: Function Baseline

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar Constraint

concepts.definition: A **Scalar Baseline** is a Baseline expressed on a defined scale of measure. It records the current or historical reference-level performance of an attribute as a numeric value on a specified scale, anchoring all subsequent target and constraint specifications.
concepts.overview: A **Scalar Baseline** (*490) is the numeric, scale-expressed form of a Baseline (*351). Where a Baseline establishes a reference point in general terms, a Scalar Baseline pins that reference point precisely on a defined Scale of Measure (*132) with a specific numeric level. In Planguage, the most common scalar baseline parameter is `Past` — the previously measured or currently observed level. It serves as the zero-point from which Percentage Impact (*306) is calculated and against which targets are evaluated. Tom Gilb noted an open editorial question about whether Scalar Baseline and Benchmark (*007) are truly distinct concepts; this has not been fully resolved in the glossary.

relatedConcepts.name: Failure Limit

concepts.definition: A **Scalar Constraint** is some kind of limitation on the delivered level of a defined Scale of Measure. It marks regions on the scale that must not be entered — or must not be exceeded — under penalty of failure, unacceptability, or catastrophe.
concepts.overview: A **Scalar Constraint** (*468) is a Constraint (*218) expressed on a continuous scale of measure rather than as a binary pass/fail condition. It defines specific thresholds and ranges on a scalar scale that trigger different severity levels of non-compliance — from the tolerable minimum (Must Do Level, >>) through Failure (!, !!) and Survival ([ ], [=====]) to Catastrophe (•). Unlike a Scalar Target (*470) which describes where you want the system to go, a Scalar Constraint describes where the system absolutely must not go. The family of scalar constraint sub-types provides a rich vocabulary for engineering safety and reliability requirements.

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Target

relatedConcepts.note: the scale on which the target level is expressed

concepts.definition: A **Scalar Target** is a performance target or resource target level specification expressed on a defined scale of measure. Scalar targets define stakeholder-valued levels of system performance and development costs, and are distinct from scalar constraints (like Fail) and benchmark levels (like Past).
concepts.overview: A **Scalar Target** (*470) is the aspiration side of scalar specification — it defines where the system should go on a scale of measure, rather than where it must not go (Scalar Constraint, *468) or where it currently is (Scalar Baseline, *490). Planguage provides four ordered scalar target parameters: Goal, Budget, Stretch, Wish, and Ideal — each expressing a different degree of ambition for the same attribute. Goal (*109) and Budget (*481) are the primary commitments; Stretch (*404) and Wish (*244) are ambitious aspirations; Ideal (*328) represents the theoretical maximum. Targets apply equally to performance attributes (how good the system performs) and resource attributes (how much it costs to build or run).

concepts.name: Scalar

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure

relatedConcepts.name: Binary

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar Baseline

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar Target

relatedConcepts.note: performance and resource attributes are scalar

concepts.definition: A **Scalar** is an adjective used to describe objects that possess or are measured using at least one scale of measure. Numeric levels on a scale of measure are described as *scalar* values, contrasting with binary objects that exist only in one of two discrete states.
concepts.overview: A **Scalar** (*198) describes any object that can be positioned on a continuous scale of measure — it has at least one measurable dimension. Performance attributes, resource attributes, and any requirement expressed as a numeric level are scalar. Scalars can be elementary (one scale only) or complex (multiple scales). The defining contrast is with binary objects (*249), which cannot be placed on a continuum because they exist in exactly one of two states (present or absent). The keyed icon `---------->` represents the open arrow of a scale: a direction without a fixed endpoint.

concepts.definition: A **Scale Context** is all the additional information that applies to a Scale of Measure, in addition to the units of measure. It includes qualifiers, conditions, definitions, and any other specification elements that make the scale precisely applicable to a specific measurement situation.
concepts.overview: A **Scale Context** (*640) extends the bare units of a scale into a fully specified measurement framework. Units of Measure (*560) tell you what you are counting — milliseconds, percentages, dollars. Scale Context tells you *when*, *for whom*, *under what conditions*, and *by what method* you count it. Context can be defined in the Scale parameter itself, in qualifiers used by referencing parameters (such as Goal or Past), in referenced definition files, or in any specification that references the Scale. Without a defined Scale Context, a measurement may be technically valid but practically ambiguous. Tom noted (as of 2003-09-02) that Scale Parameter conditions were not yet formally defined — pointing forward to Scale Qualifier (*381) and Scale Qualifier Conditions (*666) as the formal mechanism.

concepts.definition: A **Scale Impact** is an absolute numeric value on the scale of measure for a scalar requirement. It represents the level estimated or actually achieved when a specified design idea (or set of design ideas, or Evo Step) is implemented — including all effects of previously implemented designs.
concepts.overview: A **Scale Impact** (*403) is the absolute, scale-anchored view of what a design idea achieves. Where Percentage Impact (*306) shows *how much of the gap* between baseline and goal a design idea closes, Scale Impact shows *where on the scale* the system will actually land after the design is implemented — incorporating the effects of all previously implemented designs. Together, they form two complementary views in an Impact Estimation Table (*638): Scale Impact for real-world result, Percentage Impact for stakeholder-intelligible progress tracking. The keyed icon `-|-|->` is composed from the Scale icon `-|-|-` and the Impact arrow `->`.

concepts.definition: **Scale Qualifier Conditions** are Qualifier Conditions (*666) embedded within a defined Scale of Measure. They are the specific qualifier conditions that a Scale Qualifier (*381) introduces into the scale definition — conditions that must be explicitly bound (by a Scale Qualifier Definition, *446) in every parameter statement that references the scale.
concepts.overview: **Scale Qualifier Conditions** (*666 + *132) sit at the intersection of two concepts: the general notion of Qualifier Conditions (*666) and the Scale of Measure (*132). When a Scale Qualifier (*381) is written into a scale definition — for example `[Task]` in "time to complete a defined `[Task]`" — the conditions that `[Task]` can take are Scale Qualifier Conditions. They are the variable slots embedded in the scale, waiting to be resolved by Scale Qualifier Definitions (*446) in each referencing parameter statement. Tom Gilb wrote this entry as "*666 + *132", signalling it as an intersection concept: it is both a qualifier-condition concept and a scale-structure concept. The entry was first formalised in June 2021 and is brief — reflecting its status as an early draft combined entry.

concepts.definition: A **Scale Qualifier Definition** is the specific term assigned to finally define a qualifier condition for a corresponding Scale Qualifier. For example, in `Scale: time to complete a defined [Task]`, the Scale Qualifier is `[Task]` and `Update` is a Scale Qualifier Definition when the Goal statement reads `Goal [Task = Update]: 30 minutes`.
concepts.overview: A **Scale Qualifier Definition** (*446) is the binding act: it takes the generic placeholder of a Scale Qualifier (*381) and assigns a specific, concrete value to it at the point where the Scale is used. Where the Scale Qualifier says "fill this in with something specific," the Scale Qualifier Definition says "here is the specific thing." If a Scale Qualifier has no corresponding Scale Qualifier Definition in a given statement — and no declared default exists — that statement is defective. Scale Qualifier Definitions are also Specification Variables (*456): they carry meaning only when their own definition is resolved elsewhere in the specification. Tom Gilb added the synonym "Scale Qualifier Set" in 2020, reflecting that a statement can bind multiple scale qualifiers simultaneously.

concepts.definition: A **Scale Qualifier** is an optional term within the *definition* of a Scale of Measure that defines generic conditions — such as `[Task]` or `[Stakeholder]` — that must be specifically assigned (bound) in any parameter statement that references the Scale. Scale Qualifiers make scale specifications reusable and generalisable.
concepts.overview: A **Scale Qualifier** (*381) is the generic placeholder within a Scale of Measure specification that signals: "this condition must be given a specific value every time this scale is referenced." If a Scale says "time to complete a defined `[Task]`", then `Task` is the Scale Qualifier. When a Goal statement uses this scale, it must bind the Task to a specific value: `Goal [Task = Update]: 20 minutes.` The specific binding value ("Update") is the Scale Qualifier Definition (*446). Scale Qualifiers allow a single scale definition to serve multiple measurement contexts — changing only the qualifier definition, not the scale itself. Tom Gilb also calls this concept a "General Term" and "Umbrella Term" (added 2020), emphasising its role as a reusable placeholder across many instances.

concepts.definition: A **scale type** is a classification of the mathematical structure of a scale of measure — for example, whether the scale uses ordinal ranking, interval measurement, or ratio measurement with a true zero.
concepts.overview: Every Scale of Measure (*132) has an implicit or explicit scale type that determines what mathematical operations are valid on values expressed along it. An ordinal scale supports ranking but not arithmetic; a ratio scale supports all arithmetic, including meaningful percentage comparisons. Recognising scale type prevents analytical errors such as averaging ordinal ranks or computing ratios on interval scales without a true zero. Scale Type is a property of the Scale definition, not of any individual numeric level placed on the scale. As a relatively early-draft concept in the Planguage glossary, Scale Type is expected to be developed further in future editions.

concepts.definition: A **scale uncertainty** is an estimate of the error margins for a specific scale impact — the plus-and-minus range on the scale of measure over which an impact estimate can possibly vary — allowing calculation of best-case and worst-case borders.
concepts.overview: Quantitative specifications rarely carry exact numeric values; they carry estimates with inherent uncertainty. Scale Uncertainty formalises this by attaching an explicit error range to any Scale Impact value. This enables honest worst-case and best-case reasoning rather than treating point estimates as certainties. Experience data (with named sources) should back the specified uncertainty range. Uncertainty margins need not be symmetric — a system may be easier to improve than to degrade, producing asymmetric bounds such as +30% / −40%. Acknowledging and specifying uncertainty is a mark of specification maturity, not weakness.

concepts.definition: A **scale of measure** defines a single scalar attribute dimension — the common reference framework against which all numeric levels (benchmarks, goals, constraints, estimates) for that attribute are expressed.
concepts.overview: The Scale of Measure is the foundational quantification device of Planguage: it defines *what* is being measured before *how much* is specified. Every numeric requirement, estimate, or measurement in a Planguage specification is expressed relative to a defined scale. A scale is conceptual — it describes a variable, trackable, observable dimension of reality — while the Meter is the physical means of sampling that dimension. Generic scales include Scale Qualifiers that act as placeholders, allowing the same scale definition to be reused across multiple goal or benchmark parameters with different qualifier bindings. Because a good scale accurately reflects stakeholder values, choosing the right scale is arguably the most important specification decision a team makes.

concepts.definition: A **scope** describes the extent of influence of something — a specification, a system, a project, or any other defined entity — expressed using Planguage qualifiers (time, place, event, stakeholder, etc.) or any other useful terms.
concepts.overview: Scope sets the boundary within which a specification or system applies. Without an explicit scope, requirements and designs silently expand to fill all conceivable situations — a primary cause of specification ambiguity and project overrun. Scope can be declared globally (affecting everything within a defined system unless overridden) or locally (restricting influence to a defined sub-system). Scope is not an alternative to Qualifiers; it is a high-level container declaration that Qualifiers refine. Scope declarations interact with Authority, Mission, and Context to form the complete situational envelope of any specification.

concepts.definition: The **scribe** writes up the Editor Advice Log or other team notes during an SQC (Software Quality Control) meeting — capturing editorial advice and decisions so they are not lost after the meeting ends.
concepts.overview: The Scribe is the note-taker of an SQC session: a lightweight, rotating role that any team member can fill. The Scribe's primary output is the Editor Advice Log — the record of editorial issues, decisions, and action items raised by the Editor during the meeting. Who scribes is not a critical assignment; the Team Leader scribes by default if no one else is designated. The Scribe role prevents the common failure mode of good SQC insights evaporating as soon as participants leave the room.

concepts.definition: **Serial development** is a development process in which work proceeds on only one Evo Step at any one time — each step completes before the next begins.
concepts.overview: Serial development is one of three modes of Evolutionary Project Management (Evo), alongside Parallel Development (*363) and Platform Development (*362). Its defining characteristic is strict sequencing: only one Evo Step is active at any given time. The key advantage is that lessons learned from each step are fully available before the next step begins, enabling tight learning loops. The disadvantage is an extended Time Between Successive Products (TBSP) — the market must wait longer for subsequent product variants. Serial development suits contexts where learning from each step is critical, lead times are short, or parallel team capacity is unavailable.

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder

concepts.definition: A **server stakeholder** is a stakeholder who attempts to deliver results in order to satisfy the needs of a client stakeholder.
concepts.overview: In the Planguage stakeholder model, every relationship between parties can be framed as a client-server pairing: the client stakeholder (*650) has needs, and the server stakeholder attempts to meet them. This pairing is relational — the same individual or organisation may be a server stakeholder in one relationship and a client stakeholder in another. The server stakeholder's effectiveness is ultimately judged by whether the client stakeholder's needs are actually satisfied, not merely by whether a service was delivered. This distinction is critical for performance measurement and accountability in system design.

concepts.definition: A **service** is the provision of a facility to meet the needs or for the use of a person or thing (Oxford English Dictionary). In Planguage terms, providing the service is *why* a system does something — the purpose that a function exists to fulfil.
concepts.overview: Service, Function, and Mechanism form the fundamental "why-what-how" triad of system description in Planguage. A service answers the question "why does this system capability exist?" — it is the value delivered to a stakeholder or another system. The function answers "what does the system do?" — the observable behaviour. The mechanism answers "how does the system do it?" — the means of realisation. Confusing these three levels leads to requirements that specify implementation (mechanism) instead of purpose (service), producing brittle specifications that constrain design unnecessarily.

concepts.definition: A **set** is a list of terms that belong together in some defined sense — a named collection of related items, expressed using curly-brace notation `{ }` in Planguage.
concepts.overview: The Set parameter is Planguage's mechanism for grouping related items under a single name. It provides a compact, readable way to declare collections — whether of people, systems, conditions, or any other enumerable entities — without repeating each member name wherever the group is referenced. Sets are defined once and referenced by name, reducing specification verbosity and ensuring consistency. The curly-brace notation `{ }` is the keyed icon and standard syntax for Set declarations.

concepts.definition: A **sibling** is a "parallel kid" — a specification artifact (process, function, system, delivery step, or other entity) that shares the same parent as another artifact at the same level of derivation.
concepts.overview: The Sibling relationship is the horizontal peer relationship in Planguage's hierarchical specification structure. Where Parent (*267) expresses a vertical "owns" relationship and Kid (*266) expresses "is a child of," Sibling expresses "is at the same level as." Two artifacts are siblings if and only if they share the same parent. Sibling relationships matter for scope analysis (siblings do not inherit from each other — only from their shared parent) and for decomposition completeness (a well-decomposed parent should have a complete and non-overlapping set of siblings covering its full scope).

concepts.definition: A **Side Effect** is an impact by a design idea on any requirement attribute, other than the direct impact(s) we primarily intended.
concepts.overview: Side effects arise whenever a design idea touches requirement attributes beyond its primary target — they are the collateral consequences of engineering decisions. Contrary to common usage, side effects are not always negative; they may be intended, unintended, positive, neutral, or negative. Engineers must systematically identify and evaluate side effects at design time, not only discover them at testing or operation. The Planguage keyed icon `*.->` captures this precisely: `*` for multiple impacts and `->` for the Impacts symbol, signalling that any design may ripple across multiple attributes.

concepts.definition: **Significant Specification** refers to any specification content which, if wrong, misinterpreted, or missing, represents a potential for non-trivial downstream cost to correct and suffer.
concepts.overview: The Significant Specification concept draws a sharp line between specification content that truly matters and mere commentary. Only specification elements whose errors would cause non-trivial downstream costs — in rework, failure, or risk — qualify as "significant." The complementary concept, Non-significant Specification (Comment *018), covers introductory text, footnotes, and background material where defects are minor and cheap. This distinction focuses Specification Quality Control (SQC) effort on the content that truly drives engineering decisions, avoiding wasted review energy on commentary. Generic Planguage rules require a visible distinction between the two categories.

concepts.name: Simple

relatedConcepts.name: Simplicity

relatedConcepts.name: Complex

concepts.definition: **Simple** is the adjective form of Simplicity (*690): a quantified level of performance, for a defined task, by a defined stakeholder, in a defined environment, that has been achieved or targeted.
concepts.overview: Simple is not a vague quality impression — in Planguage it is an adjective derived from a measurable scale. To call something "simple" is to assert that it scores at or beyond an acceptable level on the Simplicity scale for a defined task, agent, and environment. Without specifying the scale, the agent, and the conditions, the word "simple" is meaningless. The companion concept Simplicity (*690) defines the noun and provides the scale template; Simple is the adjective applied when a system, design, or process achieves a quantified simplicity level. The antonym Complex (*021) sits at the opposing end of the same dimension.

concepts.name: Simplicity

relatedConcepts.name: Simple
relatedConcepts.note: adjective form of the same concept — paired bidirectionally

relatedConcepts.name: Complex
relatedConcepts.note: antonym; the opposite end of the same scale

concepts.definition: **Simplicity** is a numeric level, stated on a defined Scale of Measure, for defined conditions, including Who, How, Where and When.
concepts.overview: Simplicity in Planguage is not an impression — it is a measured quantity. Like any quality attribute, it must be expressed as a numeric level on a defined scale, with specified conditions for the agent (Who), the task (How), the environment (Where), and the time (When). The conventional scale template for Simplicity uses average effort to complete a defined task — typically time, error rate, or cognitive load — by a defined user class in a defined context. The companion concept Simple (*689) is the adjective derived from this noun; Complex (*021) is the antonym. Without a scale and conditions, any claim of "simplicity" is meaningless as engineering specification.

concepts.definition: A **Softcrafter** is a person who practices the craft of programming software for computers — commonly known as a programmer or coder.
concepts.overview: Tom Gilb coined "Softcrafter" to name clearly what a computer programmer actually does: practice a craft. Programming is a skilled craft, not an engineering discipline, and calling programmers "software engineers" is a category error comparable to a skilled carpenter calling themselves a structural engineer. The Softcrafter concept draws a sharp distinction between craft (writing code that works) and engineering (designing systems that deliver quantified stakeholder value within resource constraints). The Softect (*567) and Software Engineer (*571) represent genuine engineering roles; the Softcrafter does not. The term is deliberately not derogatory — craft has genuine value — but precision requires honest naming.

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architect
relatedConcepts.note: the generic architect role; Softect is the software-specific instance

concepts.definition: A **Softect** is one who does software or IT systems architecture — a concatenation of *software* and *architect*.
concepts.overview: The Softect is the necessary synchronisation and co-ordination function for specialist software engineers and builders in a large software engineering environment. Where there are many specialists working in parallel, the Softect maintains architectural coherence — ensuring that the technical solution set satisfies the multiple, often conflicting objectives of users as fully as possible. The Softect is also a specialist Software Engineer, but with a specific speciality: overall control of a complex engineering process. The companion concept Softecture (*566) names the activity the Softect performs. The term was coined by Tom Gilb in *Principles of Software Engineering Management* (1988), alongside the analogous Systect (*565) / Systecture (*564) pair for systems-level architecture.

concepts.name: Softecture

relatedConcepts.name: Softect
relatedConcepts.note: the person who performs Softecture — paired concept coined together in Gilb88

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: the generic architecture concept; Softecture is the software-specific highest-level instance

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architecture (Systecture)
relatedConcepts.note: systems architecture activity above Softecture; sets constraints for Softecture

relatedConcepts.name: Systect
relatedConcepts.note: person who performs Systecture and co-ordinates the Softect

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architect
relatedConcepts.note: the generic architect; Softect is the software-specific instance

relatedConcepts.name: Designer
relatedConcepts.note: Softecture is the highest level of design activity in a software engineering project

relatedConcepts.name: Software Engineer
relatedConcepts.note: Software Engineering encompasses Softecture as a sub-discipline

relatedConcepts.name: Software Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: the broader engineering discipline within which Softecture is the top design tier

relatedConcepts.name: Softcrafter
relatedConcepts.note: the programmer whose work is architecturally constrained by Softecture
