relatedConcepts.note: information system architect — analogous role coined alongside Softect in Gilb88

relatedConcepts.name: Infotecture
relatedConcepts.note: information architecture — analogous activity coined alongside Softecture in Gilb88

concepts.definition: **Softecture** is a concatenation of *software* and *architecture* — the highest level of design activity in a software engineering project, or in the software area of a systems engineering activity.
concepts.overview: Softecture names the top-tier design discipline within software engineering, coined by Tom Gilb in *Principles of Software Engineering Management* (1988). Just as Architecture (*192) is the highest-level design discipline generically, Softecture is its software-specific expression. The Softect (*567) is the person who performs Softecture — the two terms are a paired concept: activity (Softecture) and actor (Softect). Softecture operates below Systecture (*564), the systems-level architecture that sets constraints for it. The term forms part of a family of Gilb-coined professional vocabulary designed to bring engineering precision to role and activity naming in software and systems work.

concepts.name: Software Engineer

relatedConcepts.name: Software Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: the discipline the Software Engineer practices — paired bidirectionally

relatedConcepts.name: Software
relatedConcepts.note: all non-hardware types for machines and people — the material domain

relatedConcepts.name: Softcrafter
relatedConcepts.note: a computer programmer; not an engineer; commonly misuses this title

relatedConcepts.name: Softect
relatedConcepts.note: the design specialist within software engineering; narrower territory than Software Engineer

relatedConcepts.name: Softecture
relatedConcepts.note: the architecture discipline performed by the Softect, within Software Engineering scope

relatedConcepts.name: Systect
relatedConcepts.note: the systems architect who co-ordinates software engineering at the systems level

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architecture (Systecture)
relatedConcepts.note: systems architecture setting constraints for software engineering work

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Engineer
relatedConcepts.note: the analogous engineering role at the systems level — same discipline, broader scope

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: the broader systems engineering discipline that software engineering interfaces with

relatedConcepts.name: Logicware
relatedConcepts.note: computer programs — the specific type of software most directly produced

concepts.definition: A **Software Engineer** is an engineer with specialty in software — characterised by the ability to assemble software components based on quantified attributes, meeting multiple quantified requirement performance levels within specified resource constraints.
concepts.overview: The Software Engineer is the central professional role in software engineering, distinguished from both the Softcrafter (*573) and the Softect (*567) by a broader and distinctly engineering-oriented accountability. Where the Softcrafter practices the craft of programming and the Softect focuses on architectural design, the Software Engineer thinks in measurable system performance characteristics, costs across the full lifecycle, and value delivered to a balanced set of stakeholders. Software Engineers must know how to access and measure the multiple quantified attributes of design components — this is the defining engineering capability that separates the role from programming. The discipline they practice is Software Engineering (*572).

concepts.name: Software Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Software Engineer
relatedConcepts.note: the person who practices Software Engineering — paired bidirectionally

relatedConcepts.name: Software
relatedConcepts.note: all non-hardware types for machines and people — the material domain

relatedConcepts.name: Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: the generic engineering discipline; Software Engineering is a specialisation

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: the broader systems engineering discipline; Software Engineering interfaces with it

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: balanced set of stakeholders is a defining obligation of Software Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Value
relatedConcepts.note: balanced set of values delivered to stakeholders is the goal of Software Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Softect
relatedConcepts.note: the design specialist within Software Engineering; Softecture is a sub-discipline

relatedConcepts.name: Softecture
relatedConcepts.note: the top design tier within Software Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Softcrafter
relatedConcepts.note: computer programmer; a sub-process Software Engineering controls but does not reduce to

relatedConcepts.name: Systect
relatedConcepts.note: systems architect who co-ordinates Software Engineering at the systems level

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Engineer
relatedConcepts.note: the analogous engineering role at the systems level

concepts.definition: **Software Engineering** is the engineering discipline of enabling and motivating software systems to deliver a balanced set of values, directly or indirectly, to a balanced set of stakeholders, throughout their lifecycle.
concepts.overview: Software Engineering is defined in Planguage by its outcome obligation — delivering balanced stakeholder value — not by its technical activities. It includes determining stakeholder requirements, designing new and adapting existing systems, subcontracting for components, interfacing with systems architecture, testing, and measurement. Crucially, Software Engineering *controls* sub-processes like computer programming (Softcrafting *573), quality assurance, and requirement specification — it is not reducible to any of them. The two key phrases in Gilb's definition are deliberate: "balanced set of values" (to prevent fixation on narrow technical deliverables) and "balanced set of stakeholders" (to prevent optimising for only one party at the expense of others). The Software Engineer (*571) is the person who practices this discipline.

concepts.name: Software

relatedConcepts.name: Software Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: the discipline that produces and maintains software

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: software documentation and plans are a component of software

relatedConcepts.name: Documentation
relatedConcepts.note: plans and specifications made by people concerning software

concepts.definition: **Software** refers to the 'non-hardware' aspects or components of a system. It specifically includes computer programs, data (computer-readable files and databases), and software documentation and plans (any form of specification or plans made by people concerning software).
concepts.overview: Software is the non-physical layer of a system — programs, data, and all documentation that governs how that system behaves. It contrasts with hardware, which is the tangible physical substrate. In Planguage, software is treated as a material component alongside hardware, people, and processes within any engineered system. Because specifications and plans are explicitly included in the definition, the quality of software is inseparable from the quality of its documentation. This broad definition ensures that measurement and improvement efforts address the full scope of what software actually consists of.

concepts.name: Solution Level
concepts.definition: Solution Level is the layer where implementation choices (Designs, Strategies, Means) are specified. Solutions are the means by which Products are realised. Solutions create Product effects; they are the cause whose effect is Product.
concepts.overview: **Solution Level** (*804) is part of HumanAgent Gilb's Value Delivery framework, an extension to Tom Gilb's original Planguage. It is not in the source PlanguageGlossary.pdf — it has been authored to capture concepts the framework needs but the PDF did not name.

concepts.name: Source

relatedConcepts.name: Source (parameter)
relatedConcepts.note: polysemy — Source-parameter.135 is the inline Planguage tag; this file covers the general SQC process-input concept sharing the same number

relatedConcepts.name: Evidence
relatedConcepts.note: source documents are the repositories in which evidence is located

concepts.definition: **Source** is a synonym for process input *information* (as opposed to process input *materials*). In SQC workflows, source specifications are contained in documents that are usually of earlier production — and typically at higher levels of authority, global scope, and abstraction — than the current work product.
concepts.overview: In Statistical Quality Control and Planguage process modelling, every work product is produced from upstream inputs. The term 'Source' names the *information* inputs specifically — the documents, contracts, requirements, and designs that a team must consult and transform into the next work product. This distinguishes information inputs from physical materials. Sources are hierarchical: contracts are sources for requirements; requirements and designs are sources for impact estimation; design is source for planning and construction. Understanding source relationships makes the traceability chain of a system explicit and auditable. Note that this general concept shares concept number *135 with the more specific Source *parameter* definition — see the polysemy note below.

concepts.name: Space

relatedConcepts.name: Time
relatedConcepts.note: the temporal scope dimension; Space is its non-temporal counterpart

relatedConcepts.name: Event
relatedConcepts.note: event-dependent scope dimension; Space is neither temporal nor event-dependent

relatedConcepts.name: Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: Space is used within qualifier expressions to define context

relatedConcepts.name: Scope
relatedConcepts.note: Space is one of the primary dimensions for defining scope

relatedConcepts.name: Place
relatedConcepts.note: geographic Place is a subset of Space; Space generalises Place to non-geographic dimensions

concepts.definition: **Space** is a specification concept that encompasses the geographic 'Place' notion and, in addition, any other *notions of group or location* — such as component, market, religion, race, or organisational unit. It refers to the set of possible scope dimensions that are neither temporal nor event-dependent, but which capture 'where' or 'who/what group' notions. Space can be used as a parameter to define any number of dimensions simultaneously.
concepts.overview: Space generalises the intuitive notion of physical location into a multi-dimensional scoping tool. Where Time (*153) answers 'when?' and Event (*062) answers 'on what trigger?', Space answers 'where?' — but broadly interpreted: geography, organisation, people types, and system components are all spatial dimensions in this sense. This makes Space a powerful qualifier ingredient, letting engineers write precise conditional requirements such as "for Buddhist Korean teenagers" or "for the radio transmitter subsystem". Tom Gilb marked this entry "DELETE" in the source, suggesting it may be a deprecated or merged concept in later Planguage editions, but the content is preserved here as extracted.

concepts.name: Specific Design

relatedConcepts.name: Function Design
relatedConcepts.note: a 'less specific' upstream design that narrows choices without making a final specific selection

relatedConcepts.name: Design / Solution
relatedConcepts.note: the general class of design of which specific design is the most concrete instance

concepts.definition: A **specific design** is a precise and definite design, intended to give the final range of performance and cost attributes resulting from that design to a real system. It is distinct from all upstream design notions, which are intended to narrow choices in an appropriate direction — but not to make a final specific choice.
concepts.overview: Specific Design is the most concrete level of the design hierarchy in Planguage. Where upstream design activities (such as Function Design *521) progressively narrow the solution space, Specific Design commits to final attribute values and implementation details for a real system. It is the design that will actually be built. Tom Gilb emphasises a three-way distinction for any design: the *intended* design, the *specified* design (which may be defective relative to intent), and the *actually implemented* design (which may differ from both). Keeping these three distinct is essential for honest quality assessment and defect classification.

concepts.name: Specific

relatedConcepts.name: Generic
relatedConcepts.note: the antonym — Generic applies broadly across a class; Specific applies to a precise, defined subset

concepts.definition: **Specific** means applicable to a precise, definite set of components. It is usually used to reduce scope to declare a component (or set of components) as being explicitly singled out as the subject for attention. A *specific constraint* is a system specification constraint that applies to a specific set of defined conditions — those conditions being typically defined in qualifier brackets.
concepts.overview: Specific is the scope-narrowing qualifier term in Planguage, standing in direct contrast to Generic (*081). Where a generic statement applies broadly across a class or system, a specific statement targets exactly one component, subsystem, user type, or context. In practice, 'Specific' is deployed within qualifier expressions in brackets to signal that the following requirement or constraint is scoped to a named, bounded set. This precision is essential in large system specifications where a single requirement might apply globally in one form and locally in another — and the difference must be unambiguous.

concepts.name: Specification Constant

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Variable
relatedConcepts.note: Scale Variable values vary as a function of time or environment; Specification Constant values do not

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: qualifiers may define the context in which a constant applies

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Variable
relatedConcepts.note: the direct contrast: a Specification Variable changes as a function of time or external environment

concepts.definition: A **specification constant** is a Tag in a specification which always translates to a specific, stable definition. The definition might be updated or improved over time, but it does not vary as a function of time or external environment. It is the stable counterpart to a Specification Variable (*456).
concepts.overview: When a Tag in a Planguage specification resolves to the same definition regardless of when or where it is evaluated, it is a Specification Constant. The definition can be refined or corrected through a deliberate revision process, but it does not depend on runtime conditions, agreements, or environmental context. This stability is what makes a constant suitable for use in formal requirements: readers and tools can rely on a single, unambiguous meaning. A Specification Constant contrasts with a Specification Variable (*456), whose value is explicitly time- or context-dependent, and with a Scale Variable (*446), whose measurement values shift with environment.

concepts.name: Specification Content Review

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Review Rule
relatedConcepts.note: Content Rules that govern what is checked in an SCR; the rule set the SCR applies

relatedConcepts.name: Review Criteria
relatedConcepts.note: the criteria used to judge content during an SCR

relatedConcepts.name: Spec QC / Inspection
relatedConcepts.note: the broader SQC inspection process of which SCR is a specialised review class

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Intelligibility Review (SIR)
relatedConcepts.note: must succeed before SCR is run — clarity precedes content judgment

relatedConcepts.name: Design Content Rules
relatedConcepts.note: the Design Rules applied when conducting a Design Concept Review (SCR variant)

relatedConcepts.name: Content
relatedConcepts.note: the subject of the review — the ideas and substance of the specification

relatedConcepts.name: Review Focus
relatedConcepts.note: defines what the review is looking at; SCR focuses on content quality, not format

concepts.definition: A **Specification Content Review (SCR)** is a class of specification review that focuses on the *goodness of the ideas* specified, regardless of *how well* they are specified. It asks: 'Is this the right stuff to do?' It looks at *content of concept* — not format or packaging — and uses Content Rules to determine what to review in a particular type of content review.
concepts.overview: The SCR occupies a distinct and demanding position in the Planguage review hierarchy. Clarity reviews (*607) come first: a specification must be judged well-written, clear, and complete before senior people invest time judging its content. Once clarity is established, the SCR asks the harder question — not 'is it written well?' but 'is it the right thing to do?'. The SCR applies Content Rules (such as Design Rules *593) to count and characterise violations, producing a quantified basis for exit decisions (e.g., 'no more than 1.0 Major defects/page'). Multiple SCR variants exist — Design Concept Review, Requirement Concept Review, Architecture Concept Review, Test Plan Concept Review, and Value Review — each applying domain-specific content rules. Note: Specification-Review-Rule.543 was labelled 'Content Rules' in the source; it is the canonical rule set for this review.

concepts.name: Specification Element

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: A Specification Element is a constituent part of a Specification.

relatedConcepts.name: Statement
relatedConcepts.note: A Statement is one of the three primitive forms a Specification Element can take.

relatedConcepts.name: Expression
relatedConcepts.note: An Expression is one of the three primitive forms a Specification Element can take.

relatedConcepts.name: Term
relatedConcepts.note: A Term is one of the three primitive forms a Specification Element can take.

concepts.definition: A **Specification Element** is any distinct element, however elementary or complex, of a specification. A specification element can be a statement, an expression, or a term.
concepts.overview: The Specification Element concept provides the atomic building-block vocabulary for analysing and describing the content of any Planguage specification. Every piece of textual information in a specification can be classified as one of three primitive forms: a Statement, an Expression, or a Term. This decomposition supports systematic quality checking because reviewers can identify what kind of element is at issue when raising a specification issue. The concept is deliberately neutral with respect to complexity — an element may be a single keyword (a Term) or an elaborate multi-parameter block (a complex Statement).

concepts.name: Specification Issue
synonyms: Issue *529 (short informal form used in SQC context; actually an abbreviation)

relatedConcepts.name: Issue
relatedConcepts.note: The parent concept; a Specification Issue is an Issue detected during specification review rather than in a running system.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rule
relatedConcepts.note: A Specification Issue arises when a Specification Rule is suspected to have been violated.

relatedConcepts.name: Error
relatedConcepts.note: An Error (slip/mistake) by the author is the typical upstream cause of a Specification Issue.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Defect
relatedConcepts.note: A Specification Issue becomes a confirmed Specification Defect only once the author or editor accepts it as such.

relatedConcepts.name: Fault
relatedConcepts.note: If a Specification Defect survives into the system, it can manifest as a Fault.

relatedConcepts.name: Malfunction
relatedConcepts.note: The end-user-visible failure at the top of the defect chain that begins with a Specification Issue.

relatedConcepts.name: Resolution
relatedConcepts.note: The outcome of reviewing a Specification Issue; it either becomes a confirmed defect or is dismissed.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control (SQC)
relatedConcepts.note: The disciplined process within which Specification Issues are raised and resolved.

concepts.definition: A **Specification Issue** is a checker-perceived potential defect in any form of documentation or system development specification. When resolved by the author or editor, a specification issue either becomes an acknowledged defect or is dismissed.
concepts.overview: The Specification Issue concept provides a deliberately non-accusatory mechanism for SQC checkers to flag potential defects without asserting that a defect is certain. By declaring "I think this *might* be a problem," the checker preserves professional courtesy and leaves the final determination to the author or editor. Specification Issues can be embedded directly inside the specification using the `Issue:` parameter, paired with a `Resolution:` parameter to record the author's response. This keeps the QC dialogue visible in context and auditable. The chain runs: Error/Slip → Specification Issue → Specification Defect → Fault → Malfunction.

concepts.name: Specification Language

relatedConcepts.name: User Defined Term
relatedConcepts.note: User-Defined Terms are the product-specific vocabulary layer that is integrated onto Specification Language's formal skeleton.

relatedConcepts.name: Process Language
relatedConcepts.note: A project's Specification Language must be distinguished from its Process Language, which captures the 'process standards for doing the project.

relatedConcepts.name: Project Language
relatedConcepts.note: The set of all Process Language, Product Language and Specification Language artifacts used by a defined project; within Project Language, a variant of Basic Planguage's Specification Language can be used to express specific project specifications.

relatedConcepts.name: System Description Language (SDL)
relatedConcepts.note: The subset of Planguage for describing systems, including 'processes viewed as systems with attributes'; a specialisation within Specification Language.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Language provides the formal structures for writing a Specification.

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage Concept
relatedConcepts.note: Planguage Concepts are the semantic content that Specification Language structures carry.

concepts.definition: **Specification Language** provides the structures and formats used to express Planguage specifications. Its formal skeleton — Planguage parameters, icons, concept definitions, and specification conventions — is the framework onto which product language is integrated.
concepts.overview: Specification Language is the syntactic and structural layer of Planguage, distinct from the semantic content (Product Language) and the process standards (Process Language) that also make up a full Project Language. It defines the grammar: which parameters exist, what icons mean, how concepts are declared, and what conventions govern layout and cross-reference. Practitioners who write specifications use it implicitly; people who develop or customise specification standards use it explicitly. The rationale for naming it separately — as Tom Gilb noted — was a felt need to distinguish the different aspects of Planguage so that each could be formally discussed, extended, or adapted without conflating concerns.

concepts.name: Specification Maturity

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Status [Specification]
relatedConcepts.note: Quality Status is a distinct concurrent view of a specification; Specification Maturity does not express quality.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Level
relatedConcepts.note: Quality Level measures defect density; Maturity measures evolutionary stage — both are orthogonal views.

relatedConcepts.name: Status [System]
relatedConcepts.note: The generic Status parameter of which Specification Maturity is a specification-branch specialisation.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Maturity is a parameter used to describe the level of evolution of a Specification.

concepts.definition: **Specification Maturity** is the level of evolution of a specification, standard, or process artefact. It is a parameter used to describe how far along the lifecycle a specification has progressed, and is explicitly *not* a measure of specification quality.
concepts.overview: Specification Maturity provides a lifecycle stage label for any specification artefact, allowing teams to communicate unambiguously how far a specification has evolved — from initial capture to final availability. This is orthogonal to Specification Quality Level, which measures defect density, and to Quality Status, which is a broader assessment status. A mature specification may still have many defects; a high-quality specification may still be in an early lifecycle stage. Keeping these dimensions separate avoids the common confusion of treating "we finished writing it" as equivalent to "it is good." The parameter was developed and popularised by Nokia practitioner Leo Hippeläinen in 2002.

concepts.name: Specification Meeting

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control (SQC)
relatedConcepts.note: The Specification Meeting is one of the three main SQC sub-processes; it follows the individual Checking sub-process.

relatedConcepts.name: Scribe
relatedConcepts.note: The Scribe records the issues and outputs during the Specification Meeting.

relatedConcepts.name: Editor
relatedConcepts.note: The Editor produces the Editor Advice Log, the primary written output of the Specification Meeting.

relatedConcepts.name: Question of Intent
relatedConcepts.note: Questions of Intent raised during individual checking are surfaced and discussed in the Specification Meeting.

relatedConcepts.name: Checker
relatedConcepts.note: Checkers report their individual checking results at the start of the Specification Meeting.

relatedConcepts.name: Editor Advice Log
relatedConcepts.note: The principal written output of the Specification Meeting, produced by the Editor.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Issue
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Issues are the primary content discussed and logged during the Specification Meeting.

concepts.definition: A **Specification Meeting** is an SQC sub-process — a meeting of checkers and a team leader, scheduled after the individual Checking sub-process. Its overall purpose is to evaluate the results from the individual checking activity and to produce an Editor Advice Log as written output.
concepts.overview: The Specification Meeting is the collective phase of Specification Quality Control, coming after each checker has independently reviewed the specification and before the editor consolidates defect reports. Its purposes include: initial reporting of individual checking results, surfacing and analysing issues and Questions of Intent for the author or writer, reporting process improvement suggestions, and enabling additional checking in a brainstorming mode. The meeting is calibrated at its outset — if the checking data analysis shows minimal findings, the meeting may be cut short or skipped. The primary output is the Editor Advice Log. Unlike a formal design review, the meeting has the flavour of collaborative exploration rather than final verdict.

concepts.name: Specification Quality Control

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: SQC is the specification-domain specialisation of the general Quality Control discipline.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Defect
relatedConcepts.note: SQC is the process that detects, measures, and drives the removal of Specification Defects.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rule
relatedConcepts.note: Specifications are checked against Specification Rules; violations are Specification Defects.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Review Rule
relatedConcepts.note: A different type of rule used in SQC to check specification readiness for review (business or technical).

relatedConcepts.name: Review
relatedConcepts.note: SQC is a formalised, rule-based form of Review focused on specification quality.

relatedConcepts.name: Defect Detection Process (DDP)
relatedConcepts.note: One of the two core sub-processes of SQC; defined in detail in [GILB93].

relatedConcepts.name: Defect Prevention Process (DPP)
relatedConcepts.note: The second core sub-process of SQC; extends scope to quality assurance when active.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Meeting
relatedConcepts.note: A key SQC sub-process: the collective meeting phase following individual checking.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Issue
relatedConcepts.note: The polite, non-accusatory flag raised by a checker during SQC when a potential defect is found.

concepts.definition: **Specification Quality Control (SQC)** is a rigorous specification quality control discipline concerned with defect detection, defect measurement, defect removal, process improvement, and entry/exit controls. It is based on evaluating specification conformance to specification rules.
concepts.overview: SQC applies the Shewhart/Deming tradition of statistical quality control to specifications rather than manufactured products. Specifications are checked against defined Specification Rules (*129); violations are objectively classified as defects; defect density is measured using the Specification Quality Level parameter. SQC includes a Defect Detection Process (DDP) and a Defect Prevention Process (DPP). When the DPP is active, SQC extends from quality control into quality assurance. By default, SQC does not judge the *relevance* or *profitability* of the requirements — only their clarity, completeness, and consistency. A separate layer using Specification Review Rules (*543) can extend SQC to check specification readiness for business or technical review. The same process is historically known as "Inspection" [GILB93] and "Peer Review."

concepts.name: Specification Quality Level

relatedConcepts.name: Status
relatedConcepts.note: Status is the broader lifecycle parameter; Specification Quality Level provides a specific quality dimension alongside it.

relatedConcepts.name: Remaining Major Defects/Page
relatedConcepts.note: The operational measure used to calculate Specification Quality Level.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Defect
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Defects are what the Quality Level counts and tracks.

relatedConcepts.name: Major Defect
relatedConcepts.note: Only Major Defects are counted in the Quality Level metric; minor defects are excluded.

relatedConcepts.name: Logical Page
relatedConcepts.note: The normalisation unit for the Quality Level metric — defects per logical page.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Maturity
relatedConcepts.note: Maturity is orthogonal to Quality Level; a specification can be mature and still have high defect density.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control (SQC)
relatedConcepts.note: SQC uses Specification Quality Level as the primary output metric to determine specification fitness.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rule
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Rules define what constitutes a defect; Quality Level measures how many such violations remain.

concepts.definition: The **Specification Quality Level** is a measure of a specification's conformance to any specified relevant standards. Operationally, it is the estimated number of remaining major defects per logical page — the primary output metric of the SQC process.
concepts.overview: Specification Quality Level provides a single, objective number that expresses how defect-dense a specification currently is. By counting only major defects and normalising by logical page, it gives teams a comparable, repeatable metric for tracking improvement across SQC cycles and for setting exit criteria. A Quality Level of 0.0 means no remaining major defects are estimated; higher values indicate a specification that still needs work. This metric is deliberately orthogonal to Specification Maturity — a specification can reach late lifecycle stages while still having a poor Quality Level, and vice versa. The metric drives the SQC process toward measurable goals rather than subjective impressions of quality.

concepts.name: Specification Reference

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Variable
relatedConcepts.note: A Specification Variable is a user-defined Tag that changes value; a Specification Reference is a user-defined Tag that cross-references a defined term.

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Variable
relatedConcepts.note: Scale Variable (*446) is a user-defined scaling qualifier; distinct from a Specification Reference.

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: Scale Qualifiers provide additional context to scale values; a Specification Reference can cross-link to a defined Scale Qualifier.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Constant
relatedConcepts.note: A Specification Constant is a user-defined Tag with a fixed value; like a Specification Reference but value-bearing rather than cross-referential.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: Specification References appear within a Specification to cross-link defined terms without duplicating their definitions.

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: A Specification Reference is specifically a user-defined Tag; it does not include Planguage parameters.

concepts.definition: A **Specification Reference** is any user-defined Tag which cross-references a defined term elsewhere in the specification. This does not include Planguage parameters.
concepts.overview: Specification References enable within-specification hyperlinks — a way to point from one part of a specification to a defined term without repeating its definition. They are user-defined Tags, meaning the naming convention is chosen by the specification author, not prescribed by Planguage itself. The exclusion of Planguage parameters is important: parameters like `Goal:`, `Scale:`, or `Rationale:` are part of Specification Language, not Specification References. A Specification Reference is part of the product-level tagging system — the author's own cross-referencing infrastructure layered on top of the Planguage skeleton.

concepts.name: Specification Review Rule

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control (SQC)
relatedConcepts.note: SQC can be extended by using Specification Review Rules to check specification readiness for business or technical review.

relatedConcepts.name: Review
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Review Rules specify best practices for engineering review; they both instruct the engineer and guide the reviewer.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rule
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Review Rules are a different type of rule from Specification Rules: they judge *what* is specified (content and engineering soundness), not just *how well* it is written.

relatedConcepts.name: Standard
relatedConcepts.note: A Specification Review Rule is a type of standard.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Content Review
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Content Review is the process that directly applies Specification Review Rules to evaluate specification content.

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Objective
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Review Rules check whether specified designs address stakeholder Strategic Objectives.

concepts.definition: A **Specification Review Rule** specifies the official known best practices for deriving a systems engineering concept (for example, a design) from other information (such as requirements and known technology). A specification review rule is used both to instruct the engineer in how to carry out a systems engineering process, and then consequently to instruct reviewers on how to evaluate the resulting specification.
concepts.overview: Specification Review Rules extend the SQC framework beyond craftsmanship quality into engineering soundness and content adequacy. While ordinary Specification Rules (*129) ask "Is the specification well written?", Specification Review Rules ask "Is what is specified the right thing?" They encode engineering best practices — covering architecture content, design content, risk coverage, and stakeholder alignment — and serve the dual purpose of guiding engineers as they work and providing an objective checklist for reviewers after the work is done. Like all Specification Rules, a Specification Review Rule is a type of standard. When applied in an SQC process, they extend it into quality assurance territory.

concepts.name: Specification Rule

relatedConcepts.name: Standard
relatedConcepts.note: A Specification Rule is a type of Standard; it should be versioned and maintained with the same rigour.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control (SQC)
relatedConcepts.note: SQC is the process that applies Specification Rules to detect, measure, and classify defects.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Review Rule
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Review Rules are a different type: they judge *what* is specified (content), while Specification Rules judge *how well* it is written.

relatedConcepts.name: Rule
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Rule is a domain-specific specialisation of the general Rule concept.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Defect
relatedConcepts.note: A violation of a Specification Rule is, by definition, a Specification Defect.

relatedConcepts.name: Major Defect
relatedConcepts.note: Many Specification Rules pre-classify their violations as Major Defects (severity code M).

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Issue
relatedConcepts.note: When a checker suspects a rule violation, they raise a Specification Issue; confirmation determines whether it is a Specification Defect.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Level
relatedConcepts.note: Defect counts from Specification Rule violations feed the Specification Quality Level metric.

concepts.definition: A **Specification Rule** focuses on the question: "Is the specification well written?" A set of specification rules states how we should both ensure and check such things as the completeness, unambiguousness, accuracy, and intelligibility of information in a specific type of specification. In particular, a specification rule does not go deeply into an engineering process in the way that a specification review rule does.
concepts.overview: Specification Rules are the atomic quality standards that drive the SQC process. Each rule specifies a testable property that every specification of a given type must satisfy — for example, "all quality requirements must be quantified using a defined scale of measure." When a specification violates a rule, that violation is classified as a Specification Defect. The density of such defects, measured by the Specification Quality Level metric, becomes the objective measure of specification quality. Specification Rules concern *craftsmanship* — the quality of writing — not the engineering soundness or business value of the content. That latter question is the domain of Specification Review Rules (*543), which serve as a complementary and distinct standard layer.

concepts.name: Specification Variable

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Constant
relatedConcepts.note: The direct contrast: a Specification Constant has a stable, non-context-dependent definition; a Specification Variable changes with time or external environment

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Variable
relatedConcepts.note: Scale Variable values vary as a function of time or environment — analogous variation at the measurement level

relatedConcepts.name: Scale Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: Scale Qualifiers define the conditions under which a variable's value applies

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: A Specification Variable is a term within a Specification whose interpretation requires external reference

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage-Term
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Variables are Planguage terms that require a definition lookup to resolve

concepts.definition: A **Specification Variable** is any term in a specification which references another term — whose definition we must look up in order to interpret the specification. The variable's value is not fixed; it can be resolved differently depending on time, context, or an external agreement. For example: `Use [Latest Version] of the Server Software` — where "Latest Version" is a variable that must be defined elsewhere and may resolve differently at different times.
concepts.overview: In Planguage, not all terms in a specification are self-contained. A Specification Variable is a named term whose full meaning is held externally and may change as a function of time, customer agreement, or environmental context. The variable is written in brackets or as a tag in the specification, and its definition must be consulted to determine its current value. This is in contrast to a Specification Constant (*457), which always translates to the same, stable definition — regardless of when or where it is evaluated. Specification Variables make explicit the fact that some parts of a specification are dynamically resolved: they are a transparency mechanism, not a weakness. Without them, hidden dependencies on changing external values would be buried silently in specification text.

concepts.name: Specification Writer

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: The Specification Writer produces and owns the Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Quality-Control
relatedConcepts.note: The SQC process applies rules to the Specification Writer's output

relatedConcepts.name: Checker
relatedConcepts.note: The Checker reviews and quality-controls the Specification Writer's work

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Rule
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Rules define the standards the Specification Writer must meet

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Language
relatedConcepts.note: The Specification Writer uses Planguage as the specification language

relatedConcepts.name: Designer
relatedConcepts.note: The Specification Writer often overlaps with the Designer role in engineering projects

concepts.definition: A **Specification Writer** is the person responsible for articulating, composing, and maintaining a specification — translating stakeholder needs, engineering decisions, and system requirements into formal, written Planguage specifications. Synonyms: Author, spec writer, cognizant engineer.
concepts.overview: The Specification Writer (*004) is the author role in the Planguage process — the person who produces the written specification that communicates system ideas to an intended audience. Tom Gilb's source entry for this concept is notably brief: the concept appears as a bold title with concept number, date, and a synonym line. The brevity reflects that the role itself is conceptually simple — the Specification Writer is whoever is responsible for the written output. In practice, the role carries significant responsibility: the Specification Writer must be familiar with Planguage parameter conventions, understand the intended audience, apply relevant Specification Rules (*129), and produce output that will survive SQC (*051) review by a Checker (*014). In Tom Gilb's engineering context, the term "cognizant engineer" comes from US defence systems engineering practice, where the cognizant engineer is the person who "owns" and is responsible for a given specification or technical document.

concepts.name: Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Writer
relatedConcepts.note: The author role responsible for producing a Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Checker

relatedConcepts.note: Standard is the parent type in the Standards hierarchy; Specification is one of its component types

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Language
relatedConcepts.note: Planguage — the formal language used to write Specifications

relatedConcepts.name: Specify-To
relatedConcepts.note: The act of specifying — what a Specification Writer does to produce a Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Type
relatedConcepts.note: The class/kind of a Specification (Quality Requirement, Design, etc.)

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Variable
relatedConcepts.note: A term in a Specification whose value is context-dependent

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Constant
relatedConcepts.note: A term in a Specification with a stable, non-varying definition

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Element
relatedConcepts.note: An elementary unit of a Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement-Specification
relatedConcepts.note: A Specification sub-type for requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Issue
relatedConcepts.note: An issue raised during Specification review or evaluation

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Content-Review
relatedConcepts.note: A review process targeting the content of a Specification

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Review-Rule
relatedConcepts.note: Rules for reviewing Specification content (vs. form)

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Maturity
relatedConcepts.note: The degree to which a Specification has been completed and refined

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Rule
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Rule as sub-type within the Standards hierarchy diagram

concepts.definition: A **specification** communicates one or more system ideas and/or descriptions to an intended audience. A specification is a formal, written means for communicating information. It can address requirements (what the system must achieve), design ideas (how it will be achieved), constraints, costs, resources, or any other system characteristic. In Planguage, a specification is always structured using defined parameters that make its content unambiguous, measurable, and reviewable.
concepts.overview: Specification (*137) is one of the most fundamental concepts in Planguage — the central artefact of the entire engineering communication system. Every Planguage process produces, refines, or evaluates a Specification. A Specification has a declared type (Quality Requirement, Function, Design, Constraint, etc.), a Specification Writer (*004) who is accountable for its content, and a set of parameters that structure its content in machine- and human-readable form. Specifications sit in the Standards hierarchy (*138) as a peer of Rule, Concept, Policy, and Process — meaning that the standard governs not just what goes into a system, but what goes into the document that describes the system. In Planguage, all of the sub-concepts prefixed "Specification-" (Specification-Element, Specification-Type, Specification-Variable, Specification-Constant, Specification-Language, Specification-Maturity, and more) are aspects or parameters of this central concept.

concepts.name: Specify, To

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: The written output produced when one specifies

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Writer
relatedConcepts.note: The role of the person who specifies

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: Planguage is the formal language used when specifying in written form

relatedConcepts.name: Specification-Language
relatedConcepts.note: The specification language (Planguage) used in formal written specification

relatedConcepts.name: Specify-To
relatedConcepts.note: Note: *239 is a verb concept (the act of specifying), not a noun concept

concepts.definition: To **specify** means to articulate an idea. Specifying can be done in writing or orally, using text and/or symbols. In Planguage, specifying typically refers to the act of producing a formal, structured written specification — but oral specification (e.g., capturing stakeholder needs in an interview) is also a recognised form of specifying.
concepts.overview: "Specify, To" (*239) is the verb concept in the Planguage specification framework — it names the *act* of articulating a system idea, in contrast to Specification (*137), which is the *noun* (the resulting artefact). Tom Gilb's source definition is deliberately broad: to specify is to articulate an idea. This encompasses the full range from informal oral expression to rigorous written Planguage parameter structures. In practice, Planguage is a system of *written* specification — structured, parameterised, audience-declared, and rule-governed — but the concept of specifying is grounded in the more fundamental cognitive act of making an idea explicit. Oral specification is recognised as a valid input mode: stakeholder interviews and verbal discussions can be "specifications" in the sense that they articulate system ideas, even if they must subsequently be formalised in writing. The Specification Writer (*004) is the role that performs the act of specifying in the formal Planguage sense.

concepts.name: Sponsor

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: Sponsor is a type of Stakeholder — the sub-class that actively contributes resources toward system change

relatedConcepts.name: User
relatedConcepts.note: Non-sponsor stakeholder type — uses the system but does not inject resources into the development activity

relatedConcepts.name: Client
relatedConcepts.note: Non-sponsor stakeholder type — sets requirements or commissions the system

relatedConcepts.name: Owner
relatedConcepts.note: Related stakeholder role — typically has authority and may also be a Sponsor

relatedConcepts.name: Decision-Maker
relatedConcepts.note: Related stakeholder role — makes decisions; may or may not be a Sponsor

relatedConcepts.name: Designer
relatedConcepts.note: Internal stakeholder who implements what Sponsors fund

concepts.definition: A **sponsor** is a person or group who has an interest in supporting the achievement of specific system change — and who contributes, or is willing to contribute, resources toward that achievement. Resources can include financial budget, people, materials, reputation, or vocal/political support. A sponsor is a type of Stakeholder (*233).
concepts.overview: The Sponsor (*396) is the stakeholder sub-class defined by active resource contribution. All sponsors are stakeholders, but not all stakeholders are sponsors — the defining criterion is the willingness to invest resources (financial, human, political, or material) in the system change activity. Non-sponsor stakeholders have an interest in the system outcome but do not inject resources into the work. In a Planguage specification, identifying sponsors is important because they are the people who can provide continued or increased support, who can mobilise resources when obstacles arise, and whose expectations the specification must satisfy to maintain project viability. A system can have multiple sponsors at different levels — for example, one sponsor for the overall initiative and a different sponsor for a specific stretch goal. The Sponsor parameter can be attached to any elementary specification or to a set of specifications, making sponsorship explicit and traceable throughout the specification hierarchy.

concepts.name: Stakeholder Level
concepts.definition: Stakeholder Level is the layer where each stakeholder group's needs and values are quantified. Stakeholders consume Products; what they value rolls up to create Business value. Stakeholder requirements are expressed as quantified values on scales.
concepts.overview: **Stakeholder Level** (*802) is part of HumanAgent Gilb's Value Delivery framework, an extension to Tom Gilb's original Planguage. It is not in the source PlanguageGlossary.pdf — it has been authored to capture concepts the framework needs but the PDF did not name.

relatedConcepts.name: Designer

relatedConcepts.name: Client-Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: 2017 classification: stakeholder with needs that a server stakeholder satisfies

relatedConcepts.name: External-Stakeholder

concepts.definition: A **stakeholder** is any person, group, or object that has some direct or indirect interest in a *defined* system. Stakeholders can exercise control over both the immediate system operational characteristics and long-term system lifecycle considerations (such as portability, lifecycle costs, environmental considerations, and decommissioning). The `Stakeholder:` parameter can be used to specify one or more stakeholders explicitly, attached to any elementary specification or set of specifications.
concepts.overview: Stakeholder (*233) is one of the most fundamental role concepts in Planguage — the umbrella concept for all parties (human, organisational, or object-level) with an interest in a defined system. Every requirement, design decision, and quality target exists in relation to stakeholders: they set requirements, evaluate quality, use the system, impose regulatory constraints, and determine whether the system succeeds or fails. Tom Gilb's definition is deliberately broad — it includes not just the obvious parties (customers, users, developers) but any entity with a stake, including objects (e.g., laws, regulatory frameworks). The concept includes a rich sub-classification: by role (User, Client, Sponsor, Designer, Owner, Decision-Maker), by position (Internal, External), and by function in the 2017 framework (Client Stakeholder, Server Stakeholder). The Stakeholder parameter is first-class in Planguage — it can be attached to any specification to make audience and accountability explicit.

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rule
relatedConcepts.note: Rules are one element class that a Standard contains

relatedConcepts.name: Policy

relatedConcepts.name: Process

relatedConcepts.name: Form
relatedConcepts.note: Forms are one element class that a Standard contains

relatedConcepts.note: Templates are one element class that a Standard contains

relatedConcepts.name: Work Process Standard
relatedConcepts.note: Full synonym — Tom assigns both names to concept *138

concepts.definition: A **standard** is an official, written specification that guides a defined group of people in doing a process. It is a best-known practice. Standards include: {rule, policy, process, entry condition, procedure, exit condition, form, template}.
concepts.overview: A Standard in Planguage is the canonical wrapper concept for all forms of process guidance. It codifies best-known practice into a documented, shareable, and enforceable specification that a defined audience can follow. Because it contains rules, policies, processes, forms, and templates, it functions as the top-level container for operational discipline. Tom Gilb defines standards in the Oxford sense: "a thing serving as a recognized example or principle to which others conform or by which the accuracy or quality of others is judged." The concept shares concept number *138 with Work Process Standard, which is a full synonym — not a distinct concept.

concepts.name: Starts

relatedConcepts.name: Ends
relatedConcepts.note: Icon • — the complementary temporal boundary; Starts (*) marks begin, Ends (•) marks completion

relatedConcepts.name: Before
relatedConcepts.note: Icon => — used to express ordering relative to a Starts event

relatedConcepts.name: After
relatedConcepts.note: Icon => — used to express ordering relative to a Starts event

relatedConcepts.name: In Process
relatedConcepts.note: Icon ^ — distinguishes events still in-progress from those that have merely started

concepts.definition: **Starts** indicates the condition where a defined event begins. It marks only the initiation boundary of an event — it says nothing about duration, whether the event is still in progress, or whether it has been completed.
concepts.overview: Starts is a temporal sequence parameter used in Planguage to anchor the beginning moment of an event, distinct from its completion or ongoing state. Its keyed icon is `*` (an explosion symbol), contrasted with `•` (the Ends icon *316) which marks completion. Starts can be combined with Before *312 and After *313 to specify ordering relationships between events: "A before B starts" and "B after C starts" express precise temporal dependencies. The distinction between Starts and In Process *113 (`^`) is critical — `*` means the event has begun, but `^` means it is still underway.

relatedConcepts.name: False

concepts.definition: A **state** is a defined status of a specified system or component. States can vary in operation or during projects. A State parameter documents a basic specification qualifier for planning or design, anchoring a scalar measurement or goal level to a particular operational condition of the system.
concepts.overview: State is a Planguage scalar concept used to qualify measurements and specifications by the condition of the system at the time the measurement applies. The keyed icon `[!]` is derived from `[?]` (a condition being queried) that has been determined (`!` = resolved). Planguage predefines nine State values: On, Off, Undetermined, Undeterminable, Unknown, Unstable, Changing, True, and False. Custom states (e.g., Black, Hot, Closed) may also be defined. State shares concept number *174 with Status — State being the more general concept (a defined system condition), Status being the outcome of an evaluation against a condition. Both are cross-linked bidirectionally.

concepts.name: Statement

relatedConcepts.name: Term
relatedConcepts.note: A Term is a component of expressions and statements

relatedConcepts.name: Expression
relatedConcepts.note: One or more Expressions connected form a Statement

relatedConcepts.name: Definition
relatedConcepts.note: A Definition is a type of Statement that anchors meaning

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: A Specification communicates one or more system ideas and can consist of many Statements

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter
relatedConcepts.note: Parameters are the keyed elements inside a Planguage Statement

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: A Tag opens a Statement by naming the concept being specified

relatedConcepts.name: Keyed Icon
relatedConcepts.note: Keyed Icons are the compressed parameter markers inside Statements

concepts.definition: A **statement** is one or more Planguage expressions connected to form a meaningful and complete specification. Numerous classes of Planguage statement exist, including: Requirement, Design, Plan, Relationship, Note, Parameter, Condition, and Function.
concepts.overview: The Statement is the fundamental syntactic unit of Planguage — the smallest complete communicative act in a specification. Where an Expression *302 is a sub-unit (a single keyed element or phrase), a Statement aggregates one or more expressions into a whole that conveys a complete specification idea. Statements normally begin on a new line and end with a period. They are the building blocks from which a Specification *137 is assembled. Tags *146 name what a statement is about; Parameters *105 supply structured values within it; Keyed Icons *144 compress those parameters into compact notation.

concepts.name: Statistical Process Control

relatedConcepts.name: PDSA Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: Plan-Do-Study-Act Cycle — the iterative improvement cycle that SPC data informs

relatedConcepts.name: Continuous Process Improvement
relatedConcepts.note: SPC is a primary analytical tool within CPI

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: Statistical Quality Control — broader discipline of which SPC is a subset focused on process data

relatedConcepts.name: Special Causes
relatedConcepts.note: SPC distinguishes special causes (individual, assignable) from common causes

relatedConcepts.name: Common Causes
relatedConcepts.note: SPC distinguishes common causes (systemic, organizational) from special causes

concepts.definition: **Statistical Process Control (SPC)** is a method for analysis of statistical process data that aims to improve performance levels and reduce the variability of results. Emphasis is placed on distinguishing between systemic problems — which can only be cured by changing the system — and special causes of results — which need to be addressed at the individual level, not the organizational level.
concepts.overview: SPC was developed by Walter Shewhart and taught by his students W. Edwards Deming and Joseph Juran. It is a core analytical method within Continuous Process Improvement *424, providing the statistical foundation for understanding whether a process is stable or being affected by assignable (special) causes. The critical insight of SPC is that blaming individuals for systemic problems — or trying to fix the system for individual errors — are both mistakes with high cost. SPC uses control charts and statistical tests to classify variation as either Common Causes *020 (inherent system noise) or Special Causes *019 (assignable outliers). The PDSA Cycle *168 and SQC *051 are closely related frameworks.

concepts.definition: **StatusToGoal** is the numeric gap between the current [[Now.513|Status *513]] and the [[Goal.109|Goal *109]] level. It measures how far the current performance is from the committed success target — the threshold at which success is declared and no further improvement priority is given.
concepts.overview: **StatusToGoal** (*700) is the success-distance signal in the [[Tolerable.539|STG (Status · Tolerable · Goal)]] model. When StatusToGoal is **positive**, the project is alive and working toward Goal — this gap is the work remaining. When StatusToGoal **reaches zero**, [[Goal.109|Goal]] has been reached: success is declared for this attribute, and it receives no further improvement priority. Resources are freed for attributes still in the Tolerable or Intolerable Range.

relatedConcepts.name: Status

relatedConcepts.name: Tolerable
relatedConcepts.note: Tolerable *539 is the project-viability threshold — the target point of the StatusToTolerable gap

relatedConcepts.name: StatusToGoal
relatedConcepts.note: StatusToGoal *700 is the companion gap — from Status to the committed success level (Goal)

relatedConcepts.name: Gap
relatedConcepts.note: StatusToTolerable is a specific Gap *359 instance: the unfulfilled distance from Status to the Tolerable threshold

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe Range

concepts.definition: **StatusToTolerable** is the numeric gap between the current [[Now.513|Status *513]] and the [[Tolerable.539|Tolerable *539]] threshold. It measures how far the current performance is from the project-viability line — the boundary below which the whole project fails.
concepts.overview: **StatusToTolerable** (*699) is the most critical priority signal in the [[Tolerable.539|STG (Status · Tolerable · Goal)]] model. A **positive** value means the project is alive — Status is above the Tolerable threshold, and the project has that much margin above the failure line. A **zero or negative** value means the project is in the **Intolerable Range** — Status has fallen below Tolerable — the entire project is failing, not merely one attribute. StatusToTolerable drives the highest-priority improvement work.

concepts.name: Step Element

relatedConcepts.name: Step Task
relatedConcepts.note: A Step Task is one class of Step Element — the process overhead components of an Evo step

relatedConcepts.name: Step Level
relatedConcepts.note: Step Level specifies the intermediate scalar targets for an Evo step; co-cluster with Step Element and Step Task

concepts.definition: A **step element** is any component of a step specification. In practice this can be one or more of: a design idea (including strategies, architecture, solutions); a function requirement; a step specification defined elsewhere but reused in a new qualifier context (e.g., Step-ABC [Utah]); or a step task *347.
concepts.overview: Step Element is the catch-all container concept for any content item that can appear inside an Evo delivery step specification. It is more general than Step Task *347 — a Step Task is a specific sub-class of Step Element covering process overhead activities (planning, measuring, testing, training). A Step Element can also be design ideas, function requirements, or reused step specifications applied in a new context qualifier. Together with Step Task *347 and Step Level *535, Step Element forms the three-concept Step cluster describing what an Evo step contains and how its targets are expressed.

concepts.name: Step Level

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Step Level is a sub-class of Goal level — an intermediate, approximate milestone rather than a primary target

relatedConcepts.name: Path Plan
relatedConcepts.note: Step Levels are used in conjunction with Path Plans to define evolutionary development stages

relatedConcepts.name: Step Element
relatedConcepts.note: Step Level specifies the target for the step; Step Element specifies the content; both are Step cluster concepts

relatedConcepts.name: Step Task
relatedConcepts.note: Step Task is the process overhead within a step; Step Level defines what the step is trying to achieve; both are Step cluster concepts

concepts.definition: A **step level** specification is a sub-class of a Goal level. A Step Level is intended for specification of intermediate scalar levels of both performance and resources, where these levels are not primary product or system targets in themselves — they are approximate plans for evolutionary steps or other increments of project or system maintenance plans.
concepts.overview: Step Level is an experimental Planguage concept (explicitly flagged by Tom Gilb as not included in the Competitive Engineering book) that provides a way to specify intermediary milestone targets during evolutionary development. Unlike a Goal *109 — which is a primary, final target — a Step Level is deliberately provisional. It motivates engineers to make incremental progress and provides feedback when progress falls short, while emphasizing that these are staging posts, not destinations. Step Level pairs with Path Plan *534, which describes the overall evolutionary trajectory, and sits in the Step cluster alongside Step Element *409 and Step Task *347.

concepts.name: Step Task

relatedConcepts.name: Step Element
relatedConcepts.note: Step Task is a sub-class of Step Element — the process overhead category of step content

relatedConcepts.name: Step Level
relatedConcepts.note: Step Level specifies the scalar targets for the step; Step Task specifies the process activities to achieve them; both are Step cluster concepts

concepts.definition: A **step task** is any component of an Evo delivery step that has to be carried out in order to deliver the planned impact, but is not itself a specific design idea or function (step content) to be delivered to the host system. Step tasks are the process overhead components of a delivery cycle.
concepts.overview: Step Task is a sub-class of Step Element *409 covering the process overhead activities — not the deliverable content — of an Evo step. While design ideas and function requirements are what gets delivered into the host system, Step Tasks are everything else required to make that delivery happen: planning, measuring, getting approval, training, quality control, and testing. Tom Gilb uses the metaphor of a cook: purchasing, measuring, heating, mixing, tasting, and serving are all step tasks — they are not the food (the design/function content) but they are essential to getting it to the table. Together with Step Element *409 and Step Level *535, Step Task forms the three-concept Step cluster.

concepts.name: Story: Stakeholder Story

relatedConcepts.name: Vision
relatedConcepts.note: Stories are narratively related to Vision — Vision *422 is the high-level ambition; a Story is a specific stakeholder articulation of a piece of that vision

relatedConcepts.name: Ambition
relatedConcepts.note: Ambition *423 is the 'management BS level'; Stories are more concrete than Ambition but still informal compared to a full Planguage requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: Every Story must contain at least one identified Stakeholder

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: A Story is a high-level informal Requirement — the starting point for a proper formal requirement specification

relatedConcepts.name: Design Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: Solution Stories express a desired technology or solution — analogous to Design Constraint *181 (note: Tom's source text cites '*523' for Design Constraint, which appears to be a number drift; the correct file is Design-Constraint.181.md)

concepts.definition: A **story** (§) is a very high-level definition of a requirement, containing just enough information so that: it can be made more structured and better clarified as a proper formal requirement if necessary; it enables a rough understanding of expected value, stakeholders involved, and costs involved; and it contains at minimum some notion of an interested stakeholder, some notion of a requirement of any type, and some notion of "why" — justification, purpose, expectation, or knock-on result.
concepts.overview: Story in Planguage is Tom Gilb's bridge between informal agile practice and formal specification. A Story is explicitly positioned as a starting point — not a destination. It is the minimum viable requirement statement: one stakeholder, one requirement hint, one "why." The keyed icon § (section sign, also the "SS" of Stakeholder Story) marks a Story as a deliberate new thought in a specification text. Tom classifies four sub-types: User Story (identical to Scrum/Cohn), Stakeholder Story (broadens to any stakeholder class), Value Story (introduces a quantified variable), and Solution Story (a technology preference analogous to Design Constraint *181). The purpose is to capture informal intent before it evaporates — then to clarify it into formal Planguage requirements for estimation and delivery.

concepts.name: Strategic Constraints

relatedConcepts.name: Fundamental Constraints
relatedConcepts.note: constraints imposed externally at the fundamental level; Strategic Constraints are self-imposed at our own level

relatedConcepts.name: Means Constraints
relatedConcepts.note: constraints imposed at the means/implementation level; Strategic Constraints are at the strategic level

relatedConcepts.name: Strategy
relatedConcepts.note: strategies must operate within strategic constraints

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Management Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: the Strategic Management Cycle enforces and monitors strategic constraints

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Objective
relatedConcepts.note: strategic constraints and strategic objectives together define the strategic frame

concepts.definition: **Strategic Constraints** are constraints we have imposed at our own level, over which we have control.
concepts.overview: Strategic Constraints represent the self-imposed boundaries a team or organization sets at its own strategic level — in contrast to fundamental constraints (externally imposed laws and physics) and means constraints (implementation-level rules). Because strategic constraints are self-imposed, they can in principle be changed by the decision-makers at that level, making them different in kind from the constraints handed down from above. Together with strategic objectives, they define the decision space within which strategies are designed and evaluated. Understanding the level at which a constraint sits is essential: misclassifying a self-imposed policy as a fundamental law prevents the organization from questioning assumptions that are actually within its control.

concepts.name: Strategic Management Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Result Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: the Strategic Management Cycle is the 'head' component of the Result Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Objective
relatedConcepts.note: the Strategic Management Cycle approves changes against strategic objectives

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Constraints
relatedConcepts.note: the Strategic Management Cycle filters proposals against strategic constraints

relatedConcepts.name: Strategy
relatedConcepts.note: proposed strategies are reviewed and approved within the Strategic Management Cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Evo
relatedConcepts.note: the Strategic Management Cycle is the controlling head of the Evo result cycle

concepts.definition: A **strategic management cycle** is a cycle within a result cycle concerned with controlling and monitoring the overall change process. It approves proposed changes against strategic objectives and adopted high-level strategies, co-ordinates with other programs and projects, acquires development budgets, analyzes feedback measurements, and decides the next step.
concepts.overview: The Strategic Management Cycle is the governance "head" of the Evo result cycle — the decision-making wrapper that controls what work is approved, resourced, and sequenced. Where the "body" of Evo (development, production, and delivery cycles) executes incremental change, the Strategic Management Cycle ensures that each step remains aligned with the organization's strategic objectives and constraints. It closes the feedback loop by analysing measurement data from completed steps and adjusting direction accordingly. This concept reflects Tom Gilb's insistence that evolutionary development cannot be ad hoc: without a competent strategic management function, individual increments may succeed locally while failing to deliver systemic value.

concepts.name: Strategic Objective

relatedConcepts.name: Fundamental Objective
relatedConcepts.note: strategic objectives support fundamental objectives — they are the operational layer beneath the highest-level goals

relatedConcepts.name: Means Objective
relatedConcepts.note: means objectives support strategic objectives — they are at the implementation layer

relatedConcepts.name: MOE
relatedConcepts.note: Measure of Effectiveness — used to quantify progress toward strategic objectives

relatedConcepts.name: MOP
relatedConcepts.note: Measure of Performance — operational metric tied to strategic objective achievement

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Constraints
relatedConcepts.note: strategic constraints and strategic objectives together define the strategic decision frame

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Management Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: the Strategic Management Cycle approves changes against strategic objectives

relatedConcepts.name: Strategy
relatedConcepts.note: strategies are selected to impact strategic objectives

concepts.definition: **Strategic Objectives** are the objectives which are our main responsibility. They support fundamental objectives and are themselves supported by means objectives.
concepts.overview: The Strategic Objective is the middle tier of Tom Gilb's three-level objectives hierarchy: above it sit Fundamental Objectives (*229) — the highest-level goals of stakeholders and society; below it sit Means Objectives (*215) — the operational outputs of specific strategies. Strategic objectives are the "main responsibility" of the team or organization: the set of measurable outcomes they are directly accountable for delivering. They are defined with sufficient precision to be measurable (via MOE and MOP), to be linked to strategies that will drive them, and to be reviewed within the Strategic Management Cycle. This middle tier prevents the common failure of tracking only process metrics (means) while losing sight of real stakeholder value (fundamental).

concepts.name: Strategy

relatedConcepts.name: Solution
relatedConcepts.note: polysemy — *047 is shared; Solution is the evaluated form of a design idea / strategy

relatedConcepts.name: Design Ideas
relatedConcepts.note: polysemy — *047 is shared; engineering-culture synonym

relatedConcepts.name: Means Concept
relatedConcepts.note: polysemy — *047 is shared; older Planguage synonym for any means toward an objective

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: synonym — Strategy is the broader management term; Architecture is the engineering equivalent

relatedConcepts.name: Process Improvement Suggestion
relatedConcepts.note: synonym — a PIS is a strategy specifically targeted at improving a process

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Objective
relatedConcepts.note: a strategy is selected to impact strategic objectives

relatedConcepts.name: Strategic Constraints
relatedConcepts.note: strategies must operate within self-imposed strategic constraints

concepts.definition: A **strategy** is any 'means' specified with the intent to impact defined objectives.
concepts.overview: A strategy is the fundamental Planguage answer to "how do we get there?" — any specified means that is intended to move one or more measurable attributes toward their targets. Tom Gilb deliberately chose a culturally neutral vocabulary: 'strategy' bridges the management world and the engineering world, sitting alongside 'design idea', 'means concept', and 'solution' as synonyms under concept number *047. The polysemy is intentional — the same idea carries different cultural labels, and Planguage refuses to privilege any one discipline's terminology. A strategy is not a vague aspiration; it must be specified well enough that its expected impact on quantified objectives can be evaluated, typically via a Value Decision Table (VDT).

concepts.name: Stretch

relatedConcepts.name: Need
relatedConcepts.note: a Need drives the requirement; Stretch is a target level defined above the committed Goal

relatedConcepts.name: Target
relatedConcepts.note: Stretch is a type of Target — the ambitious tier above Budget and Goal, below Wish

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Goal is the committed target; Stretch is set above Goal as a more ambitious aspiration

relatedConcepts.name: Budget
relatedConcepts.note: Budget is the minimum acceptable level; Stretch is far above it

relatedConcepts.name: Wish
relatedConcepts.note: Wish is the ultimate ideal; Stretch is below Wish but above Goal

relatedConcepts.name: Resource Target
relatedConcepts.note: Resource Targets can also have Stretch levels for ambitious resource efficiency goals

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Target
relatedConcepts.note: Stretch is a Performance Target type — specifically the ambitious tier

concepts.definition: A **Stretch** parameter is used to define a somewhat more ambitious target level than the committed Goal or Budget levels.
concepts.overview: Stretch is a named target level in the Planguage scalar target hierarchy, positioned above the committed Goal and Budget but below the idealistic Wish. Where the Goal represents the committed minimum for project success, a Stretch represents what the team could achieve with exceptional performance — an aspirational but realistic target that motivates beyond the baseline. The concept originated in practice at Nokia (Dallas, 1999) and was later adopted with the label "Outstanding" by Intel (2003). In a full Planguage scalar target specification, Stretch appears alongside Budget, Goal, Wish, and Worst Case to create a complete picture of acceptable, desirable, and aspirational performance across the entire value range.

concepts.name: Structure

relatedConcepts.name: Component
relatedConcepts.note: a structure is the observable implementation of a system component — Component is what; Structure is how it is built

relatedConcepts.name: Design
