relatedConcepts.note: structure is the observable realisation of a design idea — Design is the intent; Structure is the built result

relatedConcepts.name: Impact
relatedConcepts.note: structure can be evaluated for its impact on system attributes

concepts.definition: A **structure** is the observable implementation of a system component — the way it is built.
concepts.overview: Structure is a Planguage logical structure parameter that describes the concrete, observable form that a system component takes when implemented. It bridges the design world (what we intend) and the physical or logical reality (what we actually built). In a Planguage specification, Structure is used to document the architectural decisions that give a system its observable shape: the layering of components, the topology of connections, the decomposition into subcomponents. Because Structure is observable, it can be tested and measured — making it a more concrete object of specification than an abstract design idea. Structure is to a component what anatomy is to an organism: the actual physical arrangement that determines how it works.

concepts.name: Study [PDSA]

relatedConcepts.name: PDSA Cycle
relatedConcepts.note: Study is the third phase of the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Plan
relatedConcepts.note: Plan is the first PDSA phase; Study analyses what Plan predicted vs. what Do delivered

relatedConcepts.name: Do
relatedConcepts.note: Do is the second phase; Study observes and gathers data on the results of Do

relatedConcepts.name: Act
relatedConcepts.note: Act is the fourth phase; it uses Study findings to decide the next action

relatedConcepts.name: Evo
relatedConcepts.note: PDSA underpins the Evo evolutionary process — Study is the feedback analysis step

relatedConcepts.name: SPC
relatedConcepts.note: Statistical Process Control is the technical discipline behind the Study phase measurement

concepts.definition: **Study [PDSA]** is the third phase of the Plan-Do-Study-Act Cycle (*168). The Study phase observes and gathers data concerning the results of the Do phase.
concepts.overview: Study is where learning happens in the PDSA cycle. After Plan (*169) has articulated a hypothesis and defined the experiment, and Do (*170) has executed the change on a small scale, Study steps back from action and asks: what actually happened? It collects measurements, compares actuals to predictions, and surfaces the gap between what was expected and what was observed. In Planguage and Evo, Study is the feedback analysis step that closes the loop — it is the source of the empirical information the Act phase uses to decide whether to adopt, adapt, or abandon the change. Without rigorous Study, the cycle collapses into repeated doing without learning; Study is what makes PDSA evolutionary rather than merely iterative.

concepts.name: Sub-Process

relatedConcepts.name: Supra-Process
relatedConcepts.note: a sub-process is contained within a supra-process — the two are inverses in the process hierarchy

relatedConcepts.name: Process
relatedConcepts.note: a sub-process is a process at a lower level of decomposition within a containing supra-process

concepts.definition: A **sub-process** is a process contained in a supra-process.
concepts.overview: A sub-process is the lower component in a two-level process decomposition: it is a fully defined process that sits within — and is directed by — a supra-process (*257). The relationship is hierarchical and containment-based: the supra-process sets the context, sequence, and purpose; the sub-process carries out a bounded portion of the supra-process's work. This decomposition pattern is fundamental to Planguage's process modelling: complex processes are made tractable by identifying their constituent sub-processes, assigning each a defined scope, and specifying each independently. Any sub-process may itself be a supra-process relative to finer-grained processes below it, making the hierarchy as deep as the system requires.

concepts.name: Subjective

relatedConcepts.name: Objective [Adjective]
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — Objective describes independence from individual judgment; Subjective describes dependence on it

relatedConcepts.name: Subjectivity
relatedConcepts.note: Subjectivity is the noun form; Subjective is the adjective; together they form the subjective pole of the objectivity spectrum

relatedConcepts.name: Objectivity
relatedConcepts.note: Objectivity is the opposite pole; all measurement exists on a spectrum between full subjectivity and full objectivity

concepts.definition: **Subjective**: dependent on defined stakeholder value judgment. Not 'Objective'.
concepts.overview: In Planguage, *subjective* is a characterisation applied to a measurement, specification element, or judgment that depends on the personal opinion, taste, cultural context, or value system of a defined stakeholder — rather than on an observer-independent standard. Subjectivity is not inherently bad: stakeholder value is by definition subjective, and making that value explicit, attributed, and defined is better than pretending it does not exist. What Planguage resists is *hidden* subjectivity — specifications that appear objective while resting on unexamined personal judgments. The discipline is to name the stakeholder whose judgment applies, define the criteria as precisely as possible, and acknowledge the degree of subjectivity explicitly so that readers can calibrate their confidence in the specification.

concepts.name: Subjectivity

relatedConcepts.name: Subjective
relatedConcepts.note: Subjective is the adjective form; Subjectivity is the noun — the underlying system property

relatedConcepts.name: Objectivity
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — Objectivity is the complementary system property at the opposite end of the spectrum

relatedConcepts.name: Objective [Adjective]
relatedConcepts.note: Objective (adjective) is the antonym of Subjective; observer-independent vs. observer-dependent

concepts.definition: **Subjectivity** is that which is predominantly a matter of personal opinion, or taste, or state of mind.
concepts.overview: Subjectivity (*387) is the system property that characterises data, judgments, or specifications whose content is shaped by individual or cultural perspective rather than by observer-independent fact. As a system property, Subjectivity is not a bug to be eliminated but a reality to be acknowledged and managed. Planguage engineering does not pretend that all relevant information can be made fully objective; stakeholder value, aesthetic judgment, and contextual expertise are inherently subjective. The discipline is to distinguish where subjectivity is unavoidable from where it is merely convenient, to attribute subjective judgments to named stakeholders, and to reduce hidden subjectivity through explicit scales, meters, and sources. For the full treatment of the subjective/objective spectrum, see *657 Subjective and *388 Objectivity.

concepts.name: Subset

relatedConcepts.name: Consists Of
relatedConcepts.note: Consists Of defines what a whole is made of; Subset names one of those parts

relatedConcepts.name: Component
relatedConcepts.note: A Component is a specific kind of Subset within a system

relatedConcepts.name: Includes
relatedConcepts.note: Includes is the verb form — a thing Includes its Subsets

concepts.definition: A **Subset** is a specified, or defined, part of a specified, or defined, larger whole.
concepts.overview: In Planguage, a Subset is a named partition of a larger entity — a system, a requirement set, a stakeholder group, or any defined collection. Specifying a Subset is useful when you need to apply requirements, measures, or constraints to only a portion of a whole, rather than the entirety. Subsets are typically referenced within Consists Of or Includes relationships to trace how a whole breaks into its parts. Precision in defining a Subset prevents scope ambiguity: every member of the Subset must be identifiable, and the Subset boundary must be unambiguous.

concepts.name: Success Range

relatedConcepts.name: Failure Range
relatedConcepts.note: The region below the Fail level; the opposite of Success Range

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe Range
relatedConcepts.note: The region below Catastrophe-Range-Start; worse than Failure Range

relatedConcepts.name: Acceptable Range
relatedConcepts.note: The band between Fail and Goal; adjacent to but below Success Range

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: The minimum tolerable boundary; Success Range lies well above Survival

relatedConcepts.name: Landing Zone
relatedConcepts.note: The preferred sub-region within the Success Range

relatedConcepts.name: Survival Range
relatedConcepts.note: The band between Survival and Fail; adjacent to but below Acceptable Range

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: General concept of a bounded interval on a scale

relatedConcepts.name: Tolerable
relatedConcepts.note: Tolerable is the lower STG threshold (project-viability); Success Range begins at Goal — above the Tolerable Range

relatedConcepts.name: Status
relatedConcepts.note: Status in the Success Range means success is declared and no further improvement priority is given to this attribute

relatedConcepts.name: StatusToGoal
relatedConcepts.note: StatusToGoal = 0 when Status reaches Goal, placing the attribute in the Success Range

concepts.definition: A **Success Range** is meeting the Goal level or better — any measured value at or above the Goal level on a scalar performance scale.
concepts.overview: Planguage structures scalar targets as a layered set of ranges arranged along a measurement scale, each range carrying a different consequence. The Success Range is the most desirable tier: a measured result landing here means the Goal has been achieved or exceeded. Below the Success Range lies the Acceptable Range (*545), then the Survival Range (*585), the Failure Range (*546), and finally the Catastrophe Range (*603). The Success Range has no upper bound unless a specific ceiling is defined — more is simply more successful. Within the Success Range, the Landing Zone (*605) can identify a particularly preferred sub-region. Knowing the Success Range is essential when evaluating whether an Evo step or a design has truly met its objective.

concepts.name: Sum for Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Percentage Impact
relatedConcepts.note: Sum for Requirement aggregates the individual Percentage Impacts across designs

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Factor
relatedConcepts.note: Safety Factor is applied against the Sum for Requirement to determine headroom

relatedConcepts.name: Safety Deviation
relatedConcepts.note: Safety Deviation is derived from the Safety Factor and the Sum for Requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Sum of Benefits
relatedConcepts.note: Sum of Benefits is the vertical sum of performance impacts; Sum for Requirement is the horizontal sum for a given requirement

relatedConcepts.name: Sum of Costs
relatedConcepts.note: Sum of Costs aggregates resource impacts in the same table structure

concepts.definition: A **Sum for Requirement** is, for a given set of design ideas, the sum of their estimated or measured percentage impacts on a single performance or resource attribute.
concepts.overview: In an Impact Estimation table, each column represents a design idea and each row represents a requirement (performance or resource attribute). The Sum for Requirement is the horizontal aggregation across design columns for one specific requirement row. It answers: "How much total percentage improvement do all the selected designs together deliver for this one requirement?" This makes the Sum for Requirement the per-requirement view of combined design impact, complementing the Sum of Benefits (*008), which is the per-design vertical sum across requirements. Safety Factors (*131) and Safety Deviations (*405) are then applied to the Sum for Requirement to produce risk-adjusted estimates.

concepts.name: Sum of Costs

relatedConcepts.name: Sum of Benefits
relatedConcepts.note: Sum of Benefits is the complementary vertical sum for performance attributes; Sum of Costs is the denominator in the Performance to Cost Ratio when Sum of Benefits is the numerator

relatedConcepts.name: Sum of Performance
relatedConcepts.note: Sum of Performance is the polysemous synonym of Sum of Benefits; both serve as the performance numerator against which Sum of Costs is divided

relatedConcepts.name: Performance to Cost Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: Derived by dividing Sum of Performance by Sum of Costs for the same design idea

relatedConcepts.name: Value to Cost Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: A related ratio concept that compares value (often stakeholder benefit) against cost

relatedConcepts.name: Cost
relatedConcepts.note: The underlying concept of cost / resource consumption that Sum of Costs aggregates

relatedConcepts.name: Percentage Impact
relatedConcepts.note: The individual resource-impact cells that are vertically summed to produce Sum of Costs

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation
relatedConcepts.note: The method within which Sum of Costs is computed

concepts.definition: Within an Impact Estimation table, for a specific design idea (or set of design ideas or Evo step), the **Sum of Costs** is the vertical sum of the percentage impacts of selected scalar resource attributes.
concepts.overview: The Impact Estimation table organises design ideas as columns and both performance and resource requirements as rows. The Sum of Costs is the vertical column total across only the resource attribute rows for a given design idea — the arithmetic sum of all percentage impacts on cost-related attributes such as development time, hardware expenditure, or operational cost. It is the cost-side counterpart to the Sum of Benefits / Sum of Performance (*008), which totals the performance-side impacts. Together, these two column sums form the inputs to the Performance to Cost Ratio (*010): a high ratio indicates a cost-efficient design. The Value to Cost Ratio (*635) extends this to a value-broader comparison. The synonym "Resource Impact" underscores that "costs" in this context means resource consumption, not financial cost alone.

concepts.name: Sum of Performance

relatedConcepts.name: Sum of Benefits
relatedConcepts.note: Polysemous twin — shares concept number *008; both refer to the vertical sum of performance impacts in an Impact Estimation table; the terms are used interchangeably in Planguage practice

relatedConcepts.name: Sum of Costs
relatedConcepts.note: Sum of Costs is the complementary vertical sum for resource attributes; together with Sum of Performance it forms the basis of the Performance to Cost Ratio

relatedConcepts.name: Performance to Cost Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: Derived by comparing Sum of Performance to Sum of Costs for the same design idea

relatedConcepts.name: Sum for Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: Sum for Requirement is the horizontal aggregation across designs for one requirement; Sum of Performance is the vertical aggregation across requirements for one design

relatedConcepts.name: Percentage Impact
relatedConcepts.note: The individual cells that are vertically summed to produce Sum of Performance

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation
relatedConcepts.note: The method within which Sum of Performance is computed

concepts.definition: Within an Impact Estimation table, the **Sum of Performance** is the total quantitative impact on the specified performance targets made by a specific design idea (or set of design ideas or Evo step).
concepts.overview: The Impact Estimation table organises design ideas as columns and performance requirements as rows. The Sum of Performance is the vertical column total for a given design idea — the arithmetic sum of all its individual Percentage Impacts (*306) across every performance attribute. It measures how much collective performance improvement a design idea delivers across the system's goals. The Sum of Performance is a canonical synonym of Sum of Benefits (*008) — both share concept number *008 and both refer to the same calculation. The distinction, where one is made, is terminological rather than conceptual: "performance" emphasises the type of attribute being summed; "benefits" emphasises the positive outcome for stakeholders. Together with the Sum of Costs (*128), the Sum of Performance feeds the Performance to Cost Ratio (*010), enabling rational ranking of design alternatives.

concepts.name: Supplementary Designs

relatedConcepts.name: Alternative Designs
relatedConcepts.note: Alternative Designs are a different kind of design set — options to choose between; Supplementary Designs are additions needed to close a gap toward targets

relatedConcepts.name: Specific Design
relatedConcepts.note: A Supplementary Design is itself a Specific Design — it is additional rather than alternative

relatedConcepts.name: Performance Design
relatedConcepts.note: A Supplementary Design is often added specifically to boost a Performance Design toward its Goal level

relatedConcepts.name: Function Design
relatedConcepts.note: A Supplementary Design may supplement a Function Design to meet functional requirements

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation
relatedConcepts.note: Impact Estimation reveals the gap that motivates the addition of Supplementary Designs

concepts.definition: **Supplementary Designs** are needed to move the set of designs towards the design Goal levels, other target levels, or towards meeting other requirements (constraints, functions).
concepts.overview: In Planguage Evo practice, the current set of selected designs may not be sufficient to reach all performance Goals, Constraints, or functional requirements. Supplementary Designs are additional design ideas proposed specifically to close the remaining gap — they are not alternatives to what is already selected, but genuine additions. They arise when Impact Estimation (*283) shows that the existing design set's Sum of Benefits (*008) is insufficient to reach a target level for a given requirement. Supplementary Designs must themselves be evaluated, estimated, and ranked like any other design idea; they are not automatic inclusions simply because a gap exists. The concept is closely paired with Alternative Designs (*588), which addresses the selection among competing options rather than the supplementation of an insufficient set.

concepts.name: Support System

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: A Support System's performance impacts a defined Stakeholder environment

relatedConcepts.name: Measure of Effectiveness
relatedConcepts.note: Measure of Effectiveness evaluates whether the Support System achieves its intended stakeholder benefit

relatedConcepts.name: Measure of Performance
relatedConcepts.note: Measure of Performance quantifies the system-level attributes of the Support System

relatedConcepts.name: Benefit
relatedConcepts.note: The Support System is intended to contribute to the stakeholder Benefit level

relatedConcepts.name: Performance
relatedConcepts.note: The Support System has Performance levels that are the mechanism of its contribution

relatedConcepts.name: Supports
relatedConcepts.note: Supports (*415) is the relationship parameter that names what the Support System supports

relatedConcepts.name: System
relatedConcepts.note: A Support System is a specialised kind of System focused on stakeholder impact

relatedConcepts.name: Environment System
relatedConcepts.note: The environment in which the Stakeholder operates; the Support System impacts this environment

concepts.definition: A **Support System** is any system that has performance levels that impact a defined stakeholder environment. A Support System is intended to contribute to the stakeholder benefit level.
concepts.overview: In Planguage, a Support System is defined by its relationship to a Stakeholder (*233) and that stakeholder's environment. Rather than specifying a system by its internal structure, the Support System concept specifies it by its external impact: does it have measurable performance levels that affect what the stakeholder experiences? If so, it qualifies as a Support System. The intent is always to contribute positively to the stakeholder's Benefit (*009) level — the support system exists for the benefit of stakeholders. This framing is important for requirements engineering: it shifts focus from what a system does internally to what it delivers outwardly to those who depend on it. The related concept Supports (*415) names the directional relationship; Measure of Effectiveness (*486) evaluates whether the support has been achieved; Measure of Performance (*482) quantifies the system's internal performance levels.

concepts.name: Supported By

relatedConcepts.name: Supports
relatedConcepts.note: Supports is the directional inverse — where Supported By lists what contributes to a requirement, Supports names what an attribute is intended to support

relatedConcepts.name: Impacts
relatedConcepts.note: Impacts is a broader relationship; Supported By is the positive-contribution specialisation

relatedConcepts.name: Impacted By
relatedConcepts.note: Impacted By is the general inverse of Impacts; Supported By is the positive-contribution inverse of Supports

relatedConcepts.name: Support System
relatedConcepts.note: A Support System is the entity whose attributes appear in the Supported By list

concepts.definition: **Supported By** is used to list the tags of any and all specifications that contribute usefully to the accomplishment of a defined requirement.
concepts.overview: Planguage provides paired directional relationship parameters for expressing mutual contributions between specifications. Supported By (*414) is attached to a requirement (or any specification) and lists the tags of other specifications — designs, sub-requirements, systems, or attributes — that actively contribute to its accomplishment. It is the receiving end of the relationship: the requirement "looks back" and names everything that helps it. The complementary parameter Supports (*415) is the contributing end: an attribute "looks forward" and names what it is intended to support. Together they form a bidirectional traceability mechanism that allows readers to navigate from a requirement to its supporting specifications and vice versa. The parameter Impacted By (*412) is a more general cousin that covers any influence, positive or negative; Supported By implies positive, useful contribution.

concepts.name: Supports

relatedConcepts.name: Supported By
relatedConcepts.note: Supported By is the directional inverse — where Supports names what an attribute is intended to support, Supported By lists from the requirement's perspective what contributes to it

relatedConcepts.name: Impacts
relatedConcepts.note: Impacts is a broader directional relationship; Supports is the positive-contribution specialisation

relatedConcepts.name: Support System
relatedConcepts.note: A Support System is defined by having attributes that support stakeholder requirements; Supports is the keyword that makes this explicit

relatedConcepts.name: Impacted By
relatedConcepts.note: Impacted By is the general inbound form; Supported By (*414) is its positive-contribution specialisation, paired with Supports

concepts.definition: **Supports** is used to indicate what an attribute is mainly intended to support.
concepts.overview: Planguage provides paired directional relationship parameters for expressing mutual contributions between specifications. Supports (*415) is attached to an attribute — a design, a sub-requirement, a system parameter — and names the tag of the requirement or goal it is primarily intended to help accomplish. It is the contributing end of the relationship: the attribute "looks forward" and declares its intended beneficiary. The complementary parameter Supported By (*414) is the receiving end: a requirement "looks back" and lists everything that helps it. Together, Supports and Supported By form a bidirectional traceability pair that allows navigation from any specification in both directions. The keyed icon `>>` signals a forward-pointing contribution. The more general relationship Impacts (*334) covers any direction of influence; Supports is the positive, intended-contribution specialisation.

concepts.name: Supra-process

relatedConcepts.name: Supra
relatedConcepts.note: prefix that forms 'Supra-process' — any component type with sub-components

concepts.definition: A process that contains other defined processes.
concepts.overview: A **Supra-process** (*257) is any lifecycle process that acts as a container for one or more defined sub-processes. The prefix *Supra-* (see [[Supra.264]]) signals upward containment: the Supra-process is the parent from which child processes inherit scope and sequencing context. Recognising which process is the Supra-process clarifies authority and decomposition boundaries — something sub-processes cannot define for themselves. The concept is the process-level application of the general Supra relationship that applies to any component type in Planguage.

concepts.name: Supra

relatedConcepts.name: Parent
relatedConcepts.note: Supra is the upward-facing side of a Parent/Kid relationship

relatedConcepts.name: Kid
relatedConcepts.note: the sub-component produced when Supra- is applied

relatedConcepts.name: Subset
relatedConcepts.note: complementary containment relationship for subsets rather than components

relatedConcepts.name: Supra-process
relatedConcepts.note: process-level application of the Supra prefix

concepts.definition: 'Supra-' is a prefix, which can be attached to any component type that has its own sub-components (kids).
concepts.overview: **Supra** (*264) is a Planguage prefix that designates any component type as a container for sub-components (kids). Attaching 'Supra-' to a component type name signals that the named entity has one or more children that inherit its scope and operate under its authority. Supra is the upward-facing half of the parent/kid relationship — you can think of it as a formal way of saying "this thing owns that thing." The concept is recursive: a Supra-component can itself be a kid of a still-higher Supra. The prefix is defined generically so it applies equally to processes, requirements, functions, or any other named Planguage component.

concepts.name: Survival Range

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe Range
relatedConcepts.note: the range beyond Survival Range where system death occurs

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: the state that Survival Range defines and protects

relatedConcepts.name: Limit
relatedConcepts.note: Survival Range is implemented as a pair of scalar Limits

concepts.definition: A Survival Range is the numeric range of a scalar attribute that indicates survival of the system, with respect to that attribute alone.
concepts.overview: A **Survival Range** (*585) is the bounded numeric interval of a scalar attribute within which a system can continue to exist. Values inside the range represent [[Survival.440|Survival]]; values outside represent system death via [[Catastrophe-Range.603|Catastrophe Range]]. The "with respect to that attribute alone" qualifier is critical: each Survival Range is defined per attribute, and overall system survival requires *all* monitored attributes to remain within their respective ranges simultaneously. Survival Range is expressed using the keyed-icon notation `[ ]` at both ends and gives engineers a precise, quantified boundary at which an emergency response or shutdown must trigger.

concepts.name: Survival

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: Fail is the minimum acceptable performance level; Survival is the absolute floor below which the system cannot exist

relatedConcepts.name: Limit
relatedConcepts.note: Survival is implemented as a pair of scalar Limits

relatedConcepts.name: Catastrophe
relatedConcepts.note: breaching Survival produces a Catastrophe — system death

relatedConcepts.name: Survival Range
relatedConcepts.note: the numeric interval that defines whether the system is in a Survival state

concepts.definition: Survival is a state where the system can exist. Outside the survival range is a 'dead' system caused by a specific attribute level being outside the survival range.
concepts.overview: **Survival** (*440) is the state in which a system is capable of existing — meaning all monitored scalar attributes remain within their respective [[Survival-Range.585|Survival Ranges]]. When any single attribute crosses its survival limit, the system is declared "dead" with respect to that attribute: not degraded, not impaired, but non-existent in any functional sense. Survival is the hardest of all Planguage performance constraints, harder than [[Fail.098b]] (minimum acceptable performance) and distinguishable from Fail precisely because crossing a Survival limit is not merely unacceptable — it is catastrophic. The keyed icon `[ ]` wraps an attribute's scale to mark the two survival limits.

concepts.name: Symbol

relatedConcepts.name: Icon
relatedConcepts.note: a Symbol with a primarily pictorial convention

relatedConcepts.name: Drawn Icon
relatedConcepts.note: an Icon realised as a drawn or illustrated mark

relatedConcepts.name: Keyed Icon
relatedConcepts.note: an Icon realised as typed characters — Planguage's primary form

relatedConcepts.name: Sign
relatedConcepts.note: broader category; includes Symbols but also natural signs that need no convention

relatedConcepts.name: Symbology
relatedConcepts.note: a defined collection (system) of Symbols

relatedConcepts.name: Diagram
relatedConcepts.note: a composition of Symbols conveying structure

relatedConcepts.name: Pattern
relatedConcepts.note: a recurring Symbol or arrangement

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage Concept
relatedConcepts.note: Symbols are how Planguage Concepts are visually expressed

concepts.definition: A **Symbol** is any defined representation of information, concrete realities, or abstractions such as emotion.
concepts.overview: A **Symbol** (*162) is any defined representation of information, a concrete reality, or an abstraction — where "defined" is the operative word. Without a shared convention, a mark is just a mark; the convention is what makes it a Symbol. In Planguage, Symbols appear as [[Keyed-Icon.144|Keyed Icons]] (e.g., `>` for Goal, `[ ]` for Survival), in [[Diagram.228|Diagrams]], and are organised into [[Symbology.209|Symbologies]]. A Symbol is distinct from a [[Sign.195b|Sign]]: a Sign can arise naturally (smoke signals fire without any agreement), whereas a Symbol always requires a deliberately defined convention. Symbols are atomic units that compose into Symbologies, Diagrams, and Patterns.

concepts.name: Symbology

relatedConcepts.name: Icons
relatedConcepts.note: Icons are key members of a Planguage Symbology

relatedConcepts.name: Keyed Icons
relatedConcepts.note: Keyed Icons are the primary typed-character members of Planguage's Symbology

relatedConcepts.name: Concepts
relatedConcepts.note: Planguage Concepts are what the Symbology's Symbols represent

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: Planguage has its own defined Symbology of Icons, terms, and Symbols

relatedConcepts.name: Symbol
relatedConcepts.note: a Symbology is a defined system composed of individual Symbols

relatedConcepts.name: Diagram
relatedConcepts.note: Diagrams are composed using a Symbology

concepts.definition: The system of symbols representing ideas, which includes {terminology, icons, symbols}.
concepts.overview: A **Symbology** (*209) is a defined system of symbols used to represent ideas, comprising terminology, [[Icon.161|icons]], and [[Symbol.162|symbols]]. Where a single [[Symbol.162|Symbol]] is an atomic defined representation, a Symbology is the structured collection that gives a set of Symbols a shared, coherent meaning — a notation language. Planguage has its own Symbology built from [[Keyed-Icon.144|Keyed Icons]] (e.g., `>` for Goal, `[ ]` for Survival), defined terminology, and drawn icons. A Symbology is a Description Parameter — something you can specify as part of a document or system, stating explicitly which convention system is in use. Without a declared Symbology, readers cannot reliably decode the symbols they encounter.

concepts.name: Symmetry

relatedConcepts.name: Monster
relatedConcepts.note: Monster is the upside-capture component of Symmetry

relatedConcepts.name: Trigger
relatedConcepts.note: Trigger is the mechanism that activates the upside-capture right

concepts.definition: Explicit pairing of downside protection with upside capture rights. Downside Limit = Tolerable (we already have this). Upside Capture = Monster (new).
concepts.overview: **Symmetry** (*695) is the explicit pairing of a downside protection constraint (Tolerable — the limit below which loss is unacceptable) with an upside capture right ([[Monster.694|Monster]] — the extraordinary upside opportunity). Without Symmetry, most specifications protect only against bad outcomes and leave good fortune to chance; Symmetry demands that both sides of an outcome distribution be deliberately designed. The [[Trigger.696|Trigger]] is the mechanism that activates the upside-capture right when Monster conditions are met. Coined in the context of *Precise Heresies* (suggested by Grok, 2025-11-26).

concepts.name: Systect

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architecture (Systecture)
relatedConcepts.note: Systecture is the discipline a Systect practises — systems architecture

relatedConcepts.name: Architect
relatedConcepts.note: Systems Architect is the conventional role equivalent to Systect

relatedConcepts.name: Designer
relatedConcepts.note: Designer is a related role; a Systect is distinguished by system-level scope and architectural authority

concepts.definition: A **Systect** is a person who does Systecture (systems architecture) — a systems architect. It is a conjunction (systems architect).
concepts.overview: A **Systect** (*565) is a person who practises [[Systems-Architecture.564|Systecture]] — the coined Planguage term for systems architecture. The word is a deliberate portmanteau of "systems" and "architect," analogous to the way [[Systems-Architecture.564|Systecture]] compresses "systems architecture" into a single, precise term. Using Systect instead of "systems architect" is a small economy that becomes significant in documents where the role appears repeatedly — and it signals familiarity with the Planguage vocabulary in which the role is defined. A Systect is related to but distinct from a [[Designer.190|Designer]]: the Systect operates at system-level scope with architectural authority, whereas a Designer may operate at component or solution level.

concepts.name: System Container

relatedConcepts.name: System Interface
relatedConcepts.note: a System Container is a physical or conceptual interface to a set of components — closely related to System Interface

concepts.definition: **System Container** is any physical or conceptual system component which physically or logically serves as an interface to a defined set of system components.
concepts.overview: A **System Container** (*691) is any physical or conceptual component that acts as an interface boundary to a defined set of system components — either physically (a hardware chassis, a network node) or logically (a software module, a conceptual boundary). The System Container is distinct from the components it contains: the container defines the *boundary and interface*, while the contained components perform the internal functions. As a Scope & Context Parameter, declaring a System Container explicitly fixes the system boundary — what is inside the container is in scope; what is outside is the environment. This concept closely overlaps with [[Interface.194|System Interface *194]], which is noted as a partial synonym.

concepts.name: System Definition Rule

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rule
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — a System Definition Rule is a kind of Specification Rule

concepts.definition: A **system definition rule** is any statement which specifies a rule of any kind for the design or action of any system.
concepts.overview: A **System Definition Rule** (*518) is a Specification Rule whose scope is the entire system — covering both how a system is designed and how it behaves in action. Because it applies to any rule "of any kind," the concept is deliberately broad: a rule about performance targets, a constraint on interfaces, a design mandate, and an operational policy all qualify. This breadth matters because it unifies diverse governance statements under a single auditable class. The key engineering insight is that defining a system requires more than listing features; it requires articulating governing rules that constrain and direct every aspect of design and operation. A system without clear definition rules is a system that can drift silently in any direction its implementers choose.

concepts.name: System Description Language

relatedConcepts.name: Basic Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: SDL is built on the foundation of Basic Planguage

relatedConcepts.name: Process Language
relatedConcepts.note: Process Language is a sibling subset of Planguage alongside SDL

relatedConcepts.name: User-Defined Term
relatedConcepts.note: SDL supports user-defined terms to extend the core vocabulary

relatedConcepts.name: Project Language
relatedConcepts.note: SDL is the foundation for project-specific language extensions

concepts.definition: **SDL** is the subset of Planguage for describing systems, including 'processes viewed as systems with attributes'.
concepts.overview: The **System Description Language** (*183), abbreviated SDL, is the specialised subset of Planguage dedicated to specifying *systems* — including any process that can be viewed as a system with measurable attributes. SDL sits alongside the Process Language (*246) as a bounded subset of the larger Planguage framework, and it extends Basic Planguage (*225) with the vocabulary, keywords, and structural conventions needed to define system properties, boundaries, and behaviours. By treating processes as systems with attributes, SDL unifies hardware, software, organisational, and process descriptions under one coherent specification idiom. The practical value is that any entity a team needs to quantitatively describe — be it a software service, a manufacturing line, or an acquisition process — can be specified in SDL using the same measurable, testable language.

concepts.name: System Descriptor

relatedConcepts.name: Attribute
relatedConcepts.note: Attribute is the general concept; System Descriptor is its system-scoped specialisation

relatedConcepts.name: System
relatedConcepts.note: a System Descriptor is a descriptive dimension of a System

concepts.definition: A **system descriptor** is any external or internal attribute {performance, quality, cost, function, constraint, design or other notion} which is used in some way to describe or characterize a system.
concepts.overview: A **System Descriptor** (*384) is any attribute — whether externally observable or internally structural — that is used to describe or characterise a system. The concept is intentionally broad: performance, quality, cost, function, constraint, design, and any "other notion" all qualify. This breadth reflects the Planguage principle that a system must be specifiable in *all* relevant dimensions, not merely the functional ones. The practical value of naming System Descriptors as a class is that it gives teams a disciplined inventory category: for any claim about a system, one can ask "which descriptor class does this belong to?" and thereby organise, prioritise, and measure it. A system that cannot be described across all relevant descriptor classes is a system that cannot be fully specified.

concepts.name: System Element
concepts.definition: System Element is the taxonomy class for things-in-the-system (as opposed to specifications about the system). Sub-groups: System Boundary, Partitioning, Component & Object, Software & Technology Material, Agent & Mechanism, System Property, Lifecycle Phase.
concepts.overview: **System Element** (*832) is part of HumanAgent Gilb's Value Delivery framework, an extension to Tom Gilb's original Planguage. It is not in the source PlanguageGlossary.pdf — it has been authored to capture concepts the framework needs but the PDF did not name.

concepts.name: System Rules

relatedConcepts.name: Business Rules
relatedConcepts.note: Business Rules is a sub-class of System Rules

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Rule
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Rule is a sub-class of System Rules

concepts.definition: **System Rules** is the generic concept containing the sub-class business rules and specification rules.
concepts.overview: **System Rules** (*531) is the generic parent class that contains both Business Rules (*532) and Specification Rules (*609) as sub-classes. Where Business Rules govern the operational logic and policies of a business domain, and Specification Rules govern the structure of Planguage specifications, System Rules is the umbrella concept that recognises both as forms of governing rule applied to a system context. The shared keyed icon `[ ] ->` (condition-to-action syntax) expresses the common logical structure: a condition block triggers a set of rule actions. Understanding System Rules as a class helps engineers audit their rule inventories systematically — any governing statement about a system should be classifiable as either a Business Rule or a Specification Rule under this umbrella.

concepts.name: System

relatedConcepts.name: Attribute
relatedConcepts.note: Attributes are the descriptive dimensions used to specify a System

relatedConcepts.name: System Descriptor
relatedConcepts.note: a System Descriptor is any attribute used to characterise a System

relatedConcepts.name: Object
relatedConcepts.note: Object is a synonym for System in Planguage

relatedConcepts.name: System
relatedConcepts.note: hub concept — referenced by most system-branch concepts

concepts.definition: A **system** is any useful subset of the universe that we choose to specify. It can be conceptual or real.
concepts.overview: A **System** (*145) in Planguage is any useful subset of the universe that we choose to define a boundary around and specify. The definition is radically broad: a system can be physical hardware, a software service, an organisation, a process, a business domain, or any conceptual entity — as long as it is useful and we choose to specify it. The keyed icon `[ ---->O----> ]` represents inputs flowing through the system boundary to produce outputs. This breadth is deliberate: Planguage is a language for specifying *any* kind of system, and the System concept must therefore be as general as possible. The critical engineering implication is that the act of choosing what to call a system — drawing the boundary — is itself a specification decision, one with profound consequences for what gets measured, what gets governed, and what gets ignored.

concepts.name: Systemic

relatedConcepts.name: Root Causes
relatedConcepts.note: Systemic problems arise from Root Causes embedded in the whole system

relatedConcepts.name: Process Improvement
relatedConcepts.note: systemic causes require systemic Process Improvement responses

relatedConcepts.name: Chance Causes
relatedConcepts.note: Chance Causes are contrasted with systemic causes — random vs. structural

relatedConcepts.name: DPP
relatedConcepts.note: DPP (Defect Prevention Process) addresses systemic causes of defects

relatedConcepts.name: SPC
relatedConcepts.note: SPC distinguishes systemic (common-cause) variation from special-cause variation

concepts.definition: **Systemic** means 'of', or 'relating to', the entire system.
concepts.overview: **Systemic** (*262) is an adjective meaning "of or relating to the entire system" — as opposed to local, component-level, or random. In engineering and quality contexts, calling a problem or cause "systemic" indicates that it is embedded in the system's structure or process, not attributable to a single anomalous event or individual. The distinction between systemic causes and chance causes (*019) is foundational to Statistical Process Control (*466) and Defect Prevention Process (*042): systemic causes require structural intervention — changing the system itself — whereas chance causes require only local response. Understanding whether a problem is systemic is therefore the first diagnostic question in any serious improvement effort.

concepts.name: Systems Architect

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: a Systems Architect is the agent who carries out Systems Architecture work

relatedConcepts.name: Designer
relatedConcepts.note: Designer is the broader role; Systems Architect is a specialisation focused on architecture

concepts.definition: A **systems architect** is a person or group, who carries out the work tasks of systems architecture (a process).
concepts.overview: A **Systems Architect** (*193) is the person or group responsible for carrying out the work tasks of Systems Architecture (*564) — the process that produces strategic frameworks, models, standards, and design constraints for implementing and maintaining systems. The definition deliberately includes both individuals and groups: systems architecture at scale is often a team function, not a solo role. The Systems Architect is a specialisation of the broader Designer role (*190), scoped specifically to the architectural level — concerned with the mandatory and recommended best-practice structures that govern how systems are built, rather than the detailed design of components. The key insight is that the role is defined by its *work tasks* (a process), not by a title or seniority level.

concepts.name: Systems Architecture

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: Systems Architecture is the set of artefacts produced by Architecture Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Systecture
relatedConcepts.note: Systecture is Tom Gilb's coined portmanteau for Systems Architecture — coined July 2002; synonym entry

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture
relatedConcepts.note: Architecture *192 is listed as a synonym; see Architecture.192

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Architect
relatedConcepts.note: the agent who carries out the Systems Architecture process

concepts.definition: **Systems Architecture** is the set of artifacts produced by Architecture Engineering. A systems architecture is a strategic framework and consists of models, standards and design constraints specifying mandatory and recommended best practice for implementing and maintaining systems.
concepts.overview: **Systems Architecture** (*564) — also known as **Systecture**, Tom Gilb's portmanteau coined July 2002 — is the artefact set produced by Architecture Engineering (*499) and the strategic framework that governs how systems are implemented and maintained. It consists of three elements: *models* (structural and behavioural representations), *standards* (governing rules for how systems are built), and *design constraints* (mandatory and recommended best-practice limitations). The distinction between mandatory and recommended best practice is important: a Systems Architecture does not dictate every detail of every implementation — it provides the governing envelope within which design decisions are made.

concepts.name: Systems Engineer

relatedConcepts.name: Systems Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: Systems Engineer is defined by the practice of Systems Engineering

concepts.definition: One who practices systems engineering (*223) or is qualified to do so.
concepts.overview: A **Systems Engineer** (*574) is any person who practises Systems Engineering (*223) or is qualified to do so. Like the Systems Architect (*193), the role is defined by its practice — the work of managing all relevant stakeholder requirements, design solutions, and technology, economic, and political considerations across the system lifecycle. The phrase "or is qualified to do so" acknowledges that a Systems Engineer may hold the qualification without currently exercising it — the role is not solely situational. This is the simplest and most direct role definition in the Planguage engineering-role hierarchy: the Systems Engineer *is* their practice.

concepts.name: Systems Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: Engineering is the broader discipline; Systems Engineering is a process within it

relatedConcepts.name: Architecture Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: Architecture Engineering is a sub-process domain of Systems Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: Requirement Engineering is a sub-process domain of Systems Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Design Engineering
relatedConcepts.note: Design Engineering is a sub-process domain of Systems Engineering

relatedConcepts.name: Evo
relatedConcepts.note: Evo is Tom Gilb's evolutionary delivery method compatible with Systems Engineering practice

concepts.definition: **Systems Engineering (SE)** is an engineering process, encompassing and managing all relevant system stakeholders requirements; as well as all design solutions; and necessary technology, economic, and political areas.
concepts.overview: **Systems Engineering** (*223), abbreviated SE, is the engineering process that encompasses and manages all relevant stakeholder requirements, all design solutions, and the technology, economic, and political areas necessary to deliver a system. The scope is deliberately total: SE does not limit itself to technical subsystems or individual engineering disciplines — it manages the *whole* problem space, including non-technical forces that shape what the system must be and can be. The key insight is that no single engineering discipline — software, hardware, mechanical, electrical — is sufficient to manage a complex system end to end; Systems Engineering provides the integrating process that coordinates all of them and ensures the final system satisfies its stakeholder requirements. INCOSE, DoD/Blanchard, and FAA each offer alternative definitions; Planguage's definition emphasises the managing function and the explicit inclusion of economic and political areas.

concepts.name: Tag

relatedConcepts.name: Term
relatedConcepts.note: a Tag identifies a Term — every Defined Term is anchored to a capitalised Tag

relatedConcepts.name: Statement
relatedConcepts.note: Tags identify individual statements or sets of statements within a specification

relatedConcepts.name: Definition
relatedConcepts.note: the Definition parameter formalises what a Tag stands for

relatedConcepts.name: Type
relatedConcepts.note: the Type parameter classifies a concept in the same way a Tag names it

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter
relatedConcepts.note: Tags are a core identification parameter within the Planguage parameter system

concepts.definition: A **Tag** is a term that serves to identify a statement, or set of statements, unambiguously.
concepts.overview: **Tag** (*146) is the unique identifier that names and anchors a Planguage concept, requirement, or specification statement. A Tag is capitalised in Planguage text to signal that a formal definition exists — the capitalisation is the reader's cue to look it up. Every entry in the Planguage Glossary carries a Tag (its English Name), and every Defined Term (*151) is anchored to its Tag. Without a Tag, a specification statement is anonymous and therefore unfindable, unreferenceable, and unmeasurable — it cannot be tracked, queried, or updated with confidence across a large document set. The Tag is thus the primary unit of identification in the Planguage specification system.

concepts.name: Tailored Planguage

relatedConcepts.name: Basic Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: Tailored Planguage is defined as modifications to Basic Planguage — Basic Planguage is the base

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: Tailored Planguage is a specialised variant of the broader Planguage system

relatedConcepts.name: Language
relatedConcepts.note: Tailored Planguage is a specific language-class variant within the Planguage language system

relatedConcepts.name: Terminology
relatedConcepts.note: tailoring often includes extending or restricting the terminology vocabulary used in a project

concepts.definition: **Tailored Planguage** is any modification to a defined version of Basic Planguage (*225) to tailor it to a specific environment.
concepts.overview: **Tailored Planguage** (*226) is the practice of adapting the standard Basic Planguage (*225) to fit the specific needs of a project, organisation, or domain. Tailoring may include translations into other natural languages, domain-specific vocabulary extensions, subsets that restrict the full parameter set to only those relevant in a given context, or variants that replace default notation conventions with organisation-specific ones. The result is a named variant of Planguage that retains the core logic of measurable, attributable specification while fitting the culture and constraints of its environment. Tailored Planguage enables broad adoption of the Planguage discipline without requiring every organisation to accept the full standard vocabulary unchanged — a pragmatic acknowledgement that real-world engineering environments are diverse.

concepts.name: Target System

relatedConcepts.name: System
relatedConcepts.note: a Target System is a defined system — the generic System concept is the parent class

relatedConcepts.name: Agent System
relatedConcepts.note: the Agent System is the entity that directs change at the Target System; they are paired concepts

concepts.definition: A **Target System** is a defined system that is the target of a defined change effort by an agent system.
concepts.overview: **Target System** (*610) identifies the system that is the subject of a deliberate change effort — the system being improved, measured, or developed. It is always paired with an Agent System (*611), which is the entity (organisation, team, or process) directing the change. The distinction matters because it clarifies accountability: the Agent System is responsible for the change; the Target System is what changes. In Planguage specification work, clearly naming both the Target System and the Agent System eliminates the ambiguity of "who is responsible for what" that plagues unclear project charters. A Target System is always defined — loosely scoped systems cannot serve as legitimate targets for measurable change.

concepts.name: Target

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: a Goal (Performance Target) is the desired level — Target is the Planguage requirement-level concept for what we plan to reach

relatedConcepts.name: Budget
relatedConcepts.note: Budget *421 (Budget-Constraint) is a related requirement class that caps cost or resource use

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: Benchmark is the current measured baseline — Target is where we plan to get to from that baseline

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: Constraint is a firm boundary that must not be violated; Target is the level we plan to achieve

relatedConcepts.name: Function Target
relatedConcepts.note: Function Target is the function-level analogue of a scalar Target

relatedConcepts.name: Function Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: Function Constraint is the function-level analogue of a Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar Target
relatedConcepts.note: Scalar Target *470 is the more specific concept; Target *048 is the general class

relatedConcepts.name: Stretch
relatedConcepts.note: Stretch is an aspirational level beyond Target — the ambitious upper bound

relatedConcepts.name: Wish
relatedConcepts.note: Wish is a desired but uncommitted level — Target implies a serious plan to reach it

relatedConcepts.name: Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: Targets are a class of Requirements — every Target is a Requirement with a commitment to reach it

concepts.definition: **Targets** are a class of Requirements that we seriously plan to reach.
concepts.overview: **Target** (*048) is the Planguage requirement-class for levels of performance or function that an organisation seriously commits to achieving. The defining characteristic is the seriousness of the plan: a Target is not a hope or a wish — it implies that resources, effort, and accountability are allocated to reach it. Targets contrast with Constraints (*218), which must not be violated, and with Wishes (*244), which are desirable but uncommitted. The keyed icon `@` marks Target values in Planguage specifications. Targets may be scalar (quantified performance levels, *470) or functional (*420), and they sit within the broader family of Requirements (*026) — statements that define what a system must deliver.

concepts.name: Task

relatedConcepts.name: Act [PDSA]
relatedConcepts.note: Act is the PDSA-cycle action step — a Task may include an Act as its defined unit of work

relatedConcepts.name: Process
relatedConcepts.note: a Process is a broader, repeatable set of activities; a Task is a defined and limited piece within a Process

relatedConcepts.name: Procedure
relatedConcepts.note: a Procedure is a defined sequence of steps; a Task may be composed of one or more Procedures

concepts.definition: A **Task** is a defined and limited piece of work.
concepts.overview: **Task** (*149) is a basic work unit in Planguage's process and lifecycle vocabulary — a piece of work that is both defined (its boundaries and purpose are explicit) and limited (it has a finite scope). Tasks differ from Processes (*113) in scale and repeatability: a Process is an ongoing or repeatable pattern of activity, while a Task is a specific, bounded instance of work. Tasks relate to Procedures (*115), which prescribe the steps to perform a Task, and to the Act (*172) in the PDSA cycle, which represents an improvement action taken as a result of planning. In Planguage specifications, Tasks appear in schedules, method descriptions, and improvement plans where discrete, bounded actions must be identified and assigned.

concepts.name: Team Leader

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: the SQC process the Team Leader is responsible for managing

relatedConcepts.name: Quality Control
relatedConcepts.note: SQC Team Leader manages a specialised quality control process — Quality Control is the broader concept

concepts.definition: A **Team Leader** is responsible for managing a specification quality control (SQC) process.
concepts.overview: **Team Leader** (*281) is the authority role responsible for managing the Specification Quality Control (*051) process in a Planguage context. The Team Leader plans, runs, and closes the SQC session, ensuring that the process is executed with discipline and that results are properly recorded. The role is equivalent to the "Moderator" in IBM's Inspection process — the person who keeps the review on track, prevents it from becoming a design discussion, and ensures that exit criteria are met. In SQC, the Team Leader is distinct from the author of the specification under review and from the stakeholders who identify defects — the Team Leader manages the process, not the content.

concepts.name: Technology

relatedConcepts.name: Design Ideas
relatedConcepts.note: Design Ideas are the specific design choices that constitute the Technology of a system — the means by which quality levels are achieved

concepts.definition: **Technology** is the methods and materials used to construct or modify a system. The design ideas and functionality.
concepts.overview: **Technology** (*352) in Planguage refers to the methods, materials, and design ideas used to construct or modify a system — not technology in the popular sense of "software or electronics," but in the engineering sense of the technical means by which a system achieves its required functions and qualities. Technology is a system element: it is part of what a system is made of. Design Ideas (*047) are the specific technology choices that a designer selects to deliver required performance levels. Planguage treats Technology as a system-branch concept because the technology of a system is part of its definition — understanding what a system is requires understanding not just what it must do but what methods and materials it uses to do it.

concepts.name: Template

relatedConcepts.name: Form
relatedConcepts.note: a Template is a type of Form — Template is the model or example version; Form is the general concept

concepts.definition: A **Template** is an example or 'model' of something, which can be used to help people to tailor or make something, based on that model.
concepts.overview: **Template** (*254) is a model or example document structure that helps people create their own instances by tailoring it to their specific needs. In Planguage, Templates serve as the standardised starting points for specifications, forms, and process documents — providing a consistent structure so that practitioners do not have to invent the format each time, while remaining flexible enough to be adapted to the context at hand. A Template differs from a Form (*068) in that a Form is the general concept of a structured document type, while a Template is a specific, filled-in (or partially filled-in) example of that Form that can be copied and adapted. Templates embody collective experience about what a good instance of a document type looks like.

concepts.name: Term

relatedConcepts.name: Defined Term
relatedConcepts.note: same concept number — Defined Term is the alias entry for Term *151; both share *151 per Planguage polysemy convention

relatedConcepts.name: Statement
relatedConcepts.note: a Term appears within Statements — the smallest meaningful unit of a specification statement

relatedConcepts.name: Expression
relatedConcepts.note: an Expression is a set of Terms combined with operators or syntax to form a meaningful specification unit

relatedConcepts.name: Definition
relatedConcepts.note: a Definition (the Defined As parameter) is what transforms a Term into a Defined Term with formal meaning

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: a Term becomes a Defined Term when it is anchored to a capitalised Tag in specification text

relatedConcepts.name: Terminology
relatedConcepts.note: Terminology is the collective vocabulary of Planguage Terms used in a project or system

concepts.definition: A **Planguage Term** is a minimum set of words and/or symbols (icons) that has a defined Planguage meaning.
concepts.overview: **Term** (*151) is the atomic unit of Planguage vocabulary — the smallest set of words or symbols that carries a distinct, formally defined meaning within the Planguage system. Every concept in the Planguage Glossary is identified by its Term (its English Name/Tag), and every Term that has been formally defined with a written Definition (*044) becomes a Defined Term (*151 — same concept number, Planguage polysemy convention). The minimality criterion is important: a Term is not a sentence or a phrase — it is the smallest meaningful unit that can be independently defined and referenced. Terms form the building blocks of Statements (*140) and Expressions (*302), which in turn compose Planguage specifications. The entire Terminology (*210) of Planguage is the system of its Terms.

concepts.name: Terminology

relatedConcepts.name: Term
relatedConcepts.note: Terminology is the collective system of Terms — Term is the atomic unit that Terminology is composed of

relatedConcepts.name: Tailored Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: tailoring often extends or restricts the Terminology used in a specific environment

relatedConcepts.name: Basic Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: Basic Planguage defines the standard Terminology; Tailored Planguage may extend it

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage
relatedConcepts.note: Terminology is one of the defining components of the Planguage system as a whole

relatedConcepts.name: Language
relatedConcepts.note: Terminology is a language-class concept — it defines the vocabulary component of the Planguage language

concepts.definition: **Terminology** is the vocabulary of technical terms used and defined in Planguage, and in projects which make use of it.
concepts.overview: **Terminology** (*210) is the collective vocabulary of Planguage — the entire system of technical Terms (*151) that have been formally defined within Planguage, together with the Terms defined in projects that use Planguage. Terminology is a language-class concept: it represents the vocabulary component of the Planguage language system. Just as a natural language has a vocabulary (the set of words and their meanings), Planguage has a Terminology (the set of formally defined Terms and their meanings). The Planguage Glossary is the primary repository of this Terminology. Projects that adopt Planguage extend the Terminology with domain-specific Terms through Tailored Planguage (*226). A healthy Terminology is one where every term in use has been formally defined, is consistently applied, and is kept current as the project evolves.

concepts.name: Test

relatedConcepts.name: Meter
relatedConcepts.note: testing executes measurement; Meter provides the scale and method for quantifying what is observed

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: test results are interpreted against a scale of measure

relatedConcepts.name: Quality
relatedConcepts.note: testing assesses whether quality attribute levels are achieved

relatedConcepts.name: Review
relatedConcepts.note: review is a complementary quality-control process to testing

concepts.definition: To **test** is to plan and execute an analytical process on any system, product or process, where we attempt to understand if the system performs as expected, or not.
concepts.overview: **Test** (*256) is a planned, analytical quality-control process applied to any system, product, or process to determine whether it behaves as expected. Testing is not merely running software and hoping for the best — it is a structured inquiry governed by a scale of measure and pre-defined pass/fail criteria. Without a quantified expectation (a Meter and a Goal or Tolerable level), a "test" is indistinguishable from random observation. Testing is the primary mechanism by which Planguage specifications are verified against reality, closing the loop between specification and delivery.

concepts.name: Threat

relatedConcepts.name: Attack
relatedConcepts.note: an Attack is a Threat that has been realised — the active event that a Threat warns of

relatedConcepts.name: Mitigation
relatedConcepts.note: Mitigation reduces the probability or impact of a Threat materialising

relatedConcepts.name: Risk
relatedConcepts.note: Risk quantifies the probability and impact of a Threat; Threat is the source event, Risk is its measure

concepts.definition: A **threat** is something that can potentially cause some degree of project failure, lack of success or negative consequences.
concepts.overview: **Threat** (*671) names a potential source of harm — a condition, event, or actor that could, if realised, damage a project's ability to deliver value. A Threat is distinct from a Risk (*309): the Threat is the hazard source, while Risk is the quantified expression of its probability and impact. When a Threat is realised it becomes an Attack (*672). Identifying Threats explicitly is the first step toward quantifying them as Risks and designing Mitigations (*670) that reduce their likelihood or consequence. Without naming Threats precisely, risk management degenerates into vague worry.

concepts.name: Time Between Successive Products

relatedConcepts.name: Time To Market
relatedConcepts.note: TTM measures first release; TBSP measures the interval between subsequent releases

relatedConcepts.name: Time
relatedConcepts.note: TBSP is a specific application of Time as a scope/context parameter

relatedConcepts.name: Evo
relatedConcepts.note: Evo's incremental delivery model generates a sequence of successive products, making TBSP the primary cadence metric

relatedConcepts.name: Delivery
relatedConcepts.note: TBSP is the interval between successive Delivery events

relatedConcepts.name: Product
relatedConcepts.note: TBSP measures the gap between successive Product releases

concepts.definition: The **TBSP** is calculated by subtracting the release date of the earlier product from that of the later product, giving calendar days difference.
concepts.overview: **Time Between Successive Products** (TBSP, *361) measures the calendar-day interval between consecutive product releases, making it the cadence metric for incremental delivery. Where Time To Market (*365) captures the duration from project start to first release, TBSP captures the rhythm of every subsequent release — the operational heartbeat of an Evo-based programme. A short TBSP signals rapid feedback loops and frequent value delivery; a long TBSP signals that stakeholders must wait extended periods between improvements. TBSP is also known as Time To Market Prime (TTM') to distinguish it from the initial TTM measurement. Reducing TBSP is a primary organisational capability in iterative engineering.

concepts.name: Time Cycle Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Evo
relatedConcepts.note: Time Cycle Constraint governs the maximum length of an Evo Frontroom delivery cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Frontroom
relatedConcepts.note: the Frontroom cycle is the customer-visible delivery phase whose duration is bounded by this constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Backroom
relatedConcepts.note: the Backroom cycle runs in parallel; its timing is distinct from the Frontroom delivery cycle

relatedConcepts.name: Time
relatedConcepts.note: Time Cycle Constraint is a specialised constraint applied to the Time parameter

relatedConcepts.name: Time Between Successive Products
relatedConcepts.note: TBSP is the market-facing manifestation of the Time Cycle Constraint — the result of enforcing a short cycle limit

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: Time Cycle Constraint is a type of Constraint

concepts.definition: In Evo delivery cycle planning, the **Time Cycle Constraint** is the maximum-recommended duration of a Frontroom delivery cycle (as opposed to a result cycle). The average duration time that a customer has to wait for a delivery.
concepts.overview: **Time Cycle Constraint** (*154) is a design constraint that caps the maximum permissible length of a Frontroom (*343) delivery cycle within an Evo (*355) programme. It exists to enforce the discipline of short, frequent delivery: if the cycle length is unconstrained, teams naturally extend it, deferring customer value indefinitely. By treating the cycle length as an explicit, specified constraint — not a guideline — organisations commit to a cadence that limits how long any stakeholder must wait between deliveries. The constraint bridges the abstract notion of Time (*153) and the market-facing metric of Time Between Successive Products (*361).

concepts.name: Time To Market

relatedConcepts.name: Time Between Successive Products
relatedConcepts.note: TBSP (TTM') measures subsequent release intervals after first release; TTM measures the first interval only

relatedConcepts.name: Time
relatedConcepts.note: TTM is a specific scale-of-measure application of the Time parameter

relatedConcepts.name: Time Cycle Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: the Time Cycle Constraint governs delivery cycle length, which directly influences achievable TTM

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: TTM is itself a scale of measure — calendar time — applied to product delivery

relatedConcepts.name: Product
relatedConcepts.note: TTM measures the duration from project start to successful Product release

concepts.definition: The **Time To Market** (TTM) is the calendar time between the [defined] start, or initial staffing, of the project, and the project's [defined level of] product successful release to [defined] market. A scale of measure.
concepts.overview: **Time To Market** (TTM, *365) is a scalar measure of the calendar time from a project's defined start point to the moment a product successfully reaches a defined market. The bracketed qualifiers — [defined] start, [defined level of] product, [defined] market — are not decoration; they are the entire substance of the measurement. Without precise definitions of each qualifier, TTM figures are incomparable across projects and meaningless as engineering targets. TTM measures the first-release interval; subsequent release intervals are measured by Time Between Successive Products (TBSP, *361). Specifying TTM as a quantified requirement, with a Goal and a Fail level, converts it from a boardroom aspiration into an engineered outcome.

concepts.name: Time

relatedConcepts.name: Time Cycle Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: Time Cycle Constraint is a specialised constraint applied to the Time parameter in Evo planning

relatedConcepts.name: Time To Market
relatedConcepts.note: Time To Market is a specific operationalisation of Time as a scalar metric

relatedConcepts.name: Time Between Successive Products
relatedConcepts.note: TBSP is another operationalisation of Time applied to successive release intervals

relatedConcepts.name: Parameter
relatedConcepts.note: Time is a Planguage parameter — a scope/context qualifier on any specification

relatedConcepts.name: Scope
relatedConcepts.note: Time is used alongside Scope to constrain when a specification applies

relatedConcepts.name: Tag
relatedConcepts.note: Time is commonly expressed as a Tag value in Planguage specifications

concepts.definition: **Time** defines 'when'. It relates to any notion of time: clock-time or timescale.
concepts.overview: **Time** (*153) is a Planguage scope and context parameter that answers the question "when does this specification apply?" It encompasses any temporal reference — a specific clock time, a date, a duration, a phase, or a relative timescale. Because Planguage specifications are precision instruments, the implicit assumption that "this requirement applies always and forever" is rarely true in practice; Time makes the temporal scope explicit. Time is the parent parameter from which Time To Market (*365), Time Between Successive Products (*361), and Time Cycle Constraint (*154) are all derived as specialised applications. Without Time as an explicit parameter, specifications drift silently as the temporal context changes.

concepts.name: To Budget

relatedConcepts.name: Budget
relatedConcepts.note: the output of the budgeting process — a committed resource-allocation level

relatedConcepts.name: Budget Target
relatedConcepts.note: To Budget produces a full Budget Target specification (Wish, Stretch, Budget, and Fail levels)

relatedConcepts.name: Resource
relatedConcepts.note: budgeting allocates a limited Resource

relatedConcepts.name: Target
relatedConcepts.note: budgeting results in Target specifications for one or more resources

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: budgeting also produces Constraint specifications (Budget Constraint) bounding resource use

relatedConcepts.name: Plan
relatedConcepts.note: budgeting is a planning activity that produces resource allocation plans

concepts.definition: **'To budget'** refers to a process to plan the allocation of limited resources to a system. The budgeting process results in the specification of a set of target and constraint specifications for one or more resources.
concepts.overview: **To Budget** (*488) names the process by which limited resources are allocated to a system, producing a structured set of target and constraint specifications as its output. It is not merely the act of assigning a cost ceiling — it is the disciplined exercise of specifying, for each resource, the full hierarchy of Wish, Stretch, and Budget (committed) target levels alongside the outer constraint boundaries (Fail/Crash/Survival). The distinction between To Budget (the process) and Budget (*480) (the committed-level output) is the same as the distinction between designing a system and the system itself. The output of a well-executed budgeting process is a complete Budget Target (*481) specification, not just a single number. Source note: extracted from PDF p.37; the source type is listed as "Verb," reflecting the verbal/process nature of this concept.

concepts.name: Tolerable

relatedConcepts.name: Status
relatedConcepts.note: Status (current measured level) is compared to Tolerable to determine which range the attribute is in; see StatusToTolerable *699

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Goal is the committed success level above Tolerable; the Tolerable Range spans from Tolerable to Goal

relatedConcepts.name: StatusToTolerable
relatedConcepts.note: the gap from current Status to the Tolerable threshold — key priority signal when Status is approaching or in the Intolerable Range

relatedConcepts.name: Fail
relatedConcepts.note: Fail is Tom Gilb's attribute-level defect boundary; in the STG framework, Fail sits inside the Tolerable Range (above Tolerable, below Goal)

relatedConcepts.name: Survival
relatedConcepts.note: Survival is Tom Gilb's existence-threatening boundary; the STG Tolerable threshold corresponds semantically to Survival — below it the whole project fails

relatedConcepts.name: Limit
relatedConcepts.note: Limit defines the boundary; Tolerable is the acknowledged minimum level on the acceptable side of the Limit

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: Tolerable defines the three STG ranges: Intolerable (below Tolerable), Tolerable Range (Tolerable to Goal), Success Range (above Goal)

relatedConcepts.name: Scalar Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: Tolerable is a type of Scalar Constraint — the project-viability threshold

concepts.definition: The **Tolerable** level is the project-viability threshold on a scalar attribute scale. Below it, the whole project fails — not just the one attribute value. Above it, the project is still alive. It is the critical boundary that separates the Intolerable Range (project dead) from the Tolerable Range (project alive, below Goal).
concepts.overview: **Tolerable** (*539) is the single most critical threshold in the STG (Status · Tolerable · Goal) framework. It marks the line between project survival and project failure. Performance below Tolerable places the entire project in the Intolerable Range — a project-level failure, not merely an attribute-level defect. Performance at or above Tolerable keeps the project alive; the Tolerable Range (from Tolerable up to Goal) is the zone where the project is alive but has not yet reached its committed target. The concept was suggested by HumanAgent Gilb in 2003. In Tom Gilb's fuller model, the Tolerable threshold corresponds semantically to the Survival *440 boundary — the existence-threatening limit. A polysemy note applies: concept *539 is also used for Must-Do, which is a distinct concept sharing the same number — each has its own file.

concepts.name: Trade

relatedConcepts.name: Translation
relatedConcepts.note: adjacent concept in the glossary; both Trade and Translation are lifecycle/language concepts defined in the same batch

relatedConcepts.name: Product
relatedConcepts.note: a Trade involves producing or exchanging Products within a market or group context
