concepts.definition: **Trade** is a type of activity done by groups. E.g. 'The computer trade.'
concepts.overview: **Trade** (*206) names the class of collective activities performed by groups operating within a shared domain — most commonly a commercial or technical sector. In Planguage, Trade enters primarily as a context parameter: when a specification references a market, industry, or sector (e.g. "the computer trade"), it is invoking Trade as a scope-defining concept. The definition is deliberately minimal — Tom Gilb treats Trade as a foundational contextual category rather than a richly specified engineering concept. Its key role is to anchor language about sectors, industries, and market groups within specifications that need to distinguish one commercial domain from another.

concepts.name: Translation

relatedConcepts.name: Trade
relatedConcepts.note: adjacent concept; both Translation and Trade are foundational Planguage context/language concepts

relatedConcepts.name: Language
relatedConcepts.note: Translation operates between Languages; Language is the parent class of which Translation is a process

relatedConcepts.name: Document
relatedConcepts.note: Translation produces a translated Document from a source Planguage document

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: Planguage Specifications are the primary candidates for translation to other human languages

concepts.definition: A **translation** is a translation from (usually US English, the default language) a Planguage document to another major human language. Note: Planguage to UK English would be a dialect 'tuning' not a translation.
concepts.overview: **Translation** (*205) names the process and output of converting a Planguage document from its default language (US English) into another major human language. The concept is precisely bounded: moving between national languages constitutes a Translation, while adjusting for regional dialect variants (US English → UK English) is a "tuning" — not a Translation. This distinction matters because a Translation requires different expertise, different quality-assurance processes, and potentially different reviewer profiles than a dialect adjustment. Since Planguage specifications must be exact to be useful, a mistranslation is not merely a stylistic issue — it is a specification defect that can propagate incorrect requirements into downstream engineering decisions.

concepts.name: Trend

relatedConcepts.name: Benchmark
relatedConcepts.note: Trend is a subtype of Benchmark — a benchmark derived from historical or projected data

relatedConcepts.name: Level
relatedConcepts.note: Trend expresses how a Level is expected to change over time

concepts.definition: A **Trend** parameter is used to specify how we expect or estimate attribute levels to be in the future. It is used as a benchmark.
concepts.overview: **Trend** (*155) is a scalar benchmark that captures how an attribute level is expected to evolve over time, derived from historical data or reasoned estimation. Rather than stating a fixed past measurement, Trend projects a directional pattern — rising, falling, or stable — that serves as a reference for future planning and target-setting. It is keyed with the icon `?<`, where `<` denotes the past direction and `?` acknowledges inherent doubt about perfect prediction. Trend was first suggested by HumanAgent Thomas Gilb in May 1995, and is essential for calibrating specifications against realistic futures rather than naive snapshots.

concepts.name: Trigger

relatedConcepts.name: Monster
relatedConcepts.note: A Trigger fires when a Monster is approaching — it is defined relative to the Monster's threshold

relatedConcepts.name: Symmetry
relatedConcepts.note: Symmetry provides the paired upside counterpart to the Monster's downside; Trigger monitors Monster proximity

concepts.definition: A **Trigger** is a quantified early-warning signal that the monster is approaching, defined while we still have time to re-allocate resources.
concepts.overview: **Trigger** (*696) is a quantified threshold that fires an early warning when a Monster (*694) is becoming imminent — before the catastrophic outcome has already arrived. It is defined proactively, at a time when the team still has meaningful room to redirect resources, change course, or activate contingency plans. Unlike a reactive alert triggered after harm, a Trigger is a forward-looking instrument: crossing it is a signal to act, not a notification of failure. It was introduced for the *Precise Heresies* book (suggested by Grok, 2025) and belongs to the decision and estimation process family.

concepts.name: Type

relatedConcepts.name: Specification Type
relatedConcepts.note: Polysemy: Specification-Type shares *398 and classifies specifications; Type classifies concepts

concepts.definition: **Type** specifies the category of a Planguage concept.
concepts.overview: **Type** (*398) is an identification parameter that assigns a concept to its named category within the Planguage taxonomy. Every Planguage concept belongs to a Type — Scale, Parameter, Benchmark, State, Process, and so on — and this classification governs how the concept is interpreted, how it may be combined with other concepts, and what rules apply to it. Type is one of the core metadata fields in the glossary itself, appearing in the YAML frontmatter of every concept file. Number *398 is shared (polysemy) with Specification-Type (*398), which performs an analogous classification role for specification documents rather than individual concepts.

concepts.name: Ultimate

relatedConcepts.name: Ultimotive
relatedConcepts.note: Ultimotive is the highest-level motivation; Ultimate is the highest-level system component — complementary apex concepts

concepts.definition: The systems engineering component, at the highest level worthy of consideration, is the **ultimate** component.
concepts.overview: **Ultimate** (*442) designates the highest-level systems engineering component that is still meaningful to consider in a given analysis. It is a scoping concept: it marks the apex of the system hierarchy from which all lower-level components, constraints, and decisions derive their context. By naming and specifying the Ultimate component, engineers establish the widest boundary of relevance — preventing both the error of ignoring important higher-level constraints and the error of pursuing scope beyond any useful limit. The concept was suggested by HumanAgent Gilb in connection with the Whirlwind manuscript in July 2001.

concepts.name: Ultimotive

relatedConcepts.name: Ultimate
relatedConcepts.note: Ultimate names the highest-level system component; Ultimotive names the highest-level motivation — complementary apex concepts

concepts.definition: An **ultimotive** is the highest level of motivation in a defined chain of motivations.
concepts.overview: **Ultimotive** (*444) names the apex motivating purpose in a hierarchical chain of motivations — the "why behind all other whys" within a defined scope. It is a system property that anchors the motivational hierarchy in the same way that Ultimate (*442) anchors the structural hierarchy: by naming the highest level explicitly, engineers make all lower-level goals, objectives, and functions answerable to it. Ultimotive was concocted by Tom Gilb in conversation with HumanAgent Gilb on July 22, 2001, and brings the same naming discipline to motivation chains that Planguage brings to performance attributes.

concepts.name: Uncertainty

relatedConcepts.name: Risk
relatedConcepts.note: Risk is the negative consequence of Uncertainty materialising; Uncertainty quantifies the degree of doubt, Risk quantifies its cost

relatedConcepts.name: Undetermined
relatedConcepts.note: Undetermined is a State value meaning the determination has not been attempted; Uncertainty is a quantified degree of doubt about a known estimate

relatedConcepts.name: Undeterminable
relatedConcepts.note: Undeterminable is a State value meaning determination was attempted but yielded no clear result; Uncertainty quantifies partial knowledge rather than total absence

concepts.definition: **Uncertainty** is the degree to which we are in doubt about how an impact estimate, or measurement, of an attribute reflects reality.
concepts.overview: **Uncertainty** (*310) is a quantification parameter that captures the epistemic doubt surrounding an estimate or measurement of an attribute — specifically, how faithfully the stated value reflects the true state of reality. It is keyed with the icon `±?`, where `±` denotes deviation and `?` denotes doubt, encoding both the bidirectional nature of error and the acknowledgement that precision is partial. Uncertainty is distinct from Risk (*309): Uncertainty is about knowledge quality (how confident are we in the number?), while Risk concerns the negative consequences if that number is wrong. By explicitly quantifying Uncertainty, Planguage forces engineers to report not just their estimates but how much to trust them.

concepts.name: Undeterminable

relatedConcepts.name: State
relatedConcepts.note: Undeterminable is a predefined value in the State scalar type

relatedConcepts.name: Undetermined
relatedConcepts.note: Undetermined means determination has not yet been attempted; Undeterminable means it was attempted but yielded no clear result

relatedConcepts.name: Unknown
relatedConcepts.note: Unknown is a related predefined State; check Unknown.629 for the closely adjacent concept

relatedConcepts.name: Uncertainty
relatedConcepts.note: Uncertainty quantifies degree of doubt about a known estimate; Undeterminable represents total absence of determinable state

concepts.definition: **Undeterminable** is a predefined State. Attempt to determine has been made and the result is no clear state information is available.
concepts.overview: **Undeterminable** (*628) is a predefined State value that records a specific epistemic situation: a determination was attempted, but the attempt produced no clear state information. It differs critically from Undetermined (*627), which records that no attempt has yet been made. Undeterminable is therefore not a placeholder — it is a finding. It tells the reader that the system has been probed, measured, or analysed, and the result of that investigation is that the state cannot be established. This distinction matters for specification management: an Undeterminable state may require a different escalation path than an Undetermined one.

concepts.name: Undetermined

relatedConcepts.name: State
relatedConcepts.note: Undetermined is a predefined value in the State scalar type

relatedConcepts.name: Undeterminable
relatedConcepts.note: Undeterminable means determination was attempted but yielded no clear result; Undetermined means the attempt has not yet been made or concluded

relatedConcepts.name: Unknown
relatedConcepts.note: Unknown is a closely adjacent predefined State in the same epistemic cluster

relatedConcepts.name: Uncertainty
relatedConcepts.note: Uncertainty quantifies degree of doubt about a known estimate; Undetermined records the absence of any estimate attempt

concepts.definition: **Undetermined** is a predefined State. The state determination has either not been attempted or is not concluded yet.
concepts.overview: **Undetermined** (*627) is a predefined State value that honestly records the absence of completed measurement or determination for a given attribute — either because the determination has not been started, or because it is still in progress. It is a placeholder State, used legitimately during specification development, but which must eventually be replaced by a real value or by Undeterminable (*628) if determination fails. Unlike Undeterminable, which reports the *outcome* of a failed attempt, Undetermined records *prior to* any conclusive attempt. Its presence in a specification is a signal to reviewers that work remains.

concepts.name: Units Context

relatedConcepts.name: Units of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: Units of Measure specifies the measurement unit; Units Context specifies where and when that unit is applicable

relatedConcepts.name: Units Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: Units Qualifier modifies the unit; Units Context specifies the scope of applicability

relatedConcepts.name: Scale
relatedConcepts.note: Units Context is part of the Scale class family; it defines the applicability domain of a Scale

concepts.definition: A **Units Context** defines where the scale of measure is applicable. It primarily contains place, space, event; secondarily contains sources, authority, priority.
concepts.overview: **Units Context** (*559) is a scale-class component that specifies the domain of applicability for a given unit of measure — the conditions of place, space, and event under which the measurement is valid and meaningful. Without a Units Context, a measurement is decontextualised: a latency figure measured in a test lab under low load is a different thing from the same figure measured in production under peak load, even if the Units of Measure (*560) are identical. Units Context makes the domain of validity explicit, preventing the attribution of measurements to contexts where they do not apply. It is part of the tripartite Units cluster alongside Units of Measure (*560) and Units Qualifier (*561).

concepts.name: Units Qualifier

relatedConcepts.name: Units of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: the base unit that this qualifier limits or contextualises

relatedConcepts.name: Units Context
relatedConcepts.note: cluster sibling specifying measurement environment

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: parent structure containing the full Units cluster

concepts.definition: **Units Qualifiers** specify in a Scale of measure which dimensions apply to the units of measure.
concepts.overview: **Units Qualifier** (*561) is the sub-field of a Planguage Scale that constrains *how the unit of measure is dimensioned* — typically expressing a denominator or partitioning dimension such as "per year," "per user," or "per release." It transforms a raw unit into a rate or density that is meaningful in context. Without a qualifier, a measurement like "100 errors" is ambiguous — 100 per minute is catastrophic, 100 per decade is fine. Together with Units of Measure (*560) and Units Context (*559), the Units Qualifier completes the three-part cluster needed to produce a fully unambiguous scale.

concepts.name: Units of Measure

relatedConcepts.name: Scale of Measure
relatedConcepts.note: parent structure that contains Units of Measure

relatedConcepts.name: Units Qualifier
relatedConcepts.note: specifies dimensional limits on these units

relatedConcepts.name: Units Context
relatedConcepts.note: specifies the sampling or measurement context for these units

concepts.definition: **Units of Measure** define the basic units to be used for measurement in a scale of measure.
concepts.overview: **Units of Measure** (*560) is the component of a Planguage Scale that declares the fundamental measurement unit applied to all numeric values in that scale — for example, "seconds," "dollars," or "errors." It anchors every quantified requirement to a concrete, observable dimension. Without declared units, a number like "95" carries no meaning and cannot be measured, compared, or verified. Together with the Units Qualifier (*561) and Units Context (*559), it forms the three-part Units cluster that fully characterises how a scalar value is to be interpreted.

concepts.name: Unknown

relatedConcepts.name: State
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept; Unknown is a predefined State value

relatedConcepts.name: Undetermined
relatedConcepts.note: epistemic sibling — state exists but has not yet been determined

relatedConcepts.name: Undeterminable
relatedConcepts.note: epistemic sibling — state cannot in principle be determined

relatedConcepts.name: Unstable
relatedConcepts.note: related predefined State — state is changing unpredictably

concepts.definition: **Unknown** is a predefined State. The state is not known.
concepts.overview: **Unknown** (*629) is one of Planguage's predefined values for the State parameter, signalling that the current value or condition of the thing being specified is not known to the specifier at this time. It is distinct from Undetermined (*627), where the state exists but simply has not yet been found out, and from Undeterminable (*628), where no measurement method can in principle establish it. Declaring a state as Unknown is an honest, useful act in specification: it flags a gap in current knowledge without implying whether that gap is temporary or permanent, preventing readers from assuming a default value that was never established.

concepts.name: Unstable

relatedConcepts.name: State
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept; Unstable is a predefined State value

relatedConcepts.name: Unknown
relatedConcepts.note: related predefined State — the state is not known

relatedConcepts.name: Undetermined
relatedConcepts.note: related predefined State — state exists but not yet determined

relatedConcepts.name: Undeterminable
relatedConcepts.note: related predefined State — state cannot be determined

concepts.definition: **Unstable** is a predefined State. The state is changing in unpredictable ways.
concepts.overview: **Unstable** (*630) is one of Planguage's predefined values for the State parameter, signalling that the current value or condition of the specified entity is not merely unknown or unmeasured — it is actively changing in ways that cannot be predicted or reliably tracked. Marking a requirement or system attribute as Unstable communicates that any measurement or specification made right now is likely to be invalid by the time it is used. It is a flag to stakeholders and engineers that stabilisation is a prerequisite to meaningful quantification, and that the design, environment, or requirements need to be settled before work on the related attribute can proceed productively.

concepts.name: Until

relatedConcepts.name: Or Worse
relatedConcepts.note: related range operator — open-ended lower bound

relatedConcepts.name: Or Better
relatedConcepts.note: related range operator — open-ended upper bound

relatedConcepts.name: Range
relatedConcepts.note: parent concept; Until is the operator used to express scalar ranges

concepts.definition: **Until** is a logical operator that is used to limit the extent of a scalar range of values.
concepts.overview: **Until** (*551) is the Planguage operator that connects two scalar levels to form a closed Range — the lower bound "until" the upper bound. Its keyed icon is `->` (a right arrow), so `A -> B` means "from value A until value B," defining an acceptable band of performance rather than a single target point. Using Until forces specifiers to be explicit about the full acceptable range, preventing the common error of specifying only a nominal target while leaving the acceptable limits unstated. It pairs naturally with Or Worse (*549) and Or Better (*550) for ranges with one open end.

concepts.name: Upstream

relatedConcepts.name: Downstream
relatedConcepts.note: antonym — refers to any later processes than the current reference point

concepts.definition: **Upstream** refers to any earlier processes than the one currently identified (the current reference point).
concepts.overview: **Upstream** (*291) is a Planguage Relationship Parameter that identifies any process, activity, or system component that occurs *before* the current reference point in a flow or sequence. Its keyed icon is `~>`, read as "A ~> B means A is upstream of B." Declaring upstream relationships makes process dependencies explicit in specifications, allowing engineers and stakeholders to trace how outputs from earlier steps flow into and constrain the current step. It is the structural complement of Downstream (*052), and together they map the causal flow of any process chain.

concepts.name: User-Defined Term

relatedConcepts.name: Planguage Term
relatedConcepts.note: contrasting concept — a native Planguage term, not user-defined

relatedConcepts.name: Project Language
relatedConcepts.note: the broader vocabulary system within which user-defined terms live

concepts.definition: In Planguage, a **user-defined term** is a definition of a term made by a Planguage user. It is not a Planguage term (like Scale or Goal), nor a customer-tailored Planguage term, such as a new Parameter, Parameter Synonym or grammatical variation.
concepts.overview: **User-Defined Term** (*530) is any term that a Planguage practitioner defines specifically for their project or domain — a concept that belongs neither to the native Planguage vocabulary (*211) nor to the category of customer-tailored Planguage extensions (new parameters, parameter synonyms, or grammatical variants). User-defined terms populate the Project Language (*247) alongside standard Planguage terms, filling in the domain-specific concepts that the methodology cannot anticipate. They are the project team's vocabulary additions: a "FMEA rating," a "sprint velocity," or a "tier-1 customer" defined precisely so all stakeholders share one meaning. Without user-defined terms, specifications must either co-opt standard vocabulary imprecisely or leave domain concepts undefined.

concepts.name: User

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: parent class — User is a specific type of Stakeholder

relatedConcepts.name: Client
relatedConcepts.note: sibling Stakeholder subtype — may commission the system without using it

relatedConcepts.name: Consumer
relatedConcepts.note: sibling Stakeholder subtype — receives system outputs without necessarily operating it

concepts.definition: A **user** is a person or group, who actually will make practical use of a system.
concepts.overview: **User** (*234) is the Planguage Stakeholder subtype that identifies the person or group who will actually operate and make practical use of the system — as opposed to the Client (*235), who commissions or pays for it, or the Consumer (*038), who receives its outputs without necessarily operating it. Distinguishing Users from other Stakeholder types is essential because Users have distinct performance requirements: their experience is governed by response times, usability, task completion rates, and the moment-to-moment interface with the system. Requirements that conflate Users with Clients or Consumers systematically underspecify usability and operational quality.

concepts.name: Validation

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: parent quality control process framework within which Validation operates

relatedConcepts.name: SCR
relatedConcepts.note: Specification Content Review — a primary vehicle for performing Validation

relatedConcepts.name: Verification
relatedConcepts.note: complementary QC process — Verification checks correctness; Validation checks completeness and real-world alignment

concepts.definition: **Validation** is a process of confirming that a specification is complete and correct.
concepts.overview: **Validation** (*601) is the Planguage quality control process that confirms whether a specification is complete and correct — not just internally consistent, but aligned with stakeholder needs, real-world constraints, and engineering feasibility. It is the inward-looking complement to Verification (*321): where Verification asks "did we build it right?" Validation asks "did we specify the right thing?" A specification can pass every internal consistency check (Verification) and still be wrong if it specifies a system that does not address what stakeholders actually need. Validation catches that class of error. It is typically performed through Specification Content Reviews (SCR, *542) and operates within the broader Software Quality Control (SQC, *051) framework.

concepts.name: Value Chain

relatedConcepts.name: Value
relatedConcepts.note: the concept of value that the chain propagates and makes explicit

relatedConcepts.name: Impacts
relatedConcepts.note: the multi-target impact parameter that a value chain may express

relatedConcepts.name: Impact
relatedConcepts.note: single-target impact; a value chain sequences these causal steps

relatedConcepts.name: Supports
relatedConcepts.note: related relationship parameter — value chains express support relationships

concepts.definition: A **value chain** is a sequence of two or more defined objects. The initial object produces value, as defined by the second object's value.
concepts.overview: **Value Chain** (*591) is a Planguage Quantification Parameter that makes explicit how value propagates through a sequence of defined objects — how one entity's output produces the value that defines the next entity's worth, and so on through the chain. Its keyed icon is `+>`, expressing that "A +> B" means A produces value that flows into B. Value chains are the Planguage mechanism for tracing the causal logic that connects engineering choices to stakeholder outcomes: why does improving a database response time improve customer satisfaction? The value chain makes those intermediate steps explicit, quantifiable, and auditable. Without it, claimed value delivery is asserted rather than argued.

concepts.name: Value To Cost Ratio

relatedConcepts.name: Value
relatedConcepts.note: the value component of the ratio

relatedConcepts.name: Cost
relatedConcepts.note: the cost component of the ratio

relatedConcepts.name: Value to Cost Score
relatedConcepts.note: simpler scoring variant using 0–9 scale

relatedConcepts.name: Performance to Cost Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: analogous ratio for performance rather than value

concepts.definition: The **value to cost ratio** is a numeric expression of perceived stakeholder value to estimated or actual costs, for a set of design ideas or for an Evo step.
concepts.overview: **Value To Cost Ratio** (*635) expresses how much stakeholder value is obtained per unit of cost invested, producing a numeric ratio that can be compared across design alternatives or Evo steps. It combines perceived value (*269) with estimated or actual cost (*033) into a single comparable figure. The ratio supports prioritisation decisions: a higher ratio signals that a design idea or delivery increment delivers more benefit per resource consumed. Unlike the simpler Value-to-Cost Score (*349), which uses a 0–9 ordinal scale, the ratio can be computed from actual measurement data. It is a cornerstone of evolutionary delivery prioritisation, helping teams choose which increments to do first.

concepts.name: Value to Cost Score

relatedConcepts.name: Value to Cost Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: the more rigorous computed-ratio counterpart

relatedConcepts.name: Value
relatedConcepts.note: the value dimension being scored

relatedConcepts.name: Cost
relatedConcepts.note: the cost dimension being scored

concepts.definition: The **value to cost score** is a simple numeric scoring mechanism, sometimes used in meetings to share opinions, and to arrive at a consensus about the value and cost of Evo steps. The scale is 0 to 9, where 9 is the score representing highest value, or highest cost.
concepts.overview: **Value to Cost Score** (*349) is a lightweight collaborative tool that enables a group to rapidly rank Evo steps by assigning each one two scores on a 0–9 ordinal scale: one for perceived value and one for estimated cost. High-value, low-cost steps float to the top of the delivery queue. The score is intentionally simple — designed for use in a meeting, not for engineering precision — making it more accessible than the computed Value To Cost Ratio (*635). Its power lies in surfacing consensus quickly across stakeholders who may not agree on much else. The scores must be treated as opinions, not measurements, and should be revisited as delivery proceeds.

concepts.name: Value

relatedConcepts.name: Benefit
relatedConcepts.note: value is perceived benefit — the subjective experience of benefit

relatedConcepts.name: Impacts
relatedConcepts.note: impacts are the changes that generate or destroy value

relatedConcepts.name: Values
relatedConcepts.note: Values (plural) are the cultural principles that determine what is considered valuable

relatedConcepts.name: Quality
relatedConcepts.note: quality is the degree to which a system delivers its intended value

relatedConcepts.name: Value To Cost Ratio
relatedConcepts.note: uses Value as the numerator in prioritisation

relatedConcepts.name: Value to Cost Score
relatedConcepts.note: the ordinal scoring tool for value in meetings

concepts.definition: **Value** is perceived benefit: that is, the benefit we think we will, or do, get from something.
concepts.overview: **Value** (*269) is the perceived benefit that a stakeholder believes they receive from a system, product, or action — it is inherently subjective and stakeholder-relative. Because value is perceived rather than objective, different stakeholders may assign very different values to the same outcome. Planguage uses the keyed icon `+>` to express "adds value to," signalling that something contributes positively to a stakeholder's goals. Value is closely related to, but distinct from, Benefit (*009): benefit is what is actually delivered, while value is what is perceived. Quantifying value — however roughly — is essential for rational prioritisation, as captured in the Value To Cost Ratio (*635) and the Value to Cost Score (*349).

concepts.name: Values

relatedConcepts.name: Value
relatedConcepts.note: Value (singular) is the scalar outcome; Values (plural) are the principles that determine what is considered valuable

concepts.definition: **Values** are human culture guidelines that help individuals or groups make choices. They are the principles, standards and paradigms that we consider when choosing alternatives.
concepts.overview: **Values** (*592) are the collectively held principles, standards, and paradigms that a human culture or organisation uses when evaluating and choosing between alternatives — they are the criteria behind decisions, not the outcomes of those decisions. Unlike Value (*269), which is a scalar measure of perceived benefit for a specific outcome, Values are plural and normative: they describe what a group considers important in general. An organisation that Values transparency will consistently evaluate options differently from one that Values efficiency above all else. In Planguage, making Values explicit enables stakeholders to understand why certain requirements are prioritised and provides a stable foundation for value modelling. Source concept credited to Ralph Keeney [KEENEY92].

concepts.name: Variability

relatedConcepts.name: Commonality
relatedConcepts.note: the dual concept; together Commonality and Variability define a product-line architecture

concepts.definition: Any development artifacts or components that do not have identical corresponding artifacts in another product represent **variability** between the products.
concepts.overview: **Variability** (*582) identifies the development artifacts or components that differ between two or more products in a product family — it is the complement of Commonality (*580), which captures what is shared. Together they define the architecture of a product line: what must be built fresh for each variant versus what can be reused. Quantifying variability enables engineering teams to estimate how much of a new product is truly new work, and how much can be inherited from the shared platform. The concept was contributed by Stefan Ferber of Bosch in July 2002, reflecting industrial product-line experience.

concepts.name: Variant
concepts.definition: A **variant** is a special variation of a Planguage artifact {handbook, slides, etc.}.
concepts.overview: **Variant** (*203) is an identification and naming parameter that labels a Planguage artifact as a specialised version adapted for a particular audience, company, or trade context. Where a Version (*332) captures a time-based revision history, a Variant captures a context-based fork: the same artifact expressed differently for Nokia versus a software engineering audience, or for a healthcare regulator versus a retail buyer. Variants allow a single underlying specification structure to be maintained while the surface presentation, examples, or emphasis differs for each target context.

concepts.name: Verification

relatedConcepts.name: Validation
relatedConcepts.note: validation asks 'did we build the right thing?'; verification asks 'did we build it right?

relatedConcepts.name: SQC
relatedConcepts.note: software quality control; the broader process of which verification is a component

relatedConcepts.name: Evo
relatedConcepts.note: evolutionary delivery; verification is applied at each Evo step exit

concepts.definition: A **verification** process tries to confirm that the output of a process corresponds to expectations.
concepts.overview: **Verification** (*321) is the quality control process that checks whether the output of a development step matches its specified expectations — it asks "did we build it right?" Verification is distinct from Validation (*601), which asks "did we build the right thing?" — that is, whether the system satisfies actual stakeholder needs. Verification is an internal, process-facing check: the specification set what was expected, and verification confirms the output conforms. In Planguage practice, verification operates at the exit boundary of each Evo step, ensuring that the delivered increment meets its stated quantitative requirements before the team proceeds. Credit for this concept definition is given to Lawrence Day, Boeing.

concepts.name: Version
concepts.definition: A **version** is an initial or changed specification instance.
concepts.overview: **Version** (*332) is an identification and naming parameter that tracks successive instances of a specification as it is initially created or subsequently changed. In Planguage practice, every specification artifact — a requirement, a design decision record, a test plan — may carry a Version label that distinguishes its current state from all prior states. Versioning enables traceability: when a requirement changes, the old version remains accessible for audit, comparison, and regression analysis. Unlike Variant (*203), which distinguishes audience-based forks, Version is strictly temporal — each new version supersedes the previous one for the same specification target.

concepts.name: Veto Constraint

relatedConcepts.name: Demand Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: the positive counterpart: 'Do X'; Veto is 'Do not do X

relatedConcepts.name: Constraint
relatedConcepts.note: parent class; a Veto Constraint is a specific form of Constraint

concepts.definition: A **veto** is a negative constraint; the type 'Don't do X'.
concepts.overview: **Veto Constraint** (*462) is the negative, binary form of a Constraint (*218) — it specifies what a system or design must not do, rather than what it must achieve. Where a Demand Constraint (*461) says "do X," a Veto says "do not do Y under any circumstances." Veto constraints are non-scalar and binary: the system either violates the veto or it does not. Because a veto represents an absolute prohibition — often driven by legal, ethical, safety, or contractual obligations — it functions as a filter that eliminates otherwise valid design alternatives outright, before value and cost calculations begin. Also known as Prohibition, Taboo, or simply "a 'Do Not' constraint."

concepts.name: View

relatedConcepts.name: Scope
relatedConcepts.note: a View selects which aspects of a system are visible; Scope defines the boundary of the system itself

relatedConcepts.name: Viewpoint
relatedConcepts.note: a Viewpoint defines the frame of reference that produces a View; the View is the result

relatedConcepts.name: Description
relatedConcepts.note: a View is expressed through one or more Descriptions

relatedConcepts.name: Specification
relatedConcepts.note: a Specification may contain multiple Views of the same system

relatedConcepts.name: Subjectivity
relatedConcepts.note: different stakeholder Views introduce subjectivity into system understanding

concepts.definition: A **view** is any useful perspective regarding a defined system.
concepts.overview: **View** (*484) is a Planguage parameter that designates a selected perspective on a defined system — any coherent, useful angle from which a system can be described, analysed, or evaluated. A single system may support many views simultaneously: a security view, a performance view, a stakeholder-value view, a cost view. The choice of View determines which aspects of the system are rendered visible and which are set aside. This concept is related to but distinct from Viewpoint (*644): a Viewpoint is the frame of reference or set of concerns that generates a View; the View is the resulting projection. IEEE 1471-2000 provides an alternative architectural definition of view, confirming the concept's place in international standards practice.

concepts.name: Viewpoint

relatedConcepts.name: View
relatedConcepts.note: a Viewpoint is the template that governs construction of a View

relatedConcepts.name: Template
relatedConcepts.note: a Viewpoint acts as a reusable template for generating Views

relatedConcepts.name: Form
relatedConcepts.note: Viewpoints may specify the forms used within a View

relatedConcepts.name: Standard
relatedConcepts.note: Viewpoints embody standards for how a particular perspective is rendered

relatedConcepts.name: Rule
relatedConcepts.note: Viewpoints encode rules that constrain how a View may be constructed

relatedConcepts.name: Stakeholder
relatedConcepts.note: different Stakeholders require different Viewpoints

relatedConcepts.name: Impact Estimation Table
relatedConcepts.note: IETs can be structured as a Viewpoint on impact data

concepts.definition: A **Viewpoint** captures the rules for constructing and analyzing a particular kind of view. It is a template for a view and can be reused across many architecture descriptions.
concepts.overview: **Viewpoint** (*644) is the meta-level specification that governs how a particular kind of [[View.484|View]] is built, what it must contain, and how it must be analyzed. Where a View is a single instance of a perspective on a system, a Viewpoint is the standing rule-set for constructing any View of that type. Because Viewpoints are reusable templates, they save architecture teams from reinventing the same conventions every project and ensure consistency across all Views of the same kind. Different [[Stakeholder.233|Stakeholders]] require different Viewpoints — the security auditor's Viewpoint differs from the end-user's. Defining Viewpoints explicitly turns ad hoc diagramming into a governed, repeatable practice.

concepts.name: Vision

relatedConcepts.name: Core Ideology
relatedConcepts.note: Core Ideology is the stable foundation from which a Vision is projected

relatedConcepts.name: Story
relatedConcepts.note: a Story can give narrative form to a Vision, making it communicable

concepts.definition: A **Vision** is an idea about a future state, which is very long range, and probably idealistic, maybe even unrealistic.
concepts.overview: **Vision** (*422) is the highest-level aspirational statement in Planguage — an idea about a long-range future state that is deliberately idealistic, perhaps even unrealistic in the short term. Vision is not a requirement and not a plan; it is a direction-setting aspiration that gives coherence to all lower-level goals, strategies, and functions. It draws its authority from [[Core-Ideology.664|Core Ideology]] (*664), which supplies the stable values and purpose that make the Vision credible over time. A Vision should be bold enough to inspire and vague enough to accommodate many different paths toward it, while still being specific enough to reject options clearly incompatible with it. Without an explicit Vision, organisations optimise locally and drift strategically.

concepts.name: Waterfall Method

relatedConcepts.name: Evo
relatedConcepts.note: Evo (Evolutionary Project Management) is the iterative alternative to Waterfall Method

concepts.definition: The analogy in the term **Waterfall Method** refers to a series of waterfall stages as the 'water' (project progress) flows downstream.
concepts.overview: **Waterfall Method** (*311) is Planguage's label for the traditional sequential development process in which phases — requirements, design, construction, testing, deployment — are treated as discrete stages that complete before the next begins, like water cascading over a series of falls. Planguage defines it in explicit contrast to [[Evo.355b|Evo]] (*355), the Evolutionary Project Management method that delivers value in small, measured, feedback-driven increments. The Waterfall Method's core problem, in Gilb's analysis, is that it delivers feedback on whether the right thing was built only at the end — when changing direction is maximally expensive. Its apparent orderliness is an illusion: the real chaos is deferred, not eliminated, and lands at integration and acceptance testing.

concepts.name: Wish

relatedConcepts.name: Wish Budget
relatedConcepts.note: polysemy sibling — same number *244; Wish Budget is the resource/budget form of an uncommitted stakeholder desire

relatedConcepts.name: Need
relatedConcepts.note: a Need is a committed requirement; a Wish is the uncommitted version of a stakeholder desire

relatedConcepts.name: Target
relatedConcepts.note: Wish is a type of Target parameter — the scalar value being wished for

relatedConcepts.name: Goal
relatedConcepts.note: Goal is the committed form of a performance target; Wish is the uncommitted form

relatedConcepts.name: Budget
relatedConcepts.note: Wish Budget (*244 & *480) is the resource counterpart: an uncommitted budget desire

relatedConcepts.name: Stretch
relatedConcepts.note: Stretch is an ambitious but committed target; Wish is ambitious and uncommitted

relatedConcepts.name: Ideal
relatedConcepts.note: Ideal is the best theoretically achievable value; Wish is a stakeholder desire that may approach the Ideal

concepts.definition: A **Wish** parameter is used to specify a stakeholder-valued, not-committed target level for a scalar attribute.
concepts.overview: **Wish** (*244) is a Planguage Performance Target parameter that records a stakeholder's desired level for a scalar attribute without committing to that level as a planned deliverable. The keyed icon `>?` signals "a perhaps questionable goal" — a value worth noting and tracking but not yet agreed as the engineering target. Wish is the uncommitted counterpart to [[Goal.109|Goal]] (*109): where a Goal is a committed performance target, a Wish is an aspiration that has not yet been negotiated into a binding specification. This distinction prevents stakeholder desires from being silently elevated to requirements while also ensuring desires are not silently lost. The polysemy sibling [[Wish-Budget.244b|Wish Budget]] (*244 & *480) applies the same uncommitted-desire concept to resource budgets.

concepts.name: Work Hours
concepts.definition: **Work Hours** is the total hours of work, irrespective of clock-hours, or number of people involved. The cost of doing something.
concepts.overview: **Work Hours** (*156) is a Planguage Effort & Time resource parameter that measures the total amount of human work expended on a task or project, independent of how many people were involved or how long the calendar clock ran. One hundred work hours is one hundred work hours whether it was produced by one person over 100 days or ten people over ten days. This person-agnostic, calendar-agnostic definition makes Work Hours the consistent unit for costing and estimating human effort. The source entry notes that the old term "man-hours" is not politically correct; Work Hours is the preferred gender-neutral equivalent.

concepts.name: Work Process

relatedConcepts.name: Work Process Standard
relatedConcepts.note: a Work Process Standard governs and specifies how a Work Process must be executed

relatedConcepts.name: Standard
relatedConcepts.note: Standard (polysemy sibling of Work Process Standard at *138) provides the abstract standard concept that governs processes

concepts.definition: A **Work Process** is a defined process for carrying out human work.
concepts.overview: **Work Process** (*182) is the Planguage concept for any formally defined sequence of human activities directed toward a specific outcome. The definition is deliberately minimal — "a defined process for carrying out human work" — because the distinguishing characteristic of a Work Process in Planguage is that it is defined: explicit, documented, and bounded. An undefined process may still get work done, but it cannot be measured, improved, or governed. Work Processes are governed by [[Work-Process-Standard.138b|Work Process Standards]] (*138), which specify how the process must be executed, under what entry and exit conditions, and at what rates. The Work Process concept provides the subject for which standards, measurements, and improvement targets are written.

relatedConcepts.name: Performance

concepts.definition: A **Workload Capacity Requirement** is a need to achieve specific work capability levels for a system: 'how much' work a system should do.
concepts.overview: **Workload Capacity Requirement** (*544) is a formal Planguage requirement specifying what level of work capacity a system must achieve — the "how much" of system performance. It is a specialised [[Performance-Requirement.100c|Performance Requirement]] (*100) applied specifically to the capacity dimension: how many transactions per hour, documents per minute, or requests per second a system must be able to handle. The attribute being specified is [[Workload-Capacity.459|Workload Capacity]] (*459); this concept is the requirement wrapper that creates the accountability structure (scale, meter, benchmark, goal, worst) around that attribute. Without a Workload Capacity Requirement, a system's capacity is an aspiration rather than an engineering commitment subject to test.

relatedConcepts.name: Workload Capacity Requirement
relatedConcepts.note: formal Planguage requirement that specifies what Workload Capacity level must be achieved

concepts.definition: **Workload Capacity** is a performance attribute. It is used to express the capacity of a system to carry out its workload, that is 'how much' a system can do, did, or will do.
concepts.overview: **Workload Capacity** (*459) is a Planguage performance attribute expressing the supply side of the capacity equation: "how much" a system can handle, has handled, or is required to handle. It is closely related to — and shares a concept number with — [[Workload.459b|Workload]] (*459), which foregrounds the demand placed on a system. Workload Capacity foregrounds what the system can sustain. As a scalar value, it must be expressed in concrete units (transactions per second, documents per minute) on a defined measurement scale, with a benchmark from measured reality and a target for the future. The formal requirement that specifies what Workload Capacity level a system must achieve is [[Workload-Capacity-Requirement.544|Workload Capacity Requirement]] (*544). Workload Capacity is foundational to system sizing, capacity planning, and acceptance testing.

concepts.definition: A Planguage-defined abbreviation meaning 'cross reference'.
concepts.overview: **XREF** (*258) is a Planguage identification parameter that marks a cross-reference — a pointer from one location in a specification to another defined concept, requirement, or parameter elsewhere in the document or document set. It belongs to the Identification & Naming family alongside [[Abbreviation.454|Abbreviation]], [[Tag.146|Tag]], [[Type.398|Type]], and [[Class.017|Class]]. Unlike a [[Specification-Reference.458|Specification Reference]] (which is a user-defined cross-referencing Tag), XREF is a Planguage-defined abbreviation — part of the standard vocabulary, not the author's own tagging system. Its purpose is conciseness: wherever a specification needs to say "see also" or "this relates to that," XREF provides a terse, standardised marker. Proper use of XREF keeps specifications navigable without duplicating definitions.
